title: The cursed cruise: how the dream of never-ending luxury at sea became a nightmare | Cruises | The Guardian
description: The MV Odyssey was billed as the ultimate escape from Donald Trump. Instead, the oil shock caused by his war has left passengers unceremoniously dumped in Cambodia
Author: Oliver Holmes
Headline: The MV Odyssey was billed as the ultimate escape from Donald Trump. Instead, the oil shock caused by his war has left passengers unceremoniously dumped in Cambodia
Content: The company pulled the plug on the cruise after it said monthly fuel costs per cabin had gone from $1,800 to as much as $8,000.Illustration: Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenThe company pulled the plug on the cruise after it said monthly fuel costs per cabin had gone from $1,800 to as much as $8,000.Illustration: Guardian DesignThe Saturday readCruisesThe cursed cruise: how the dream of never-ending luxury at sea became a nightmareThe MV Odyssey was billed as the ultimate escape from Donald Trump. Instead, the oil shock caused by his war has left passengers unceremoniously dumped in CambodiaOliver Holmesin Bangkok,Daniel Boffeyin London andAdeshola Orein MelbourneFri 30 Oct 2026 23.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 10.27 EDTShareThe idea was a never-ending retirement at sea, a continuous voyage around the globe. The promise to the passengers of the MV Odyssey cruise ship – many approaching the autumn of their lives – was that on the open seas they could cut loose from the troubles of the world. But the world had other ideas.The end came in an announcement as stark as it was brief: they had seven hours to get off. They were going no further thanCambodia.The Odyssey, owned by Florida-based Villa Vie Residences, which had first set sail from Belfast, Northern Ireland, in October 2024, made an explicit offer:Donald Trumphad been re-elected to the White House, and this was a way for those ill-disposed to the president to enjoy a four-year “skip forward”.View image in fullscreenPassengers disembark from the Odyssey at Sihanoukville port in Cambodia.Photograph: Kith Serey/EPAFor $319,998, a couple seeking such an escape could head off to the high seas for the length of a presidential term and come back from their journey to nowhere when the danger had passed – or not. For those who had simply had enough, there was a permanent residency option for a few hundred thousand more. Depending on the package, there were also monthly fees on top, which covered food, drinks, wifi, wellness programmes and room cleaning. They would have access to a pool, a pickleball court, a theatre, several bars and a gym. Exotic port destinations would be visited along the way.It was by no means cheap – but the Odyssey was quite accurately billed as the “affordable” option for those interested in such a cocoon. The pioneer in the world of “residential ships”, a vessel called MS The World, offered apartments that typically ranged from $2m to $15m, with the pampered passengers getting to choose where it would go. For that experience, there was a waiting list.The Odyssey was not in that league. Rather than built as a residential ship, it had previously been a traditional cruise liner named MS Braemar. Under that name, it had been turned away from several ports in the Caribbean during the pandemic when its passengers became ill. Cuba finally allowed it to dock, but the vessel never went into service as MS Braemar again. It was sold off by Fred Olsen cruises and adapted by its new owners. Villa Vie described the three-decade-old restructured vessel as “an intimate residential cruise ship offering a new way to live”.View image in fullscreenPassengers onboard the then-MS Braemar wait to disembark in Mariel, Cuba, in March 2020.Photograph: Adalberto Roque/AFP/Getty ImagesAt 642ft (196 metres) long, it was a relatively small ship, but at such prices, and with the world being held firmly at bay, what could go wrong? Neither the more than 200 passengers on the Odyssey nor its cruise operator foresaw the consequences of Trump’s war in Iran. The reality was, there was no escaping the US president.On Tuesday, Villa Vie Residences issued a statement. It had run out of money owing to the soaring price of oil. Monthly fuel costs per cabin in parts of Asia had risen to as much as $8,000 from $1,800, placing it “under unsustainable financial pressure”, it announced.graphic“Since the conflict began in late February, we have taken significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port,” the company said, explaining the slow death of its business model. “Those measures have not been enough to offset the extraordinary increase in fuel costs, and we have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses.”View image in fullscreenThe Villa Vie Odyssey cruise ship leaves Belfast.Photograph: Liam McBurney/PAThe Odyssey’s passengers were told to pack up their belongings before being transported on buses into the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville on the Gulf of Thailand. “We are working with residents to coordinate disembarkation and temporary living arrangements, and are supporting residents, crew, and employees as we evaluate restructuring and recapitalisation alternatives over the next 60 days,” the company said.Map graphic“People were shell-shocked, numb, crying,” said one passenger, Kit Cassingham from the US, who spent two years on the ship with her husband, Randy. They had made their cabin into a home, putting down their own rugs and pictures on the wall. “People were angry. They were hysterical. They were sad … Disbelief,” she added. “I mean, that whole gamut of, what is it, the five stages of grief.”Most of the passengers on the Odyssey were Americans, travelling with an international group of 156 crew members, including a ship’s doctor and two nurses. Many of the passengers were retired or digital nomads. One woman, Holly Hennessy, had been living happily with her cat, Captain, since the ship set sail two years ago.View image in fullscreenHolly Hennessy with her Siamese cat, Captain, in Belfast.Photograph: Liam McBurney/PAOne couple, Lanette Canen and Johan Bodin, who said they had bought a cabin with a 15-year guarantee, had beendocumenting their life at sea on YouTube, including the lead-up to the fateful announcement. The signs of financial distress had been apparent for weeks, they said.“I’m Mr Super Positive, and I’ve felt really drained the last two months,” Bodin recounted in a video.Footage from inside the ship’s lounge on the final night showed residents drinking, as rumours spread that their voyage might be over. Cruise ship staff had requested each passenger contribute $1,800 to ensure the ship had funds to travel to Bangkok.The next day, the couple postedan updateshowing the inside of their cabin as a voice on the loudspeaker said the ship’s operator had “unfortunately” been “unable to secure the fuel necessary to continue operations”. An email was sent requesting that everyone disembark by 2pm.“We knew the worst-case scenarios, but we didn’t think it would come to reality, which it did,” said Rina Cavazza, a pilates instructor from Brisbane, Australia.View image in fullscreenRina Cavazza’s cabin on the Villa Vie Odyssey.Photograph: suppliedAnother passenger, Sherrie Cornett, wrote on Facebook that they were “dropped unceremoniously in the middle of town, left to our own devices”.The company has not provided financial aid, passengers said, or even supplied a list of hotels in Cambodia. It later offered tickets for a charter flight to the US, although many passengers had already left. The company has been contacted for comment.Kit and Randy Cassingham, now in a hotel in Cambodia, reflected on how life changed on the ship once the Iran war began, with ominous signs that the company was running out of money. The food quality began to deteriorate, and there was less of it; there were fewer excursions on shore, they said.View image in fullscreenRandy and Kit Cassingham: ‘Live life while you can because you don’t know how the adventure will turn out.’Photograph: Tang Chhin Sothy/AFP/Getty Images“I realised as soon as the strait of Hormuz incident came along, the energy of the ship changed,” Kit said. “I think it was because the ship management realised how much more this was going to cost. And then they were starting to do cutbacks that we weren’t aware of yet.”Far from being a haven, the ship became a microcosm for the global economic turmoil. “I watched the world, and I don’t even pay attention to the news, but I’ve watched it just kind of crumble and shatter,” said Kit. “And I’m thinking, ‘it’s going to be difficult no matter what’.”Randy said the writing had long been on the wall. They were, after all, on a ship that “drinks petrol by the metric tonne”. “You know, literally they’re buying 150 metric tonnes of fuel at a time,” he said. “We’re talking about $800,000 if we tried to get a full tank.”While docked in Singapore in August, passengers had already been told the company did not have enough money to continue cruising, and several of the residents had contributed their own funds to get it moving again.“Very few expect to get any money back because we know that they [the company] have been in terrible money problems from the beginning,” said Randy. Passengers had also passed a jar around for money for the crew, who are also stuck in Cambodia, he said.Will the story of the Odyssey put people off cruises? It is unlikely, said Prof Andrew Coggins, an industry analyst, who pointed to an unprecedented boom since the end of the Covid pandemic, with global passengers reaching a historical high of 37.2 million in 2025.Those numbers were in part because of “pent up demand” from those who had been unable to enjoy a cruise during the pandemic years, he said. But it was also the case, he said, that a cruise could offer good value for money. “You get to be pampered, you pack and unpack once, but you see different places, you eat better food than you would get at home, and then you have the romance of going to sea,” he said.View image in fullscreenGoing nowhere: the Villa Vie Odyssey at Sihanoukville port in Cambodia.Photograph: Kith Serey/EPAResidential ships such as the Odyssey were, though, in a very small category of their own, Coggins added. “The World is the only other one I know about and I think there are a couple that are trying to start up,” he said. But the finances are notoriously difficult. In 2023, a three-year cruise offered by MirayCruises, with fares starting at $30,000 per person per year, including accommodation, food, drinks, laundry and even health care, was cancelled weeks before its due departure date owing to an inability to make the sums add up.To survive choppy world markets, charges to the passengers have to be high, necessitating a concomitant level of luxury. “The World was actually built as a residential ship,” Coggins said. “The cabins or the state rooms are much bigger.”Speaking earlier in the week, Mikael Petterson, who launched Villa Vie Residences in 2023, accepted that he was the “villain in the story” but said he was doing everything he could to help the stranded passengers. “Nobody that’s tried residential cruising has succeeded and we have gone further than anyone else,” he said. “But I think we would have been absolutely fine and we would have seen this through, if there was no Iran war.”Back in Cambodia, Randy has been blogging to keep people updated while they work out what to do next. But he isn’t bitter. For all the promises, he said, all good things must come to an end. “Our message is that we’re not saying ‘poor me’. We know that people are having trouble, that they’re trying to put fuel in their cars, food in their mouths. And we’re very lucky. We’re not crying in our soup. So we are completely aware that we’re very lucky and that we’re going to land on our feet and be OK.”Kit, a transformation coach, agreed. “This isn’t a pity party for us,” she said. “We actually want to say to people: ‘Live your dreams. Go for the gusto. Live life while you can because you don’t know how the adventure will turn out’.”Explore more on these topicsCruisesThe Saturday readShipping industryDonald TrumpCambodiaWater transportShare

title: ‘We freed Patrick Stewart!’ Star Trek’s Marina Sirtis on breaking in her beloved but very serious co-star | Patrick Stewart | The Guardian
description: She was scared of him but soon loosened the Shakespearean up – then watched him give Star Trek depth, even insisting scenes be rewritten for her. Captain Picard’s right-hand woman salutes her fabulous friend
Author: Tim Jonze
Headline: She was scared of him but soon loosened the Shakespearean up – then watched him give Star Trek depth, even insisting scenes be rewritten for her. Captain Picard’s right-hand woman salutes her fabulous friend
Content: ‘Star Trek was a punchline before he came along’ ... from left, LeVar Burton, Stewart and Sirtis.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Star Trek was a punchline before he came along’ ... from left, LeVar Burton, Stewart and Sirtis.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyPatrick Stewart‘We freed Patrick Stewart!’ Star Trek’s Marina Sirtis on breaking in her beloved but very serious co-starShe was scared of him but soon loosened the Shakespearean up – then watched him give Star Trek depth, even insisting scenes be rewritten for her. Captain Picard’s right-hand woman salutes her fabulous friendMarina Sirtis as told toTim JonzeSat 31 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’d been warned about Patrick by friends who’d worked with him at the Royal Shakespeare Company. They said: “Marina, you can’t beyouaroundPatrick Stewart. He’s all about the work. He takes itveryseriously and he won’t abide you mucking about and trying to make people corpse.”We had been cast together onStar Trek: The Next Generationand, because of what I’d heard, I was a bit scared, a bit intimidated. And let’s be honest – Patrickwasvery serious about the work. But there was a concerted effort by the rest of us to beat it out of him. We were from a younger generation and we wanted to shake up this Englishman who was so typical of his generation – stiff upper lip and a Yorkshireman to boot. You know, the kind of person who was not exactly renowned for showing their emotions. Early on Patrick told us all that we weren’t there to have fun, and you should have seen the looks he got. I’m a cockney: I’ve got a Spurs tattoo and we all looked at him in the same way I look at an Arsenal fan. But we did loosen him up. And – he’s said this himself – I think we actually freed him. We gave him a freedom that he said he’d never really felt before.double quotation markHe told the writers he really had to look into my eyes – not Data’s – to reach the emotions he neededOf course it went both ways. We learned so much from him, how could you not? We learned from his professionalism and his absolutely insane talent. He brought gravitas to the role.Star Trekwas a bit of a punchline before Patrick came along – it’s not any more. Patrick gave it depth – here was this consummate Shakespearean actor playing the captain of a starship. It just shifted everything.View image in fullscreen‘It was the absolute privilege of my life to work with him’ … Sirtis and Stewart at the Sag awards in 2011.Photograph: Abaca Press/AlamyHe had reservations about taking the role, and his friends – who loved him and were looking out for him – told him not to do it. They thought it would be the end of his career, whereas it was probably the best decision in showbusiness at that time. He handled fame with grace. He didn’t flaunt it. Never got too big for his boots. Early on, a review in a paper described him as an “unknown Shakespearean actor” and we blew it up and stuck it on his trailer door. Someone less self-deprecating might not have liked that but he left it up there for years. He knew it was all good fun.Before meeting Patrick I was just a jobbing actor who did a bit of telly. I’d grown up dirt poor and had a difficult childhood, so we came from very similar backgrounds. I kept my cockney accent because I wanted people to know where I came from. Patrick was the same – not through his voice, but through his demeanour and actions. He was down to earth, a regular bloke. The fact that he supportedHuddersfieldTown shows you who he is – he didn’t go for Leeds or one of the glamour clubs.We’d both experienced childhood trauma and came out with our stories after we had finished working together. We never sat down and went into it all. But when people have gone through something like that, there’s something in their demeanour, something that you can see in them, that you feel in them.A month before Covid hit, my husband died. I was on my own in my house in Los Angeles for a year with just my dogs for company. Patrick was one of the very few people who invited me over for lunch, socially distanced in his garden. It had occurred to him that I was grieving and on my own – and he did something about that. It’s a mark of who he is.View image in fullscreen‘Our relationship on screen was a two-way street’ … in Star Trek: The Next Generation.Photograph: APC/THA/ShutterstockHe was always on my side. In one of the Star Trek movies we did there was a scene written for Picard and Data, where Picard tells the story of how his family were burned in a fire. Patrick went to the writers and producers and asked if they could rewrite the scene to have me be in it instead of Brent Spiner. He said that Brent’s character Data was an android, and that he really needed to look into my eyes in order to reach the emotions he needed. So our relationship on screen was a two-way street, which sounds ridiculous saying that out loud! I don’t know how I’ve got the cheek to say that when I’m talking about Patrick Stewart! But we did help each other.It’s also because of Patrick that I am now in the annals of my football team. When Tottenham played Huddersfield in 2018, we both did interviews about the game and it was officially named in the match day programme as the Star Trek derby. That’s now a part of Tottenham history and, as anyone who knows me will tell you, that means more to me than winning an acting award!It was the absolute privilege of my life and my career to work with him. We were very, very close and stayed in touch right to the end, even though it became difficult to speak to him on the phone because of his health. He went quickly in the end and it makes me very sad that I didn’t get a chance to say goodbye. To say: “Thank you Patrick. Thanks for everything, mate.”Explore more on these topicsPatrick StewartStar TrekTelevisionHuddersfieldTottenham HotspurfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The moment I knew: He loved to travel, I had a fear of flying. I expected him to skol his beer and wish me well | Australian lifestyle | The Guardian
description: On Danni Smith’s first date with Kev, she made a few disclosures and expected him to skol his beer and wish her well – but his response surprised her
Author: Doosie Morris
Headline: On Danni Smith’s first date with Kev, she made a few disclosures and expected him to skol his beer and wish her well – but his response surprised her
Content: ‘It was all very easy between us, so about half an hour in, not wanting to waste our time, I thought I should make a few disclosures’: Kev and Danni Smith on their first trip away to the Mornington Peninsula in 2024.View image in fullscreen‘It was all very easy between us, so about half an hour in, not wanting to waste our time, I thought I should make a few disclosures’: Kev and Danni Smith on their first trip away to the Mornington Peninsula in 2024.The moment I knewAustralian lifestyleThe moment I knew: He loved to travel, I had a fear of flying. I expected him to skol his beer and wish me wellOnDanni Smith’sfirst date with Kev, she made a few disclosures and expected him to skol his beer and wish her well – but his response surprised herFind more stories fromthe moment I knew seriesDanni Smith, as told toDoosie MorrisSat 31 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 21.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn September 2023 I’d been divorced for about a year. At 59 I thought to myself, “surely there’s got to be a little bit more love that I could give in my life”. But I was also keenly aware that not many people find romance organically these days.I gave Bumble a go, had some pretty average dates and thought it wasn’t for me, but I decided to give it one last shot. It was Kev’s smile and his eyes that caught my attention. His profile said travel was really important to him, which gave me a bit of a laugh because I have huge anxiety issues around holidaying of any sort. We exchanged a few texts and decided to arrange a date. It was nothing fancy, just a few drinks at a bar in a bayside suburb of Melbourne.It was all very easy between us, so about half an hour in, not wanting to waste our time, I thought I should make a few disclosures. First I told him that as a divorcee twice over, I obviously wasn’t very good at relationships. He surprised me by saying we were on par there. Then I went on to explain my pathological fear of flying, and that I wouldn’t be a great travel buddy.The moment I knew: I admitted I had a crush on her. She replied, ‘Well, that’s good. Isn’t it?’Read moreI fully expected him to skol his beer and wish me well but instead he asked lots of questions about my anxiety and listened intently before saying: “Well, you don’t need to get on a plane to experience Australia!” I thought that was so nice of him and a little spark lit up in me – if he’s willing to compromise on something so important to him, maybe this could go somewhere.We caught up the next week, and then he returned home to Newcastle. We stayed in touch and I started to realise you really can learn a lot about a person over the phone. He had a great sense of humour and we were getting along so well, but about six weeks later he told me he didn’t think a long-distance relationship could work. I was sad but wished him all the best and left the door open for him to reach out if he was ever back in Melbourne.It felt brazen, but a few weeks later, I sent him a text. He replied immediately and said he would love to catch up while visiting family for Christmas. When he arrived at my door on Boxing Day, his smile had me swooning. We talked and laughed and the chemistry was palpable. We met again the next day and, thinking it would be the last I’d see of him. I wrote him a card thanking him for giving me hope and saying had circumstances been different, I would have given a relationship between us 100%.By New Year’s Eve he’d messaged to say he missed me. A few weeks later, he came back to Melbourne, where we both now live, and we went on our first road trip together.View image in fullscreen‘I’m sure he thinks I’m completely neurotic, but he never lets on’: Kev and Danni Smith during a trip to Canberra.Photograph: SuppliedThree and a half years later, Kev has never put pressure on me to fly. Instead, he’s helped me, by letting me be and warming me up for bigger and bigger jaunts. It’s all still totally anxiety-inducing for me, but it gets a little bit easier every time because he’s there encouraging me. I’m sure he thinks I’m completely neurotic, but he never lets on. Instead, he makes considerations for the most problematic triggers, like elevators or staying up high in hotels, while helping me extend myself and see places I never would have without him. We’ve just returned from Jervis Bay, and a trip to Canberra.I’ve never been in a relationship with anyone who could help me through my anxiety. I’ve always felt very alone in those experiences, but Kev’s way of dealing with it is a balm. Not only does it show me that he’s willing to accept me as I am, but he shows such compassion and patience that it reduces the anxiety itself.I don’t think I’ll ever get on a plane, but Kev’s gentle, flexible attitude to my anxieties has helped me spread my wings. We plan to set off to central Australia in 2027.Tell us the moment you knewShare your experienceShare your love storyDo you have a romantic realisation you'd like to share? title: Is AI your new wingman? How chatbots are transforming dating | Dating | The Guardian
description: Almost 40% of British singles are using AI for romantic advice, from writing messages to assessing potential partners
Author: George Francis Lee
Headline: Almost 40% of British singles are using AI for romantic advice, from writing messages to assessing potential partners
Content: Illustration: Anaïs Mims/Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenIllustration: Anaïs Mims/Guardian DesignDatingIs AI your new wingman? How chatbots are transforming datingAlmost 40% of British singles have used AI for romantic advice, from writing messages to assessing potential partnersGeorge Francis LeeandDan MilmoSat 31 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 08.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter Sam’s ex joked that her sister found him ugly, he turned to AI. Google Gemini had a look at the photo and politely disagreed. AI has been his wingman ever since, aiding his dating life by giving pep talks and vetting his messages.The 27-year-old from Stoke-on-Trent is not the only AI-assisted romantic – a survey of 3,000 British singles published this month by Match Group, the owner of theTinderand Hinge platforms, found 39% had used AI in their dating lives.Relying on AI is bad, Sam tells the Guardian, adding he would rather begin dating in person, but there is a “paradigm shift in dating that’s occurring, which is really odd, where everything is expected to start online”.The proportion of AI use in dating is even higher for younger generations, rising to 66% for members of gen Z (people born in the mid 1990s to early 2010s), and 53% of millennials (those born in the early 1980s to mid-90s).Sam says pressure to make a good impression on dating apps means a misunderstood message could risk him losing out on dates. “Online dating … as a guy it’s a bit of a ghost town,” he says. “Rather than saying: ‘Hey, how’s your weekend going?’ it’s thinking about what I can pick up that might get a response.”The most common use of AI across all cohorts, according to Match, is to get advice about someone they are talking to, plan date ideas, practise conversations, write a dating profile or messages, and vet whether profiles or photos are genuine. Using AI to alter a photo is a no-no for the majority of singles, the survey says.View image in fullscreenSome singles are turning to AI to navigate online dating, using chatbots to plan dates and check whether profiles are genuine.Photograph: oatawa/Getty Images/iStockphotoA single mother from New Zealand, who asked to remain anonymous, says she has used AI as a dating mentor. “I did not really date before I met my ex-husband … with ChatGPT I set it up to coach me to become more secure – to not panic about any delay in messaging, to not rush into anything,” she says.One man from Melbourne, Australia, who began dating after his 20-year marriage ended, says AI made finding his current partner faster by assessing people he “matched” with and testing his responses. “It was getting [to be] quite a lot of work, like all the chats and the profiles. So I thought: ‘How can I use AI just to sort of speed it up a little bit?’” he says.The 51-year-old adds that the chatbot he was using helped him think twice about profiles he’d overlooked. “[With] my current partner, it was really aggressive with me saying that: ‘Nah, she’s your vibe, she just takes shit photos.’ And then I meet her at a cafe and she’s absolutely drop-dead gorgeous,” he says.When he told his partner he had used AI in their exchanges, she also admitted to using Anthropic’s Claude chatbot to analyse his responses. He says she joked that the “two Claudes were probably just chatting away behind the scenes”. It is a risky admission, though – about a third of UK singles said they would end a date if they found out AI had been used to write a potential paramour’s messages.But, while a few singles like to discuss how their date went with a chatbot (7%), far more prefer a group chat (29%) or their parents (20%), according to the Match survey. “Maybe our friends are becoming more distant because of technology, a little more hands off, compared to the generation before us [who] would get together in their flat or the pub and just absolutely dish the dirt,” says Dec, 31, from London, who uses ChatGPT as a “sounding board” when chatting with single men.Dec says he uploaded his dating conversations to ChatGPT and gave it prompts such as: “Tell me what you think the red flags there are”, and: “What does this connection look like?”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAlthough deploying the chatbot charmer led to a number of dates, Dec worries that his “brain feels like it’s rotting because everything’s just offloaded to AI now”. He adds: “We all know it’s going to be a bit of a yes man sometimes.”View image in fullscreenAbout a third of British singles say they would end a date if they discovered the other person had used AI to write their messages.Photograph: Maskot/Getty ImagesThe Match survey also hinted at a robotic romantic future where autonomous AIs do people’s dating work for them. More than a quarter of respondents liked the idea of two people’s assistants talking to each other and reporting back before the people speak – even if a majority think the idea is “unacceptable”. Match’s head of trust and safety, Yoel Roth, says the company is taking a “hard stance” against bot-to-bot dating.“In a world where people say that they’re more alienated than ever, are hungrier for connection than ever, we don’t get closer to that goal of human connection by having robots talk to each other,” he says.Sam agrees that AI can only enhance his prospects by so much: “If I replace my humour with AI I think I’ve died as a person.”Explore more on these topicsDatingAI (artificial intelligence)ChatbotsTinderComputingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘The sexy stuff has got to be coming to an end, right?’: Rivals star Aidan Turner on beards, ballroom dancing and putting Poldark to bed | Aidan Turner | The Guardian
description: His dashing lead role in Jilly Cooper’s bonkbuster didn’t hurt the actor’s pin-up status, but now, he protests, he’s 43 – and a dad
Author: Rebecca Nicholson
Headline: His dashing lead role in Jilly Cooper’s bonkbuster didn’t hurt the actor’s pin-up status, but now, he protests, he’s 43 – and a dad
Content: All portraits: Stephanie Siân Smith/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAll portraits: Stephanie Siân Smith/The GuardianAidan TurnerInterview‘The sexy stuff has got to be coming to an end, right?’: Rivals star Aidan Turner on beards, ballroom dancing and putting Poldark to bedRebecca NicholsonHis dashing lead role in Jilly Cooper’s bonkbuster didn’t hurt the actor’s pin-up status, but now, he protests, he’s 43 – and a dadSat 31 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAidan Turner has a tactical beard. For the last two decades or so, the actor has found himself in roles that have made him a smouldering pin-up. Audiences really love to look at him. You can buy mugs that say, “Today I don’t feel like doing anything … exceptAidan Turner.” There are entire Reddit forums dedicated to sharing photographs of him looking hot. He knows this about himself, just like he knows that people want to ask him about it. “I do get asked these questions,” he says, a little wearily. “I do get the, you know, word ‘smoulder’ or ‘sexy’, and all that kind of shit.” So right now, he has a full beard, in the hope that he will not be accused of, for example, smouldering. “I thought it wouldn’t happen so much with the beard,” he sighs. “I thought I could get away with it. I was going for ‘dad’.”The job of actors is to sell a story as well as they possibly can, and over the years plenty of the stories that Turner has sold have involved romance and sex. He appeared in Les Liaisons Dangereuses at the National Theatre in London this summer, and even the New Yorker noted how much he smoulders. In some ways, Turner is one of those male performers who is, well, a little bit objectified. The fact that he is a good actor, and also known for being sexy, places him in a peculiar bind. If he doesn’t gamely play along, if he points out that he’s getting a bit tired of it actually, then he risks being seen as a killjoy. Sure, there are worse burdens to bear, but at times the star ofPoldarkandRivalsfinds himself in a curious position.Turner is 43 now. (He is literally a dad – he and his wife, the American actor Caitlin FitzGerald, have got a small son.) His early roles showed off his ability to handsomely, pensively brood. He was a vampire in the sci-fi seriesBeing Human, and played Dante Gabriel Rossetti in Desperate Romantics, writing moody poetry in soft light. Then, in 2015, he starred in the BBC’s hugely popular adaptation of Poldark, which turned him into a household name. As Ross Poldark, an 18th-century soldier, he loved, fought and, very famously, swung a scythe. The attention that came with it made his career, but it also put him off sexy roles for a while. Then a few years later, Rivals came along.View image in fullscreenTurner with his wife, Caitlin FitzGerald, in 2024.Photograph: Kate Green/Bafta/Getty Images for BaftaRivals is outrageously fun and smutty. It adapts Jilly Cooper’s Rutshire Chronicles novels, the kind of books that would once have been known as bonkbusters, into big, brash television. In her fictionalised version of the Cotswolds in the 1980s, Cooper brought together aristocrats, MPs and cut‑throat television executives. Everyone is having sex with everyone; everyone is ready to stab their neighbour in their back, and probably have sex with them at the same time. Everyone, that is, except Turner’s character, Declan O’Hara, a serious‑minded broadcast journalist who is unusually faithful to his wife, Maud – and also dashingly handsome. So here Turner is again, fielding questions about intimacy coordinators, sex scenes and his very full moustache.double quotation markJilly Cooper’s parties were exactly what you would imagine. The champagne never stopped flowing, and her dogs were everywhereThe moustache was his idea. “Isayit was my idea,” he begins, then corrects himself. “It fuckingwasmy idea.” Turner swears like it is going out of fashion. He has just finished today’s photoshoot, so we have gone to find a quiet spot to chat, and have ended up in a basement, surrounded by bikes and cleaning products and tools. He is out of the fancy clothes and back in his east London dad uniform of white T-shirt, navy chore jacket and jeans. He explains that he had turned up for the Rivals job with a full beard, and if they were going to shave it off, he told them, he had no intention of using a stick-on prosthetic. “You end up eating hairs all day and if you smile it falls off,” he says. “I think everyone on set has now learned the lesson of no stickies.” So they shaved him down to a moustache first, and decided they liked it, and that’s what stuck. It also gave Declan a bit more gravitas. “I don’t want to make this about getting into character or anything. All that stuff gives me the creeps, actors talking about that,” he says, squirming. “But [the moustache] is really helpful, because Declan feels older to me. Like, he’s a bit more of a grownup than I am.” Turner grew up in Dublin and has the accent to prove it, but Declan has a Westmeath accent, a bit deeper than his own, which he borrowed from his father, Pearse. “So with that, and the geography teacher outfits, everything feels more mature.”View image in fullscreenRivals has been a juggernaut for all involved. The TV series is nostalgic and knowing, horny and hilarious, but the new episodes find the show in a more gloomy mood. It opens with a funeral – don’t panic; I counted, and it only takes 15 minutes to get to a sex scene – and trouble is brewing for Declan and Maud’s marriage. “It’s a big one,” Turner nods, though spoiler etiquette dictates he cannot say too much.The fact that Rivals can swing so comfortably between profound grief, camp backstabbing and joyful infidelity gives it a very particular tone. Why does Turner think that audiences have lapped it up? “I mean, I was born in ’83, and there is this yearning for that nostalgia, I suppose. And Jilly Cooper has a certain tone. She was looked over for many years. It was seen as this low-rent, smutty kind of literature, and I don’t know if a lot of people gave it a chance. That doesn’t seem to be the case any more.” He has noticed that it appeals to lots of age groups, and for the first time in a while people in their 20s are coming up to him in the street. “Rivals is funny, and it knows exactly what it is,” he offers. “It’s unapologetic. It’s on the front foot and it’s out there, going, this is what we’re doing, this is who we are.”View image in fullscreenTurner as Declan O’Hara in Rivals.Photograph: Robert Viglasky/ Disney+Cooper was heavily involved in the first season, and they were in the middle of shooting the second whenthe author diedsuddenly, at the age of 88. Turner has fond memories of her. “She was famous for throwing these parties at her house in the Cotswolds that were just exactly what you would imagine,” Turner says. “They were so much fun. The champagne never stopped flowing, and her dogs were everywhere. She was so spirited.” He was filming the immediate aftermath of those funeral scenes when he sensed that something was going on. “It was eerie already, and I mentioned to Victoria [Smurfit, who plays Maud] that this feels weird. It feels very dark, and,like, not Rivals. And then we took a break, and I knew something was up.” The line producer broke the news to the cast that Cooper had died.Five weeks earlier, Turner says, he had been at one of those famous parties. “And she was making speeches and drinking champagne and introducing me to people. She was her brilliant, funny, filthy self.” Cooper would often swing by the set. “I’m just glad that she got a chance to see the show, to see where it was going and how it was looking, and she was really proud of it.”Given the amount of sex involved in Rivals, it is no surprise that they use intimacy coordinators to assist with the choreography. Turner remembers the time before intimacy coordinators were commonplace, and he finds it much better, and much easier, now that they are readily available on sets. In the past, he remembers working with directors who were hands-off or awkward when it came to sex scenes. “They just kind of leave it to you. And I don’t know whether that’s a really good thing, you know, because it’s, like, what the fuck do we do? And is this OK? And does this work?” Having a professional who is there to figure that out is really useful. “I think it’s important, especially in a show like this, to sell the scene and to do what we’re doing, because there are so many different types of sex in this show. It helps us a lot.”Turner was in his early 30s when he got the lead in Poldark, the BBC’s second adaptation of the Winston Graham novels, about a soldier returning home from the American revolutionary war. It turned you into a pin-up, I suggest. He takes a breath so deep that it could fill a Cornish tin mine. “I suppose they were positioning Ross to be that,” he concedes, carefully. “There was a sex in Ross, wasn’t there, I suppose,” he says, with a chuckle, “that previously wasn’t there.” He mentionsthe photographof him taken behind the scenes, in a field, topless, with a scythe. For the last 10 years, it has appeared again and again, which, he says, is “all quite embarrassing. It kind of went everywhere.” In it, Turner is being touched up by the show’s makeup artist Jacqui Fowler, who is often airbrushed out of the shot, much to his disdain. “She’s there with the makeup brush, brilliant Jacqui, and I don’t know what she’s doing … ”Was she painting his muscles? (I meant enhancing them, rather than adding them.) “No! That was something I fucking worked hard for,” he laughs. “I was 12 years younger. It was probably a lot easier to get in shape. But I was, like, no, this guy is a farmer. He’s on the horse all the time. We never really see him eating. When he is, it’s fucking gruel. He’s probably quite lean.” So Turner decided that he needed to get in shape, too. As with the Rivals moustache, it was his idea to go topless in the scything scene, and he had no idea that it would still be talked about a decade later. “I made some friends on the show that I’m still friends with now, and I’m proud of it. It had a really strong audience, and we tried to do something different with it, and I think we did. But all of that stuff wasembarrassing, because it just kind of follows you around a little bit. But it might not have been successful if we didn’t have any of that at all.”View image in fullscreenTurner as Ross Poldark with Eleanor Tomlinson as Poldark’s wife, Demelza.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyFor a few years afterwards – until Rivals, in fact – Turner resisted taking roles that he knew would require him to be sexy. DidPoldarkput him off? “It did, yeah,” he says. In photoshoots now, for example, he might politely decline to pose in a way that seems suggestive. “It just feels different, at 43, and being a dad,” he shrugs. Then again, he admits, he is here to talk about Rivals. Also, he has just finished Les Liaisons Dangereuses, that famously sex-focused play, in which his character Valmont manipulates women into bed, for sport and for the sheer sociopathic thrill of it. “And you’re, like, well, I mean, you’re asking for it, dude!” he laughs. He is nothing if not self-aware. “But then, I feel like this sexy stuff has got to be coming to an end. Right? Tell me it’s done.” I think that’s up to him. “For sure, and it is. But the roles are getting more interesting, and less about … that.”Turner has never done social media and says he has never felt any pressure to sign up to it. “No. You would definitely get more free shit if you had a few million followers on Instagram. I do meet people and I’m, like, where did you get that? And they’re, like, oh, it got sent to me.” But he knows it’s not worth it. “I don’t need those trainers. Most people I know are on it, but I don’t really want to share those things. And I don’t think I’d be very good at doing it. I would probably get it wrong. I’d probably either overshare, or not do it enough.”Turner does not strike me as an oversharer. He mentions early mornings taking his son to school after a late night at the theatre, or trips with him to the West End to see The Lion King and Paddington, but otherwise he is tight-lipped on life outside work. “I draw the line at the personal stuff. And plus, I’ve always just felt, like, who wants to hear from me? I always felt that, in the early days of Twitter or X or whatever. It takes so much confidence, doesn’t it, to go, ‘People want to hear exactly what I have to say in this sentence.’ Wow. Theballson that. Jesus. I’d love some of that courage.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhen not being forced to examine the embarrassment of being objectified as a man in your 40s by horrible, intrusive journalists, Turner is great company. He is funny; he is as charming, as you might expect; and he is more than happy to discuss big, state‑of-the-world stuff. Take this morning. He was listening to a podcast aboutMeta’s new AI assistant, he says. “They will do shit for you. They’ll order food and deliver it to a friend of yours, and they’ll make sure that if you want to get paid, you’ll get paid, and they’ll make sure your mortgage gets done every month, and they’ll do everything. But you’ve just got to give them all of you.” He realised, for the first time, that he was scared of what might happen next. “There could be a moment where it’s, like, no, sorry, Aidan, there is no money for you. We need that money for a datacentre.” The podcast talked about how helpful AI could be, as well as how destructive. “But this has already been downloaded by millions of people, and I’m, like, we’re walking straight into this fire, aren’t we? This might be coming for us faster than I thought.”double quotation markI was actually quite a shy kid, and there’s still a lot of that in thereView image in fullscreenDoes he worry about AI coming for his job? The late Gene Wilder’s voice has been reactivated for a Netflix reality show;Tilly Norwood, the world’s first AI actor, has been unleashed on Hollywood, to middling results. “It will get better and better, and it’s about how comfortable we are when it does get amazing and we can’t tell the difference,” he says. “I don’t know whether I want to read a novel from an AI author. I want the human. I want the connection.” Maybe he is showing his age, he says, “but I don’t want to write us off yet. I don’t want a painting that’s been generated by AI. I want to see oil and canvas and acrylic. Call me old school, but I want the humans to win that battle.”Turner lives in London now, with FitzGerald and their son. He moved to the city in his 20s, after a few years of doing theatre in Dublin. “My first TV job brought me over, and I never really went back,” he says. “I love London. For me, it’s still one of the most exciting cities in the world.” The couple have lived in the US for short periods of time, too, though neither was keen on settling there. For political reasons? “I’m not going to lie.  Guns scare me, and we have a young child, and I don’t want to worry about that every day. I know we have our own problems in this country, but the guns thing scares me. I think the healthcare system is completely fucked [in America]. God forbid you’re not very wealthy, because if you get sick and you don’t have much money, or even if you’re doing all right, it will take everything. That just seems crazy to me.”Turner grew up in Clondalkin, in the west of County Dublin, with his brother and his parents. “We were a working-class family. My dad retired a few years ago, but he was an electrician, and my mum is an accountant.” He had a grandmother who did amateur dramatics, but otherwise there was no history of performing in the family. When Turner realised he wanted to go to drama school, at 18, “there was a certain mould being broken, there”. But, he says, he did have some experience of being on stage. “It would be remiss of me not to say that there was an unusual part of my childhood where I danced,” he begins.View image in fullscreenHe was not just a casual dancer. He danced ballroom and Latin American from the age of six to 17, and at one point he came third in the All-Ireland dance championships. “That’s weird as fuck,” he laughs. “I mean, not odd, but just not the norm for a kid from west Dublin, which is quite poor. My mum and dad spent a lot of money to fund that.” He describes the world of competitive dancing in vivid detail. “There were trophies everywhere, and we went to a competition and it was tails and suits and numbers on the back, and fake tan and Elnett hairspray and pushy mums.“I went to schools that were quite rough, and I danced right up until I was 17,” he continues. “And I told everyone!” Was he given a hard time for it? “I don’t think they believed me, that’s my theory.” He has seen old friends who have since read about his dancing years, and they told him that they didn’t think he was being serious. “These are working-class boys, who are 14, 15, and we’re all drinking cider on a Friday night and smoking cigarettes and doing whatever else. And you tell them that you’re away to Blackpool this weekend, that you dance, and theymightbelieve you. But they don’t want to take part in this conversation. They move away. They still want to be your mate, but they don’t have the faculties to deal with this conversation.” He gave up dancing when his dance partner got injured, and while on a break, he applied on a whim for drama school. “I was actually quite a shy kid, and there’s still a lot of that in there,” he says. Acting made him less self-conscious, and he knew straight away that it was the life for him.View image in fullscreenStyling: Lewis Munro, assisted by Louis Wesnes. Grooming: Jessica Doyle. Brioni blazer; Burberry shirt; Mithri trousers; Giorgio Armani pocket square; Jimmy Choo shoes; Gieves and Hawkes tie. Blue Celine shirt; Loewe checked jacket. Black shirt: Mithridate; black scarf: Soho Scarves; cream trousers: BrioniRivals season two review – if I could give this exquisite bonkbuster 10,000 stars, I wouldRead moreTurner has roles coming up that take him beyond the heart-throb. He is waiting for work to start on Grendel, the live-action adaptation of the 1971 novel, which tells the story of Beowulf from the monster’s perspective. Is he playing a monster? “No, no, he’s a warrior. He’s a shit warrior,” he jokes. “I don’t even know how much I can talk about that. I hope it’s still happening.” He also plays the Apostle Andrew in Terrence Malick’s forthcoming biblical epic, about the life of Jesus Christ, currently known as The Way of the Wind, though Malick is, famously, not a fast worker, and it was filmed in 2019. “Surely it’s coming out soon? I don’t know,” he says.But he has also, briefly, returned toThe Diplomat, Netflix’s popular political thriller, reprising his role as the British spy Callum Ellis. And there is no denying it: Callum is a sexy guy. “Oh, come off it. I amnotsexy in The Diplomat,” he says, firmly. “That is all you.” He really does think, or hope, that this era is almost behind him. “It must be coming to an end,” he says. But what if he’s got another 20 years of it left? “Ohno,” he says, laughing. Then groans, as if he cannot think of anything worse.Rivals season two returns to Disney on 11 November.Explore more on these topicsAidan TurnerTelevisionPoldarkBeing HumanPeriod drama (TV)DramainterviewsShareReuse this content

title: From gold rush to cosmic questions: a South Dakota mine and the search for the secrets of the universe | Particle physics | The Guardian
description: A mile beneath the Black Hills, scientists are building giant detectors to analyse neutrino particles – and possibly find the answer to existence
Author: Ian Sample
Headline: A mile beneath the Black Hills, scientists are building giant detectors to analyse neutrino particles – and possibly find the answer to existence
Content: The proto-Dune experimental programme is designed to test the technology in the construction of the Dune research facility under Lead, South Dakota.Photograph: Maximilien Brice, CernView image in fullscreenThe proto-Dune experimental programme is designed to test the technology in the construction of the Dune research facility under Lead, South Dakota.Photograph: Maximilien Brice, CernParticle physicsFrom gold rush to cosmic questions: a South Dakota mine and the search for the secrets of the universeA mile beneath the Black Hills, scientists are building giant detectors to analyse neutrino particles – and possibly find the answer to existenceIan SampleScience editorSat 31 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 07.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor more than a century, the mining town of Lead, in the Black Hills ofSouth Dakota, attracted workers with a taste for gold. Now, a flagship experiment being built in the old mine is drawing scientists in search of more intriguing riches: answers to the deepest mysteries of the universe.Construction of the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (Dune) in the former Homestake mine is due to start on Monday. Engineers will begin assembling four giant detectors inside caverns blasted from rock a mile underground.Once switched on, the detectors will quietly spark and flicker as ghostly particles called neutrinos hurtle through them. Some will arrive from the sun and distant supernovae, others in an intense beam sent through 800 miles (1,300km) of rock from a government laboratory near Chicago, Illinois.View image in fullscreenProject members visit the old mine, where construction is soon to start.Photograph: Landin Burke, Destyn Humann/FermilabObserving the neutrinos could uncover entirely new science and shed light on cosmic spectacles, such as the death of stars and the birth of black holes. Scientists are particularly hopeful of solving one of the most enduring puzzles in nature: why everything around us is made from matter and not its “evil twin”, antimatter. In other words, why we, and why anything, is here at all.Dune graphic“It’s a super exciting time to be working on this,” said Dr Kate Shaw, an experimental particle physicist on Dune from the University of Sussex. “Neutrinos do not make sense yet and they could open a door to new physics.”Neutrinos are the most abundant matter particles in the universe, outnumbered only by photons, the massless particles of light that illuminate the universe. They are produced in natural nuclear reactions, such as those that power the sun, in radioactive decay and in particle accelerators.Even by physicists’ standards, neutrinos are oddballs. The chargeless particles barely interact with other matter: about a trillion pass unnoticed through your body each second. Neutrinos come in three varieties, all with minuscule but different masses. Weirdly, they change from one variety to another, a process called oscillation, as they travel. “It’s a very strange behaviour,” said Shaw. “It’s like me throwing you an apple and it turns into a banana.”Lead has a history with these peculiar particles. In the 1960s, the physicist Ray Davis followed miners down the shaft and built a detector from a 100,000-gallon tank filled with dry-cleaning fluid. Shielded so deep beneath the ground, the detector became the first to record neutrinos from the sun as they struck chlorine atoms in the fluid and turned them into argon.The mine closed in 2001 and transitioned, thanks to visionary forethought, into a dedicated subterranean laboratory, the Sanford Underground Research Facility (Surf). It is already home to the Lux-Zeplin (LZ) experiment which last month reported thefirst potential detectionof dark matter.View image in fullscreenThe Lux-Zeplin dark matter experiment main detector in a surface lab before installation underground.Photograph: Matthew Kapust/Sanford Underground Research Facility/Reuters“We’ve gone from mining the Earth to helping scientists explore the universe,” said Robin Lucero, Lead’s city administrator, whose family has lived locally for generations. “We’re incredibly proud and lucky that Dune is happening here, and Surf, which has other experiments like LZ. Having world-class science brings new opportunities, new people and new possibilities for our local businesses and especially our young people.”Unlike Davis’s apparatus, the Dune experiment is enormous. Made from more than 4,000 tonnes of steel, the detectors will stand up to five-storeys high and hold a combined 70,000 tonnes of liquid argon that must be chilled to -200C. Assembling the detectors should take nearly three years. Filling them with liquid argon, another year.“This is a heavy duty engineering operation,” and a partnership with the skilled local workforce, said Prof David Newbold, of the UK’s Science and Technology Facilities Council and a Dune spokesperson. “It’s like building a ship underground.” The UK is the largest international partner in the US-led experiment and is making core detector components, critical computing to reconstruct events in the detectors, and the graphite target needed to generate neutrinos at Femilab, a particle physics facility in Illinois.View image in fullscreenThe LBNF-Dune underground site.Photograph: Landin Burke, Destyn Humann/FermilabOnce operational, Dune will study an intense beam of neutrinos sent from Fermilab through 800 miles of the Earth’s crust and mantle. Most neutrinos will shoot straight through, but every so often one will strike an argon atom, creating a flicker of light and a pulse of electric charge. Analysing these will reveal intimate details about the mysterious particles.One big question surrounds the masses of different neutrinos. Which is lightest and which heaviest? The answer could reveal fundamental new forces of nature. And in an attempt to answer the matter v antimatter question, Dune will look for subtle differences between neutrinos and their antimatter twins, antineutrinos.Beyond the beams of particles sent from Fermilab, Dune will also study neutrinos arriving from space, carrying with them fresh information on stellar explosions and the formation of black holes.Earlier this month, the Nobel prize for physics honoured the Belgian researcher Francis Halzen, who useda cubic kilometre of Antarcticato detect high-energy neutrinos from deep space. But detection is far from the end of the story. “This really is going to be a golden era,” Newbold said. “There’s a lot more of that to come.”Explore more on these topicsParticle physicsPhysicsSouth DakotafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: UK police should not have let US force take over airbase trial, MoD documents show | UK news | The Guardian
description: According to documents obtained by the Guardian, officials accused Cambridgeshire force of breaching US-UK deal by handing over case of woman strangled by US pilot
Author: Rob Evans
Headline: According to documents obtained by the Guardian, officials accused Cambridgeshire force of breaching US-UK deal by handing over case of woman strangled by US pilot
Content: The Guardian uncovered a series of cases showing how US military personnel are not being brought to justice in British courts.Photograph: Kathy images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe Guardian uncovered a series of cases showing how US military personnel are not being brought to justice in British courts.Photograph: Kathy images/ShutterstockBase justiceUK newsUK police should not have let US force take over airbase trial, MoD documents showAccording to documents obtained by the Guardian, officials accused Cambridgeshire force of breaching US-UK deal by handing over case of woman strangled by US pilotRob Evans,Harry Davies,Louisa LoveluckandEmine SinmazSat 31 Oct 2026 09.30 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 09.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMinistry of Defence officials have privately accused a UK police force of wrongly handing over the investigation of an American fighter pilot who strangled a British woman to the US military, according to documents obtained by the Guardian.Cambridgeshire police allowed the US military police to quickly take control of the investigation into Capt Jacob Wulfson after he had been accused of sexuallyassaulting Sarah Steele in his Cambridge flat.The decision meant Wulfson was not tried in an English criminal court. Instead he wasprosecuted in a military tribunal on a US airbasein neighbouring Suffolk.View image in fullscreenAn all-male jury of Capt Jacob Wulfson’s fellow air force officers convicted him of strangling an intimate partner but acquitted him of sexual assault.Photograph: United States Air Forces CentralMinistry of Defence officials said the Cambridgeshire force should “absolutely” not have let theUS militarypolice take over the investigation in a clear breach of a long-established agreement with the US.The disclosure of the case by the Guardian in June provokedimmediate criticism from Downing Street, which said it was “deeply distressing” and “very concerning” that the UK authorities were not involved in prosecuting Wulfson.‘Degrading’: why did a US fighter pilot avoid British trial after strangling a woman in England?Read moreThe government to set up a high-level inquiry to examine how and why police forces have been transferring investigations into serious crimes to the US military police.The Ministry of Defence, which is responsible for handling the military relationship with the US, is one of the key departments taking part in the inquiry.A batch of documents, disclosed via the Freedom of Information Act, revealed the private views of MoD officials about the Steele case, which centres on an obscure agreementsigned bythe US and the UK decades ago.Under the terms of the agreement, police in the UK have the primary right to investigate alleged crimes byAmericans stationed in the country.The MoD officials made it clear the agreement was “pretty unambiguous” and only permitted the US militaryto acquire jurisdiction over investigationsin a “narrow set of circumstances”. These circumstances are: if the offences were committed while the Americans were on duty, or if they were committed against another member of their armed forces or property.In a memo written on 8 July, MoD officials based in Washington wrote: “The Steele case does not, on the surface, appear to meet the bar for a visiting force to be awarded jurisdiction.” In the agreement, the US military is formally known as a visiting force.Four days earlier, the MoD officials had referred to the Steele case in an email to colleagues, saying: “The decision-making on this specific case seemed at odds with what is very clear” in the agreement.Another MoD official agreed that “as best as we understand the facts, this should absolutely have been for the UK courts”.An unidentified Greater Manchester police officer wrote in an email to MoD officials on 6 July that Cambridgeshire police had “wrongly, in my view” handed over the Wulfson investigation to the US military.Cambridgeshire police said they were conducting a review of the case with what they called “the assistance of material provided” by US Air Force lawyers. The force said it “remained engaged with the victim”.“We are working with government, wider policing and criminal justice partners to ensure greater clarity of jurisdictional decision making,” they added.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHow the US bypasses British courts to try its military over crimes in the UKRead moreThe US military aims to prosecute as many of its personnel as possible within the boundaries of its agreement with the UK.The Americans often ask police in the UK if they can take over the prosecution of their military personnel – requests the police agree to, even when they have primary responsibility for investigating them.A series of cases uncovered this year by the Guardian have highlighted concerns that British victims are required to give evidence in US courts martial, an unfamiliar legal system that often does not afford the same protections as that of a court in the UK.Wulfson was off-duty when he assaulted Steele in his Cambridge flat in December 2023 after the pair talked on the Tinder dating app.Steele testified at Wulfson’s court martial, which was held on his airbase at Lakenheath, Suffolk in April, that her experiencewas “degrading and distressing”.The verdict and sentence were decided by an all-male jury of Wulfson’s fellow air force officers. All the lawyers were American. Steele was subjected to invasive and aggressive questioning by Wulfson’s lawyer.Wulfson was convicted of strangling an intimate partner but acquitted of sexual assault. He was dismissed from the US Air Force and confined to a military jail on Lakenheath for six months.Thecross-government inquiry, which includesofficials from the Home Office, Ministry of Justice and Foreign Office, is looking at how US military personnel are not being brought to justice in British courts.The inquiry, which also involves police chiefs, is scrutinising a series of cases uncovered by the Guardian this year.In each case, police handed over the investigations to US military police even though the American perpetrators were off-duty and the British victims had no connection to the armed forces.They were tried in US courts martial on American bases.Tyrion Davis allegedly rapedtwo women in Suffolk. He was convicted of one charge of sexual assault, but cleared of 10 further counts of sexual assault and abusive sexual contact.Hannes Marschalekallegedly exposed himself to a 16-year-old girland four young women in Littleport, Cambridgeshire. He negotiated a plea bargain at a court martial and admitted a charge of indecent conduct. He won an appeal in a US military court that quashed his conviction on technical grounds. This ruling is now being challenged.The US has more than 12,000US militarypersonnel in the UK, stationed in at least 15 bases and facilities. The two biggest bases are at Lakenheath and Mildenhall, in Suffolk. Significant numbers of American military personnel live in East Anglia.Explore more on these topicsUK newsBase justicePoliceUS militaryCrimeMilitaryMinistry of DefenceCambridgeshirenewsShareReuse this content

title: Judge dismisses Trump lawsuit against Wall Street Journal over Epstein birthday letter | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: Ruling ‘with prejudice’ means US president may not amend or refile his lawsuit over his alleged birthday letter to Jeffrey Epstein
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Ruling ‘with prejudice’ means US president may not amend or refile his lawsuit over his alleged birthday letter to Jeffrey Epstein
Content: Jeffrey Epstein and Donald Trump at Mar-a-Lago in Palm Beach, Florida, on 22 February 1997.Photograph: Davidoff Studios Photography/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJeffrey Epstein and Donald Trump at Mar-a-Lago in Palm Beach, Florida, on 22 February 1997.Photograph: Davidoff Studios Photography/Getty ImagesDonald TrumpJudge dismisses Trump lawsuit against Wall Street Journal over Epstein birthday letterRuling ‘with prejudice’ means US president may not amend or refile his lawsuit over his alleged birthday letter to Jeffrey EpsteinMarina DunbarSat 31 Oct 2026 16.31 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 16.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA US judge dismissed Donald Trump’s lawsuit against theWall Street Journalwith prejudice on Saturday, according to a court filing, bringing an end to his legal challenge over the newspaper’s reporting on his alleged birthday letter to Jeffrey Epstein.The decision follows anearlier dismissalin April that had allowed Trump to revise his complaint. As of Saturday, the case is dismissed with prejudice, meaning the lawsuit cannot be amended or refiled.The case stemmed from aWall Street Journal articlealleging that Trump had sent a “bawdy” letter to disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein in 2003. Trump denied the letter was real, insisting instead it had been fabricated.Throughout the proceedings, the court repeatedly pointed to the newspaper’s efforts to obtain Trump’s response before publication and its inclusion of his direct denials as evidence that it had followed appropriate reporting standards.Judge Darrin P Gayles issued thefinal dismissalon Saturday after determining that Trump’s amended complaint still failed to establish “actual malice”, the high legal threshold public figures must meet when pursuing defamation claims.View image in fullscreenA 238-page ‘birthday book’ contained messages from many of Epstein’s friends, including a letter carrying a signature resembling US president Donald Trump’s.Photograph: UNpixs/Courtesy of House oversight committee“As President Trump has not plausibly alleged that each Defendant made defamatory statements with actual malice, the Amended Complaint must be dismissed,” the ruling said. “And because this is President Trump’s second attempt to allege his claims, the Court finds that dismissal with prejudice is appropriate.”Trump, who has frequently pursued legal action against media organizations both during and outside his time in the White House, has maintained that the lewd drawing described in the Journal’s report was fake.A spokesperson for Trump’s legal team shared a statement following the ruling: “President Trump will continue to press forward in his powerhouse lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal and all of the other defendants. The President will continue to hold those who mislead the American People with Fake News and smears accountable for their actions.”A Dow Jones spokesperson said: “We’re pleased with the court’s decision.”Representatives for the Journal had asked the judge to dismiss the claim, arguing that the story was accurate and that it did not meet the bar for defamation. They argued that the reporters had neither knowingly published false information nor proceeded with the belief that the material was likely to be false.The lawsuit attracted particular attention because it named Rupert Murdoch, one of Trump’s most prominent media allies, among the defendants. Murdoch’s News Corporation media empire owns the Journal. Before the article was published on 17 July 2025, Trump personally contacted Murdoch in an effort to stop its publication.The report was published under the headline “Jeffrey Epstein’s Friends Sent Him Bawdy Letters for a 50th Birthday Album. One Was From Donald Trump.”The Journal did not originally publish the image, though it was released by the House oversight committee in September after it was provided by Epstein’s estate.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpWall Street JournalJeffrey EpsteinUS justice systemUS politicsLaw (US)US press and publishingShareReuse this content

title: Man in Belfast charged with possessing explosives and firearms | Belfast | The Guardian
description: The 35-year-old was charged after police searched properties in Shankill Road and Edwina Street areas
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: The 35-year-old was charged after police searched properties in Shankill Road and Edwina Street areas
Content: Police and army during a security operation on Riga Street off the Shankill Road in north Belfast, 30 October 2026.Photograph: Rebecca Black/PAView image in fullscreenPolice and army during a security operation on Riga Street off the Shankill Road in north Belfast, 30 October 2026.Photograph: Rebecca Black/PABelfastMan in Belfast charged with possessing explosives and firearmsThe 35-year-old was charged after police searched properties in Shankill Road and Edwina Street areasNadeem BadshahSat 31 Oct 2026 16.21 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 16.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA man has been charged under the Explosives Act and Firearms Order after police searched properties in Belfast.The 35-year-old was charged with offences including two counts of possessing explosives under suspicious circumstances, and possession of a prohibited weapon (discharge of electricity or noxious gas).He is due to appear before Belfast magistrates court on Monday, the Police Service of Northern Ireland said.The charges follow searches at properties in the Shankill Road and Edwina Street areas of north Belfast on Friday and Saturday.DCI McCallum said: “Following these searches a number of suspicious devices, along with other items, were located and seized by officers for forensic examination.“Local residents who were evacuated as a precaution have now been allowed to return home following the public safety operation conducted alongside ammunition technical officers.“All cordons have now been lifted from the area, and we thank local residents for their patience as inquiries were conducted yesterday and into today.”McCallum added: “As we continue to investigate the circumstances surrounding this incident, we would appeal to anyone who may have information that could assist with inquiries to contact us on 101, quoting reference number 261 30/10/26.”Explore more on these topicsBelfastNorthern IrelandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Oleshky evacuees reunite with families after truce allows crossing back into Ukraine | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Residents of nearby villages line highway waving flags to greet the evacuees’ convoy from the Russian-occupied city
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Residents of nearby villages line highway waving flags to greet the evacuees’ convoy from the Russian-occupied city
Content: People evacuated from the Russian-controlled city of Oleshky arrive in Ukraine at an undisclosed location.Photograph: EPAView image in fullscreenPeople evacuated from the Russian-controlled city of Oleshky arrive in Ukraine at an undisclosed location.Photograph: EPAUkraineOleshky evacuees reunite with families after truce allows crossing back into UkraineResidents of nearby villages line highway waving flags to greet the evacuees’ convoy from the Russian-occupied cityAssociated PressSat 31 Oct 2026 15.17 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 15.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEvacuees from Russian-occupied Oleshky have been reunited with their families after crossing into Ukrainian-held territory on Saturday.The major rescue operationbegan on Fridayand was carried out under the most significant truce since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine four and a half years ago.Evacuees wrapped in Ukrainian flags stepped off buses at the Ukrainian-Belarusian border to be reunited with family members. Volunteers with hand-drawn welcome signs handed coffee to the weary people who had travelled by bus and plane through Russia and Belarus. Residents of nearby villages lined the highway waving flags and torches to greet the convoy.Evacuation of civilians begins in besieged Ukrainian city of OleshkyRead moreTetiana Leonidivna, 71, thanked the Ukrainian soldiers who helped her to flee. “We love them, we love them,” she said through tears. “We know that they are protecting us. And a deep bow to them, and a deep bow to their parents, for having such children. I am proud, I am simply proud.”The ceasefire in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region began early on Tuesday and was expected to continue through Sunday evening. The White House said the first lady Melania Trump helped broker the localised deal, while Pope Leo XIV pressed Russia andUkraineto allow aid deliveries and evacuations.Relatives and volunteers with the Red Cross, Médecins Sans Frontières and World Central Kitchen welcomed the evacuees as they arrived at the border, ready to provide aid and food, including for their pets.View image in fullscreenDmytro and Larysa were delighted to return to Ukrainian-controlled territory.Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/ReutersHolding a cigarette between shaking fingers, 48-year-old Ivan Yevhenovych described his last months in Oleshky. “It was very difficult. There were a lot of drones. It was hard to move around the streets,” he said. “Since spring, there hasn’t really been any staple food left. People had a little bit of their own reserves. We are thrifty people.”He said landmines or drone strikes were killing residents every day.An estimated 2,000 people remained in Oleshky when the temporary truce took hold. They were offered the choice of being evacuated to Ukrainian- or Russian-held territory, or remaining in the city with replenished food and medical supplies.“Many people stayed behind and didn’t want to leave,” Yevhenovych said. “Some for their houses, some for their animals.”View image in fullscreenRelatives and volunteers welcomed the evacuees at the border, ready to provide aid and food, including for their pets.Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/ReutersUkrainian authorities, seeking to protect those who remained and safeguard future humanitarian missions, have not said how many residents evacuated Oleshky and have restricted details of their route. Melania Trump posted on social media on Friday that the humanitarian convoy could safely evacuate more than 750 people.Liza Paliy, 19, waited at the border for her father, whom she last saw more than two and a half years earlier when she fled the occupied city with her mother and sister. “We thought at that time that it would be a month, two maximum, and we would return, but unfortunately two years have already passed,” she said.Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, hailed the humanitarian mission as a win.“This is an extremely important moment. Behind us are difficult negotiations, agreements, preparations, and an enormous amount of work. But most importantly, the people who waited so long to be rescued are finally safe,” he said in an online post.Lubinets said evacuees ranged in age from just over one year old to 94, and they brought pets, including dogs, cats, a parrot and a raccoon. He said he hoped the Oleshky truce could be replicated elsewhere, saying it “could form the basis of a new mechanism for responding to the most difficult humanitarian crises”.View image in fullscreenEvacuees ranged in age from just over one year old to 94.Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/ReutersYana Lantratova, Russia’s human rights commissioner, said both sides have agreed to conduct regular humanitarian missions in and around Oleshky. Lubinets did not mention this development.“The mission has concluded, but, unfortunately, living conditions in Oleshky remain extremely difficult,” she said. “We will make every effort to support those residents who have made the decision to stay.”Some Oleshky evacuees who chose to move to Russian-occupied territory were taken to a temporary shelter in Simferopol, Lantratova said. The city is in Ukraine’s Crimean peninsula, which Moscow annexed in 2014.“After everything they have endured and a long journey, it is essential for these people to rest, recover and feel cared for. However, support should not be limited to just a roof over their heads and a hot meal,” she said in a social media post.View image in fullscreenPets, including dogs, cats, a parrot and a raccoon, were also evacuated.Photograph: Danylo Antoniuk/Anadolu/Getty ImagesA Ukrainian drone attack killed a 30-year-old woman and a 41-year-old man in Russia’s western Bryansk region, the local governor, Yegor Kovalchuk, said on Saturday. Five others were wounded, he said.Local officials also reported Ukrainian drone attacks in the Russian republic of Bashkortostan. Russian media outlets said there was a fire in the region’s capital, Ufa, home to several oil refineries.The Russian defence ministry said on Saturday its forces had shot down 433 Ukrainian drones overnight.The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said Moscow launched drone attacks on energy and railway infrastructure across Ukraine overnight, leaving 280,000 households in Dnipro and Kyiv regions without power.Explore more on these topicsUkraineRussia (Football)EuropeRussia (World news)newsShareReuse this content

title: Streeting says he began stockpiling food weeks ago amid rising threat to UK | Defence policy | The Guardian
description: Defence secretary says value for money and modernisation key for spending to ‘fight the wars ahead’
Author: Kevin Rawlinson
Headline: Defence secretary says value for money and modernisation key for spending to ‘fight the wars ahead’
