Content: Wes Streeting (right) and the chancellor, John Healey, on board HMS Glasgow during a visit to BAE Systems Govan in Glasgow.Photograph: Jane Barlow/PAView image in fullscreenWes Streeting (right) and the chancellor, John Healey, on board HMS Glasgow during a visit to BAE Systems Govan in Glasgow.Photograph: Jane Barlow/PADefence policyStreeting says he began stockpiling food weeks ago amid rising threat to UKDefence secretary says value for money and modernisation key for spending to ‘fight the wars ahead’Kevin RawlinsonSat 31 Oct 2026 06.57 EDTFirst published on Sat 31 Oct 2026 06.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe defence secretary,Wes Streeting, says he started stockpiling food and water weeks ago in case of a national emergency, as he talked up the threats to the UK and said his department had already begun ramping up its spending in response.Streeting spoke after thechancellor, John Healey, said he wanted defence spending to reach 3%of GDP by 2030 and 3.5% by 2035; having already asked Whitehall departments to find 1% cuts in their budgets for long-term investment to fund defence spending.“I’m glad the message is getting through because my mum got in touch and said ‘payday is coming up, how much do you think I need to buy because I’m just budgeting to the end of the month?’ I’m glad that people are beginning to think about their own household resilience, making sure we’ve got sufficient supplies of bottled water, canned goods, battery-powered torches. These are all just commonsense things for the everyday challenges,” Streeting told the Times.View image in fullscreenWes Streeting has stocked up on pulses and tinned fish in preparation for an emergency.Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/ShutterstockThe defence secretary says he has bottled water, a first aid kit and a battery-powered torch on standby. He added that he was stockpiling baked beans, sweetcorn, red kidney beans, tuna, protein bars and nuts. Streeting, whorecently urged all Britons to follow suit, said he had started setting aside the supplies because he wanted to “lead by example”.He told the Times he was determined the UK should be able to deter its adversaries and “should deterrence fail, to be ready to defeat them”. Streeting said: “That is the core job. We should never lose sight of that,” adding that any additional spending must be done carefully. “Spending more money badly is not virtuous,” he said. He also told the newspaper that value for money and modernisation needed to be balanced in order to ready the UK to “fight the wars ahead”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘Autonomy, not flesh’: RAF chief outlines AI drone-powered futureRead moreIn June, Healey’sresignation as defence secretarywas one of the final nails in the coffin of Keir Starmer’s premiership. The man who now serves as chancellor in Andy Burnham’s government accused Burnham’s predecessor, as well as the former chancellor Rachel Reeves, of putting the country’s security at risk with inadequate funding for the defence investment plan (Dip).“You have been unable and the Treasury has been unwilling to commit the resources that the nation needs to defend the country at this time of rising threats. I would not be able to accept a Dip settlement that does not give our forces the resources they need. I am now left with no other option than to submit my resignation as your defence secretary,” he wrote.Announcinghis first budget on Wednesday, Healey said he was now fully funding the defence investment plan. He reiterated the target of defence spending reaching 3% of GDP; prompting the Nato secretary general, Mark Rutte, to say the UK was on “a credible path towards meeting the commitment made by all Nato allies in The Hague”. But Healey was criticised for leaving details of his plan to reach that target until next year’s spending review.Besides spending, Streeting also discussed oversight of service personnel, telling the Times the courts were in the middle of an “active campaign” to “smear the reputation and integrity of our special forces”. He also left the door open to scrutiny of special forces and the UK’s nuclear weapons by MPs and peers on the intelligence and security committee, saying they could be trusted.Explore more on these topicsDefence policyWes StreetingJohn HealeyMilitaryBudgetnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK charity shop profits plummet amid shift in secondhand clothes market | Charities | The Guardian
description: British Heart Foundation describes ‘exceptionally challenging’ trading after retail profit reportedly fell 23% amid rise of platforms such as Vinted
Author: Harry Cockburn
Headline: British Heart Foundation describes ‘exceptionally challenging’ trading after retail profit reportedly fell 23% amid rise of platforms such as Vinted
Content: An Oxfam shop in London. Oxfam’s retail head said the shift had been ‘challenging …  and it is going to be painful for the sector’.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAn Oxfam shop in London. Oxfam’s retail head said the shift had been ‘challenging …  and it is going to be painful for the sector’.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianCharitiesUK charity shop profits plummet amid shift in secondhand clothes marketBritish Heart Foundation describes ‘exceptionally challenging’ trading after Oxfam’s retail profit reportedly fell 23% amid rise of platforms such as VintedHarry CockburnSat 31 Oct 2026 11.10 EDTFirst published on Sat 31 Oct 2026 10.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleProfits at some of the UK’s best-known charity shops have plummeted as they face a number of pressures, including from online secondhand clothes platforms, prompting claims that a key part of the sector’s fundraising model could be under threat.According to unpublished accountsseen by the Financial Times, Oxfam’s retail profit fell 23% to £4.9m in the last financial year, compared with £6.4m in the previous year.The British Heart Foundation (BHF), which has the biggest high street presence of any charity in the country,has announced plansto close 150 stores after they made a £3.3m loss in the last financial year. Cancer Research UK and Scope have also closed, or are closing, some of their shops.But these losses come despite UK spending on secondhand clothing having quadrupled over the past decade, rising to £8.8bn a year, according to GlobalData.The shift has come alongside the rise of websites such as Vinted and Depop, suggesting that people who might previously have donated clothes to charity shops are instead selling them directly to other consumers and profiting themselves.View image in fullscreenThe British Heart Foundation, which has the biggest high street presence of any charity in the country, has announced plans to close 150 stores.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianAlongside this change, Chinese companies are selling more clothes in developing countries, particularly in Africa, which has long been a major market for unwanted secondhand clothing.“It has been challenging … and it is going to be painful for the sector,” Lorna Fallon, the head of Oxfam’s retail operation, told the Financial Times.Oxfam’s latest filings reveal that for every £100 people spend in its shops, just £6 now goes towards the charity’s work on alleviating global poverty. As recently as 2022, the figure was £22, the FT reports. However, the organisation’s focus on books and music means it has no plans to reduce its number of shops.In June, BHF carried out a major review of its retail arm, which employs almost 3,700 staff, after profits from its shopsplungedfrom £18.8m in 2024 to £3.6m in the year to 31 March 2025.The charity cited “an exceptionally challenging trading environment”, and said it was aiming to close 90 stores by the end of March 2027 and another 60 by the following March.The rapid change in fortunes for charity shops also highlights their limitations in the face of greater competition. Whereas Vinted and Depop directly connect sellers with buyers, charity shops remain at the mercy of high street and warehouse rents and other associated costs and inefficiencies, including collecting, sorting, pricing and storing clothes.Another issue hampering high street charity shops is that the clothes being donated are increasingly substandard. Speaking to the Guardian earlier this month, Tansy Hoskins, the author of Charity Shop World,describedthe sector as dealing with “avalanches” of poor-quality clothes across the country, as people use charity shops as convenient dumping grounds for unwanted purchases.“Quality is the big change marker – it’s gone through the floor. You’re just fighting against the waste,” Hoskins said.Robin Osterley, the chief executive of the Charity Retail Association, said: “Fast fashion has had an impact on donations quality, there’s no question about that.”View image in fullscreenOxfam’s focus on books and music means it has no plans to reduce its number of shops.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockBut he added: “We don’t see Vinted or any of the other online platforms as an issue at all. It might be having a little bit of an effect – where people have one bag for charity shop donations and one for Vinted – but we believe these effects are significantly mitigated by two things.“The first is that Vinted and other platforms are having a very positive effect on people’s attitudes towards secondhand shopping, and creating an environment where it’s much more normalised. A rising tide floats all ships.“The second factor is that there are a lot of people who buy things from charity shops to sell on the online platforms. Our members get a significant income from them.”Bafta trustees may have broken charity law by accepting free guest ticketsRead moreOsterley instead suggested theNovember 2024 budgethad had a much larger impact on bricks and mortar charity shops, in which national insurance increases and the lowering of the national insurance threshold – affecting more part-time staff – has had a “really significant” effect on the costs charity shops face, as well as inflationary pressures across the economy.Richard Hawkes, Oxfam GB’s chief executive, said: “Whilst there is no getting away from the fact that the charity retail sector has been impacted by the cost-of-living crisis, like the rest of the high street, there is still much to be hopeful and positive about for the future.“The growth of secondhand presents real opportunities for the whole sector, but it also means we need to think differently about the traditional charity retail model.He added: “Our shops also offer much more than just an income. They give us a presence in communities where we might not otherwise be, while providing opportunities to engage with more than 20,000 volunteers. This wider role remains a vital part of what makes charity retail so valuable.”Explore more on these topicsCharitiesRetail industryOxfamVoluntary sectornewsShareReuse this content

title: Almost 140 arrested at protest against Palestine Action ban outside US embassy in London | UK news | The Guardian
description: Met alleges demonstrators ‘meeting to purposefully commit a crime’ in largest such gathering under Burnham
Author: Sammy Gecsoyler
Headline: Met alleges demonstrators ‘meeting to purposefully commit a crime’ in largest such gathering under Burnham
Content: A demonstrator is removed by police during a protest in support of Palestine Action outside the US embassy in London on Sunday.Photograph: Carlos Jasso/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA demonstrator is removed by police during a protest in support of Palestine Action outside the US embassy in London on Sunday.Photograph: Carlos Jasso/AFP/Getty ImagesUK newsAlmost 140 arrested at protest against Palestine Action ban outside US embassy in LondonMet alleges demonstrators ‘meeting to purposefully commit a crime’ in largest such gathering under BurnhamSammy GecsoylerSat 31 Oct 2026 14.28 EDTFirst published on Sat 31 Oct 2026 10.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlmost 140 people have been arrested at the largest mass demonstrations under Andy Burnham’s premiership opposing the proscription of Palestine Action.Hundreds of people gathered outside the US embassy in Battersea, south London, holding signs that read: “I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action.” Demonstrators also held a vigil in support of the group outside the US consulate in Edinburgh.Before the London gathering, the Metropolitan police warned those taking part “that they face arrest as part of a robust policing operation” and that anyone “playing a key role in organising the event, giving instructions to others and/or providing logistical support” would probably be committing an offence.In a statement on X, the Metropolitan police said: “139 people have now been arrested. Officers remain on scene and are continuing to make arrests.”Commander Adam Slonecki, who is leading the policing operation, said: “All those intending on coming to this event know that supporting a proscribed organisation is unlawful – they are essentially meeting to purposefully commit a crime.Defend Our Juries, the group behind the demonstrations, said the Met was “terrified of facilitating US embarrassment” andestimatedthat “around 400 people” gathered to take part.More than 4,000 arrests have been made for supporting Palestine Action since the ban came into effect, Defend Our Juries said, representing the vast majority of terror arrests since last July.Among those sitting outside the US embassy, holding a sign that appeared to express support for Palestine Action, was Sue Morhall. “The USA is complicit in most of the wars that are going on. I just feel the leaders of this world, including Trump, need to know that people are so against what’s happening in Gaza,” said the 79-year-old retiree.View image in fullscreenSue Morhall takes part in the demonstration outside the US embassy in London.Morhall believes there is a chance Burnham could rescind the proscription. “I think it’s early days. I’m hopeful, though pigs might fly,” she said. “I think he’s going to perhaps wait until the midterm elections in America. It’s a terrible shame that people who are trying to stop a genocide are being arrested.”She has been arrested “five or six” times at previous demonstrations and feels “OK” about being hauled into a police van again. “It’s the principle, and this is one that I feel very strongly about,” she said.The Rev Bill White, 72, who also held a sign that read: “I oppose genocide. I support Palestine Action,” said: “I’m appalled that Britain is helping facilitate the genocide that is happening in Palestine. We supply weapons that are being used on Palestinians.”View image in fullscreenRev Bill White also took part in the demonstration.He said he had “hoped for better” from Burnham and resigned from the Labour party after Palestine Action was proscribed as a terrorist group.As a faith leader, he said there was “no choice” other than to take part in the demonstration. “This is the right thing to do. There’s a bad law and it is wrong to criminalise people that are trying to prevent genocide,” he said. “How can I not be here?”A Defend Our Juries spokesperson said: “The Met police overzealous response outside the US embassy today only serves to further expose how far authorities in the UK will go to appease American interests. Israel’s war crimes that have caused death and injury to thousands could not happen without the US’s approval.”The protests come before an appeal at the UK supreme court against Palestine Action’s designation as a terror group on 4 November.Last month, more than 160 people were arrested or reported for summons at a similar demonstration in support of Palestine Action staged outside the Labour party conference in Liverpool.The new government has come under pressure to rescind the ban, though Shabana Mahmood, who has stood firm in favour of the group’s proscription, remained in post as home secretary.The journalist and author Sarah Helm, the wife of the prime minister’s national security adviser, Jonathan Powell, was accused of supporting Palestine Actionafter posting on X: “God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action.” Her post came in response to news that the Irish authorSally Rooneycan no longer sell her books in the UK because of her support for the group.During the Labour party conference, two activists confronted the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, during a meal at Pizza Express in the city centre where he was challenged about the arrests. Videoof the incidentshowed one of the protesters urging Miliband to declare a genocide in Gaza and de-proscribe Palestine Action.Miliband said he was happy to discuss the issue but at another time, before the protesters were ushered out.One woman, who held a sign that, bar swapping the word “authors” to “retirees”, replicated the X post by Sarah Helm, was among thosearrestedin London, despite the Met ultimatelyassessingthat Helm’s post “did not meet the criminal threshold”.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Was I not enough?’: care worker barred from meeting home secretary | UK news | The Guardian
description: Nigerian care worker Kolade says he was left in tears after being excluded from talks with Shabana Mahmood over proposed changes to immigration system
Author: Aamna Mohdin
Headline: Nigerian care worker Kolade says he was left in tears after being excluded from talks with Shabana Mahmood over proposed changes to immigration system
Content: Kolade, who moved to Britain in 2022, said he felt ‘humiliated’ after being excluded from the meeting.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianView image in fullscreenKolade, who moved to Britain in 2022, said he felt ‘humiliated’ after being excluded from the meeting.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianUK news‘Was I not enough?’: care worker barred from meeting home secretaryNigerian care worker Kolade says he was left in tears after being excluded from talks with Shabana Mahmood over proposed changes to immigration systemAamna MohdinCommunity affairs correspondentSat 31 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 10.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKolade had carefully prepared what he would tell the home secretary about the elderly people he cares for, the life his family had built in Britain and how her immigration proposals could threaten both.The meeting withShabana Mahmoodhad already been rescheduled twice. When the third date fell during a holiday, he cut his trip short to travel to London. But hours before the meeting was due to take place, it was cancelled after Mahmood declined to allow him to attend.The rejection left him in tears. “It was a feeling of humiliation,” Kolade said. “I cried because I felt like someone saw me less to be in the same room with her.“Was I not enough to be in the same room with the home secretary? It’s not right to have treated anybody that way.”The meeting, scheduled for 21 October, was to be the first between Mahmood and the general secretary ofUnison, Andrea Egan, since she took office. Egan planned to attend alongside a union policy officer and Kolade, who had been selected by fellow migrant workers to represent them.Two hours before the meeting, the home secretary’s office informed Unison that Kolade would not be permitted to attend because Mahmood considered his presence “inappropriate”, according to the union.Egan said ministers should welcome opportunities to hear directly from workers about their experiences. “Kolade is a dedicated care worker and an inspirational campaigner. In other words, he’s a true representative of our migrant workers,” she said.“The government should be celebrating these brilliant people who give everything to care for our loved ones and keep us healthy. Not demonising, attacking and leaving them vulnerable to exploitation and abuse.”View image in fullscreenShabana Mahmood is facing calls to abandon proposals that would require migrant care workers to wait 15 years before qualifying for indefinite leave to remain.Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/ShutterstockA spokesperson said the government was considering more than 200,000 responses to its consultation on earned settlement, including submissions from more than 145,000 people directly affected by the proposals. “It would not have been appropriate to prioritise the views of a single individual while the responses to this are being considered,” the spokesperson added.“The home secretary hoped that the meeting could go ahead regardless. However, Unison’s general secretary cancelled.”The dispute comes amid pressure on Mahmood to abandon proposals that would force migrant care workers to wait 15 years before qualifying for indefinite leave to remain, rather than the five years they had expected.Under the proposed “earned settlement” system, the standard qualifying period would double from five to 10 years, with workers in lower-paid occupations, including social care, facing a 15-year wait.For Kolade, the row encapsulates what he believes is missing from the immigration debate: the voices of those whose lives could be upended by its policies. He has watched politicians dismiss care work as low-skilled and portray migrant workers as a burden on the British economy.“I was just going to tell her that is not correct,” he said. “We are not a burden to the British state. We are also contributing as much as we can, supporting British families.“She talked about fairness to the British people. I was going to tell her that caring for British families is our own little way to show that we are contributing, and that we have earned our rights to stay in this country, a place we’re currently calling home.”Kolade describes care work as the “most honourable work anybody can do”, a conviction shaped by his father’s death from diabetes when he was about 20. His father had concealed the severity of his illness, instructing the family not to tell Kolade until he had finished his university exams. But he died just a day before his final exam.View image in fullscreenKolade has said his job as a care worker is ‘the most honourable work anybody can do’.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The Guardian“Losing my dad at that age … created a vacuum, a space in my life to care for people,” he said. “When I started caring in the UK, I see everybody I care for from the lens I would see my dad. And this is what I would have said to Shabana Mahmood: I would give my best to that person as if I had a second chance to look after my dad.”Kolade rejected the suggestion migrant care workers were simply waiting to secure permanent residency before abandoning the sector. Many were investing in qualifications to build long-term careers in British social care, he said.“On the day that Shabana cancelled the meeting, one of us put on the group that he had just finished his NVQ 4 and passed with distinction. We were all very happy,” he said.“People are developing themselves within the industry so they can take up more senior roles. So the fear around: ‘Oh, they’re just going to leave the sector’ – that’s not what we are saying.”But he warned the proposals could push experienced workers to countries offering greater security. “I have a few years to my ILR [indefinite leave to remain], and so if they say: ‘Oh, you have to stay 15 years,’ I have to evaluate the other options I have. Today, Ireland, Canada and Australia are asking for people with my skill.“So you would have trained people and then you would lose them to these countries.”Kolade moved to Britain in 2022 with his wife, who is also a care worker, and two children. One of his children recently asked him: “If you don’t win, are we going to go back to Nigeria?”“I couldn’t explain what was going to happen to us,” Kolade said. “This is our home right now. This is what we know at the moment. Our kids know this place already.”Despite the cancelled meeting, Kolade remains committed to Unison’s campaign for a five-year route to settlement, sector-wide visas allowing care workers to change employers without risking their immigration status, and fair pay.“Confidence is never down,” he said. “We are going hard. We are not stopping until we have everything we have on our list.”Explore more on these topicsUK newsImmigration and asylumCare workersShabana MahmoodSocial careUnisonHome OfficefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A world-first focus on long-term outcomes could transform UK government – or create new spending fights | Economic policy | The Guardian
description: Tucked away in John Healey’s budget is decision to ringfence preventative projects where future savings outweigh initial cost
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: Tucked away in John Healey’s budget is decision to ringfence preventative projects where future savings outweigh initial cost
Content: The chancellor, John Healey, pictured in the Commons with Andy Burnham after delivering the budget. The new measure is being billed as a way to tackle neglected long-term issue such as rough sleeping.Photograph: House of Commons/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe chancellor, John Healey, pictured in the Commons with Andy Burnham after delivering the budget. The new measure is being billed as a way to tackle neglected long-term issue such as rough sleeping.Photograph: House of Commons/ReutersEconomic policyAnalysisA world-first focus on long-term outcomes could transform UK government – or create new spending fightsPeter WalkerSenior political correspondentTucked away in John Healey’s budget is decision to ringfence preventative projects where future savings outweigh initial costSat 31 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 11.02 EDTShareIt merited the briefest of mentions in John Healey’s speech and just one paragraph in the 166-pagebudget document, but some believe it could revolutionise not just public spending but the very process of government itself: a new focus on long-term outcomes.The idea in the broad sense is very simple. Any spending deemed to be “preventative” – that is, the initial outlay will be more than made up for by future savings – will from now on be ringfenced, meaning it cannot be raided for more immediate needs.This might sound uncontroversial, but it follows many years of long-term spending being pillaged to plug day-to-day gaps, particularly so during and after the austerity measures of the 2010 coalition government, which slashed numerous prevention-based services, not least the Sure Start programme for families with young children.But now, starting from the upcoming spending review, which kicks off next year, projects that can be shown to bring down costs in the future will be protected via a new piece of jargon – a preventative departmental expenditure limit, or PDEL.“It could end up being quite a major change in how the government runs spending reviews, and the entire spending framework,” said Stuart Hoddinott, at the Institute for Government thinktank, which had called for such a system to be implemented. Officials in the Treasury agree, with one calling it an “important reform”.That is, however, about as straightforward as it gets. The budget document uses Andy Burnham’s new spending toprevent rough sleepingas an example of the sort of thing that would qualify. A few other areas would seem likely: for example, public health programmes to prevent future illness, and Sure Start-type early years schemes.View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham’s new rough-sleeping prevention plan is the type of project that would qualify to be protected under the PDEL.Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty ImagesBut beyond that, no one really knows what might or might not qualify for PDEL status. Departments say they are waiting for Treasury guidance, which has not yet been drawn up. “A lot depends on the definition,” Hoddinott said. “While it sounds simple, it becomes quite difficult when you think about how it will work in practice, as you could make any argument that almost all types of spending are preventative.”Government officials agree, with one making the point that, in theory, the Ministry of Defence could argue all its spending is preventive, given the very obvious costs to the country of fighting a war, let alone losing one.There is therefore the potential for a new variant of the endless spending-review tussles between departments and the Treasury, as ministers try to protect their pet projects from future plunder.But what is perhaps just as important is the symbolism. Some other governments around the world protect specific preventative budgets – public health, for example – but this is believed to be the first time one has introduced this as a blanket policy.Government officials are billing the decision as part of a wider focus under Burnham to try to deal with knotty and neglected issues that have longer-term costs and repercussions, including rough sleeping and adult social care.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOne said: “Too often government departments have ended up raiding these types of budgets to fund short-term measures. This is an attempt to combat that as part of a wider push to transform the way the state operates.”Those whose work revolves around trying to generate long-term benefits to the public are cautiously delighted.“This does feel like a really good thing,” said Greg Fell, Sheffield city council’s director of public health and the president of the Association of Directors of Public Health.“There are a lot of questions about how it will work. Is it about preventing future acute demand, or creating the conditions for communities to thrive? Those are different things and they require a different mindset and way of operating. And with some spending, it might take decades to realise the benefits.“But as a country we have never been very good at this sort of thing, so it’s up to all of us to make sure it works.”Explore more on these topicsEconomic policyBudget 2026John HealeyAndy BurnhamLabourBudgetTax and spendinganalysisShareReuse this content

title: The secret behind Lula’s win in Brazil may be an ‘army’ – of social media creators | Brazil | The Guardian
description: There are many explanations for the incumbent president’s win over Flávio Bolsonaro, but analysts – and he – point to reinvention of his social media use
Author: Tiago Rogero
Headline: There are many explanations for the incumbent president’s win over Flávio Bolsonaro, but analysts – and he – point to reinvention of his social media use
Content: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva takes a snapshot during a campaign motorcade in Ceilândia, Distrito Federal, Brazil on 9 October.Photograph: Evaristo Sa/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLuiz Inácio Lula da Silva takes a snapshot during a campaign motorcade in Ceilândia, Distrito Federal, Brazil on 9 October.Photograph: Evaristo Sa/AFP/Getty ImagesBrazilThe secret behind Lula’s win in Brazil may be an ‘army’ – of social media creatorsThere are many explanations for the incumbent president’s win over Flávio Bolsonaro, but analysts – and he – point to reinvention of his social media useTiago Rogeroin BrasíliaSat 31 Oct 2026 09.37 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 09.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFour days before his stunning electoral comeback,Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Brazil’s president, got his first smartphone.Lula, who turned 81 last Tuesday, had long said he wanted to avoid an endless stream of calls during his rare moments off, and he began his presidential campaign by sticking to an old habit: using aides’ phones – only when necessary.Then he suffered an unexpected first-round defeat to the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who had neither his father Jair Bolsonaro’s charisma nor much of a record as a two–decade legislator – and Lula realised he had lost both in the ballot box and in the digital arena.The veteran leftist, who contested his first election more than 40 years ago, overhauled his digital strategy, began recording selfie-style videos – and went on to beat Bolsonaro by more than 4.4m votes.There are many explanations forhow he managedto boost turnout and win over other candidates’ voters. Some analysts point to an organic student mobilisation that held mass protests across Brazil, others to a package of government benefits Lula approved at the last minute in a transparent attempt to use government spending to curry favour with the electorate.But many analysts, and the president himself, point to the incumbent’s reinvention of his social media use as a key reason for his victory.View image in fullscreenLuiz Inácio Lula da Silva delivers a speech at La Moneda Palace, in Santiago Chile, on 21 July 2025.Photograph: Cristobal Basaure Araya/Sopa Images/LightRocket/Getty ImagesInterestingly, neither Lula’s campaign created nor ran what was ultimately the driving force behind the shift: a WhatsApp group called “Lula’s Army”.In the days leading up to the vote, its nearly 11 million followers – up from just 60,000 after the first round – received daily “missions” to try to win over voters and make pro-Lula content perform well on social media.Leading the “army” was the man Lula praised in his victory speech as “our general”, whose role was “raising the morale of our troops every day”: 42-year-old congressman André Janones.“I have no doubt that Lula’s army determined the outcome of the election,” Janones said, saying that he is not modest “because modesty sometimes comes very close to hypocrisy. I know how much bigger I came out of this election.”In his view, the contest had three main fronts. The first was candidate versus candidate, “and on that Lula was winning by a mile because he had much more experience”. The second was mobilisation on the streets, “and we were bringing many more people out to the protests”.But the third: “You don’t have to be very clever to realise that we were losing on social media.”Although Lula had more followers, Bolsonaro’s content generated up tofive timesmore engagement.The incumbent’s campaign also complained to the electoral court of alleged interference by Meta in the senator’s favour, including a24-hour periodin which Lula was unable to boost ads on Instagram, which the company later acknowledged but blamed on a technical error.Janones said he realised the solution was to boost organic engagement among Lula’s voters.2:54How students and social media delivered Lula a historic comeback in Brazil – videoOne of his most successful strategies came a week before the election, when “soldiers” were told to post a photo making an “L” sign for Lula with their thumb and index finger while wearing the yellowBrazilfootball shirt, a national symbol that had been appropriated by Bolsonaro supporters over the past decade.Domestic worker Sidneia dos Santos Araujo, 63, took part “because the shirt of Lula supporters is the Brazilian one. Bolsonaro supporters should be wearing the United States shirt,” she said this week, citing the Bolsonaro clan’s“subservience” to US president Donald Trumpand noting how the senatorfled to Miami.A day after Lula’s victory, Araujo created a template on Google Drive that allowed followers of the “army” to create their own “certificate”, which would declare that during their “military service” they “maintained excellent performance and exemplary conduct … and are therefore deserving of this distinction as a ‘soldier’”. The certificates, which went viral, came complete with copies of the signatures of “marshal” Lula and “commander” Janones.Janones said that, above all, he wanted to create a “sense of community: the feeling that we are not alone”.View image in fullscreenLula uses his wife’s phone at a campaign rally in Natal, Brazil, on 10 October.Photograph: Adriano Machado/ReutersAccording to Raquel Recuero, a researcher at the Federal University of Pelotas, this was one of the channel’s biggest achievements: it gave voters “a sense of purpose and the chance to channel their energy into doing something to help Lula”.Other young, digitally native politicians have also been credited with reshaping Lula’s social media strategy, including21-year-old Ana Elisa Santos, known as Ana Elisa, who became the youngest congresswoman elected from Minas Gerais in this election.The night after Lula’s first-round defeat, Elisa recorded a hugely popularvideosaying the left needed to be more “humble” and to “learn” how to use social media because “there is no longer any separation between social media and the streets … The grassroots are also on Instagram and TikTok.”She was called to a meeting with Lula and is said to have persuaded the president to record the selfie-style videos he had previously refused to make.Meanwhile, Janones urged each WhatsApp group member to bring in one more person. One day, while recording a video alongside the president, the congressman said that if they reached 5 million followers, Lula would buy a mobile phone and join the “army” himself.“People think we only say that for the cameras, but it’s real: Lula really didn’t have a mobile phone,” said Janones.The group hit its target, and when an allied politician gave the president a phone as a gift, Lula finally joined it. “I’m not going to say he’s an expert now, but he’s there, following it, and has been sending some content,” said Janones.Recuero believes it will be difficult to keep “Lula’s army” engaged now because there is a “social cost” to being so digitally committed – Janones himself suffered a cardiac arrhythmia after the first presidential debate and had to spend 24 hours in hospital. It was the only day the group went silent.But Janones believes there is a path forward for the group, perhaps not engaged 24/7 as it had been, but focused on special moments, such as trying to secure passage of legislation important to Lula.“We can’t leave the campaign trail any more,” he said, noting that despite Lula’s election, Bolsonaro’s party secured an unprecedented number of seats in congress. The “army”, he said, is what will “guarantee Lula’s ability to govern”.Explore more on these topicsBrazilLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaSocial mediaAmericasfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: It’s closer to Beijing than Washington – and residents of this Alaskan outpost are reeling from Trump’s policies | Alaska | The Guardian
description: On the Bering Sea, Unalaska is the US’s most productive seafood port, employing thousands of workers. But Trump’s cuts, and his disastrous war with Iran, have caused chaos – and put Republican control of Congress at risk
Author: Chris Stein
Headline: On the Bering Sea, Unalaska is the US’s most productive seafood port, employing thousands of workers. But Trump’s cuts, and his disastrous war with Iran, have caused chaos – and put Republican control of Congress at risk
Content: Unalaska, in the Aleutian Islands, is further west than Hawaii, and most visitors arrive on flights from Anchorage.Photograph: Brian Adams/The GuardianView image in fullscreenUnalaska, in the Aleutian Islands, is further west than Hawaii, and most visitors arrive on flights from Anchorage.Photograph: Brian Adams/The GuardianAlaskaIt’s closer to Beijing than Washington – and residents of this Alaskan outpost are reeling from Trump’s policiesOn the Bering Sea, Unalaska is the US’s most productive seafood port, employing thousands of workers. But Trump’s cuts, and his disastrous war with Iran, have caused chaos – and put Republican control of Congress at riskChris Steinin Unalaska, AlaskaSat 31 Oct 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 12.02 EDTShareIt was less than 17 hours until the start of Alaska’s lucrative Bering Sea crab season, and Oystein Lone was standing on a dock in the city of Unalaska, preparing to embark in rough conditions.The problem wasn’t the next day’s forecast of 60mph gusts, which would kick up white-capped swells and make crabbing, alreadyone of the most dangerous jobsin the United States, even more hazardous. Nor was it the question of whether there’d be enough red king, tanner and snow crabs to go around – state regulators had, in fact, announced higher quotas for the season.What was bothering Lone, as the sun sank lower in the sky that Wednesday evening, was the question of how to make the numbers work when diesel costmore than ever, thanks to the war with Iran.“This is the most challenging time I’ve seen,” said Lone, who has been fishing since 1989. He had already spent $86,000 to put 12,000 gallons of the fuel in one of his two boats, but the price had climbed higher since then, and if he wanted to fill up again, he expected to spend $100,000.Located further west than the Hawaiian islands, Unalaska is closer to Beijing, Tokyo and Seoul than Washington DC. Most visitors arrive on flights from Anchorage, which cost at least $1,600 round trip and are prone to cancellation, due to the region’s unpredictable storms and fog.But Unalaska is by no means a backwater. It has been the country’s most productive seafood port by volume for more than two and a half decades, and when its crab and pollock seasons are open, thousands of deckhands and processors arrive from elsewhere to work tough but well-paying jobs on boats offshore and in seafood plants crowded in the city.View image in fullscreenOystein Lone, the captain of the Pacific Mariner.Photograph: Brian Adams/The GuardianEven here, the impacts of Donald Trump’s efforts to remake the US government in his image can be felt. Since Trump returned to the White House, the library, museum, public radio station and local government have had funding they relied on disrupted or canceled altogether. Longshoremen have been tasked with loading empty containers on to ships to avoid tariffs. And thesoaring pricefor diesel has squeezed not just the seafood industry, but all of the nearly 4,300 residents of the city, who rely on the fuel for electricity.“This whole town runs on diesel,” said Daneen Looby, a longtime Unalaska resident who sits on the city council and owns the Norwegian Rat Saloon. With distributors upping the fuel surcharges she pays for food and alcohol shipments, Looby is thinking of raising her menu prices. “I didn’t want to, but I kind of have to, otherwise I’m going to become a charity.”The midterm elections are on Tuesday, and Alaska is set to play a major role in determining if the president’s Democratic foesregain control of Congress. Alaska resoundingly backed Trump in the 2024 election, as did a majority of Unalaska voters, but Democrats believe the president’s plunging public approval ratings together with rising fuel prices have put its two-term Republican senator, Dan Sullivan,at riskof losing re-election to their nominee Mary Peltola, even asscandalsrockher campaign.Candidates only occasionally make the trip to Unalaska, and there are just a handful of campaign signs up around town, but outrage over the direction the country has taken since Trump returned to office is prevalent.“I feel like we have a rogue government right now, and I don’t feel like theRepublicansare doing their job,” Looby said. “I don’t understand why Congress isn’t getting more involved.”‘In furtherance of the president’s agenda’The name Unalaska derives from a word in the language of the Unangax̂ people who have lived on the island for thousands of years, and roughly translates to “near the mainland” for its proximity to Alaska’s southwestern peninsula.Russian fur traders arrived in the middle of the 18th century, and eventually established a colony that came under American control when Washington purchased the Alaska territory in 1867. As the second world war approached, the US military built bases on the large, mountainous island of Unalaska and the smaller Amaknak island next to it, which were connected by a single bridge in the 1970s. In June 1942, Japan staged back-to-back air raids that killed dozens, and there are still concrete pillboxes and bunkers strewn all over town and on the tops of its treeless, windswept hills.In 2023, the most recent year for which data is available, more than 780m pounds of catch valued at nearly $225m came through its port, Dutch Harbor, according to theNational Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. Pollock, a versatile white fish, is the main product, and if you’ve eaten fish sticks, imitation crab or a Filet-O-Fish sandwich at a McDonald’s in Asia or the United States, its ingredients may well have been processed on Unalaska. The different species of crab found in the Bering Sea are also offloaded here, and the travails of that work are documented every year by camera crews who embark from Dutch Harbor to film the reality seriesDeadliest Catch.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenTop: A king crab on display in Amelia’s restaurant. Bottom: Crab pots wait to be unloaded.Photograph: Brian Adams/The GuardianAs soon as he took office in 2025, Trump began signing executive orders billed as rooting out waste from the federal government, together with the efforts of Elon Musk’snow-shuttered“department of government efficiency”. Democrats and good governance groups said the campaign undermined important functions of government, and were ofdubious legality.One of Trump’sorders, signed in March 2025, attempted to dismantle a slew of federal agencies, including the Institute of Museum and Library Services (IMLS). The little known office is the source of a yearly grant that Unalaska’s public library receives to buy books, and librarian Karen Kresh expected $6,000 last year, only to be told the money would not be coming.“It had been stable and been reliable for years and years, and that was sort of a surprise to see that instability come up with that grant,” she said.The main repository in the United States for cultural and natural history objects from the island chain is the Museum of the Aleutians in Unalaska. When Trump arrived in office, its staff was at work cataloging a large collection of artifacts dating back to the Russians’ first contact with the Unangax̂, funded by more than $347,000 in grant money from the National Endowment for the Humanities (NEH).At the beginning of April, the museum’s executive director, Virginia Hatfield, received a message saying the grant was being canceled because it “no longer effectuates the agency’s needs and priorities”, and that the funds would be reallocated “in a new direction in furtherance of the president’s agenda”. The cut put the project on hold, and Hatfield was forced to lay off six people.“It’s very heartbreaking, and it kind of truncated important work,” she said.Weeks later, Republicans in Congressapprovedlegislation ending funding for public media outlets, which they have long accused of broadcasting news with a liberal bias. The decision had significant implications for Alaska, the largest state in the country which is full of small, remote communities – like Unalaska – unreachable by road, and where cellphone service can be unreliable.That makes radio the best way to get word out when an emergency strikes, and the same day the Senate began debating whether to cut funding, the island’s public broadcaster KUCB was putting out warning of a potential tsunami. The wave did not arrive, and the station lost half of its budget after Trump signed the bill, said Lauren Adams, the general manager. In the months that followed, KUCB, along withother public media outletsnationwide, experienced a surge in giving from outraged listeners. It was also among more than a dozen Alaska stations to receivetemporary fundingfrom the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA).View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenLauren Adams of KUCB radio pictured in Unalaska.Photograph: Brian Adams/The GuardianThe station now has reserves in the bank, Adams said, but no long-term solution to the question of how to stay open, with annual federal funding gone.“When you get just this windfall fundraising from around the United States, what’s the sustainability of that?” Adams asked. “Eventually, we’re going to run out of those reserves and things that kept us going.”Lost opportunitiesThe second Trump administration hasn’t solely been a disruptive force in Unalaska.Iliuliuk Family & Health Services is the city’s only clinic, and deals with everything from checkups to emergencies. Soon, they will open a pharmacy that can replace the mail-order drugs most residents rely on, thanks to more than $400,000 from the federal Rural Health Transformation Program.Created by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Trump’smain domestic policy legislation, the program was conceived to address concerns from Republicans that cuts to the Medicaid health insurance program for poor and disabled Americans included elsewhere in the legislation would put rural hospitals out of business.Most of the Medicaid provisionshave not taken effect yet, but hospitals nationwide remainconcernedthat even with the Rural Health Transformation money, they could lose patients vital to keeping their doors open. Christy Fassbender, Iliuliuk’s chief operating officer, said that is unlikely to be an issue in Unalaska.“We have a very small Medicaid population. We are less than 6% for Medicare and Medicaid, and that is because this is a working town,” Fassbender said.Nor has the chaos the federal government experienced when Trump first began his term been permanent. In June of this year, the Museum of the Aleutians was notified that the grant from the NEH was back on, though in the time that the funding was canceled, the project director and outreach specialist Hatfield hired found other work, and the professor who had excavated the artifacts providing a glimpse into Unalaska’s past died.The IMLS eventually restored the funds the library uses to buy books. But recently, Kresh learned that the Federal Communications Commission wasconsideringending E-Rate, a program that helps the library and Unalaska’s school district provide internet access. If that were to happen, she said, the library would have to look for another way to cover the expense of offering the only free, public wifi in town, which residents and visitors rely on to apply for jobs and stay connected to the world. NEH grants that had been cut nationwide were restored after alawsuit, and a different suithaltedthe closure of the IMLS.Unalaska has felt other consequences of Trump’s presidency, for which there appears to be little recourse.At Unisea, one of the largest seafood processors in the city, they’re rebuilding their workforce after shifting away from foreign guest workers, visas which have long been hard to get and eventually became too unreliable, director of Alaska operations Ron Kjorsvik said.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenUnalaska has felt the consequences of Trump’s presidency.Photograph: Brian Adams/The GuardianThe only foreigners still doing the difficult work of processing pollock, crab, black cod and halibut are 15 Ukrainians on a special visa for nationals of the war-ravaged country, but they’ll be leaving soon – none had their visas renewed, Kjorsvik said.A group of congressional Democrats led by Virginia’s James Walkinshaw hadcomplainedto US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) in March about delays processing such applications, and in a reply seen by the Guardian, the agency’s director said USCIS had “many competing priorities and urgent requests for consideration daily”, and could not “prioritize” Ukrainians with U4U visas.Seafood processing plants on the islands, meanwhile, have their own generators supplying electricity, while the rest of the city runs on a separate, generator-powered grid. Unalaska’s leaders have long contemplated alternatives, including the possibility of tapping geothermal power from a nearby volcano.Under Joe Biden, the Department of Energy (DOE) established the Office of Clean Energy Demonstrations, and Unalaska’s utility director, Erik Hernandez, said the city was in the process of applying for funds to install five one-megawatt wind turbines and a battery system on a windy parcel of land, which could have replaced most of their diesel generators. But after Trump took office, the DOE stopped communicating about the grant, and in June 2025, the city was informed the money was no longer available.The DOE did not respond to a request for comment. Earlier this year, the US Government Accountability Officefoundthat the Office of Clean Energy Demonstrations had lost 85% of its staff over the first six month’s of Trump’s second term, and placed a stop work order on all contracts.The city was as reliant on diesel as ever when the Iran war began and crude oil prices rose in tandem, and the fluctuating rate that Unalaska charges power users to cover the cost of fuel has climbed almost two thirds, from $0.22 per kilowatt hour last year, to as much as $0.36 now, Hernandez said.The fuel price increase has furthered the stress on a fishing industry that was already not having a great year. Pollock in 2026 have been small and scarce, and storms have been frequent. That has meant less work for Dutch Harbor’s longshoremen who move refrigerated shipping containers filled with seafood onto ships bound for Asia or the US west coast. Shawn Schomer, the International Longshore and Warehouse Union’s shop steward at Matson, one of the major shipping lines serving the port, said he’s recently been getting a new and unusual request from his superiors.Certain shipping containers that remain for too long in the United States are considered imports, and thus subject to the tariffs Trump has slapped on trading partners globally.“We got to get these tariff cans out of here. That’s what the management tells us,” when it asks for the containers to be loaded on outgoing vessels, Schomer said.“It can’t be good business to bring in empties and then have to sort them and ship them back out empty,” he said. A spokesperson for Matson declined to comment.‘We’re at the bottom’Lone, 58, has spent his adult life fishing, and expects the high price of diesel to ripple through his industry. Crew members can make six figures in a season, and will see less money, since vessels’ overhead impacts their pay, and the price boats get for their catch could also fall, because processors and shippers will similarly be looking to offset their fuel costs.“Unfortunately, we’re at the bottom. We take the beating,” Lone said. “Everybody else just passes on their cost to us.”He wonders if some of the Republicans he had previously trusted to stand up for Alaska’s interests in Washington DC were doing their job.“I support Sullivan and Begich, but I’m not too sure if they’re doing much for us,” he said, referring to the state’s junior senator and congressman, Nick Begish, respectively. While Lisa Murkowski, the senior senator, has opposed the Iran war and the effort to cut public media funding, Sullivan and Begich supported both, and are facing fierce challenges to their re-elections this year.View image in fullscreenCaptain Chris Studeman of the Kevleen K boat pulls out of the harbor to go crabbing.Photograph: Brian Adams/The GuardianAs he waited to unload a 135-ton haul of pollock, CJ Peterson, captain of the trawler the Pacific Challenger, said he had been contemplating how much more his business could take. One of Alaska’s native corporations owns his vessel, and Peterson knows the grim economics could some day keep him and his crew on land.“If the fish price doesn’t match the fuel costs, they’ll shut us down,” Peterson said.Captain Chris Studeman was not waiting for that to happen. The evening before the noontime start of crab season, he gassed up his boat, the Kevleen K, at one of Unalaska’s marine fuel terminals, and tried not to think about how much more he was paying this year than last.“Don’t have much choice,” Studeman yelled from the bridge, as his crew prepared the vessel, painted white and green and laden with crab pots, to cast off. “Can’t really change your plan. You just got to go for it.”And with that, he turned to port and headed north-east, away from Unalaska and into the Bering Sea.View image in fullscreenThe Kevleen K pulls away from shore.Photograph: Brian Adams/The GuardianExplore more on these topicsAlaskaUS politicsChinaDonald TrumpRepublicansUS SenateUS midterm elections 2026Share

title: Ads accusing Republican candidates of protecting Epstein fill airwaves in final midterm push | US midterm elections 2026 | The Guardian
description: But select Democrats, too, are being accused of having ties to the late sex offender as country prepares to vote
Author: Ariana Baio
Headline: But select Democrats, too, are being accused of having ties to the late sex offender as country prepares to vote
Content: Politicians of all stripes appear eager to associate their opponents with the late sex offender.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenPoliticians of all stripes appear eager to associate their opponents with the late sex offender.Photograph: ReutersUS midterm elections 2026Ads accusing Republican candidates of protecting Epstein fill airwaves in final midterm pushBut select Democrats, too, are being accused of having ties to the late sex offender as country prepares to voteAriana BaioSat 31 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 11.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn races across the country, Democratic candidates or groups that support them have released ads accusingRepublicansof protecting pedophiles by voting against legislation to release files related toJeffrey Epstein.The ads appear intended toevoke an emotional responseby accusing candidates of “protecting” Epstein, a notorious pedophile accused of running a sex-trafficking ring involving minors.Ananalysis from CNNfound that candidates and outside groups have spent more than $35m on Epstein-related ads. Anotherfrom the Washington Postfound that Democrats spent more than $40m on Epstein-related ads across six key Senate races.The Epstein files are a sledgehammer for the US midterms | Katie PhangRead moreIn Colorado,ads targeting Republican Jeff Cranknote that the lawmaker voted against releasing the Epstein files.In one, the family members of Virginia Giuffre, a woman who survived abuse at the hands of Epstein and died by suicide last year, claim Crank “covered up Epstein’s crimes to protect Donald Trump”.Ashley Hinson, a Senate candidate in Iowa,was accusedof voting to “protect her donors” by refusing to vote to release the Epstein files.“This week I had to explain to my boys, ‘No, Mom does not protect pedophiles,’” Hinsonsaid in a campaign adresponding to attacks over the Epstein files.Anad targeting Mike Collins, the Republican running for a Georgia Senate seat, says “Mike Collins voted against releasing the Epstein files even after he knew Epstein’s sex-trafficking operation exploited 14-year-old girls for sex”.Florida Republican Jimmy Patronisfaced an attackfrom his Democratic opponent, claiming he called investigating Epstein “a waste of his time”.A spokesperson for Crank’s campaign accused the Epstein-related ad of being “intentionally vague”, in a statement tothe Washington Post,because his position was that he would vote against the file’s release until he could be confident that victim information was properly redacted. The campaign also said it was “unfortunate” that his opponent, Jessica Killin, was “preying on a grieving family with the help of the Washington Democrats”.Crank’s staff invited and met with Giuffre’s family, though Crank himself did not meet with them in person, theNew York Times reported.Crank’s campaign also said it offered to meet with Epstein victims before the vote on the legislation.Last year, Democrats and a select few HouseRepublicanstried to force a vote on the Epstein files through a discharge petition – a procedure used in Congress to bypass the traditional steps of legislation and force a vote on the House floor.Donald Trump,who knew Epstein in the 1990sand early 2000s, opposed the discharge petition for the files,reversing his campaign promiseto increase government transparency. House Republicans largely aligned themselves with him, prompting anger from high-profile Trump voters.Eventually, under pressure from allies, Trump supported the legislation, giving Republican lawmakers the go-ahead to vote for it. All but one House Republican voted for the Epstein Files Transparency Act.Many of the ads omit the fact that nearly every House Republican voted to release the Epstein files when the Epstein Files Transparency Act came to the floor, although at that point Trump had agreed to sign the legislation and release the files. Instead, the ads refer to Republicans opposing early attempts to force the legislation to the floor.Republicans have pointed to this fact when disputing the attack ads.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Of course I voted to release the Epstein files,” Hinson said in a direct-to-camera ad, accusing her opponent, Josh Turek, of lying. While Hinson voted for the final Epstein Files Transparency Act, she did not sign on to the discharge petition.Patronis, meanwhile, never called the investigation a “waste of time”, buttold a local radio stationthat while he had “no problem getting everything all released”, the issue was a “massive energy and time suck at the end of the day”.Melissa Stone, a spokesperson for Patronis’s campaign, highlighted his work with Trump to obtain disaster funding after Hurricane Isaias and said his opponent, Gay Valimont, was “still talking about a dead pedophile in a sad web video than helping the people of [the first congressional district] recover.”Some Republicans and groups supporting the GOP have sought to flip the script, accusingDemocratsof taking money from donors who had ties to Epstein.During a Georgia Senate debate, Collins accused his opponent, Jon Ossoff, of accepting campaign donations from Reid Hoffman, a tech billionaire who had ties to Epstein. Hoffman hassaidhe only knew Epstein through fundraising relationships and regrets it.“You can claim to fight against the Epstein class, but I’m going to tell you, this call is coming from inside the house and the Epstein class is on stage right now and it’s you,”Collins said.In New Mexico’s gubernatorial race, an outside groupreleased an adaccusing Democratic candidate Deb Haaland of accepting a ride on Epstein’s private jet and taking “tens of thousands of dollars from Epstein businesses” and then “asking for more”.Haaland did not fly on Epstein’s jet, but did take a flight booked by one of Epstein’s companies in 2014.Haaland has saidshe was unaware the chartered flight was owned by an Epstein-owned company.Explore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026Jeffrey EpsteinRepublicansDemocratsUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: The staggering $446m Elon Musk has spent on the US midterms – visualized | US midterm elections 2026 | The Guardian
description: The tech mogul’s midterm donations backing Republicans have made him the largest single-cycle political donor in modern US history
Author: Nick Robins-Early
Headline: The tech mogul’s midterm donations backing Republicans have made him the largest single-cycle political donor in modern US history
Content: LoadingUS midterm elections 2026The staggering $446m Elon Musk has spent on the US midterms – visualizedThe tech mogul’s midterm donations backing Republicans have made him the largest single-cycle political donor in modern US historyNick Robins-Early,Andrew Witherspoon,Will Craft, Alvaro Dominguez, andDaniel WolfeSat 31 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 06.01 EDTShareElon Musk has poured so much money into US politics this midterms election cycle that his donations could fund half a dozen SpaceX rocket launches or buy thousands of Tesla Cybertrucks. At theTesla Diner in Los Angeles, Musk could order more than 31.9m cheeseburgers with the money he has spent on the midterms.Musk, the world’s richest person, has funnelled at least $445.77m into Republican-aligned political action committees (Pacs) and groups since last year, according to US Federal Election Commission data as of 29 October. The contributions have made him the Republicans’ most prominent financial backer and the largest single-cycle political donor in modern US history.Musk’s spending is a staggering example of the SpaceX and Tesla CEO’s political influence, as he seeks to help Donald Trump’s administration retain control of Congress in the upcoming midterm elections, though currentpolls predict Democratsachieving a majority. The contributions are at a scale that is difficult to fathom and dwarf efforts from big name megadonors like George Soros or Michael Bloomberg, setting a new precedent for how the rich and powerful attempt to shape politics.a diagram shows Elon Musk’s $446m flowing to midterms campaigns across US statesView image in fullscreenPhotograph: The GuardianOnly last year, Musk claimed he would step away from making large scale political donations after putting nearly $300m towards Trump’s 2024 presidential election campaign. FEC data since then shows he has not only leaned back into financing campaigns, but that his spending has dramatically ramped up as election day approaches, increasing by about $200m in the final two months of campaigning.Musk’s money has primarily flowed into several Republican-alignedSuper Pacs, with his largest contribution of $216m going intohis own America Pac. The Pac has targeted 43 House and Senate races across the US, blanketting voters with television commercials, digital ads, text messages and mailers.America Pac made 839 independent expenditures in House races and 623 in Senate races in 17 states across the country.The spending varies greatly depending on the state, however, with campaigns in battlegrounds such as Michigan and Arizona receiving more of the Pac’s support.Musk’s Pac has spent the most in his home state of Texas, where a closely fought Senate contest between Democratic candidate James Talarico and RepublicanKen Paxtonhas turned into the most expensive race of the midterms. America Pac has overall poured more than $33m into efforts toelect Paxton, while Musk also made a $168m contribution to the Senate Leadership Fund which supports the Paxton campaign.A large portion of America Pac’s output focuses on attack ads against Democratic candidates such as Talarico, often accusing them of being radical socialists or targeting them over supporting transgender rights. The Pac has spent $28m on anti-Talarico content, including between $300,000 and 350,000 in October on a single Google ad targeting the Texas Senate candidate.“James Talarico supports parents being charged with child abuse if they do not support transitioning their children,” stated the ad, which was shown more than 10m times over an eight day period.Musk has also reposted America Pac’s content to his more than 200m followers on X, the social media platform he owns. One of Musk’s posts in October amplified an America Pac attack ad and claimed: “Talarico wants to trans your kids and destroy the border.”The nearly $446mthat Musk has donated this election cycle far exceeds his contributions in the 2024 presidential race, when the tech mogul also held rallies and appeared on stage next to Trump during the campaign. While Musk has been a less visible presence in the midterms, potentially reflecting theUS public’s dislike of him, behind the scenes he has greatly upped his financial support for Republicans.Musk’s spending far outpaces all other donors in the elections, including fellow tech and finance moguls like Marc Andreessen, who also started his own Super Pac. Musk has put more money into this election cycle than what every top Silicon Valley donor, including himself, spent on the 2024 presidential election combined.Area circle chart shows Elon Musk’s 2026 political contributions surpass top tech donors, including himself, from the 2024 general election.View image in fullscreenThe stakes of the midterm elections are potentially high for Musk, who has closely aligned himself with the Trump administration and benefited from its lax policies toward regulating tech and artificial intelligence. SpaceX has also intertwined itself into the government more extensively, landing lucrative contracts this year for Trump’s missile defense program and the use of Musk’s Grok AI chatbot in the Pentagon.Despite the immense and unprecedented scale of Musk’s political spending, his contributions this election are still only a tiny fraction of the centibillionaire’s overall assets.A closing line to the story. It says: Musk’s net worth is hovering around $924bn —meaning that his $445.8m in political donations account for less than 0.05% of his total wealth. Alongside it is a cutout of Elon Musk sitting on a pile of cash.View image in fullscreenExplore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026US politicsElon MuskUS political financingThe super-richRepublicansSuper PacsShare

title: Days away from a national verdict on Trump 2.0, we check in with nine voters across the political spectrum | US midterm elections 2026 | The Guardian
description: Millions will vote to decide which party controls Congress – which will have a huge impact on Trump’s final years in office
Author: Rachel Leingang
Headline: Millions will vote to decide which party controls Congress – which will have a huge impact on Trump’s final years in office
Content: The Guardian’s 2026 midterm voter panel.Composite: The Guardian/Getty Images/Caleb Davis/David Ferrari/Sally Rasmussen/Patti Fucci/Justin Daniels/Sharon Anderson/Scott Akridge/Yajaira MartinezView image in fullscreenThe Guardian’s 2026 midterm voter panel.Composite: The Guardian/Getty Images/Caleb Davis/David Ferrari/Sally Rasmussen/Patti Fucci/Justin Daniels/Sharon Anderson/Scott Akridge/Yajaira MartinezUS midterm elections 2026Days away from a national verdict on Trump 2.0, we check in with nine voters across the political spectrumMillions will vote to decide which party controls Congress – which will have a huge impact on Trump’s final years in officeRachel Leingang,George Chidi,David Smith,Fabiola Cineas,Dani AnguianoandEd Pilkington, with graphics byAndrew WitherspoonSat 31 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 09.58 EDTShareLoadingUS voters will soon deliver a national verdict on the second presidency ofDonald Trump. On 3 November, millions of Americans will vote in midterm elections to decide control of the House of Representatives and Senate, as well as the governorships in 36 states and state legislatures across the country. The results could have a huge impact on Trump’s final two years in office.Our reporters haveinterviewednine voters across the country and the political spectrum about extremism in US politics, their confidence in the US voting system, what they hope Congress will tackle first and their views of the president’s secretary of defense, Pete Hegseth.The answers – highlights of which are published below – offer insight into the national mood days before voters head to the polls. The Guardian will return to its voter panel after final votes are cast.Do you think this election cycle has seen more extreme candidates? If so, who?View image in fullscreenSally RasmussenSally Rasmussen62; Medford, Wisconsin; independent/progressivedouble quotation markThe times that we’re living through has created a certain extremism. My bias is that I see the extremism on the right. I see the extremism of Trump’s influence on the candidates, on the electorate and the people that I live with every day here in Taylor county. I’ve not been a fan of Tom Tiffany, the Republican candidate for governor in Wisconsin. He showed his extremism from the very start, seeking to undermine the 2020 election, voting for war, supporting tariffs, never swerving from the lockstep Maga extremist playbook, essentially.David FerrariDavid Ferrari19; Tallahassee, Florida; Democrat/progressivedouble quotation markIt depends on what you mean by extreme. We have certainly seen way more candidates than usual making it out of the Democratic primaries who do not take billionaire or foreign lobby money, like Angie Nixon [in Florida] or Abdul El-Sayed [in Michigan]. While this shift is seen as electorally threatening to some, most of these candidates who are typically the ones labeled as “extreme” have policy prescriptions that are very close to the average American’s views, especially when it comes to topics like healthcare reform or participation in forever wars. Looking at the other side of the aisle, I do think there has been an emergence of candidates who display an “extreme” level of corruption and bigotry typically only seen coming from the White House these days. Mike Rogers [Republican Senate candidate for Michigan] comes to mind, with his main campaign strategy seemingly being a desperate bid to tie El-Sayed to anything radical or Islamist, and so does Vivek Ramaswamy’s notable doubling-down on a campaign ad implying his gubernatorial opponent [in Ohio] lied about her childhood sexual abuse.Sharon AndersonSharon Anderson70; Etowah, Tennessee; Maga Republicandouble quotation markMost of the Democratic candidates are extreme. This political cycle has produced more extreme candidates than ever before. I’m 70 years old and I’ve never been involved in active politics. I’ve always voted since I was 18 and I’ve always voted conservative Republican but I’ve never seen anything that’s so extreme. Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan is one that stands out and some have already been elected like the mayor of New York [Zohran Mamdani]. I never thought I would see someone that far left voted in.Do you think this election will be free and fair?View image in fullscreenSally RasmussenSally Rasmussen62; Medford, Wisconsin; independent/progressivedouble quotation markI believe that at the most local level, it will overwhelmingly be free and fair. And by that I mean that I have a great deal of faith in the town clerks and the county clerks, the people who, at the ground level, oversee elections and whose livelihoods, whose reputations are on the line. On the national level, I have every expectation that the extremists that are currently in power will do whatever they can to, well, to cheat, to break the law, to violate constitutional rights of the people, and to try to deny election results, as happened after the 2020 election.View image in fullscreenPatti FucciPatti Fucci46; Roswell, Georgia; independent/moderatedouble quotation markThe election itself will be free and fair as it’s conducted. However, we’re already seeing all the multiple attempts in the past two weeks of different types of intimidation from the justice department trying to interfere with elections. And we’ve seen that in California, we’ve seen it right now in Alaska, we’ve seen it here. So, they’re using the many tactics of intimidation and meddling and propaganda to interfere in the elections. But when I look at the amount of people that have already voted early, I think that’s the biggest guardrail that this election has.Sharon AndersonSharon Anderson70; Etowah, Tennessee; Maga Republicandouble quotation markI can only hope. I’m thankful for the steps that the Republican party has followed with monitors and people watching the polls because, if an election is won fair and square, I am thrilled. That is the way of the people but, if there’s any cheating going on or one vote that is fraudulent, that vote should be thrown out because that’s not what this nation is based on. In some countries, people have died for fair elections and, unless we have fair elections, it’s to the good of no one.Morgan AkinMorgan Akin85; Redding, California; Democrat/moderatedouble quotation markBeing a poll worker and observing what goes on, I think [elections] go on pretty well anywhere in the country. I think you will see a fair election. Unfortunately, maybe, delayed or not approved by the Trump administration. He’s saying if the GOP loses in Alaska, he’s not going to recognize it. [But] I think the Democrats have been anticipating this all along and have been putting together different ways of challenging him in the courts.If your party wins next week, what are you hoping they will do first?David FerrariDavid Ferrari19; Tallahassee, Florida; Democrat/progressivedouble quotation markI am hoping Democrats immediately reinstate and expand the ACA, [the Affordable Care Act], pass a war powers resolution to end engagement with Iran, pass an AI datacenter moratorium, end all military aid to Israel, reverse the White House’s cancellation of federally approved funding, undo the blanket tariffs, release the Epstein files, and scrutinize and impeach the cabinet and president. I also hope they fight to advance Medicare for All, a substantial increase in the federal minimum wage, and robust federal job and housing programs.View image in fullscreenYajaira MartinezYajaira Martinez43; Pharr, Texas; independent/disaffected Trump voterdouble quotation markWhichever party wins, I really hope they focus on doing the right thing and bring ICE under control. Right now, here in the Rio Grande valley, ICE is profiling individuals of a certain color, Hispanic people, and they are chasing them down, arresting and assaulting them. I’m not saying that they shouldn’t deport people, but it’s got to be done the right way, the legal way.Morgan AkinMorgan Akin85; Redding, California; Democrat/moderatedouble quotation markI hope they will first [address] gas prices, food prices, medical costs and interest rates, and all of the things that are hurting the economy right now. I don’t think it’s time to talk about impeachment or anything like that. It would just cause more problems than necessary.View image in fullscreenJustin DanielsJustin Daniels45; Detroit, Michigan; Democrat/progressivedouble quotation markBring civility back to society. It seems as though there’s something going on in society, and there’s a race to the bottom. Democrats had power before, and they spend so much time arguing amongst themselves. I think that when Democrats win, the speed of which society is collapsing will slow down, but it will not stop.View image in fullscreenCaleb DavisCaleb Davis22; Greenville, South Carolina; Republican/conservativedouble quotation markIf the Republican party wins next week, I hope they will focus on bringing a swift and decisive victory in Iran. They seem to be allergic to winning, whether in individual races, a national agenda or geopolitics, and they need to grow a spine.View image in fullscreenScott AkridgeScott Akridge60; Marietta, Georgia; Democrat/liberaldouble quotation markStop ICE by any means necessary. Their harmful impact is threatening the lives of innocent people daily, and it makes us look like we’re run by a third world cartel. Obama deported just as many illegal immigrants, focusing on actual criminals and not using unchecked violence against families. No civilians were casually murdered on his watch.Next, start impeachment proceedings and investigations into all the blatant and rampant corruption that the GOP has repeatedly ignored. If I had my choice, I would choose [Trump’s son-in-law Jared] Kushner as the first target and Trump’s sons to avoid the courts getting in the way with presidential privilege.
