If they do go after Trump, they should impeach both him and Vance simultaneously since they are in it together.What do you think of Pete Hegseth? What was your reaction to the idea of livestreaming an execution?David FerrariDavid Ferrari19; Tallahassee, Florida; Democrat/progressivedouble quotation markI think Pete Hegseth is unfit for the job in almost every possible way. If you can look past his vitriolic attitude toward women and every minority – I find that difficult – he is clearly an incompetent buffoon chosen purely for his loyalty to the president over any real consideration of his capabilities. The livestreamed execution idea is just one of the latest in a series designed to propel America back into some of the darkest chapters of our history. As Jamelle Bouie of the New York Times succinctly put it: “That’s a lynching.”Sharon AndersonSharon Anderson70; Etowah, Tennessee; Maga Republicandouble quotation markWe need a strong leader in any position that we have in the country. If my house is on fire, I wouldn’t want to follow someone who says: ‘Maybe we need to go this way, but I don’t know, let’s sit here and talk a minute and discuss it and find out what we need to do.’ I want somebody to get me by the hair of the head and say: ‘Let’s get the hell out of the house.’ I think that’s Hegseth. I was all for the livestreamed execution. When I first heard it I said: ‘Yeah, I’m going to watch it.’ I’m a mother of five children. Mothers look at things differently. People said, how are you going to protect the children? How many children watched Charlie Kirk get his neck blown out? Now, that wasn’t a choice but that is a part of this world and I believe if someone commits a crime, they should suffer the consequences.View image in fullscreenCaleb DavisCaleb Davis22; Greenville, South Carolina; Republican/conservativedouble quotation markPete Hegseth is a force to be reckoned with. I appreciate his restoration of military culture away from the effeminate mockery of itself that it was under Levine [Admiral Rachel Levine, who is transgender and led the public health corps during the Joe Biden administration]. I’m equally pleased to see the war department retake its original, unashamed title. We’ve been sitting while everyone else pretends not to play the game for too long, and Pete Hegseth has called the world’s bluff. As to the public execution of the traitor that killed several American soldiers, I simply believe it should have been done a long time ago. America is a joke if it can’t execute justice.Morgan AkinMorgan Akin85; Redding, California; Democrat/moderatedouble quotation markI think he’s the most inadequate person that has ever been in that position. I was in the Marine Corps for 15 years. I’ve seen different secretaries of war, as they like to put it, and he has come up with the most ridiculous things I’ve ever seen. No 1, he is prejudiced. He’s as prejudiced as Trump is about certain things, women in the military, minorities in the military. He’s gotten rid of many of the top generals and most of them are women, Black people or Latinos. He’s really downgraded the military, and he has no idea what he’s doing in terms of carrying out operations like the one in Iran. I think it was a very poor judgment on his part to even consider something like that. Because again, we’ve never done that in our history. I think it would just be another black mark on his ability to carry out his job.Explore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026US politicsTrump administrationUS CongressPete HegsethUS voting rightsShare

title: Yaga review – this erotic witchy thriller starring Hudson Williams is a total head-messer | Television | The Guardian
description: The Heated Rivalry actor plays two people in this genre-bending mystery. And Carrie-Anne Moss is fantastic as a horny author – who might have supernatural powers
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: The Heated Rivalry actor plays two people in this genre-bending mystery. And Carrie-Anne Moss is fantastic as a horny author – who might have supernatural powers
Content: Spooky … Hudson Williams in Yaga.Photograph: Bell Media/SkyView image in fullscreenSpooky … Hudson Williams in Yaga.Photograph: Bell Media/SkyTV reviewTelevisionReviewYaga review – this erotic witchy thriller starring Hudson Williams is a total head-messerThe Heated Rivalry actor plays two people in this genre-bending mystery. And Carrie-Anne Moss is fantastic as a horny author – who might have supernatural powersLucy ManganSat 31 Oct 2026 17.40 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 17.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWell, here’s an unexpected answer to the question of what Hudson Williams did next: the overnight megastar created by the smash-hit success ofHeated Rivalry(hot young men bang each other for seven episodes, emotional connection also glossed, intermittent hockey scenes) appears as two characters in the spooky thriller Yaga.Williams plays Henry Park, the missing scion of a powerfully rich family in the spooky Canadian coastal town of Whittock, and Henry’s spookily looky-likey roommate Logan, who lives in the Parks’ staffed mansion rent-free in return for helping Henry with his podcasts, parties and possible bisexuality. There is a lot of all three about these days among the young, I’m told. Usually by their podcasts.Private investigator and family employee-friend Charlie Rapp (Noah Reid) is sent by Henry’s parents, who are now visiting Japan, as Henry has a history of disappearing on jaunts abroad. Rapp, intended to be cocky yet charming, joins forces with by-the-book beat cop Carson (Clark Backo), whom he soon deduces may be a lesbian – because this is a reworking, by Canadian playwright Kat Sadler, of the misogyny-suffused Slavic legend about Baba Yaga, a misunderstood, baby-eating devil woman, and you can’t really do that without at least a dash of Sapphism in the mix. Off they go to find a way to work together despite their very different lives, temperaments, approaches to the job and abilities to dress for coastal Canadian weather.View image in fullscreenOn the case … Clark Backo as Carson (centre) and Charlie Rapp as Noah Reid in Yaga on Sky Atlantic.Photograph: Sphere Abacus/SkySoon they are amassing clues, suspects and folk-horror mainstays in roughly equal proportions. Henry’s passport, laptop, fancy watch and $15,000 (£11,000) are gone but he left his beloved camera behind. Also a narked ex-girlfriend, Pam (Ezra Franky), which is still apparently a viable name in British Columbia, who – along with other townswomen – emerges as a force to be reckoned with. She is not bothered by Henry’s missingness. “Shitty guysshouldbe dead,” she says. I like a girl who knows where she stands.They meet Carrie-Anne Moss (the show’s executive producer) as uber-mysterious, super-charismatic, fantastically old (“I’m 60”) professor Katherine, who specialises in bones. She has written a book called Sexy Bones, because Yaga is a series in which – just as things are beginning to hang together – something like this occurs to make your suspension of disbelief just that bit less willing. (See also Rapp’s success with the laydeez of Whittock – as instant and incessant as it is inexplicable, given his mindless bro energy. I would remind you that Canada is the birthplace of Ryans both Gosling and Reynolds. It is not an underinformed or undersupplied country.) Even at her advanced age, the professor is still sexually active. With younger men! It seems impossible that she can be doing this without witchcraft, but we’ll just have to wait and see.View image in fullscreenWitchy business? … Carrie-Anne Moss in Yaga.Photograph: Bell Media/SkyDead and bloodied birds become a recurring motif. The investigating duo find chicken feet in Henry’s and his doppelganger’s rooms. Mysterious symbols abound. There’s a secret passageway and blood spots in the breakfast eggs they are served at the local diner. There’s a druggy party at the mansion and a variety of chemically induced visions for Rapp. Every episode opens with a guttural voiceover from a Slavic-accented woman saying things like: “A witch isn’t born. She begins.” There is a lot of mist and there are a lot of trees and a lot of nightmares where people have spiders come out of their mouths and wake with a start.Then a castrated body turns up on the beach (and I am awarding bonus points for whoever managed to get the penis stump scene past the censors – I think it is a first, though I suspect we are all in no hurry for a second) and things become a bit more police-procedural than spooky, and although fans of the supernatural vibe will be sorry, it does improve the flow, narratively speaking.The story becomes stronger and more timely as the malevolent vibe that the town carries is revealed (though still a bit too slowly), and the feminist twist on the legend gets to work. What has up until now been a solid three-star outing starts edging towards a four, and I’m going to round up and award it the latter.Yaga is such a quirky, hit-and-miss endeavour, so dependent on individual taste and the amount of goodwill in the room at any given moment that everyone should give it a shot. It’s got something – I just can’t say precisely what. Baba, of course, may be messing with my head.Yaga streams onSky Atlanticfrom Saturday 31 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewHorror (TV)Sky AtlanticThrillersreviewsShareReuse this content

title: A-listers and AI stylists: how high-street brands are staging a fashion comeback | Fashion industry | The Guardian
description: Gap, M&S, Topshop and more are taking a leaf from luxury label playbooks to satisfy savvier generation of shoppers
Author: Lauren Cochrane
Headline: Gap, M&S, Topshop and more are taking a leaf from luxury label playbooks to satisfy savvier generation of shoppers
Content: Online fashion brand Asos appointed Law Roach (left), fashion adviser to Zendaya (right), as stylist-in-residence.Photograph: Jamie McCarthy/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenOnline fashion brand Asos appointed Law Roach (left), fashion adviser to Zendaya (right), as stylist-in-residence.Photograph: Jamie McCarthy/Getty ImagesFashion industryA-listers and AI stylists: how high-street brands are staging a fashion comebackGap, M&S, Topshop and more are taking a leaf from luxury label playbooks to satisfy savvier generation of shoppersLauren CochraneSat 31 Oct 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 12.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHigh street brands that boomed in the noughties before the squeeze of both sustainably minded consumers and the rise of ultra-cheap online labels are staging a comeback.This time, rather than focusing solely on trend-led affordable designs, the names familiar to any shopper are courting luxury fashion, A-list collaborations and enhanced services in an attempt to engage consumers.Think Gap’s new collection with Victoria Beckham. Or Marks & Spencer showcasing a covetable catwalk collection at London fashion week with celebrities including Joan Collins and assorted gen Z Gallaghers in attendance, then making it available to buy immediately, with half of the pieces under £50. Topshop relaunched last year and now has concessions in 30John Lewisstores, as well as the luxury retailer Liberty.Lisa Illis, the head of design at M&S, describes their recent catwalk show as “making the buzz of London fashion week accessible to everyone”. She says “more fashion-informed seasonal collections” have seen the number of under-35s shopping at the retailer increase 16% year on year.View image in fullscreenM&S launched a covetable collection at London fashion week, with celebrities in the frow.Photograph: Katie Collins/ReutersThe Hollywood stylistLaw Roach, whose clients include Zendaya, has been appointed stylist-in-residence at Asos, where his influence will be felt not just in advertising campaigns, but also through his suggestions on different items from across the site to wear together.“In research, we found that 68% of consumers say what they need to know is how to wear something,” says Vanessa Spence, Asos’s executive vice-president of brand.Asos turns to AI stylists to win back shoppers after sales slide 12%Read moreThe online retailer has added AI stylists, virtual try-on tools and a Buy the Look option, which allows consumers to buy an outfit in one go, a feature that Spence says is very popular. “We’re helping customers find pieces that they want to wear. Then they can get more from every purchase and extend the life of their product.”Ella Baynes, insight manager at retail consultants Savvy Marketing, says the shift shows brands are adapting to the more sophisticated ways consumers are approaching fashion, particularly online. “Instead of competing directly, [these retailers] are borrowing some of luxury fashion’s cultural cues,” she says. “You’re meeting both that shopper aspiration, but also the shopper reality [with the price].”Asos’s extensive adaptive collection for disabled customers also shows this broader way of thinking. The company worked with disabled consultancy Tilting the Lens on the range. “There is an ability to develop, even for yourself, a capsule collection,” says founder and disability advocateSinéad Burke, who has achondroplasia, the most common form of restricted growth. “It’s not just one suit, it’s not just one skirt, you can customise the pieces. You can wear the magnetic waistcoat with the pants. We hope what we’re giving people is greater choice.”View image in fullscreenSinéad Burke at this year’s Met Gala.Photograph: Sarah Yenesel/EPACrucially, these items are affordable – nothing is more than £65 – which is particularly important for disabled people, 46% of whom are not in work in the UK. “Whenever we’re looking at shopper attitude, cost is absolutely king,” confirms Baynes.For Asos in particular, which registered a sharp decline in sales post-Covid and new competition from ultra-cheap brands like Shein, an overhaul was needed. Sales weredown 12% last August. A cost-cutting drive, including charging for returns, helped the site turn a corner, and they announced a 50% growth of profits this March, although the impact of a cyber-attack at the beginning of October is yet to become clear.‘It’s time for even things I love to find new homes’: how to curate your clutter for VintedRead moreAndrea Cheong, fashion commentator and author of Why Don’t I Have Anything to Wear?, regularly posts Instagram videos reviewing different items from affordable brands, in order to assess how well made they are. She has noticed that brands are not signposting their environmental credentials as much as they once did – due to a combination of criticism from campaigners, cost and the rise of conservatism. “It wasn’t something that was very lucrative once the economy was in decline, and then bring politics into it, that has a huge impact,” she says.At M&S, which first launched its eco-commitments in 2007, value and sustainability are not competing priorities. “By designing pieces with longevity in mind, from everyday wardrobe staples to more fashion-led seasonal collections, we’re helping customers build wardrobes they’ll wear and love for longer,” says Illis.But regardless of making more enduring styles, retailers are always up against changeable consumer behaviour – and damning statistics like the estimate that a garment is on averageworn seven times before it is thrown away.Even if brands are borrowing from the luxury playbook, the reality may not always match up, argues Cheong. “However much they try to elevate what it is, it is not the same [fabric] that they use at, for example, Dior.” The use of human-made fibres in ranges like the M&S catwalk collection and Asos Adaptive is just one example of the difference between high fashion and high street.View image in fullscreenMany gen Z and millennial customers shop secondhand, says Cheong.Photograph: Photononstop/AlamyCheong says a lot of gen Z and millennial customers are also shopping secondhand, with resale app Vinted now thethird biggest retailer in the UK. “I would say 70% or 80% of my audience are 25 to 35 and they are really jaded. They are a lot more savvy than brands seem to think.”Sustainability aside, perhaps this new shift shows that brands are realising consumers are more cynical now – and that they need to do more to reach their radar.Explore more on these topicsFashion industryMarks & SpencerTopshopAsosJohn LewisSheinAI (artificial intelligence)featuresShareReuse this content

title: ‘Never big enough’: inside the booming penis enlargement industry | Documentary films | The Guardian
description: In a revealing documentary, a looksmaxxing-influenced world where ‘your social capital is tied to your appearance’ has led to more men wanting more
Author: Andrew Lawrence
Headline: In a revealing documentary, a looksmaxxing-influenced world where ‘your social capital is tied to your appearance’ has led to more men wanting more
Content: ‘With very few exceptions, almost none of the partners in the movie wanted them to do this.’Photograph: World of WonderView image in fullscreen‘With very few exceptions, almost none of the partners in the movie wanted them to do this.’Photograph: World of WonderDocumentary films‘Never big enough’: inside the booming penis enlargement industryIn a revealing documentary, a looksmaxxing-influenced world where ‘your social capital is tied to your appearance’ has led to more men wanting moreAndrew LawrenceSat 31 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 11.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMan’s obsession with his member is a tale as old as time, writ large in sky-scraping edifices, in allusions that flatter (big dick energy) or offend (prick), in the countless artifacts across the ages that venerate male potency – a porn star’s description of Donald Trump’s “toadstool” penis. But it’s the booming intimate wellness industry – AKA the rash (ahem) of fillers, therapies and cosmetic procedures that have come into vogue since the little blue pill rocked the market – that most intrigued Daniel Lombroso, the esteemed documentarian who made his name at the Atlantic and the New Yorker dissecting male fragility.‘A cultural moment’: smash hit doc You Can See Everything continues to dazzle AmericaRead more“A lot of the stories I worked on at those places were kind of fringy subculture and oftentimes adjacent to white nationalism,” says Lombroso, who became aware of the rising demand for penile enhancement procedures while reporting on plastic surgery trends at the New Yorker. “I started calling all these practitioners. But to make an embedded film the way I do, you need someone who’s very open.”A 2024 study of US Google searchesnotedan increase in interest in penile-enhancement injections from 2013 through 2022. Lombroso’s 90-minute film, Manhood, puts male self-esteem issues at the heart of the trend on a cold, chafing examination table. Our guide throughout is Bill Moore, a capitalist in scrubs who gives fresh meaning to the phrase bedside manner. We meet him at home, tongue-kissing a pet lap dog while snuggled up under the covers with his male partner. We behold the full splendor of his naked body, nipped and tucked in retreat from the ravages of time and his own unforgiving eye. “Nobody would suspect I’ve ever had anything done!” he says with bracing cluelessness.We see Moore hawk outpatient penile enhancement procedures from his Dallas strip mall office for $15,000 and $20,000 a pop and tout the lowly glow-ups as career-changing, sex-life turbocharging, depression-curing – whatever patients need to hear to fork over the dough, really. “Everybody wants a boat that’s one foot longer,” one guy says as Moore sticks a long numbing needle into his nether regions. “The boat is never big enough.”We see many of these patients (though customers is the better word, since, again, Moore isnota doctor), their faces more obscured than their ink-marked private parts. The inclination toward anonymity owes as much to the physical embarrassment Moore’s clientele bring into the room as to the irony of receiving this kind of care from an out-and-proud gay man – the megachurch pastor, the border patrol agent. It’s wild to see Moore act as a machismo whisperer to men who might perceive him as less than masculine, especially as he reflects on the guilt and fear of rejection he experienced before coming out to conservative Christian family members in the deep south (not that his mother having dementia doesn’t help).Throughout the film, Lombroso manages to point out these and other paradoxes without casting judgment. “I’m not deep in the looksmaxxing world, but part of what Clavicular and those guys understand is that your social capital is tied to your appearance,” Lombroso says. “Does your penis size matter? Probably not. But there are all these stats about the huge percentage of American men who obsess over it, which was foreign to me. And it connects all these other things we talk about – like how many older American men don’t know how to make a best friend.”None of Moore’s customers embodies male loneliness quite like Ruben, a father of five who is so desperate to enlarge his penis that he moves his family in with an ex to raise money for an enhancement procedure. “I have to sell my house this weekend, and I’m going to Bill after.” Lombroso recalls Ruben telling him in a phone call. “I was like, ‘OK, I’ll be there tomorrow.’ The only way to make a film like this, because I’m in New York and this was in Texas, was to fly out on a whim every time and just capture things as they happened.”Ruben fills his days listening to Joe Rogan prattle on about the marginalization of manly men and spends nights performing at comedy open mics in bars to crickets – and zero friends in the crowd. His jokes about child abuse are as wince-inducing as the circular logic of upgrading his manhood. He believes it will help protect and provide for his family, even as it fundamentally destabilizes them. “He’s actually a very loving father,” Lombroso says. “A good guy. But he escapes into these worlds like many of us do, and I think eventually it caught up to him.”Meanwhile, Lana, Ruben’s poor wife, overwhelmed by the succession of shocks his big dick sidequest has imposed on their lives, is pushed ever closer to divorce. “With very few exceptions, almost none of the partners in the movie wanted them to do this,” Lombroso says. “You see Lana kind of against it, but not taking too strong of a stance.”But the film takes its strangest turn with David, a handsome young man who seeks out Moore’s help repairing the damage from an enhancement procedure botched by another dubious quasi-physician – Victor Loria, a gruff George Costanza-type who brags about growing up in a “connected” family (“We lived the Goodfellas life,” he says, wondering “when are we going to jail, basically”) and keeps a large malpractice insurance disclaimer nailed to his front office wall like Martin Luther’s 95 Theses. Loria is the film’s villain, in case that wasn’t clear.View image in fullscreenA still from Manhood.Photograph: World of WonderDavid seems plucked from a casting call for the reality TV series Botched, a naive keen to hit control-Z after going under the knife too young and, perhaps, steer others away from rushing down that same path. But as his arc unfolds and his OnlyFans porn-acting past is revealed, it turns out he and Moore have more in common than just deeply religious parents who viewed homosexuality as an abomination. They share a bed, too – with Moore’s partner and the dog. That David risks permanent damage from this corrective procedure only heightens the stakes around the throuple bombshell.Lombroso calls the effort to compel David’s participation in the film “one of the hardest acts of persuasion I’ve ever done. It took the entire film to convince him. We were going to use AI face replacement. But right around the rough-cut stage, when we realized he was the heartbeat of the story, we flew him into New York and showed him – and he loved it. Told his family everything. Now he’s touring with the film. It’s the best.”Weaving between David’s feelgood story, Loria’s villainy and Ruben’s allegory is Moore – the honest broker who still lulls customers into thinking he’s a doctor, who travels to conferences to show actual doctors how to get in on the male-enhancement gold rush, and who sells his wares as an antidote to all the cosmetic procedures women can get to feel better about themselves. His massive house and impressive car collection speak more plainly to his motives in this space than his riffs to customers about self-esteem or the blarney about posting their post-op results on his company website.Moore’s company PhalloFill, which specializes in “girth enhancement”, has expanded to 32 locations across the country. He hopes to make the procedure as common as Botox. “Bill tried to get me to have my penis enlarged,” says Lombroso. The thought never occurred. “I said my mom would never forgive me.”But the great shame in Manhood isn’t that Moore and other practitioners in this charcoal gray area of medicine lavish their customers with patience and empathy. It’s that few see the tender treatment for what it is: gender-affirming care. “That’s why this movie has a very light touch,” Lombroso says. “So many of these things are funny and self-evident, especially to smart viewers. It’s fun to have these tough conversations and not tell people exactly how to feel in every moment.”Manhood is now playing in select US cinemas with UK and Australia dates to be announcedExplore more on these topicsDocumentary filmsPlastic surgeryMen (Society)Men's healthMen (Life and style)Body imagefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: From Wicker to Zelda: Ocarina of Time: your complete entertainment guide to the week ahead | Culture | The Guardian
description: Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgård star in a new fantasy romance, and Nintendo’s revered 1998 classic gets a fresh coat of paint
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgård star in a new fantasy romance, and Nintendo’s revered 1998 classic gets a fresh coat of paint
Content: Wooden performance … Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgård in Wicker.View image in fullscreenWooden performance … Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgård in Wicker.Going out, staying inCultureFrom Wicker to Zelda: Ocarina of Time: your complete entertainment guide to the week aheadOlivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgård star in a new fantasy romance, and Nintendo’s revered 1998 classic gets a fresh coat of paintSat 31 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleContents1Going out: Cinema2Going out: Gigs3Going out: Art4Going out: Stage5Staying in: Streaming6Staying in: Games7Staying in: Albums8Staying in: Brain foodView image in fullscreenGoing out:CinemaWickerOut nowAnyone who has ever fantasised about having a husband made out of wicker (surely a universal dream) will want to get themselves along to this Olivia Colman romantasy about a loner fisher who does exactly that. With Alexander Skarsgård, Richard E Grant, Peter Dinklage and Elizabeth Debicki.NightbornOut nowSeidi Haarla gives a wonderfully unhinged performance as a woman convinced there is something wrong with her newborn baby: the hellish crying, her bleeding nipples … surely this child is a monster? All will be revealed in this tense but humorous supernatural drama, with Rupert Grint having fun as the sceptical new father.PrimetimeOut nowRobert Pattinson continues a recent hot streak with a characterful turn as Chris Hansen, the TV personality famous for fronting To Catch a Predator, the US hit that lured and publicly exposed men who were interested in having sex with teenagers. Directed by Lance Oppenheim (also on a hot streak with You Can See Everything).I Love BoostersOut nowShoplifting, teleportation, the consequences of sweatshop labour, designer fashion, workers’ rights and demons who suck out your soul while performing oral sex: here’s a comedy from Boots Riley that has it all. Keke Palmer, Naomi Ackie and Taylour Paige star as Bay Area shoplifters the Velvet Gang, with Demi Moore as a powerful designer.Catherine BrayGoing out:GigsView image in fullscreenSeeing red … The Avalanches.Photograph: Dean PodmorePitchfork music festival LondonVarious venues,2to 9 NovemberThe always divisive music website returns with another city festival lineup featuring the best in alternative soundscapes. Highlights include the Avalanches, Olof Dreijer, Jacob Alon and Keiyaa, plus Nigel Godrich’s new project Dragonflies, while the best band name goes to Psychedelic Porn Crumpets.Michael CraggPapa Roach1to 9 November; tour starts GlasgowTwenty-six years after their breakthrough with second album Infest, the perpetually angry nu-metallers are still going strong. Expect a heavy focus on that album – Last Resort is pretty undeniable in a live scenario – and follow-up Lovehatetragedy on this huge arena tour.MCGuildhall School’s Opera Double BillSilk Street theatre, London,2to 9 NovemberStudents on one of the country’s leading conservatoire opera courses perform two mid-century works: the UK premiere of Gian Carlo Menotti’s comic one-acter Amelia Al Ballo and Bernstein’s jazz-soaked modern classic Trouble in Tahiti. Expect high-energy professionalism and a chance to pick out the opera stars of the future.Flora WillsonFergus McCreadieThe Glasshouse, Sage Two, Gateshead,5 NovemberSince 2021, young pianist/composer Fergus McCreadie has grown in stature within the restless evolution of contemporary global jazz as a Mercury prize nominee, the traditional folk music of his Scottish homeland, and at the cutting edge of chamber music. The Glasshouse’s Innovators programme and Chamber Music Scotland showcase this adventurous wildlife-inspired co‑commission.John FordhamGoing out:ArtView image in fullscreenOn the fence … Neisser Yoel Gálvez Tabares.Photograph: James Clifford KentWinston Taylor Photo PortraitprizeNational Portrait Gallery, London,5 Novemberto 17 JanuaryThe biggest photographic portraiture prize in the country has rebranded – you might know it better as the Taylor Wessing – but is otherwise unchanged: expect the finest photography by established pros and amateurs alike, featuring work from James Clifford Kent’s long-term project Yuma, including his portrait of aspiring pentathlete Neisser Yoel Gálvez Tabares.Mad BloomsburyCharleston Firle, Lewes,4 Novemberto 11 AprilCoinciding with the centenary of Virginia Woolf’s essay On Being Ill, this show looks at how the Bloomsbury Group – the likes of Roger Fry, Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant – dealt with ideas of madness, disability and neurodiversity.Steve McQueen: ResistanceLeedsArtGallery,6 Novemberto 25 AprilDeeply moving documentation of how acts of resistance and rebellion have transformed the UK, all conceived by the brilliant Turner prize-winning artist and Oscar-winning director Steve McQueen.The Nue Black AestheticDesign Museum, London,6 Novemberto 8 AugustThis display of more than 100 objects celebrates the black creatives who are shaping the future of design in Britain, including Taiba Akhuetie, Ini Archibong and Tejumola Adenuga.Eddy FrankelGoing out:StageView image in fullscreenIt’s a scream … Jordan Brookes.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianJordan BrookesTouring to27 November; starts BristolIn 2019, the Surrey-raised standup expressed his long-held ambition to become “the existential Michael McIntyre”. In his excellent new show, The Part of You That’s Always Screaming, Brookes reaches those heights, with an unlikely combination of laugh-out-loud observational comedy and genuinely terrifying evocations of the abyss.Rachel AroestiPeanut Butter and BlueberriesLeeds Playhouse, to 7 NovemberAfter opening to strong reviews at Kiln theatre, Suhaiymah Manzoor-Khan’s thoughtful romcom transfers to Leeds. It’s about two university students and practising Muslims who move to London from the north, fall in love – but come up against harsh realities and rumbling racism.Miriam GillinsonHamlet Hail to the ThiefBarbicantheatre, London, to 23 JanuarySteven Hoggett and Christine Jones’s music- and movement-infused Hamlet lands in London. The backbone of the show is Radiohead’s 2003 album Hail to the Thief, which frontman Thom Yorke has stripped back, rewired and threaded through the show with electrifying intent.MGLuail: NōsThe Mac, Belfast,to 7 NovemberOnly formed two years ago, Luail is Ireland’s all-island national dance company, spanning Northern Ireland and the Republic. Their triple bill includes works by Belfast’s own Oona Doherty, Liz Roche and a classic from Akram Khan.Lyndsey Winshipskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenStaying in:StreamingView image in fullscreenSeeing double … Hudson Williams in Yaga.Photograph: Bell Media/SkyYagaSky Atlantic,31 October, 9pmHudson Williams swaps romance for folklore fantasy as he follows his star-making turn in Heated Rivalry by playing two characters – the missing scion of a wealthy family and his odd housemate – in Kat Sandler’s adaptation of her own play. Could a witchy professor be the key to it all?The Rise of the Rockstar ChefBBC Two/iPlayer,5 November, 9pmThe collective yearning for 2000s monoculture continues to be stoked with this documentary series about three of the decade’s rule-breaking, gamechanging chefs: Marco Pierre White, Heston Blumenthal and Gordon Ramsay (whose own production company is behind the show). Catnip for 00s nostalgists.The GreatestPrime Video,4 NovemberBoxing dramas are a Hollywood mainstay, but this year the genre is migrating to the small screen with the likes of Fightland, A Thousand Blows and this new Muhammad Ali biopic, whose first season chronicles the vertiginous early 1960s rise of the then Cassius Clay (Jaalen Best).Allies in ExileBBC Four/iPlayer,3 November, 10pmBBC Four’s Storyville strand has long brought the world’s best feature-length documentaries to television. Now briefer films will be showcased too, starting with this one following the arduous journey of two Syrian film-makers through the UK’s asylum system. An Unknown Substance, about the poisoning of a Russian politician, airs afterwards.RAStaying in:GamesView image in fullscreenMissing Link … The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.Photograph: NintendoThe Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of TimeSwitch 2; out5 NovemberThe only major game challenging GTA 6 this month is this lively, stylish remake of Nintendo’s 1998 adventure classic, in which series hero Link becomes a time traveller to save the land of Hyrule from evil warlock Ganondorf. A nostalgic treat for the ages.Wherethe Seeds FallPS5, Switch 2, PC; out5 NovemberAn intriguing action adventure which follows the human inhabitants of a vast tree as they set out to descend its branches and rediscover the land they were once forced to flee. Part mystical role-playing game, part climbing challenge.Keith StuartStaying in:AlbumsView image in fullscreenIt’ll come out in the wash … Ex:Re AKA Elena Tonra.Photograph: El HardwickEx:Re – Save AsOut nowWith her band Daughter currently between albums, Elena Tonra returns to her Ex:Re solo moniker via this second album of textural alt-rock. Songs such as Sleep creep along with a hint of menace, while opener Radio Station spins off into a trippy road trip anthem.DIIV – Zirp!Out nowAmerican alt-rock curios DIIV return with this AG Cook-produced fifth album. While steeped in their typically opaque, shoegazey textures, songs such as the pop-adjacent Kid and chunky lead single The Fountain dial up the melodies and frontman Zachary Cole Smith’s hushed vocals.Chloe Qisha – FantasizeOut nowAfter quitting a psychology degree for pop stardom, Malaysia-born, UK-based singer-songwriter Qisha found instant success with 2024’s sultry I Lied, I’m Sorry. She increases the sex chat on this debut album, specifically on gloriously overblown banger YDH, AKA young, dumb and horny.The Big Moon – ForeverOut nowLondon quartet the Big Moon return with a sunnier take on their brand of indie rock. Created as an imaginary utopia after a period of upheaval in frontwoman Juliette Jackson’s life, songs such as the buoyant Three Things and Fun offer sweet solace.MCStaying in:Brain foodView image in fullscreenProvocationsPodcastFor the numerically challenged, this new series hosted by Nihal Arthanayake is essential listening. Experts break down the big stories in finance, such as changes in lending policies and how technology can affect banking.Interior MotivesYouTubeOn the surface this video series looks like a flippant guessing game pairing pictures of domestic interiors with their owners, but it in fact uncovers fascinating truths about the ways our homes reveal our hidden selves.Concorde: The Untold StoryPBS America,2 November, 8.40pmEncompassing everything from engineering breakthroughs to espionage and political hand-wringing, this film on the race to build the first supersonic airliner between Europe, the Soviet Union and the US makes for surprisingly engaging viewing.Ammar KaliaExplore more on these topicsCultureGoing out, staying inDanceTheatreTelevisionArtGamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: From This City Is Ours to Macklemore’s Free Palestine tour: the week in rave reviews | Culture | The Guardian
description: The most fractious family in organised crime return while the US rapper embarks upon a series of benefit shows with some A-list guests. Here’s the pick of the week’s culture, taken from the Guardian’s best-rated reviews
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The most fractious family in organised crime return while the US rapper embarks upon a series of benefit shows with some A-list guests. Here’s the pick of the week’s culture, taken from the Guardian’s best-rated reviews
Content: Going gangbusters … James Nelson-Joyce as Michael Kavanagh in This City Is Ours.Photograph: BBCView image in fullscreenGoing gangbusters … James Nelson-Joyce as Michael Kavanagh in This City Is Ours.Photograph: BBCThe week in reviewsCultureFrom This City Is Ours to Macklemore’s Free Palestine tour: the week in rave reviewsThe most fractious family in organised crime return while the US rapper embarks upon a series of benefit shows with some A-list guests. Here’s the pick of the week’s culture, taken from the Guardian’s best-rated reviewsSat 31 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTVIf you only watch one, make it …Escaping Idi AminBBC iPlayer; available nowSummed up in a sentenceFour people share their shocking testimonies of what happened when the dictator gave Asians 90 days to leave Uganda.What our reviewer said“There is a happy ending, of sorts. Bharti, Paresh, Harminder and Maz never stopped missing the country they were born in, but they made a new home in Britain, and they made Britain better: it would be hard, for example, to calculate the size of the debt we owe Bharti for her 40 years as a social worker safeguarding children in care. Every minute of Escaping Idi Amin contains an urgent lesson to learn.”Jack SealeRead the full reviewPick of the restThis City Is OursBBC iPlayer; available nowSummed up in a sentenceJames Nelson-Joyce returns in this terrifically acted, high-stakes crime drama in Liverpool – and it’s as lovable as it is bloody.What our reviewer said“We can expect more of the following: convoluted drug deals conducted over congealing ragu; shouting; tiny-skulled henchmen with chests of astonishing bulbosity, as if someone had squeezed their legs like tubes of toothpaste and all the meat had been forced up to their armpits; beards.”Sarah DempsterRead the full reviewThe One About Matthew PerryNetflix; available nowSummed up in a sentenceThe star’s friends and family celebrate his life – and give respectful insight into his troubles as well as his career triumphs.What our reviewer said“It remains at heart a simple, sad story. But this unexpectedly candid, thoughtful, genuinely intimate film gives it nuance and depth, and a voice to wider sorrows – including what a shame it was that Perry could not enjoy his talent or appreciate the joy it gave as fully as his audiences always did.”Lucy ManganRead the full reviewFurther readingThe hidden life of Matthew Perry: ‘He would say: I need to stop and get help’You may have missed …LupinNetflix; available nowView image in fullscreenFormidable foe … Omar Sy in Lupin.Photograph: Emmanuel Guimier/NetflixSummed up in a sentenceThe French super-thief returns for a fourth series; the budget is bigger, the stakes are higher and there are lots of Houdini-style twists and thrills to be had.What our reviewer said“Omar Sy, whose performance is magnetic as always, has graduated to co-showrunner and wants to lean harder into the show’s “superhero”-like qualities. These include tech and set pieces which undoubtedly add a sprinkling of Marvel.”Micha Frazer-CarrollRead the full reviewFurther readingLupin’s Omar Sy: ‘We wanted to show what the French are capable of’FilmIf you only watch one, make it …A Gentle MonsterIn cinemas nowView image in fullscreenMonster bunch … Léa Seydoux and Jella Haase.Photograph: Frédéric Batier/Netflix/APSummed up in a sentenceDisquieting drama with Léa Seydoux as a wife and mother whose life unravels when police arrive to investigate her husband.What our reviewer said“This is a bleak, pessimistic film with two excellent lead performances.”Peter BradshawRead the full reviewPick of the restI Love BoostersIn cinemas nowSummed up in a sentenceSupercool outlaw women go shoplifting in Boots Riley’s frantic caper in which Demi Moore’s haute-couture maven attracts the attention of a gang of Robin Hood style clothes robbers.What our reviewer said“An entertaining, if very exhausting fantasy-caper about the fashion biz, a madcap mile-a-minute melee of unadulterated ker-aziness. You might need a couple of ibuprofen and a lie down afterwards.”Peter BradshawRead the full reviewFurther readingBoots Riley: ‘Theft is not outside of capitalism, it’s what it was built on’WickerIn cinemas nowView image in fullscreenStraw man … Alexander Skarsgård with Olivia Colman in Wicker.Photograph: Black Bear/PASummed up in a sentenceIntriguing folk-horror romance with Olivia Colman as a depressed and bullied fisher who gets the answer to her dreams: an Alexander Skarsgård made of wicker.What our reviewer said“It occupies a strange and intriguing Venn-diagram overlap between macabre horror and sentimentality. Yet devotees of bucolic British screen-scariness will note that it is, after all, about a wicker man.”Peter BradshawRead the full reviewFurther reading‘I saw the script and went: oooh!’ Olivia Colman and Alexander Skårsgard on their steamy folk-horror movie WickerPeter Asher: Everywhere ManIn cinemas nowSummed up in a sentenceBackstory of modest music industry veteran Asher who started out as one half of pop duo Peter and Gordon, and went on to produce acts such as James Taylor and Linda Ronstadt.What our reviewer said“Asher by any standards carved an amazing path through it all, making the absolute most of being in the right place at the right time.”Andrew PulverRead the full reviewThe DevilsIn cinemas nowSummed up in a sentenceKen Russell’s 1971 possessed-nuns tale stars Oliver Reed and Vanessa Redgrave giving the performances of their lives in a film that highlights the violence of power.What our reviewer said“It comes from an era when movies, playing in high-street cinemas, still had the power to shock, to position that shock in the polite cultural mainstream and to compel serious discussion about whether that shock – or, conversely, a ban – was justified.”Peter BradshawRead the full reviewBooksIf you only read one, make it …View image in fullscreenOn Another Planet They Can Save Me by Lieke MarsmanReviewed by Edward PosnettSummed up in a sentenceThe extraordinary posthumous memoir of a Dutch poet.What our reviewer said“Marsman’s language is so beautiful, and her textual references so original: she cites Leopardi, Pasolini, Alanis Morissette, Robert Musil, Spinoza, Euripides, Wittgenstein and William James.”Read the full reviewPick of the restView image in fullscreenGilgamesh: A New Verse Translation by Simon ArmitageReviewed by Philip TerrySummed up in a sentenceThe poet laureate takes on the ancient Mesopotamian epic about the adventures of a demigod king.What our reviewer said“Armitage’s tactile, visceral version is a tour de force, combining careful scholarship with poetic verve and deft linguistic meldings.”Read the full reviewView image in fullscreenThe Mystery of What Befell in the Ditch by Thure Erik Lund, translated by David M SmithReviewed by Sukhdev SandhuSummed up in a sentenceLong thought untranslatable, a portrait of a breakdown by the man Karl Ove Knausgård considers Norway’s best living writer.What our
