title: Manchester United’s capitulation at Chelsea paints picture of a club that barely exists | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: Michael Carrick is now a little more pre-doomed, pre-sacked, but is miles away from being the actual story
Author: Barney Ronay
Headline: Michael Carrick is now a little more pre-doomed, pre-sacked, but is miles away from being the actual story
Content: This is another staging point in the progress of the Manchester United ghost ship.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThis is another staging point in the progress of the Manchester United ghost ship.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianManchester UnitedAnalysisManchester United’s capitulation at Chelsea paints picture of a club that barely existsBarney Ronayat Stamford BridgeMichael Carrick is now a little more pre-doomed, pre-sacked, but is miles away from being the actual storySat 31 Oct 2026 13.54 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 18.26 EDTShareOn and on and on. And then on just a little bit more it would seem. Manchester United: always crashing in the same Carrick.The obvious question afterthis 2-0 defeat to Chelseais how much longer United will continue to lose games under the current manager, as opposed to losing games under the next one. But it is also a mark of the dysfunction of this club, its ambient levels of sadness, that this matters so little.Manchester United crisis deepens with Chelsea defeat and Martínez red cardRead moreHere we have another staging point in the progress of the Manchester United ghost ship, where even sacking a manager carries almost zero tension, where it feels like something that has basically already happened. This is a club that can make you into a relic of the past even while you’re still walking around taking training and drawing a salary.Michael Carrick is miles away from being the actual story here. For the record, the United manager is now a little more pre-doomed, pre-sacked, pretty much already lounging around in one of those holiday adverts with Tony Pulis joshing about what’s for lunch. This defeat means United haven’t won a game since early September. At full time only the fact that Coventry and Sunderland would be playing each other later in the afternoon ruled out the prospect of an end-of-day bottom place.Chuck ina Carabao Cup exitand 20th spot in the Champions League mega-table. Troubled times, then, for the latest semi-permanent navy wool suit in the United dugout. Something will now happen, most likely Carrick’s removal once the appropriate replacement is lined up. What happened here was almost by the by. Although it still provided some pretty vivid evidence of where this club is.If there was a key moment, it arrived with 48 minutes gone and the score still 0-0. At which point Morgan Rogers scored a goal that captured entirely what Manchester United is. In real time, this felt like one of those football moments, where the metaphor, the symbolism is almost too much, the nudge in the ribs a little too hard.View image in fullscreenIt is not Michael Carrick’s fault he is not cut out for this level.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianRogers took the ball on the edge of the centre circle and just kept running in a straight line through sudden empty spaces where there should have been a thing called Manchester United. Instead he found an anti-United, a non-United. Manchester United as an absence. So much analysis of this club evolves around what is it for, where should it turn, what can it be? Maybe it’s not really anything at all.We do remember Manchester United. It has a cultural memory, a set of shapes and colours, a gripping centre. Or does it? There was once a dream that was Manchester United. You could whisper its name. Anything more than a whisper and it would vanish. So Rogers just kept running in a straight line, moving fast now, finding no resistance, nothing of substance, fibre, no flesh, no will in front of him, like opening up the curtains and watching the shadows disappear.Michael Carrick insists he will still be in charge of Manchester United against RomaRead moreHow many times has this happened at this level, that a player is able to take the ball and run 40 yards through a packed opposition half without having to dribble, beat a player or even swerve around some tangible object?This is not to diminish Rogers’s skill and drive. The finish was really nice, a little dink as Senne Lammens came out and made a strange shape, as confused as anyone else by the sudden appearance of a living, moving, actual human in front of him.Teams are often described as having been found out, their patterns solved and learned. It turns out this is the way to score against Manchester United. Just run straight through the middle of them.Before long it was time for Lisandro Martínez to get sent off, again playing football that wasn’t really there.Chelseatook a corner from the right. At which point Martínez rammed his arm into Wesley Fofana’s neck with the ball miles away. Maybe Martínez just wanted to touch another human being. Sometimes you just need to feel something.View image in fullscreenMaybe Lisandro Martínez just wanted to touch another human being for his sending off.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianCole Palmer buried the penalty to make the score 2-0, with United a man down and not existing, just a little bit more. And OK, OK, you’re still thinking about the good news, aren’t you? Well, presumably Sir Jim Ratcliffe will see the material gain here, the chance to save on hotel costs with another nonexistent team. No, we don’t need any rooms. We are non-corporeal.On a more positive note, at least the players are annoyed. Really. It has been seen as a sign of dysfunction, the ravens leaving the tower, that United’s senior players have begun to speak in public. But wouldn’t it be weird if they didn’t? What is the correct human response to this state of complete, top-down lack of care, of managed disintegration?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe first half was lively enough. Bruno Fernandeswas back in the Unitedstarting XI on a lovely crisp October morning, the sun sharp but soft, the grass a deep lime green. It is said that United lack leaders. But what is a leader? Someone who shows you how to win, makes winning more likely, walks you right to the door. Well, good luck with that around here. The sub-Saharan desert also lacks grass. This isn’t really the fault of grass.And so Manchester United started with one bloke who thinks the hierarchy has betrayed the club and another who thinks the manager is tactically poor. The thing is, they’re both right. Fernandes in particular broke the code,undermining his manager, talking tactics when you are housefly playing like a performatively unhappy jack russell.But it is hard to blame the players too much for losing the run of themselves a little. This is a club that takes a bite out of everyone, that makes everything wrong, a club that spends and spends and still seems short, that is somehow ludicrously profitable, but also ludicrously in debt, where to be a supporter is to be left always feeling short-changed, owed so much more.By the end the game had basically become a shooting practice session for Chelsea, who were good, even if they were playing a team that didn’t exist. The most significant element was the performance of Estevão Willian, who tortured Diogo Dalot on the right flank. When Estevão came off the home crowd stood on all sides. He is very obviously going to be a proper player.View image in fullscreenIt is hard to blame the players too much for losing the run of themselves a little with the club taking a bite out of everyone.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianThe last knockings were accompanied by the familiar shots on the big screen of Omar Berrada and Jason Wilcox looking doomed and sombre, in a way that was arguably the most sustained United performance of the afternoon. You try looking sombre for the cameras for 90 minutes. It is at the very least a sign of some excellent media training (no, Jason, you look wistful, I need urgently alarmed).These people will now pronounce on Michael Carrick, who they hired knowing he was Michael Carrick. But who shall pronounce on them? And will it make any difference, unless someone pronounces on the people who pronounce on the people who pronounce on every single area of interim mediocrity installed at this giant ATM of a football club. Root out the problem. Well, we can do that. But we’re going to need new roots, bark, branches, leaves.When it comes to Carrick, everybody knows United are just waiting, finger hovering over the gunge tank. Alternatives are being lined up, terms thrashed out. There is an international break soon. Funny, isn’t it? An organisation of squawking, howling incompetence. But the one place you feel suddenly in the hands of the experts, safe hands, is this part. Stand back, let the experts in. Masters of the mid-season sacking. Seen it, done it. We know this world.Carrick has played his part well through all this and said all the right things. He is what he is: a coach who is not at the peak of his profession, who is engaged in weekly micro-battles with people who are. It’s not his fault he’s not cut out for this level. He didn’t hire Michael Carrick.As for the rest of this thing, the ghost players, the latest pressed men and padded overcoats in the seats of power; they continue to perform to their own level too, at an organisation that has by now fully embraced mediocrity and misdirection as a business plan.Explore more on these topicsManchester UnitedMichael CarrickChelseaanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Zion Suzuki horror own goal haunts Aston Villa to hand Fulham a point | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Zion Suzuki’s second-half own goal gave Fulham an equaliser in their 1-1 draw at Aston Villa to cancel out Nicolas Jackson’s opener
Author: Peter Lansley
Headline: Zion Suzuki’s second-half own goal gave Fulham an equaliser in their 1-1 draw at Aston Villa to cancel out Nicolas Jackson’s opener
Content: Zion Suzuki carries the ball over his own line to hand Fulham their equalising goal.Photograph: Andrew Boyers/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenZion Suzuki carries the ball over his own line to hand Fulham their equalising goal.Photograph: Andrew Boyers/Action Images/ReutersPremier LeagueZion Suzuki horror own goal haunts Aston Villa to hand Fulham a pointPeter Lansleyat Villa ParkSat 31 Oct 2026 18.15 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 19.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFulham helped cement Jamie Carragher’s argument thatAston Villawill never be Manchester United. No, they know how to grind out a point on a bad day and can go to Barcelona on Tuesday with some confidence.Villa’s goalkeeper Zion Suzuki dropped Alex Iwobi’s corner over his own goalline to deny Unai Emery’s team a fifth win in six games after Nicolas Jackson’s eighth goal of the season had promised to lift a resurgent Villa back into the top third of thePremier League. Not even John McGinn’s missed penalty had looked set to deny them as they took control in the first period.Julio Enciso strikes again to earn Ipswich a point against HullRead moreBut while Villa were made to look below par by aFulhamside making it seven points from the last nine, the home supporters sang long and loud to make their manager know how much he is appreciated.The Holte End had not waited long to voice their verdict on the spat betweenthe former England internationaland the Villa chair.Carragher had admitted that his words were “clumsy and wrong” after telling Villa fans “to shut the fuck up” as they reacted angrily to his claims that Emery should want to manage Manchester United if Michael Carrick were to be sacked after their long winless run. It seemed like a storm in a teacup to many until Nassef Sawiris issued a statement promising to initiate legal action. “As custodians of this great club, we cannot stand still while the F word is directed at Villa fans,” Sawiris said.Notwithstanding this disappointing draw, it is beyond question that Emery has done an admirable job at Villa. Even after losing another tranche of top talent, with Ollie Watkins, Morgan Rogers and Emi Martínez heading up the exits last summer afterwinning the Europa League, the former Arsenal and PSG manager has resurrected the club’s fortunes yet again. They start seasons slowly – winning only two of their last 12 league games in August and September – but once he has cast his spell and integrated the new signings, Villa tend to get going; they had won eight of their previous 10 league games in October and November.View image in fullscreenZion Suzuki fumbles the ball into the net to gift Fulham their goal.Photograph: Manjit Narotra/ProSports/ShutterstockIt must be galling to qualify for the Champions League twice in three years and yet still have your best talents lured away. So the idea that United could, in Carragher’s eyes, come and click their fingers and expect Emery to be unable to resist their faded grandeur evidently stuck in the throats of Villa fans and chair alike.Fulham’s second-half showing, in particular, merited a draw that followed their recent league wins over Hull and Coventry and kept them two points above the relegation zone in Álvaro Arbeloa’s first autumn in charge. Emery would never countenance it but perhaps Villa’s ultimate glamour trip, to Barcelona, on Tuesday before next Sunday’s visit to Old Trafford, of all places, overshadowed this game.McGinn spurned his first penalty for the club (excluding shootouts), awarded after Sander Berge was belatedly adjudged to have handled Leon Goretzka’s header, when he thundered his spot-kick against the crossbar.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenNicolas Jackson opens the scoring for Aston Villa in the first half.Photograph: Joe Giddens/PABut while Fulham had plenty of the ball, Villa appeared content to threaten on the counterattack. Indeed, they took the lead in the 39th minute after Jackson was sent running down the inside-left channel by a perfect through ball from Johan Manzambi. The £65m striker weaved into the penalty area past Timothy Castagne and David Affengruber before slotting in his fifth goal in five Premier League games.Fulham were much more dominant in the second half. “They were more aggressive than us in the first half,” Arbeloa admitted. “I told my players I know we are a team that wants to control the game through the ball. But this is the Premier League. If you want to win a game, you need to fight for every ball.” When Castagne headed on Alex Iwobi’s corner, both Gonzalo García and Shea Charles got a touch on the ball before it spooned up on to the roof of the net. Villa were riding their luck.Fulham’s dominance paid off, however, in the most unexpected fashion midway through the second half. Suzuki, who has been lauded for his early-season form, had just saved a header from Iwobi when, from the Nigerian’s ensuing corner, under no pressure, he inexplicably dropped the ball just over the line. “It’s part of football,” Emery said. “I make mistakes as coach. The players are making every match mistakes … when it’s the keeper, those mistakes are more in focus. I prefer to speak about the saves he did today.”Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueAston VillaFulhammatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Lewis Hamilton storms to his first Ferrari pole at F1 Mexican GP with Antonelli fourth | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: Lewis Hamilton took pole position at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez, his first for Ferrari, while Kimi Antonelli is well placed as he nears title confirmation
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Lewis Hamilton took pole position at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez, his first for Ferrari, while Kimi Antonelli is well placed as he nears title confirmation
Content: Lewis Hamilton competes during qualifying at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez.Photograph: Simon Galloway/LAT ImagesView image in fullscreenLewis Hamilton competes during qualifying at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez.Photograph: Simon Galloway/LAT ImagesFormula One 2026Lewis Hamilton storms to his first Ferrari pole at F1 Mexican GP with Antonelli fourthGeorge Russell second on grid after qualifyingAntonelli well placed as he nears title confirmationGiles Richardsat the Autódromo Hermanos RodríguezSat 31 Oct 2026 19.03 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 20.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEven as Formula One’s young gunKimi Antonelliremains on course to claim his first world championship on Sunday it was the veteran, seven-time champion Lewis Hamilton who gave a salutary reminder that there is very much fight left in the old dog yet as he claimed a spectacular pole position for the Mexico City Grand Prix.Hamilton delivered a superb lap for Ferrari to secure his first pole for the team and just beat Mercedes’ George Russell into second. World championin waiting Antonelli was in fourth placebut remains in position to close out the title on Sunday, although Hamilton and Russell, who must win the race to have any hope of keeping the fight alive, have at least locked out the front row.Mexican Grand Prix qualifying: Lewis Hamilton takes pole – liveRead moreIt was clearly a hugely emotional moment for Hamilton at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez to finally nail the top spot forFerrariin his second season with the team, with the 41-year-old’s 105th pole also his first since 2023.“Thank you so much, that’s been such a long time coming,” he said. “That feels good. I’m lost for words. My first pole with Ferrari. 105 poles, I like that number.“Where there’s a will, there’s a way. It’s all in the mind. For sure, you might feel aches and pains, luckily I don’t, I do all those different things to keep myself young and fit. But I love what I do, and love is not gone.”The title is all but in Antonelli’s hands but the day belonged assuredly to Hamilton who brought the crowd to their feet and earned a rapturous reception with an exemplary lap against very tough competition. His advantage over Russell was ultimately just nine-thousandths of a second.It is an extraordinary feat for Hamilton, coming after hisdebut win for Ferrari in Barcelonaand having endured a very difficult opening season with the team, showing that he has lost none of his edge when he has the right machinery beneath him.View image in fullscreenLewis Hamilton enjoys the acclaim after taking pole in Mexico.Photograph: DPPI/ShutterstockHis sheer joy in the moment was unsurprising given it had been such a long wait for the British driver. The pole is Hamilton’s first since the Hungarian GP in 2023 and Ferrari’s first since Budapest last year. It is only his second in Mexico, having last taken the top spot a decade ago in 2016.He will, of course, be looking for the win but that alone would not be enough to deny Antonelli the crown. The Italian is 123 points ahead of Russell and 124 in front of Hamilton. If he is 100 ahead after the Mexican GP he will take the title. Russell or Hamilton have to win the race to stay in the fight but even should one of them do so, Antonelli will still be champion if he finishes in ninth place or higher.Anything less than a win for Russell or Hamilton and Antonelli would still be champion even if he failed to finish. Having secured fourth place on the grid, just staying out of trouble would surely be enough for the Italian. If he seals it on Sunday he will become F1’s youngest world champion at just 20 years old and the first Italian to claim the crown since Alberto Ascari in 1953.View image in fullscreenKimi Antonelli only needs to finish ninth to clinch the title.Photograph: Florent Gooden/DPPI/ShutterstockCharles Leclerc was third for Ferrari and Max Verstappen in fourth on track but has a one-place grid penalty for a clash with Liam Lawson in practice on Friday. The New Zealander who finished in eighth also has a one-place penalty. Lando Norris was in sixth for McLaren.For the opening runs in Q3 it was close at the front of the field with no driver holding a clear advantage. The Ferraris set the pace on the opening salvoes, with Leclerc setting a very strong time of 1min 16.647sec. The two Mercedes could not match him, with Antonelli having to really work the car and managing only seventh on his opening run but Norris came close, one-tenth back. Verstappen, however, was showing great pace and came within four-hundredths of a second of Leclerc.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFor the final laps Russell found his best form of the weekend to take the top spot only for Hamilton to pip him. Leclerc could not better his teammate, while Antonelli followed them through – he improved but could not match the leaders. Verstappen had a minor lockup in the final sector, costing him his shot and with it the British driver had sealed the place.Oscar Piastri was knocked out unusually early for McLaren. Failing to make it out of Q2, he finished in 13th complaining of a lack of rear grip.Esteban Ocon, meanwhile, has denied reports of a violent altercation with his team after the Frenchman was dropped by Haas from competing in the race weekend. Haas made the shock announcement on Saturday morning that Ocon had been replaced for the rest of the weekend by Ryo Hirakawa, but offered no explanation as to why. The 32-year-old Japanese driver, who has won two World Endurance Championships and the Le Mans 24 Hours, will make his F1 race debut on Sunday.View image in fullscreenHaas staff remove the name and number of Esteban Ocon from the garage after he was dropped from competing in the race weekend.Photograph: Bryn Lennon/Formula 1/Getty ImagesOcon is set to be replaced next season by the Ferrari junior Rafael Câmara and his sudden removal from competition in Mexico suggests relations between him and the team have broken down. He had an angry exchange with his race engineer Laura Müller during FP2 on Friday, after which he returned to the Haas garage without removing his helmet.Reports followed that a disagreement between Ocon and team staff had surfaced. While Ocon admits the disagreement, he rubbished suggestions that the exchange of views turned physical.“Following the recent decision from Haas F1 Team confirming that I will not be participating in this weekend’s Mexico City Grand Prix, I wish to formally address some media reports and speculation surrounding the situation,” a statement from Ocon read. “Last night, a difference in viewpoints led to a discussion with the parties involved. Whilst I acknowledge that this took place, I categorically reject any reports or allegations suggesting that any form of physical violence was used to resolve any differences of any nature.“I strongly condemn violence in all its forms and firmly believe that disagreements should always be handled with professionalism, respect, and mutual understanding. I kindly ask that speculation be avoided while the matter is being addressed. Further updates will be communicated in due course.”Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Lewis HamiltonFormula OneKimi AntonelliFerrariMercedes GPMotor sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Mitchell injury blow adds to England’s woes as Northampton sink Gloucester | Prem Rugby | The Guardian
description: Northampton beat Gloucester 28-14 but Alex Mitchell’s injury makes him a doubt for England’s clash with Australia
Author: Gerard Meagher
Headline: Northampton beat Gloucester 28-14 but Alex Mitchell’s injury makes him a doubt for England’s clash with Australia
Content: George Hendy dives through the tackle of George Barton to score Northampton’s third try against Gloucester.Photograph: David Rogers/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGeorge Hendy dives through the tackle of George Barton to score Northampton’s third try against Gloucester.Photograph: David Rogers/Getty ImagesPrem RugbyMitchell injury blow adds to England’s woes as Northampton sink GloucesterNorthampton 28-14 GloucesterAlex Mitchell limps off with suspected hamstring pullGerard Meagherat DPD Stadium at Franklin's GardensSat 31 Oct 2026 16.05 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 17.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEngland’s injury headaches are mounting before next Sunday’s autumn opener against Australia with the scrum-half Alex Mitchell a major doubt after limping out of Northampton’s hard-fought victory over Gloucester with another hamstring problem.Searle makes difference as Leicester battle to Prem top spot at BristolRead moreIt is to the credit of Northampton that they weathered that setback, withheld Gloucester’s early onslaught to score 28 unanswered points and see off the early-season pace-setters. Northampton’s last league outing here ended with119 points scoredbut this was a victory founded on their defensive resilience with Tom Pearson, back in the England picture this autumn, outstanding throughout.If Pearson’s performance will have pleased Borthwick, Mitchell’s withdrawal will not. He is already sweating on the fitness of the Northampton fly-half Fin Smith, who sat in the stands with an injured calf here, and now has concerns over his half-back partner Mitchell. England begin a crucial autumn series against the Wallabies and Borthwick now has significant concerns in two key positions. Mitchell’s injury is all the more of a worry with Archie McParland, his Northampton team-mate and fellow scrum-half, omitted from the matchday squad againstGloucesterdue to a calf injury sustained earlier in the week at England’s training camp.It would be rough on Mitchell should he miss out considering it is a fourth hamstring injury of the year and his body language when leaving the field does not bode well. He suffered similar injuries during the Six Nations, at an England camp in May – recovering to take his place in the Northampton squad for the Prem final win over Exeter – and during the summer Test against Fiji. Jack van Poortvliet was England’s starting scrum-half for the summer given Mitchell’s lack of game time but when fit and firing the Northampton Saint is England’s first-choice No 9.Quick GuidePremiership roundup: Caluori sparks Saracens' revivalShowJoe Shaw praisedSaracens’ character as they saw off a highly competitive and scrappingNewcastleside at the StoneX Stadium. The head coach saw his team overturn a 17-7 half-time deficit to run out 39-31 bonus-point winners for their third Prem victory of the season and move up to third.Noah Caluori came on after the break to lift what had been a lacklustre home performance by racing over for a score as Sarries ran in five second-half tries to finally get the better of visitors who had threatened an upset.Shaw said: “It’s probably best to forget about that first half because it wasn’t a pretty watch and was unexpected … Fortunately, the guys improved a lot with their execution after the break and we created several fine tries.”Johann van Graan was upbeat after seeingBathreturned to winning ways with a comfortable 36-28 bonus-point victory overSaleat the Rec. After three consecutive defeats, the home side were greatly improved, playing with far more speed and efficiency than in recent weeks to entertain the sell-out crowd with a number of well-created tries. Joe Cokanasiga (pictured) scored two of them, Henry Arundell, Tom de Glanville and Louie Hennessey the others, with Finn Russell converting four and adding a penalty.Nathan Jibulu, Tom O’Flaherty, Luke Cowan-Dickie and Elia Canakaivata scored Sale’s tries, all of which George Ford converted.Van Graan, Bath's director of rugby, said: “Last week we didn’t take our opportunities, but we were much more clinical today. We had a good balance to our game, with Finn expertly using the space out wide against a big physical side. We were really positive throughout and closed the game out well."Harlequins' head coach, Jason Gilmore, said a big improvement in his side’s discipline paved the way for their 31-28 victory atExeter. Quins led 14-0 after 11 minutes but then allowed the Chiefs back into the contest by giving away nine penalties and it was 14-14 at the break.Gilmore said: “We went eight or nine penalties on the bounce against us, which was poor, and a yellow card, and we gave Exeter good field position … I said to the boys at half-time: 'If we can stop giving penalties away and get our hands back on the ball, we will be all right,' and I don’t think we gave away a penalty again until the last minute of the game.”Press AssociationPhotograph: Simon King/Shutterstock EditorialWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.“Fin and Archie are both calf, Fin probably not as bad as Archie but it remains to be seen,” said Northampton’s director of rugby, Phil Dowson. “Mitchell has hurt his hamstring but I don’t know how bad. We have to be super careful with Alex and he knows his own body.”This was always likely to be an anxious watch for Borthwick given 10 of the players on show were included in England’s mini-training camp earlier in the week. If he finds himself without both Northampton scrum-halves for the Wallabies Test, Ben Spencer would come into the frame with Harry Randall another option. Borthwick also has problems at hooker with Theo Dan going off early in Saracens’ win over Newcastle amid fitness concerns over Bath youngster Kepu Tuipulotu. Guy Pepper and Benhard van Rensburg have already been ruled out of England’s autumn campaign.View image in fullscreenAlex Mitchell looks dejected as he is replaced after sustaining an injury.Photograph: David Rogers/Getty ImagesMitchell’s withdrawal here came midway through the first half after he was caught by aGloucesterchaser when covering back to gather a loose ball. Northampton were under the pump by this stage – George Skivington’s side beginning in a manner which befitted their lofty league position.They struck first with a well-worked move after eight minutes. Gloucester’s driving maul has been a lethal weapon this season but while Northampton withstood the drive, they had no answer to the visitors’ quick hands. The captain Seb Atkinson, who this week signed a new contract until 2029, put the excellent George Barton through a gap and he offloaded to Max Llewellyn to score. Will Joseph was next over, showing his acceleration to dash under the posts after a clever pass out the back by Atkinson, who impressed throughout. The form of those two is at least solace for Borthwick, all the more so because Atkinson has just recovered from a knee problem.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionQuick GuideNorthampton 28-14 Gloucester: teams and scorerShowNorthamptonPater; Sleightholme (Hutchinson 59), Freeman, Dingwall (capt), Hendy; Belleau, Mitchell (Weimann 20); Iyogun (Fischetti 56), Langdon (smith 56), Kundiona (Neculai 56), Coles (Lockett 78), Prowse (Van der Mescht 64), Kemeny, Pearson (Pollock 68), ChickTriesPearson, Langdon, Hendy, HutchinsonConsBelleau 4GloucesterR Barton; Joseph, Llewellyn, S Atkinson (capt), W Knight (Redshaw 69); C Atkinson, Englefield (Robson 64); Rapava Ruskin (Bleuler 53), Blake (Lake 21), Fasogbon (C Knight 53), Kleyn (Trenholm 64), Clark, Thomas, Gwynne (Morgan 53), Clement (Ludlow 76)TriesLlewellyn, JosephConsBarton 2RefereeSara CoxWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Northampton had not really got going but managed to find parity at the half-time interval. Both tries came from driving mauls, finished by Pearson and Curtis Langdon. Not exactly the type of scores for which Saints are associated but evidently their canny group of coaches had done their homework.Midway through the second half Northampton turned down a straightforward penalty at goal to kick to the corner. It felt a risk given the scrappy nature of this contest but it ultimately paid off with George Hendy eventually splashing over on the left. With a spring in their step, Saints chalked up the bonus-point score after some nifty footwork from the replacement Rory Hutchinson to move into third in the table, sitting pretty as the league now takes a break until December.Explore more on these topicsPrem RugbyNorthamptonGloucesterRugby unionmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Enzo Maresca rues ‘silly’ errors after Manchester City defeat against Brighton | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: Enzo Maresca said ‘silly goals’ and individual errors are costing Manchester City after their home defeat against Brighton
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: Enzo Maresca said ‘silly goals’ and individual errors are costing Manchester City after their home defeat against Brighton
Content: Enzo Maresca’s team have lost their last two league matches.Photograph: Matt McNulty/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEnzo Maresca’s team have lost their last two league matches.Photograph: Matt McNulty/Getty ImagesManchester CityEnzo Maresca rues ‘silly’ errors after Manchester City defeat against BrightonMatheus Nunes mistake lets in Yasin Ayari for winnerMaresca: ‘We are conceding silly goals that we can avoid’Jamie Jacksonat the Etihad StadiumSat 31 Oct 2026 14.38 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 15.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEnzo Maresca said “silly goals” and individual errors are costing Manchester City after Matheus Nunes’ mistake allowed Yasin Ayari to scoreBrighton’s winner in Saturday’s 1-0 victoryhere. Ayari’s strike was made possible after Nunes, City’s right-back, missed Diego Gómez’s cross from the right, so the ball could come back across goal via Maxim De Cuyper.The2-1 loss at Aston Villacame from Gianluigi Donnarumma allowing Nicolas Jackson’s long-range winner to squeeze under his body.Ayari on target as Brighton stun Manchester City to close gap on leadersRead more“Sometimes it happens,” said Maresca. “Unfortunately, it is happening for our players, but it is part of football, it happens many times against us, we need to analyse, understand what we can do better and try to move on.“We are the second team in terms of scoring in the Premier League, but we are conceding silly goals that we can avoid and hopefully we can avoid in the next game.“It is a very similar feeling we had after the Aston Villa game – unfortunately we created enough to get some points but we didn’t score. At the moment it is like this. We did enough to deserve something. We need to move on and try to win games. For sure we are not happy.”While Maresca said he had not seen the free-kick awarded against Elliot Anderson to decide if this was fair, Brighton’s victory takes them to 19 points, two behind City, who are the leaders before Arsenal’s trip to Liverpool on Sunday.Fabian Hürzeler was delighted his players had changed the feeling ofWednesday’s Carabao Cup penalty shootout lossto City. “Every morning you can wake up and decide if you’re disappointed by something you cannot change or set the tone,” he said. “Stand up and have the belief that you’ll have a different feeling. It was brutal [the cup defeat]. We promised ourselves that we won’t have the same feeling.“We want to be satisfied. We created energy, positivity, the next day. You need this. We saw Saturday as an opportunity to come back stronger. This was the approach and how the players stuck together and built the connection through the four days is really impressive.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHürzeler was asked what is possible for Brighton this season. “The only thing we’re focused on is that we are in a big process, a process of analysing the game. title: Canelo Álvarez wins back world title as Houthi attacks cast shadow over Riyadh | Boxing | The Guardian
description: Canelo Álvarez regained the WBC super-middleweight title with a unanimous-decision win over Christian Mbilli in Riyadh despite regional security concerns
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Canelo Álvarez regained the WBC super-middleweight title with a unanimous-decision win over Christian Mbilli in Riyadh despite regional security concerns
Content: Canelo Álvarez (right) exchanges punches with Christian Mbilli during their WBC super-middleweight title fight in Riyadh early on Sunday.Photograph: Fayez Nureldine/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCanelo Álvarez (right) exchanges punches with Christian Mbilli during their WBC super-middleweight title fight in Riyadh early on Sunday.Photograph: Fayez Nureldine/AFP/Getty ImagesBoxingCanelo Álvarez wins back world title as Houthi attacks cast shadow over RiyadhMexican star wins unanimous decision over MbilliÁlvarez, 36, regains WBC title after Crawford defeatRead Bryan Armen Graham’s round-by-round reportGuardian sportand agenciesSat 31 Oct 2026 19.26 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 19.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMexico’s Saúl “Canelo” Álvarez reclaimed the WBC super-middleweight title with a unanimous-decision victory over the previously unbeaten Christian Mbilli in Riyadh on Saturday night.The fight went ahead at Kingdom Arena despite a week of heightened security concerns in the Saudi capital, where the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted missiles and drones launched by Iran-aligned Houthi forces. Several events in the kingdom were cancelled or postponed, including the Six Kings Slam tennis exhibition.Canelo Álvarez defeats Christian Mbilli for WBC super-middleweight championship – live reactionRead moreÁlvarez, 36, fighting for the first time in more than a year, relied on his trademark counter-punching and precise body shots to overcome the aggressive French champion and re-establish himself among boxing’s elite.The judges scored the contest 115-112, 116-111 and 117-110 in favor of the Mexican. (The Guardianhad it 117-110.)“It’s something unbelievable. It feels like my first title. Now, after 21 years as a professional, 16 years ago I won my first title. Now I won that title again. I’m so proud of my team,” ‌Canelo said in English.“I love boxing. That’s why I’m here, because I still love boxing and I enjoy it a lot.”Mbilli, who entered the fight with a record of 29 wins and one draw, sought to unsettle Álvarez with relentless pressure and a higher volume of punches. But the challenger landed the cleaner blows, including a sharp uppercut that staggered Mbilli in the seventh round.View image in fullscreenÁlvarez evades a right hand from Mbilli during Saturday’s fight.Photograph: Fayez Nureldine/AFP/Getty ImagesThe victory marked a significant comeback for Álvarez, who suffered only the third defeat of his professional career when Terence Crawfordoutpointed him by unanimous decisionin September 2025.That losscost Álvarez his undisputed super-middleweight crown, ending his reign as holder of the division’s four major titles.The contest took place three weeks aftera missile strike on King Khalid International Airportin Riyadh killed at least 12 people and wounded more than 300. A second projectile struck a passenger terminal the following day, according to the Saudi-led military coalition, while several international airlines suspended flights to the kingdom amid the mounting threat to civilian aviation.Turki al-Sheikh, the chairman of Saudi Arabia’s General Entertainment Authority and one of boxing’s most influential power brokers, saidearlier this monththat Álvarez had personally assured him he would go ahead with the fight regardless of the security situation. “Canelo reached out and told me he’ll still fight in Riyadh this October, no matter what happens,” Al-Sheikh wrote on social media. “He fears nothing.”View image in fullscreenÁlvarez celebrates after Saturday’s win in Riyadh.Photograph: Fayez Nureldine/AFP/Getty ImagesThe escalation threatened Saudi Arabia’s ambitions to establish itself as a global destination for major sporting events. The kingdom has become a dominant force in professional boxing under Al-Sheikh, using its considerable financial resources to attract some of the sport’s biggest names, even as its expanding sporting footprint has drawn scrutiny over its human rights record and accusations of sportswashing.Álvarez made a brief, apparently oblique reference to the circumstances surrounding the fight during his post-fight remarks, thanking family members who were watching from afar rather than ringside.“I also want to thank my family, who are watching me from afar today for the first time,” he said in Spanish. “My siblings, my parents, my daughters, my son, and my wife – who also couldn’t make it due to certain circumstances.”Álvarez did not elaborate on those circumstances or explicitly link their absence to the security situation.Mbilli, 31, had been elevated to full WBC champion followingCrawford’s departure from the division, having previously held the interim title.The Cameroon-born boxer fought to a split draw against Lester Martínez on the undercard of the Álvarez-Crawford showdown, ending a run of 29 consecutive professional victories.Saturday’s result improved Álvarez’s record to 64 wins, three defeats and two draws and handed Mbilli the first loss of his professional career.Explore more on these topicsBoxingCanelo ÁlvarezMexicoSaudi Arabia and sportTurki al-SheikhTerence CrawfordShareReuse this content

title: European football: Kane misses penalty as Dortmund share spoils in Der Klassiker | European club football | The Guardian
description: The Ballon d’Or winner Harry Kane missed a penalty and hit the post for ⁠Bayern Munich as Borussia Dortmund snatched a last-gasp equaliser through Fabio Silva for a 2-2 draw ⁠in the Klassiker
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The Ballon d’Or winner Harry Kane missed a penalty and hit the post for ⁠Bayern Munich as Borussia Dortmund snatched a last-gasp equaliser through Fabio Silva for a 2-2 draw ⁠in the Klassiker
Content: Bayern Munich's Harry Kane looks rueful at the final whistle after Dortmund’s late equaliser.Photograph: Angelika Warmuth/ReutersView image in fullscreenBayern Munich's Harry Kane looks rueful at the final whistle after Dortmund’s late equaliser.Photograph: Angelika Warmuth/ReutersEuropean club footballEuropean football: Kane misses penalty as Dortmund share spoils in Der KlassikerBayern Munich held to 2-2 draw after Silva equaliserBarcelona on top of La Liga after thrashng AlavesAgenciesSat 31 Oct 2026 18.41 EDTFirst published on Sat 31 Oct 2026 16.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Ballon d’Or winner Harry Kane missed a penalty and hit the post for ⁠Bayern MunichasBorussia Dortmundsnatched a last-gasp equaliser through Fabio Silva for a 2-2 draw ⁠in Der Klassiker on ⁠Saturday ​that kept the teams level on points at the top.Kane, who collected his prize in a ceremony ⁠in London on Monday, was an unused substitute in the 6-1 German Cup second-round demolition of Magdeburg on Wednesday ⁠but returned to the starting lineup on Saturday, missing from the spot with Bayern 1-0 up. He also hit ​the post, one of four ‌times Bayern struck ‌the woodwork. Silva snatched the equaliser in the 89th minute to leave both ‌teams on 18 points, with Bayern top on goal difference.In a rollercoaster first half Bayern hit the post through Michael Olise and Ismael Saibari missed a golden chance before the visitors had a goal ruled out by VAR.View image in fullscreenFabio Silva’s late equaliser keeps Dortmund level on points with Bayern at the top.Photograph: Alex Grimm/Getty ImagesBayern, ‌also hit by injuries to Serge Gnabry and Olise, struck in the 38th minute thanks to Konrad Laimer’s goal on ​the rebound, after his first effort was blocked by Dortmund’s Gregor Kobel.With the Bayern head coach, Vincent Kompany, recovering after his collapse last week, Bayern’s full-back Laimer was more threatening than Kane, who sent his 56th ⁠minute spot-kick against the crossbar. Dortmund scored through Serhou Guirassy on ​the hour but parity lasted only ​six minutes as Dayot Upamecano tapped in from a Kane ​assist from close ‌range.Kane’s low shot ​bounced off ​the post before Silva scored the equaliser. Bayern’s Lennart Karl still had time to see his shot in stoppage time bounce off the crossbar and cap a frustrating day for the champions.Elsewhere in theBundesliga, last season’s Europa League finalistsFreiburgbeatAugsburg2-1 thanks to Cyriaque Irié’s 85th-minute goal to stay third.RB Leipzigare close behind in fourth after beatingSchalke2-0. The league top scorer, Niclas Füllkrug, added his ninth goal asWerder BremenbeatHoffenheim2-0 to move up to fifth.Bayer Leverkusen’s strong early form hit another setback in a 4-2 loss at home toStuttgartfor back-to-back defeats.Borussia MönchengladbachandPaderborndrew 0-0.View image in fullscreenAtlético Madrid’s Alex Grimaldo (right) celebrates after opening the scoring against Levante.Photograph: Kai Forsterling/EPAIn Spain,Barcelonaenjoyed an emphatic 6-1 home win overAlaves, with Raphinha, Fermín López, Lamine ⁠Yamal and Anthony Gordon all on the scoresheet, as the hosts responded after losses to Real Madrid and Paris St Germain.Barcelona⁠top La Liga on 30 ⁠points, two ​ahead ofAtlético Madrid, who beatLevante2-0 earlier on Saturday, with Real Madrid six points off the pace before ⁠visiting Racing Santander on Sunday.The opening exchanges at Camp Nou were punctuated by frustrated shouts from the home manager, Hansi Flick, in response to ⁠Barcelona’s defending, butAlavessoon found it impossible to live with their fluid attacking play.“It was a hard week for us, there was no better place than Camp Nou in front of our fans [to bounce back],” López said. “They make the difference, Lamine and Raphinha, with them we will achieve big things.”There was a minute’s silence at the start of each of the day’s matches in memory of the 69 victims of thetrain crash in the province of Toledo.In Italy,Milan’s Diego Moreira claimed one goal and two assists as his side took three precious points with a 3-1 victory overInterin theirSerie Aderby on Saturday, whileRomaenjoyed a 5-2 victory at ⁠Udinese.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn a week when ⁠the clubs ​sharedmore details of San Siro’s replacement, Milan’s fast start earned the win that lifts them into fourth ⁠place, four points behind leaders Lazio and Inter who have 25. The result means Lazio can move three points clear of Inter when they host Cagliari on Sunday. Roma ⁠are third on 24 points.Milan made the perfect start as Christian Pulisic headed their opener after four minutes ​before Adrien Rabiot added a second six minutes ‌later. Inter pulled a goal ‌back through Alessandro Bastoni in the 22nd and the momentum was with them.View image in fullscreenMilan players congratulate Diego Moreira after his goal against Inter.Photograph: Claudio Villa/AC Milan/Getty ImagesThe next goal was always ‌going to be crucial and it went to Milan as Moreira scored with a superb free-kick just before half-time to help his side to a fourth straight win over Inter.Roma were 4-0 up in 37 minutes at Udinese as they overwhelmed the hosts, who are second-bottom on five points. Bryan Cristante headed the first goal after 10 minutes, before Matías Soulé and Donyell Malen struck the woodwork. Rodrigo Mora ‌netted the second in the 31st minute after being set up by Cristante, and two minutes later Malen scored his eighth Serie A goal of the season.Evan Ndicka ​headed the fourth from a corner before half-time after which Udinese mounted something of a comeback. Nicolò Zaniolo and Matteo Palma scored for the hosts but Daniele Ghilardi added a fifth, his first Serie A goal, for Roma.Bolognaclimbed to ninth with ​a third successive league win thanks ​to a 2-1 victory overMonza, their first home success since April. Tommaso Pobega and ​Federico Bernardeschi netted for ‌Bologna, after the ​visitors scored an early ​penalty through Gustavo Varela, the top Serie A scorer with nine goals in as many games. He had been substituted by the time Monza were awarded a second penalty in the final 10 minutes and this time Patrick Cutrone missed from the spot as they were denied a point.Explore more on these topicsEuropean club footballBundesligaHarry KaneBayern MunichBorussia DortmundSerie AInternazionalenewsShareReuse this content

title: Pakistan win tri-series final as Fakhar Zaman century denies Sri Lanka in thrilling chase | Cricket | The Guardian
description: Pakistan chased down 326 to beat Sri Lanka in an absorbing tri-series final in Lahore
Author: Taha Hashim
Headline: Pakistan chased down 326 to beat Sri Lanka in an absorbing tri-series final in Lahore
Content: Fakhar Zaman (left) salutes the crowd after reaching his century.Photograph: Sameer Ali/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFakhar Zaman (left) salutes the crowd after reaching his century.Photograph: Sameer Ali/Getty ImagesCricketPakistan win tri-series final as Fakhar Zaman century denies Sri Lanka in thrilling chaseOpener scores 127 from 99 balls in LahoreKamindu Mendis’s 131 proves in vain for Sri LankaTaha HashimSat 31 Oct 2026 12.46 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 14.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis mini-tournament has been a welcome change of pace, carrying more meaning than your bog-standard three-match white-ball slog between two teams. And then there’s the gift of a final. This was a fitting conclusion under the lights in a packed-out Gaddafi Stadium in Lahore, settled in the penultimate over as Pakistan beat Sri Lanka by three wickets to win the tri-series.Fakhar Zaman, Pakistan’s hero from the 2017 Champions Trophy final, crashed his way to 127 in a chase of 326. But plenty of work remained after his dismissal, and the new boys needed to stay calm. Arafat Minhas, 21, and Hasan Nawaz, 24, played like old-timers, their partnership of 94 securing the game. Minhas and Faheem Ashraf fell with two runs still required, but Shaheen Afridi finished the evening with a wallop over the ropes.Pakistan v Sri Lanka: tri-series cricket one-day international final – liveRead moreMinhas was particularly brutal, middling four sixes on his way to 61 off 31 balls. Pakistan have got something special brewing,Minhas having decimated England with a six-wicket haulat the start of the tri-series. His left-arm spin was expensive here, but he made up for it.With Sri Lanka setting a target for the first time in the series, Kamindu Mendis was the lead pulveriser in the first half, his 131 ultimately in vain. The left-hander had a Bradmanesque Test average a couple of years ago after hitting five hundreds in his first eight matches, but he’s been waiting for a breakthrough knock in white-ball cricket. Seven years on from his ODI debut, he finally has a hundred, more than doubling his previous career-best. He was helped by in-form colleagues, with Avishka Fernando building an opening stand of 87 and the irrepressible Pavan Rathnayake joining Kamindu for a partnership of 146 inside 20 overs.Rathnayake has had a cracking couple of weeks, and his half-century took him to 427 runs in the tri-series at 106.75, two tons against England to go with a healthy strike rate. His 77 left Pakistan looking lost on another flat one, and they relied on Salman Agha’s part-time off-breaks for their first two wickets. With Rathnayake and Kamindu pushing Sri Lanka to 255 after 41 overs, Dasun Shanaka, unrelenting in his side’s remarkable chase of 430 against England, was waiting for the final bash.Yet Shaheen brought his side back, stopping Sri Lanka from going stratospheric. The left-armer went full to dismiss Kamindu and Shanaka; Haris Rauf went short for his two late wickets as Pakistan took six in the last nine overs. “We had to score another 30 runs,” lamented Sri Lanka’s captain, Kusal Mendis. This was a target well within reach, even for a batting lineupbowled out for 110 by Sri Lanka four days earlier.View image in fullscreenSri Lanka’s Kamindu Mendis guides the ball away during his first century in ODIs.Photograph: Rahat Dar/EPAThe chase called for a Babar Azam special at his home ground but Pakistan’s most accomplished batter is struggling for runs, now nine innings without a half-century. There was no unconverted start this time, just a thick edge to a wide slip without a run to his name. Rathnayake juggled before desperately holding on.Maaz Sadaqat had already fallen to Dilshan Madushanka after an errant drive, bringing together Fakhar and Saad Baig on 14 for two. Both are freewheeling left-handers at vastly different junctures, one making his way, the other nearing the end. Both clattered the ball at a similar rate, and Baig, hours before his 20th birthday, advanced to his first international half-century off 52 balls. While Baig perished on 74 with a return catch to Maheesh Theekshana, the Sri Lanka spinner dropped Fakhar on 69 and 106.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe left-armers kept Sri Lanka alive. Madushanka’s pace snuck past Fakhar’s swinging bat with 106 still required, and Dunith Wellalage’s spin beat Agha’s sweep. The game was even and boundaries were disappearing for more than 10 overs, the drought only broken when Minhas thumped Shanaka through the covers.With 46 needed from 30 balls, a 15-run over off Shanaka turned the game completely Pakistan’s way, Minhas’ power delighting the stands before Shaheen applied the perfect finish.Explore more on these topicsCricketPakistan cricket teamSri Lanka cricket teammatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: If Mikel Arteta’s dossier is part of a deliberate strategy, it is a dangerous one for Arsenal | Mikel Arteta | The Guardian
description: The Arsenal manager is not yet in Alex Ferguson and José Mourinho’s league, but his conspiracy theories are reaching new levels
Author: Jonathan Wilson
Headline: The Arsenal manager is not yet in Alex Ferguson and José Mourinho’s league, but his conspiracy theories are reaching new levels
Content: Mikel Arteta, booked here against Sunderland, received his second yellow card of the season for leaving the technical area against Everton.Photograph: Ian Hodgson/APView image in fullscreenMikel Arteta, booked here against Sunderland, received his second yellow card of the season for leaving the technical area against Everton.Photograph: Ian Hodgson/APInside footballMikel ArtetaIf Mikel Arteta’s dossier is part of a deliberate strategy, it is a dangerous one for ArsenalJonathan WilsonThe manager is not yet in Alex Ferguson and José Mourinho’s league, but his conspiracy theories have reached new levelsSat 31 Oct 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 16.01 EDTShareEnglish football loves the word “dossier”. It doesn’t love dossiers themselves, of course; they’re for nerds – unless, that is, they’re a “secret dossier”, which have a thrilling redolence of spy dramas, invisible ink and dead drops. Non-secret dossiers, though, are inherently risible: call something a “dossier” in English football and you’re immediately signalling: this is absurd poindextering. Dossiers were preposterous when Don Revie was – imagine the pretension! – drawing up scouting reports on opposing players, and they are preposterous today asMikel Artetacollates images of rival managers stepping outside their technical area.Arteta, it should be said, did not use the word “dossier”; rather it was swiftly applied to what he had called “a massive storage of images”. DuringArsenal’s 2-0 win against Evertonlast Saturday, he received his second booking of the season for leaving his technical area. This, it turns out, is another part of the vast conspiracy against Arsenal. Yes, Arteta accepted, he left his technical area (44 times before being booked, according to the former referee Graham Scott), but other managers do it too. “There are managers who have the record in the league, 36 times in 10 minutes [they] leave the touchline – no yellows,” he said. “I am clipping all of that … so if somebody comes to me I can say: ‘I am not in the record yet.’ Somebody else has the record so let’s see. Then it’s 36 yellow cards in 10 minutes for the managers.”‘We are not in Disneyland’: Arteta warns Dowman of Arsenal’s demandsRead moreThere are two ways of looking at this. Perhaps it’s genuine. Perhaps Arteta really is a ludicrous Pooterish figure, counting the misdemeanours of others, the worst kind of neighbourhood watch curtain-twitcher who happens also to have been cursed with a persecution complex: “I got a fine because my parking permit was partially obscured, but Mr Emery at No 17 has been six inches out of his bay on at least three occasions this month and … nothing.” Or perhaps he really is an inveterate snitch, glorying in telling on his peers: “Please, Miss! Miss, Daniel’s been chewing gum again, Miss.”Or, perhaps awed by the misguided defiance of Manchester City fans after their club was found to have perpetrated the greatest act of cheating in English sporting history, he is trying to persuade his base that everybody is againstArsenalto generate a siege mentality. Declan Rice mystifyingly got away with kicking Malick Yalcouyé off the ball against Brighton, but it’s important to remember that Arsenal remain the real victims here.The history of mind games in football is long and storied. Before the 1939 FA Cup final, for instance, Major Frank Buckley, the flamboyant manager of Wolves, claimed to have injected his players with “animal secretions”. A French surgeon, Serge Voronoff, had begun transplanting tissue from monkey testicles on to human testicles as an anti-ageing treatment, and it was widely believed that it was this monkey gland treatment that Buckley was employing. In fact, he almost certainly gave his players nothing stronger than vitamins but the idea was that Wolves’ morale would be boosted, while their opponents in the final, Portsmouth, would be intimidated by the prospect of taking on players juiced up on simian fluids. It didn’t work, Portsmouth winning 4-1 despite finishing 15 places below Wolves in the table, but the logic is familiar.The monkey glands were relatively benign, little more than a publicity stunt, but it’s easy for attempts at psychological manipulation to take on a darker aspect. Before Inter played Liverpool in the second leg of the 1965 European Cup semi-final, for instance, their manager, Helenio Herrera, had 100,000 leaflets distributed claiming that at the end of the first leg at Anfield, Liverpool fans had sung “Go home, Italians” to the tune of “Santa Lucia” which supposedly was intended “to deride us and make us feel we are just a race of cheap mandolin players”. Suitably enraged, Inter fans ensured San Siro seethed with fury, which perhaps encouraged some questionable refereeing decisions (although it probably wasn’t the only factor) as Liverpool lost 3-0 and went out 4-3 on aggregate.Alex Ferguson was a master of the art, while José Mourinho openly acknowledged that the next game begins in the post-match press conference for the previous one. Mourinho, in particular, often crossed the line of professional decency. Arteta, clearly, is not at that level, at least not yet, but if his dossier is part of a deliberate strategy it is a dangerous one.View image in fullscreenArsenal fans, more so after Max Dowman’s red card at Fleetwood, remain convinced that referees have been machinating against them for years.Photograph: Carl Recine/Getty ImagesArteta’s conspiracy theory is likely to find fertile ground among certain online Arsenal fans, who remain convinced that referees have been machinating against them for years. Even on Tuesday there were those who leaped to thedefence of Max Dowmanafter he had been sent off for thrusting a knee towards Harrison Neal’s chest, even though Arteta himself appeared furious with the16-year-old’s petulance. Why, ran the argument, had Cole Palmer not been shown a straight red for retaliating against Mateus Fernandes in Chelsea’s defeat by Tottenham on Saturday? Dowman went with his knee and Palmer with his belly, which is perhaps enough to explain the discrepancy, but even if it isn’t, so what? If you don’t want to be punished, don’t go thrusting knees or bellies or anything at opponents, no matter how bad a foul they’ve just committed.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt’s not only that football is groaning under the weight of the paranoia of various fan groups, each adamant that Pro Ref is acting with the rosicrucians, the Masons, the mob, Opus Dei and the Cubans to deny their club a spot in the Europa League, a distraction that deflects from the game’s true crisis: its descent from an endeavour in which sporting merit and integrity are paramount into a grimly capitalistic vehicle to make very rich and powerful people even richer and more powerful.It’s also dangerous because a mood of insecurity, of being convinced everything is against you, is not conducive to winning league titles – as Arsenal know. In 2024-25, their title bid was undermined by their early-season ill discipline, each red card greeted not with the resilience of champions but with bleating about how it wasn’t really their fault and everybody was picking on them, including the injury gods.Abdicating responsibility rarely helps, snitches seldom prosper and, in English football, dossiers are always a bad idea.Explore more on these topicsMikel ArtetaInside footballArsenalcommentShareReuse this content

title: Why politicians chasing economic growth is a lie | Radical Thinking with Aditya Chakrabortty |  Presented by Aditya Chakrabortty with Karel Williams and Sukhdev Johal, produced by Frankie Tobi and Luke John Smith , the executive producers are Maz Ebtehaj, Kirsty Major and James Tindale | The Guardian
description: For years, UK governments have tried and failed to increase growth per person in the UK. So what’s the lesson from the great British fairytale? The rebel economists Karel Williams and Sukhdev Johal explain to Aditya Chakrabortty why they believe praying for growth is a fool’s dream – and why it won’t improve your life
Author: Karel Williams
Headline: For years, UK governments have tried and failed to increase growth per person in the UK. So what’s the lesson from the great British fairytale? The rebel economists Karel Williams and Sukhdev Johal explain to Aditya Chakrabortty why they believe praying for growth is a fool’s dream – and why it won’t improve your life
Content: 45:43Radical Thinking with Aditya ChakraborttyEconomicsWhy politicians chasing economic growth is a lie | Radical Thinking with Aditya ChakraborttyWhat if someone told you the truth about the economy? For years, UK governments have tried spending more, spending less, cutting red tape, leaving the EU, levelling up, and they have still failed to increase growth per person. So what’s the lesson from the great British fairytale? On the latest episode, the rebel economists Karel Williams and Sukhdev Johal explain to Aditya Chakrabortty why they believe praying for growth is a fool’s dream – and why it won’t improve your lifeAditya’s suggested reading list for Karel Williams and Sukhdev Johal:As we say in the podcast, I’ve championed the work of Karel and Sukhdev and their colleagues in the Guardian for many years, and some of my columns are a good introduction to their approach.In our conversation we look at what life after growth looks like for towns and suburbs, and what it should look like.This reportfrom South Wales in 2016 examines the present-day reality.For a broader analysis of how the UK has become highly unequal and increasingly stagnant, trythis.As part of the Foundational Economy collective, Karel and Sukhdev put a lot of their analysis into freely available working papers. That circumvents the leisureliness and expense of academic publishing and gets their arguments in front of a wider public. A good example isthis one on the cost of living crisis.More recently, they’ve focused on the broken water system of England and Wales in a book calledMurky Water: Challenging an Unsustainable System.Support the Guardian ► https://support.theguardian.comThe Guardian on YouTube: The Guardian ► www.youtube.com/@theguardianGuardian News ► www.youtube.com/@guardiannewsToday in Focus ► www.youtube.com/@todayinfocuspodcastStateside ► www.youtube.com/@statesidepodcastPolitics Weekly ► https://www.youtube.com/@politicsweeklyScience Weekly ► https://www.youtube.com/@scienceweeklypodFootball Weekly ► https://www.youtube.com/@FootballWeeklyPodcastPresented byAditya ChakraborttywithKarel Williamsand Sukhdev Johal, produced byFrankie TobiandLuke John Smith, the executive producers areMaz Ebtehaj,Kirsty MajorandJames TindaleSat 31 Oct 2026 03.45 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTShareExplore more on these topicsEconomicsRadical Thinking with Aditya ChakraborttyEconomic policy

title: The real problem with Britain’s Political Traitors show is that no one is very faithful to anything for long | Robert Hutton | The Guardian
description: For Westminster’s special budget edition of the series, politicians have played to their strengths. Bombast, duplicity, distrust: it’s all second nature, says journalist and author Robert Hutton
Author: Robert Hutton
Headline: For Westminster’s special budget edition of the series, politicians have played to their strengths. Bombast, duplicity, distrust: it’s all second nature, says journalist and author Robert Hutton
Content: The Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch (left) and the  Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.Composite: Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenThe Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch (left) and the  Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.Composite: Guardian DesignOpinionThe TraitorsThe real problem with Britain’s Political Traitors show is that no one is very faithful to anything for longRobert HuttonFor Westminster’s special budget edition of the series, politicians have played to their strengths. Bombast, duplicity, distrust: it’s all second natureSat 31 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 11.49 EDTShareYou join us on a steam train in Scotland as we head to the next episode of the BBC’s hit show Political Traitors. It’s like the celebrity edition, except that everyone is less comely – politics being the practice ofshow business for ugly people. For this week’s task, the players have to construct a “budget” of tiny crowd-pleasing measures, carefully balanced by invisible tax rises.What makes the show so compelling is that the players don’t know the whole story. Only those of us on the outside can see what’s really going on. WhileJohn and Andyrun around shouting about how they have faithfully met their “fiscal rules” in the third year of the forecasts, on our sofas at home we know that this incantation is entirely meaningless.But people who’ve been on the show say that when you’re in the midst of it, it feels completely real. So much so that there are ongoing questions for the producers about safeguarding. Liz, who was a sensation of chaotic energy when she briefly appeared in 2022, is the most obvious example of someone who shouldn’t have been allowed to take part. She waslast heard explaining her plan to colonise Mars.If the series has any value beyond entertainment, it’s for the insights it offers into human psychology, especially the way people convince themselves of narratives that are objectively nonsense. Take Kemi, from the current run. After the banishment of Keir earlier this year, she could be heard explaining to anyone who would listen that this was the result ofher brilliant inquisitions at the roundtable.We could all see that the other players, after debating why on earth Keir hadn’t already been stabbed in the back, had concluded that although he was 100% faithful, he was also 1000% loser.Nevertheless, there’s something rather charming about Kemi’s total conviction that she’s a masterly player on course for triumph. It’s easy for us to laugh, but you have to remember that she doesn’t have access to the information we do, such as opinion polls and byelection results.That information gap is the joy of the show. Several times Nigel hasseemingly revealed himself to be a traitor, and his close ally Nathanwas actually unmasked as one, but still no one seems able to put two and two together.View image in fullscreenThe prime minister, Andy Burnham, and the chancellor, John Healey, visiting the Rolls Royce factory in Derby, October 29.Photograph: WPA/Getty ImagesSome players adopt a strategy of trying to fly below the radar to avoid being noticed. One current player, Ed D, has been so successful that many viewers have forgotten he exists and refuse to believe he ispart of the game at all, even after his triumph in the water slide task.Each morning, the players meet over breakfast TV for a heated discussion in which they all insist that whatever has just happened proves their theory is right. Then there’s the dramatic moment of discovering who has been banished, or simply walked off the set. In one compelling episode in 2022, almost all the players quit in the hope of forcing Boris to admit he’d been lying. Even then, to viewers’ delight, he still had the support of the loyal Nadine.In last month’s “conference” task, the players were handed the severed head of a deceased teammate and had to mimic their distinctive cry. Kemi, predictably, chose Maggie, although her impersonation looked more like pastiche. Andy, on the other hand, reckons he can do a mean Harold. He’s rejected any suggestion that he should try copying Tony, one of the game’s most successful players, but he’s failed to brush aside the lingering suspicion that he’s simply doing an impression of Keir.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe format has been sold around the world, with changes for local markets. The French edition involves a runoff vote. TheIsraeli versionis so complicated that no one understands anything about it except that somehow Bibi keeps winning. And the American one is louder, brasher and far more expensive. It also seems to be played entirely by idiots who have failed, despite an impossible number of very clear clues, to identify their obvious traitor.Although the players change at an alarming rate, the one constant in the British show is the host, Lindsay. With his ridiculous outfits and his catchphrases – “Order! ORDER!” and “Mr Holden, I think you need to leave” – he is fast becoming a national treasure. And now, as he says at the end of every roundtable, the time for talk is over.I’m joking, of course. In this version of the show, the time for talk never ends.Robert Hutton is a journalist and authorExplore more on these topicsThe TraitorsOpinionKemi BadenochNigel FarageAndy BurnhamJohn HealeyLabourConservativescommentShareReuse this content

title: Britain’s housing crisis won’t be fixed without a new tax landscape | Phillip Inman | The Guardian
description: We need policies that stop treating property as a store of wealth and that allow people to move home cheaply
Author: Phillip Inman
Headline: We need policies that stop treating property as a store of wealth and that allow people to move home cheaply
Content: One academic calls the UK’s housing system ‘one of the most dysfunctional in the world’.Photograph: Mike Kemp/In Pictures/GettyView image in fullscreenOne academic calls the UK’s housing system ‘one of the most dysfunctional in the world’.Photograph: Mike Kemp/In Pictures/GettyViewpoint columnHousing marketBritain’s housing crisis won’t be fixed without a new tax landscapePhillip InmanWe need policies that stop treating property as a store of wealth and that allow people to move home cheaplySat 31 Oct 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 17.32 EDTShareJohn Healey’s critics on the right and left accused him of dodging the big questions in his firstbudget. The chancellor failed to announce reforms that might tackle some of Britain’s chronic problems, they say.Healey’s scatter-gun budget, as the Resolution Foundation called it, was more about politics than economics, and unapologetically so.Housing was one area of policy that took up a considerable chunk of his speech. And yet the measures amounted to very little, if a test of his policy changes was to ask how different will the UK be at the next election. Or, as that date is only two and a half years away, 10 years from now.Housing is more than a single element of a complex economy. It is both its driving force and a disease eating its way through the body, from the inside out.More than 80% of global investment is in property and the vast majority of that is in residential. Countries that once had a more communitarian approach, such as France and Germany, with a highly regulated mix of social, private rented and home ownership, have succumbed to building wealth through property.It doesn’t seem to matter that Japan was ruined in the 1990s by a vicious property price crash. And China is still suffering domestically after Beijing alloweda property Ponzi schemeto develop that enriched the already super-wealthy and left tens of millions of middle-income earners in negative equity.Nowhere is the situation worse than in the UK, where property prices have cooled somewhat, but remain at levels thatdeny younger generationsthe chance to find a home at a reasonable price and some financial security.UK property has also become the method by which Gen Xers pay for social care for their parents and release housing deposits for their offspring. Then there is the debilitatingleasehold/freehold split that is both a source of angry disputes and stymies investment in solar panels and insulation (who should pay?).The lack of regulation and ill-thought-out subsidies affecting new private housing means developers are incentivised to enter an arm-twisting contest with local authorities. Without robust planning guidelines, developers champion building on flood plains or erecting tower blocks that are later dubbed ovens for their lack of ventilation in hot summers.And all the while the tax system is working to make the situation worse.The Oxford academic John Muellbauer has spent almost 40 years researching the UK’s housing system. He calls it “one of the most dysfunctional in the world”.Inan academic articlepublished in September by the British Academy, he says: “Many of the UK’s current economic and social problems, including its housing affordability crisis, can be traced to decades of land and housing policy failures. The role of land markets is strongly dependent on institutions, including land use regulation, financial regulation and property taxation.”The Treasury and Angela Rayner’s Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government have considered proposals from Muellbauer and others that remodel council tax, turning it into a fairer annual levy on households and using the reform to abolish stamp duty on transactions, which has calcified the housing market.Rachel Reeves’s mansion tax is a good start. It is only a start though, because the former chancellor was persuaded to keep the council tax banding system when she should have applied a percentage to the 150,000-odd homes valued above £2m that will be captured by the new policy.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere was the potential for a database of homes valued above £2m to be the beginning of a revaluation process, carrying on until all homes were logged. With a percentage tax of, say, 0.5%, applied to all homes, a £150,000 property would pay an annual tax rate of £750 while a £3m home would pay £15,000.Of course, the real problem is not the £3m homeowner for whom policymakers will have little sympathy – it’s the professionals occupying £1.5m homes in London, the south-east and affluent suburbs around other big cities, who will see council tax rates more than double to £7,500.The professional classes will be the worst affected in the short term. Yet there will only be progress when this powerful lobby group of owner-occupiers – working and retired – are prepared to accept the trade-off with stamp duty, which would disappear for those who sell.There are plenty of people in government who understand the need to resolve housing market issues in a more fundamental fashion. The Treasury minister Torsten Bell is one. His book, Great Britain?: How We Get Our Future Back, talks about “our housing omnishambles”.However, they have had little influence on policy in this area so far. In his first budget Healey revamped a much-discreditedhelp-to-buy schemefor new-build homes, which will only boost prices and line the pockets of developers. He also gave some more money towards council housebuilding, slapped an extra tax on landlords (that will probably push up rents) and promised to tackle homelessness.Healey and Andy Burnham put all their revolutionary zeal into a long, and possibly tortuous, process of devolution from London to the regions to kickstart growth.However, it is tax incentives that are causing the problems, not whether policy decisions are made locally or centrally. Bad policy decisions can be made locally just as much as centrally. What makes the difference is a permanently reformed tax landscape that discourages treating housing as a store of wealth, allows people to move home cheaply – especially older homeowners who want to downsize – and supports the building of more truly affordable homes to buy and rent.Explore more on these topicsHousing marketViewpoint columnBudget 2026John HealeyEconomicsStamp dutyCouncil taxEconomic policycommentShareReuse this content

title: When you’re traduced, abused and gaslighted – believe me, Black History Month matters  | Hugh Muir | The Guardian
description: There is always debate about the concept’s necessity and efficacy. But with nativists in their pomp, it’s good to focus on who we are and why, says Hugh Muir, Opinion executive editor
Author: Hugh Muir
Headline: There is always debate about the concept’s necessity and efficacy. But with nativists in their pomp, it’s good to focus on who we are and why, says Hugh Muir, Opinion executive editor
