Content: Illustration: Guardian Design; ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock; Manuel Harlan; Jeff Moore/PA;  Laura McCluskeyView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian Design; ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock; Manuel Harlan; Jeff Moore/PA;  Laura McCluskeyOpinionBlack History MonthWhen you’re traduced, abused and gaslighted – believe me, Black History Month mattersHugh MuirThere is always debate about the concept’s necessity and efficacy. But with nativists in their pomp, it’s good to focus on who we are and whyWhat forces shaped four generations of Black Britons? | The panelSat 31 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 04.05 EDTSharePityBlack History Month UK, assailed on all sides. Those on the right seek to end the celebration on the basis that it amounts to special treatment for a group that doesn’t deserve it. History should be colour-blind: society should not differentiate, they say. We are not racist, we just want fairness. But often, they are – and they really don’t.On the other side of the argument are the progressives, notably minority progressives, who say the idea of a month to consider Black history is demeaning because it should already have a year-roundplace in our teaching and consciousness. There is a further view that any beneficial effect the month once had has been diluted by unimaginative repetition and commercially motivated virtue signalling. Playerstaking the kneein the Premier League? Been there, done that: yawn!I have long taken the glass-half-full approach. The ideal would be for Black history to be incorporated into the social and educational culture – and perhaps one day it will be. But in the meantime, I’ll take a mandated, month-long focus on the Black contribution to the way our society has evolved. And it seems very necessary this year, when the very notion of belonging in Britain and other major western countries has been so under attack.A year in which we have clearly seen that a political party, with pretensions to lead the country, attracts activists with ugly racist and nativist views – at national and local level – with the same efficiency that magnets attract iron filings. Our expectations are different now. When transcripts of the thingsReform folk say in privatereach the public domain, the old-fashioned Tory dog-whistle seems comparatively quaint.View image in fullscreenA book by Michelle Obama was among those removed from school shelves.Photograph: Paras Griffin/Getty ImagesThis is a year in which we have again seen the confidence and daring of those who cuddle close to pseudo-scientific theories assertingwhite superiority and black inferiority. The racial eugenicists are back from the fringes, championed down their venal path by Donald Trump, whose leadership of the free world gladhands nativists, targets Black officials androutinely belittlesBlack enemies as “low IQ”.It’s been a year in which toxic politics and the mainstreaming of intolerance – against minorities of many categories – has led to racist unpleasantness on our streets and in the workplace. There is a snapshot from the Royal College of Nursing: racist abuse of NHS nurses – including use of the N-word – up 86% in therecent past. All part of what one NHS official called “a rising tide of racism”.Another snapshot of the increasingly hostile environment is from parliament. What happened, via social media, when Labour MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy posted a video in support of Black History Month?Vile abuse, of course: “Some of a kind that I had not necessarily seen in that volume before. I had people calling me the N-word, people telling me to eff-off and go back to where I came from, and people sending monkey photographs.”Another snapshot from Chichester, Sussex, where a diverse group of actors recently went to perform A Midsummer Night’s Dreamand were shamefully menaced.“I don’t know if I have witnessed and/or experienced as much racism, xenophobia and homophobia as I saw in those six weeks,” said the actor and comedian Munya Chawawa. Britain is a good place. The vast majority of our fellow citizens are decent and kind. But it’s now easy, far too easy, to unwittingly enter hostile territory.So in years like this, when there are obvious, concerted, targeted, and well-funded attempts to undermine Black people and the Black experience – not least thetargeting of booksby Black authors by “anti woke” crusaders – it becomes more difficult to be sanguine about concepts such as Black History Month. It then becomes a good thing, perhaps an essential one, to remember and to highlight – if only over a calendar month – who we are, who has shaped us and how we have indisputably helped to shape Britain as a vibrant, diverse, first world power.Today, at the end of thisBlack History Month, Guardian Opinion has asked Black Britons representing four generations to tell us how their own Black British identities have evolved, for we have been here long enough now to compare notes on the different stages of our lives on this island. A twentysomething sees the joy and pain of being here very differently to their elderly siblings, to their parents, to their grandparents.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCall it reflection with a purpose. In a time like this, it seems more vital than ever to know who we were, who we are – and the foundations on which we all stand.Hugh Muir is executive editor, OpinionDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsBlack History MonthOpinionRaceReform UKcommentShareReuse this content

title: Christina Applegate’s multiple sclerosis misdiagnosis is not an isolated event. I should know  | Shakira Hussein | The Guardian
description: Shakira Hussein’s concerns about her bipolar diagnosis were dismissed as common among ‘women like you’. Then she was found to have MS
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Shakira Hussein’s concerns about her bipolar diagnosis were dismissed as common among ‘women like you’. Then she was found to have MS
Content: Christina Applegate revealed her neurologist now believes she does not have multiple sclerosis after all.Photograph: Matt Sayles/APView image in fullscreenChristina Applegate revealed her neurologist now believes she does not have multiple sclerosis after all.Photograph: Matt Sayles/APMultiple sclerosisChristina Applegate’s multiple sclerosis misdiagnosis is not an isolated event. I should knowShakira HusseinShakira Hussein’s concerns about her bipolar diagnosis were dismissed as common among ‘women like you’. Then she was found to have MSSat 31 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 10.03 EDTShareIn the five years since her diagnosis with multiple sclerosis, the Emmy award-winning actor Christina Applegate has become a prominent spokesperson for people living with the neurological disease. Both hermemoir, published earlier this year, and the MS-themed podcast MeSsy that she co-hosts with fellow actor Jamie Lynn Sigler have significantly raised public awareness about multiple sclerosis and the broader topic of living with disability.So Applegate’s recentrevelationthat her neurologist now believes that she does not have the disease after all came as a shock to me and to many other people living with multiple sclerosis. We understand why Applegate says that she does not regard her health update as good news. The undiagnosis is not a cure – she is just as sick as she ever was, but “back to square one” when it comes to explanations. Medical experts interviewed about Applegate’s case reassure us that most people being treated for multiple sclerosis can be confident in our diagnoses and advise those of us with concerns to consult our neurologists for reassessment.Actor Christina Applegate reveals she was misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosisRead moreBut Applegate’s experience is not an isolated event. A2024 systematic reviewfound that about 15% of the MS cases it studied were misdiagnosed, with women twice as likely as men to be diagnosed as having the disease when they did not. And underdiagnosis is also commonplace, with many patients waiting months or years for their disease to be correctly identified and treated.My own diagnosis with remitting-relapsing multiple sclerosis 20 years ago came after a long period of being misdiagnosised with bipolar disorder.I had initially been referred to the psychiatrist who (mis)diagnosed me while I was recovering from trauma. The heart-stopping panic attacks gradually subsided thanks to cognitive behavioural therapy rather than the cocktail of antidepressants and antipsychotics that I had been prescribed for bipolar disorder, but my physical health continued to decline.My psychiatrist’s response was to increase the dosage of my medication, dismissing any concerns that I expressed by telling me that “intelligent women like you” are often unwilling to accept that they have a psychiatric disorder. The words “intelligent women like you” came to sound like an insult as I heard them recited more and more often.Eventually my health reached crisis point with a flare up that left me unable to stand without a walking stick for support; even then, the first neurologist I consulted dismissed my symptoms as psychiatric – “very common in women like you”.It was the words “women like you” that motivated me to seek a second opinion.By the time I saw the second neurologist and had an MRI scan, I had put my symptoms down to a madness caused by the political upheaval and bloodshed of the early 2000s. But when I tried to explain this to the neurologist, he paused for a long moment before saying, “The scan was abnormal”.Of course, it is entirely possible (and not particularly unusual) to have both bipolar disorder and multiple sclerosis. My psychiatrist told me in our final phone call that “intelligent women like you” often seize upon the diagnosis of a physical disease to deny that they are also suffering from a psychiatric condition. But my health immediately improved once I was taken off the bipolar medication and began treatment for multiple sclerosis.double quotation markNothing that the disease has thrown at me has been as difficult as the fear and uncertainty of the pre-diagnosis periodThe years since the diagnosis have not been easy. As a disease of the brain and central nervous system, multiple sclerosis has an endless array of weapons at its disposal and the treatments have ranged from daily self-injections to monthly infusions to a demanding immune system reboot. But nothing that the disease has thrown at me has been as difficult as the fear and uncertainty of the gruelling pre-diagnosis period.The boundary between the diagnosed and undiagnosed has become the border between worthy and unworthy, deserving and undeserving, entitlement to disability support payments and destitution. Applegate’s experience illustrates how uncertain and contested this boundary is. The legions of people like her who are sick but undiagnosed deserve better than to be stigmatised as grifters and malingerers. We should not be dismissed as time-wasters because the diagnostic process is complex and lengthy.My symptoms ought to have been taken seriously regardless of whether their underlying cause was multiple sclerosis or bipolar disorder. And, once diagnosed, we should not have to fear that a doctor’s second thoughts will make us second-class patients.Explore more on these topicsMultiple sclerosisWomenHealthGendercommentShareReuse this content

title: Hear me out: maybe Norway should give Melania Trump the Nobel peace prize | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: The first lady has been praised for ‘singlehandedly’ brokering a ceasefire in a Ukrainian city – though she might have had some help
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: The first lady has been praised for ‘singlehandedly’ brokering a ceasefire in a Ukrainian city – though she might have had some help
Content: ‘If Melania can do something about her husband, I’m crowning her Michigan’s Woman of the Year.’Photograph: Aaron Schwartz-Pool/CNP/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘If Melania can do something about her husband, I’m crowning her Michigan’s Woman of the Year.’Photograph: Aaron Schwartz-Pool/CNP/ShutterstockThe Week in PatriarchyMelania TrumpHear me out: maybe Norway should give Melania Trump the Nobel peace prizeArwa MahdawiThe first lady has been praised for ‘singlehandedly’ brokering a ceasefire in a Ukrainian city – though she might have had some helpSat 31 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 08.02 EDTShareHaters be damned: Donald Trump just keeps on winning. He won the inaugural Fifa peace prize last year and was presented with the completely real, totally not made-up “Man of the Century” award at arecent rally. The president has also spent thegreater part of a decadeclaiming he was once crowned Michigan’s Man of the Year: a fantastic achievement considering there is no such award and Trump has never lived in Michigan.But despite his manytrophies, there is one honour that has proved elusive: the Nobel peace prize. Trump holds a bit of a grudge about that, recently terming Norway a “shithouse country” for passing him over for the award. In response, thecountry’s tourism boardhighlighted some of its nicest public lavatories with the tagline: “Norway makes shit houses great again!”Speaking in my capacity as Philadelphia’s Woman of the Millennium, I’ve got a modest proposal for the people of Norway. The toilet gag was excellent, but if they want to do some top-tier trolling then I think next year’s Nobel peace prize needs to go toMelania Trump.Some people would be thrilled for their spouse to be in the spotlight, but I’m not sure that’s the case with Donald. Indeed, the president hassaid: “You can only have … one star in a family; it doesn’t work with two.” If Melania got Trump’s coveted Nobel peace prize, it could spark a war in the White House.But look, I’m not just suggesting the Norwegians honour Melania because it would raise Donald’s blood pressure. No, it seems Melania has become quite the diplomat. Last week, the White Houseannouncedthat the first lady had “successfully secured a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, localized to the city of Oleshky”.How on earth did she manage that? Apparently, Melania initiated discussions with Russia andUkraineand “aligned the parties on the agreement’s objectives, technical procedures, timing, processes, and terms, in her formal role as Exclusive Intermediary”.Whatever all that means, it seems to have worked: the ceasefire went into effect on Tuesday in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city, which has been enduring a worsening humanitarian crisis.On Friday, hundreds of people were evacuated from the frontline town and emergency supplies were brought in for people who needed to stay.Melania has been widely praised for brokering this ceasefire. Melania’s adviser has claimed she “singlehandedly” secured it, adding that no other first lady has everachievedwhat Melania just pulled off, and she is “completely revamping the role of first lady … [and] saving lives.”Perhaps. But if there is one thing that the Trumps are good at it, it is taking credit for other people’s work. So is the first lady really the great peacemaker that she’s making herself out to be?To be fair, Melania has done some good work vis-à-vis Ukraine and certainly seems to be better at peacemaking than Jared Kushner is, who has made huge sums of money while operating as one of Trump’stop diplomatic envoysto the Middle East. Last year, for example, Melaniawrote a letterto Vladimir Putin pleading for Ukrainian children seized by Russia to be returned to their families. Since then, her office has said she’s facilitatednumerous roundsof family reunification.However, despite the claim that Melania “singlehandedly” secured this ceasefire, it would appear she had a little help. Pope Leo XIV alsopersonally appealedto Putin about the situation in Oleshky in early October. It’s unclear whether he had more or less sway than the first lady had, but the pope is certainly being rather more modest about his involvement.So what’s next for Melania after her success in Oleshky? In an interview with Newsmax, her adviser Marc Beckman said Melaniamight help pavethe way to “durable, everlasting peace” in Ukraine and Russia as a whole.“She’s against war, she thinks it’s senseless … she wants to see peace all over the world,” Beckman added.Does she indeed? In that case she might want to have a word with the president, who started a very bloody war against Iran and who is currently trying to use US taxpayer money to send2,000lb bombs to Israel, a country accused of genocide.Forget the Nobel peace prize. If Melania can do something about her husband, I’m crowning her Michigan’s Woman of the Year.Bad news for US women trying to manage menopause symptomsLast November, the FDA announced that menopausal hormone therapy medications would no longer require a scary “black-box” label on them, which is the highest safety-related warning a medication can have. This reassured a lot of women about the treatment and caused a surge in demand. Supply didn’t keep up, and there’s been a shortage of estrogen patches in the USall yearbecause of an uptick in demand. Now Reutersreportsthat the shortage has spread beyond estrogen patches “with some injectable and vaginal estrogen products also in short supply”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Week in PatriarchyGet Arwa Mahdawi’s weekly recap of the most important stories on feminism and sexism and those fighting for equalityEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDolores Huerta, labor leader and civil rights champion, dies aged 96Huerta co-founded the United Farm Workers union (UFW), which improved conditions for agricultural workers in the 1960s and 1970s. She isalso creditedwith coining the phrase “Sí, se puede!” (yes, we can), which was UFW’s slogan and then Barack Obama’s 2008 campaign rally cry.Kamala Harris advises Democrats not to impeach Trump if they win House and Senate“I think that going in the direction of impeachment is not a good idea,” Harris said in aMeidasTouch interview. “I was in the Senate for the last go-round, and the votes aren’t there.” In other words: don’t hold your breath that Trump will face immediate accountability if the Democrats dominate the midterms.Egypt continues crackdown on press freedom and fines editor Lina AttalahAttalah is the editor-in-chief of Madr Masar, an independent Egyptian news site that has frequently been critical of the Egyptian president Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi’s government. The government recently accused her of running a website without a license, detained her, andshut down Mada Masr. The crackdown “can only mean that Egypt’s security agencies are moving from years of harassing independent media to wiping them out completely”, one expert told the Guardian.The toxic legacy of body positivity“We are living through a strange time in the language around bodies,” writes Hannah Marriottin the Guardian. The body positivity era is over, but “much of its social training lingers.” Thanks to the GLP-1 boom, everyone is shrinking, but it’s taboo to talk about it. “What we’re left with is a world in which skinny bodies are lionized in fashion, culture and daily life, but to either admit a desire to conform, or express concern about it, feels socially verboten.”Queer romance is dead: Chrishell Stause and G Flip have broken upYou may be familiar with thisviral tweet: “I’m 50. All celebrity news looks like this: ‘Curtains for Zoosha? K-smog and Batboy caught flipping a grunt.’” I am still a mere 43, but I had my own curtains for Zoosha moment this week when I saw the headlines about G Flip, which I could have sworn was a watch. If you are similarly confused, Rebecca Shaw has anexplaineras to why some of the queer community are in mourning.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsMelania TrumpThe Week in PatriarchyUkraineDonald TrumpWomenKamala HarrisDemocratsEgyptcommentShareReuse this content

title: Relying on AI is rotting your brain. But here’s what you can do about it | Carly Dober | The Guardian
description: Each new tech product is designed to make our lives easier and keep us mindlessly entertained. Switch off: embrace discomfort – and boredom, says psychologist Carly Dober
Author: Carly Dober
Headline: Each new tech product is designed to make our lives easier and keep us mindlessly entertained. Switch off: embrace discomfort – and boredom, says psychologist Carly Dober
Content: A humanoid robot walk past a protest outside an OpenAI developers’ conference in San Francisco, California, 29 September 2026.Photograph: Heather Diehl/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA humanoid robot walk past a protest outside an OpenAI developers’ conference in San Francisco, California, 29 September 2026.Photograph: Heather Diehl/Getty ImagesOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)Relying on AI is rotting your brain. But here’s what you can do about itCarly DoberEach new tech product is designed to make our lives easier and keep us mindlessly entertained. Switch off: embrace discomfort – and boredomSat 31 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 12.20 EDTShareEver longed for your own personal assistant? In the ever quickening tech race, Meta has recently launched Muse, anew AI personal agent. Unlike traditional chatbots, this little AI tool will be able to fill out forms for you, organise calendars, pay bills and make reservations. Meta describes Muse as a personal agent “built for everyone”. The launch comes at a time when AI agents have been making headlines for hacking intogovernment websites,public agenciesand businesses. However, my immediate concern is a little closer to home.I work as a psychologist, and I’m often talking to clients about lifestyle habits that lead to short-term gain but incur long-term pain. Our brains have a beautiful way of preferring the path of least resistance, of doing what is easiest to preserve our resources. And with the demands of modern life feeling so overwhelming for so many people, the urge to scroll after a long week or defer to a chatbot because you are exhausted is incredibly seducing.Tech bros pushing their products on to us is nothing new (we all rememberthe metaverse, right?), but the message is now seemingly at fever pitch for mass AI adoption and how integral it is for human development. It is helpful to remind ourselves what we are being asked to give up, to whom and why, and to consider the potential risks before we hand over our precious data.Some technology, such as large language models (LLMs) and social media that has an infinite scroll algorithm, seem to have a dose effect: too much reliance on this technology can lead to particular cognitive biases being activated, brain chemistry beingdepleted, moods andmental health being affected, and evenneurological skillsbeing atrophied, to name but a few of the documented risks.Overusing artificial intelligence affects the brain and learning by bypassing the mental effort required to build deep neural connections, a process known as cognitive offloading. Frequent AI use fosters a passive acceptance of information, reducing the internal friction and inquiry that drive genuine curiosity and problem-solving. The brain depends on mental struggle and overcoming failure to rewire and strengthen our neural pathways. Bypassing that friction reduces our overall cognitive reserve over time.Our tendency to favour or give greater credence to information supplied by technology (such as ChatGPT or Claude), and to ignore a manual source of information that provides contradictory information (a textbook, for example) even if it is correct, illustrates the phenomenon of automation bias. Automation complacency is closely linked – an overlapping concept that refers to the monitoring of technology with less frequency or vigilance because of a lower suspicion of error and a stronger belief in its accuracy, even when we know that LLMs often generate inaccurate answers.Social media is designed to be so addictive because its business model relies on maximising user attention, while people give up their privacy because the immediate psychological rewards outweigh the abstract risk of data exposure. Most people say they value their privacy, but their behaviour says otherwise. This contradiction is known in behavioural economics as theprivacy paradox.Digital tools make life incredibly convenient – you can order a car with the touch of a button, a hot meal can be delivered to your door, and you can order and return outfits without ever exchanging a word with another person. People gladly trade their location data, contacts and browsing history in exchange for free maps, personalised shopping recommendations and seamless communication. Many individuals falsely believe that because they aren’t committing crimes, their data isn’t valuable. They don’t realise that aggregate data is used to manipulate purchasing habits, influence political votes and predict private life events.Privacy policies are also intentionally long and confusing, and written in dense legal language that is inaccessible to the vast majority of users. Users face “consent fatigue” and simply click “Accept all” whenever the pesky window pops up while they are browsing because they feel they have no real choice.There is a way out of the muck, though. Become more discerning about what information you share online; consider turning your location off unless you’re using navigation apps; reject cookies tracking you; hell, even start to poison your data if you really want to engage in some online anarchy. Does the online store you bought a T-shirt from once really need to know your full legal name and date of birth?To avoid AI overreliance, you need to startintroducing “friction”into your days – deliberate obstacles that break the automatic loop of seeking instant gratification. From a psychological perspective, AI is highly addictive because it eliminates this friction, offering immediate rewards with zero cognitive effort – and our brains need cognitive effort to remain sharp. Every time you try to work out a problem or read a book instead of the comments section, that is your brain doing a push-up.If you’re struggling to rein in your social media or AI usage, a good way to start is by logging out of online sessions. Forcing yourself to manually type your credentials every time creates a massive psychological barrier. Also, try restricting your AI usage strictly to a desktop or laptop computer: removing ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini from your phone eliminates the urge to use it while walking, lying in bed or waiting in line. Scrolling on our phones or talking to a chatbot impedes much of the necessary mind-wandering time that our brains need to function at their best.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMeta releases Muse Spark Open, a new ‘open-weight’ AI modelRead moreWhen you feel the urge to ask an AI a question or have it write something for you, force yourself to wait about 30 minutes. Use this time to brainstorm, look at a book or simply sit with the problem. Often the urge passes or you solve the problem yourself. Commit to writing the first draft of any email, letter or presentation entirely by yourself. Embrace the discomfort of maybe getting things wrong. Instead of asking an AI for a recommendation or an explanation, ask a friend or colleague, or check a reputable website. The delay in waiting for a human response builds patience, and we need to practise this skill in order to retain it.Dedicate specific hours of your day to completely screen-free activities. Read books, write with pen and paper or go for a walk without your phone and see how differently things feel for you after six weeks of consistent effort. Intentionally building friction into the frictionless online experience is hard – but I promise that your brain will thank you for it.Carly Dober is a psychologist living and working in MelbourneExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionSocial mediaMetacommentShareReuse this content

title: Nigel’s ‘chiselled cheekbones’ make the news – Reform’s the Reformer, digested by John Crace | Nigel Farage | The Guardian
description: Editor, agony uncle, crossword compiler – he even interviews himself. Our sketchwriter finds there’s no end to Farage’s talents
Author: John Crace
Headline: Editor, agony uncle, crossword compiler – he even interviews himself. Our sketchwriter finds there’s no end to Farage’s talents
Content: Nigel Farage: ‘Let me  introduce you to the team. There’s me, Nigel.’Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenNigel Farage: ‘Let me  introduce you to the team. There’s me, Nigel.’Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianDigested readNigel FarageNigel’s ‘chiselled cheekbones’ make the news – Reform’s the Reformer, digested by John CraceEditor, agony uncle, crossword compiler – he even interviews himself. Our sketchwriter finds there’s no end to Farage’s talentsJohn CraceSat 31 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTHE REFORMERWelcome toyour new super, soaraway Reformer. The paper that aims to take you back to the 1950s with all the stories that the mainstream media don’t want you to read. Free to all patriots. And those who happen to have found a copy on the floor of the bus.A message from the editor, Nigel FarageWe are living in dangerous times. The chances of finding an immigrant ahead of you in the supermarket checkout queue have never been higher. Now more than ever you need a newspaper you can trust. One that isn’t afraid to tell you the truth about Broken Britain, and where you can find a grievance on every page. So let me introduce you to the Reformer team. There’s me, Nigel. I’m the editor-in-chief. And then there are seven or eight other nobodies whose names escape me. Here is my promise to you. If you are not fully satisfied with the Reformer in the first 100 days then I will sack all the people I have already forgotten.FARMING IN CRISISbyNigel Farage, agriculture editorA sensational report that has been hushed up by establishment figures linked to the European Union reveals that migrants are responsible for the failure of this summer’s harvest. The report, which has been leaked to the Reformer by a source who wishes to go by the name of Nigel, reveals that officials have tried to blame the crop failure on climate change. “It’s a total scandal,” said Nigel. “What’s been going on is that immigrants have been bringing their hot weather over to the UK with them in small boats. Global warming is a hoax perpetuated by leftwing politicians who want to encourage unlimited illegal immigration. But there’s no denying the facts. Back in the days when you seldom saw a black or brown face, British summers were much cooler. It’s time for everyone to start telling the truth.”FOREIGNERS INCREASE THE WELFARE BILLbyNigel Farage, home affairs editorIn one of the country’s biggest surveys of two families, the Reformer can exclusively report that white people much prefer to live next to white people. The families in question say their lives are being made a misery by having a man called Zia Yusuf as their next door neighbour. “It’s got nothing to do with Zia being a brown Muslim,” said Trevor Bloke. “I don’t care what colour or religion he is. What’s intolerable is that he is a deeply unpleasant person who goes out of his way to be rude to everyone. He thinks he owns the whole street. We all just wish he would leave. It’s doing my head in. I’m now on maximum Pip payments for my anxiety and I can no longer work.”HOW TO SPOT A NIGERIAN SCAMMERbyNigel Farage, consumer affairs editorWe’ve all had it. An email from someone who is clearly black. A telephone call from someone who is also clearly black. You know they are black because deep down, every black person wants to try to scam your bank account. Not a nice feeling when you’ve just been transferred£5m as a gift from a Thai-based billionaire. It’s the new something-for-nothing society. Say what you like about Oswald Mosley, but he would never have tolerated such behaviour. Now we just accept that immigrants are trying to take over our country. What is the easiest way to spot a Nigerian scammer? Just go to the House of Commons. There you will find the criminal mastermind. A woman called Kemi. She claims to be the leader of the opposition, but all she really wants are your credit card details.INTERVIEW OF THE MONTH: NIGEL FARAGEOur features editor,Nigel Farage, interviewsNigel Farage. With additional reporting byNigel FarageIt’s late afternoon in autumn. The sun streams through the window, its rays dancing off Nigel’s chiselled cheekbones. Nigel is at his most relaxed, mainly because he has just sent his valet, Richard Tice, to the off-licence for a third bottle of champagne. He smiles kindly at me. Reform are well ahead in the polls in third place and he is busy putting the finishing touches to his first speech as prime minister. “Tell me, Nigel,” I say. “Why is it that God has sent you down into the world to save Great Britain from all the illegal immigrants? Please can you also talk me through your magnificentbyelection victory against a comedian with a bin on his head?”Continues for another 1,500 words …HARRY’S GOLDEN BOOTSbyNigel Farage, football editorIn a stunning triumph for Brexit Britain, England’s Harry Kane has seen off countless other black and foreign footballers to becrowned the world’s best footballerin a glittering Ballon d’Or ceremony in London. Speaking exclusively to Reform, Kane’s best friend, Nigel Farage, said: “It’s about time a white Englishman won this. Harry would never have been able to do this if we hadn’t left the European Union. Just think what might have happened if footballers had freedom of movement. Harry might have ended up playing for some deadbeat team like Bayern Munich. Then he would have remained an unknown. So, really, Harry owes it all to me.”THE READERS’ CHAMPIONbyNigel Farage, agony uncleDear Nigel, I recently got married and it should have been the happiest day of my life. Instead it became the worst. First,discovered that the man who had promised me he was rich enough to be worth divorcing my first husband for had only boughtpremiumeconomy seats for our honeymoon in the US. Then I discovered that British Airways – a disgrace of a national carrier – had deliberately delayed the departure of our plane to maximise our inconvenience and thenlost an item of luggage. My husband, Thicky Dicky, as I affectionately call him, yelled: “Don’t you know who I am?” and the person on the desk said: “We know exactly who you are.” Pleasehelp us seek redress. Yours, Isabel Oakeshott, DubaiDear Isabel, I am sorry to hear your distressing story. Please send me £80 and I will do a Cameo video calling for every foreign-looking baggage handler at Heathrow to be sacked. PS: BA is now owned by a private Spanish company.RACIST OF THE MONTHbyNigel Farage, competitions’ editorCall 0800 001 for Tommy Robinson who has recently been foundguilty of harassing journalistsin a massive miscarriage of justice.Call 0800 002 for cheeky chappy Raheem Kassam, who asked the Guardian to correct a sketch that said he had deleted a racist tweet.Calls will cost £5 plus normal charges. Winners will receive something worthless in bitcoin.BOOK OF THE MONTHbyNigel Farage, literary editorMy Struggle, by Nigel Farage.In which the Reform leader hilariously recounts the ways hemade antisemitic remarks in front of Jewish boysat school on his way to becoming the most consequential politician of the last 200 years.‘Almost as good as Liz Truss’s Bank Job’ – the GuardianPOTHOLE OF THE MONTHbyNigel Farage, transport editorIn the first of an ongoing series, Nigel Farage,discusses his favourite pothole and how he got it filled. “There was this fantastic pothole near my house in Kent,” he said. “We filled it up with loads of dead immigrants and the rubber of small boats the navy had sunk in the Channel.” Doing good with a smile on your face. That’s the Reform way.TRAVEL NEWSbyNigel Farage, the Reformer’s eye-in-the-skyAvoid travelling on the M6 north of Birmingham. Traffic is at a standstill due to too many foreigners driving on English roads. It’s a nightmare. And I can promise you that I will stop all immigrants driving when I become prime minister.TV LISTINGSbyNigel Farage, media editor1. Anything from GB News.2. ITV:a charming documentaryin which almost everyone at Reform HQ is found to be racist.3. Channel 4: a brilliant drama in which Farage and friends pretend they are trying to take illegal donations. With hilarious consequences for everyone.CRYPTIC CROSSWORD CLUEcompiled byNigel FarageRobert Jenrick confused Newark MP (6 letters, anag. Beginning with W)Explore more on these topicsNigel FarageDigested readReform UKNewspapersNewspapers & magazinesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: More than 50m Americans cast ballots in early voting with three days to go before midterms | US midterm elections 2026 | The Guardian
description: Record number of early votes cast, with Democrats outnumbering Republicans in states which collect that information
Author: Oliver Milman
Headline: Record number of early votes cast, with Democrats outnumbering Republicans in states which collect that information
Content: A man in Fairfax, Virginia, casts an early vote on 31 October 2026.Photograph: Jim Lo Scalzo/EPAView image in fullscreenA man in Fairfax, Virginia, casts an early vote on 31 October 2026.Photograph: Jim Lo Scalzo/EPAUS midterm elections 2026More than 50m Americans cast ballots in early voting with three days to go before midtermsRecord number of early votes cast, with Democrats outnumbering Republicans in states which collect that informationOliver Milmanand agenciesSat 31 Oct 2026 12.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere has been a surge of early voting for the US midterm elections, with millions more Americans going to the polls compared with the last such election amid a series of tight contests that will determine control of Congress.More than 50.5m early votes have been cast across the US as of Saturday morning,according to an analysis by the University of Florida. This is already nearly 5m more votes than the total number of early votes made in the last midterm elections, in 2022.Voter enthusiasm for Tuesday’s election appears to be strongest among Democrats, with 10.7 million registered Democrats having voted so far, according to the states that collate such information, compared with 7.8 million registeredRepublicans.Affordability, AI and Iran: Americans on the key issues guiding their midterm votesRead moreThese party affiliations are not indicative of actual votes cast but polling has shown widespread unhappiness with the presidency of Donald Trump and unusually close races in states usually won comfortably by Republicans.Republicans are defending a 53-47 Senate majority in a midterm election in which the battleground map has expanded significantly, withDemocratsaiming to pull off victories in traditionally conservative-leaning states such as Texas, Alaska and even Kansas that could allow them to take control of the Senate.In Texas, a state central to Democratic ambitions, more than 7 million people have already voted early, University of Florida data shows. This is already 1.5 million more people than the number who voted early in the state during the 2022 midterms.In Harris county, which includes Houston, 862,700 people had voted as of Wednesday,an Associated Press analysis found, compared with 564,500 at the same point in 2022.The surge comes in a county that has reliably voted Democratic in recent elections, though by varying margins. In 2024, Kamala Harris defeated Trump there by nearly 6% in the presidential contest, while Democratic Senate candidate Colin Allred carried the county by roughly 11% over the Republican incumbent senator Ted Cruz.This year, the state’s Republican attorney general, Ken Paxton, faces Democrat James Talarico ina closely watched Senate race, while the Republican governor, Greg Abbott, is seeking re-election against Democrat Gina Hinojosa.Hundreds of millions of dollars have poured into the Senate race as Republicans fight to defend a state where Democrats have not won a statewide election in more than three decades. Trumpvisited Texasearlier this week, his third trip there in a month.In other close-fought Senate races, early voting has also increased in these midterms, according to the AP. In South Carolina, which Trump won by nearly 18% in the 2024 president election, early voting is up 83% compared with the 2022 midterms.In Kansas, where another unusually tight Senate battle is under way in a normally reliable Republican state, early voting is up 34%, while in Maine early voting is up 44%. In Michigan, the site of another key Senate race, early voting is up 32%.The midterms will decide the composition of the US House of Representatives and Senate for the final two years of Trump’s second term, with the rising costs of food, gasoline and other essentials, as well as the Iran war and concern over government corruption, forming the backdrop to the voting.Trump, weighed down by deep unpopularity among voters, has sought to boost struggling Republican candidates with rallies held across various previously safe states. This effort has included the US president commenting repeatedly on the physical appearance of candidates and dismissing alarm over rising gasoline costs as secondary to the profits of fossil fuel companies.Trump hinted at the toil of this effort at a rally in Florida on Friday night. “I thought this was it,” he said. “I thought I could relax. Twenty-eight days of this crap in a row is a lot. It’s a lot.”Explore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026DemocratsRepublicansUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Railway engineering work over Christmas will cause 10 days of disruption | Rail industry | The Guardian
description: London Paddington and Birmingham New Street stations will shut for five days but most routes will stay open
Author: Gwyn Topham
Headline: London Paddington and Birmingham New Street stations will shut for five days but most routes will stay open
Content: The biggest work is expected on lines leading into London Paddington, including replacing a junction near Slough.Photograph: Bloomberg/GettyView image in fullscreenThe biggest work is expected on lines leading into London Paddington, including replacing a junction near Slough.Photograph: Bloomberg/GettyRail industryRailway engineering work over Christmas will cause 10 days of disruptionLondon Paddington and Birmingham New Street stations will shut for five days but most routes will stay openGwyn TophamTransport correspondentSat 31 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePassengers travelling on some of Great Britain’s busiest railway lines atChristmashave been warned of significant disruption from 10 days of engineering works.Work will close London’s Paddington station – affecting intercity trains to the west of England and Wales until January – as well asBirminghamNew Street, the UK’s busiest station outside the capital, for five days over the holiday period.Passengers travelling betweenLondon, north-east England and Scotland will have to negotiate the part closure of the east coast mainline on Christmas Eve. Direct trains from the capital to parts of Essex and Norfolk will also be cut for much of the festive period.Network Rail said most routes would still stay open and that the Christmas period, when train services generally stop for 25 and 26 December, remained the best time to conduct essential works.Engineers hope to use the quieter festive days to carry out about £152m of works to improve reliability and capacity.The biggest engineering work is expected on the lines leading into London Paddington, including replacing a junction near Slough. Most Great Western services toWalesand the west of England will start and finish at Reading, with some services diverting around Oxford to London Euston, from 27 December until 4 January.Stratford International on track to get cross-Channel trains in budget boostRead moreThe work also means Elizabeth line services west of Paddington and Heathrow Express services will not resume after Christmas until 31 January.Birmingham’s main station, New Street, will be closed from the start of Christmas Eve until 29 December to replace overhead power supplies. No trains will stop or pass through, with rail replacement buses serving the city centre.Passengers using east coast mainline services run by LNER and other operators may wish to avoid travel on Christmas Eve. Work at Doncaster means trains between London, north-east England and Scotland will be partly replaced by rail replacement buses from Newark to York, adding two hours to journeys.The Great Eastern mainline out of London Liverpool Street will be closed for 10 days from Christmas Day for track replacement in east London, meaning no Greater Anglia or Elizabeth line rains will run through the area, with no direct trains from Norwich to London.TransPennine services between Leeds and Manchester will be slowed for six weeks from Christmas Day with the closure of Huddersfield station.Network Rail’s group director, system operator, Anit Chandarana, said: “Christmas is a time when many people want to be with family and friends, and most of the railway will be open to help them get there. We have worked with train operators to keep services running wherever we can on the busiest travel days and to provide alternative journey options where work affects the usual route.“We are sorry that some passengers will face disruption. The days between Christmas and new year are by far the quietest of the year and give us the best opportunity to complete major projects such as the power supply upgrades at Birmingham and Paddington. Our teams will do everything they can to keep people moving, and we urge passengers to check their journeys before setting off.”Explore more on these topicsRail industryNetwork RailRail transportTransportLondonBirminghamWalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Starmer says UK must get closer to Europe as US relationship changes | Keir Starmer | The Guardian
description: Shift in dealings with Washington not likely to reset once Trump leaves Oval Office, former PM says
Author: Kevin Rawlinson
Headline: Shift in dealings with Washington not likely to reset once Trump leaves Oval Office, former PM says
Content: ‘A stronger Europe is vital and the UK must be at the heart of it,’ Starmer said.Photograph: ITV via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘A stronger Europe is vital and the UK must be at the heart of it,’ Starmer said.Photograph: ITV via Getty ImagesKeir StarmerStarmer says UK must get closer to Europe as US relationship changesShift in dealings with Washington not likely to reset once Trump leaves Oval Office, former PM saysKevin RawlinsonSat 31 Oct 2026 09.32 EDTFirst published on Sat 31 Oct 2026 09.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK and other European nations must draw closer together as the US becomes a less-reliable partner,Keir Starmerhas said in his first significant political intervention since leaving No 10.The former prime minister warned European leaders of the threat posed by Russia, among others, and said the shift in relations with Washington during Donald Trump’s presidency was not likely to reset once he leaves the Oval Office. He accused them of being caught out by these new realities twice already.“A strongerEuropeis vital and the UK must be at the heart of it,” Starmer told an audience at the British Irish Chamber of Commerce on Friday. “Europe has twice been caught asleep, failing to anticipate and prepare for predictable events.“First, whenRussia’s attack on Ukraineexposed longstanding European weaknesses on defence and security, and second, when President Trump made clear, once and for all, that the US will no longer bankroll our European security. We have to catch up.”Starmer had called for closer European ties beforestepping down as prime ministerin July. Three months earlier, amid Trump’s war with Iran and his threats to withdraw from Nato, Starmer said Europe represented a “partnership for a dangerous world we must navigate together”.He said those ties should go further than just defence, adding that Brexit had done “deep damage” to the UK economy, and that he wanted to be “more ambitious”, including pursuing “closer economic cooperation [and] closer security cooperation”.View image in fullscreenKeir Starmer alongside the US president, Donald Trump, at the Nato leaders’ summit in Ankara, Turkey in July.Photograph: Yves Herman/ReutersStarmer spoke after spending time in Dublin meeting senior business leaders and politicians, including the taoiseach, Micheál Martin, with whom he established the annual UK-Ireland summit.“I will say here what I have said to European leaders. This is about responding to a permanent change of affairs, not an aberration of the Trump presidency. Things will not go back to the way they were before.“That doesn’t mean the US relationship is no longer important. On the contrary, the military, security and intelligence alliance is far too strong for that. But it does mean enabling Europe to take on far more responsibility for its own defence and security.”His comments reflect a growing consensus on the left of UK politics that closer ties with Europe are essential to ensure economic and military security. Soon after taking office as Starmer’s successor,Andy Burnhamsaid that he intended to be “bolder” about closer ties with the EU.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAs Trump fans the flames of a world on fire, can diplomacy take back control?Read moreNext month,Burnham will attend a crucial EU-UK summitwhere new agreements on food standards, energy and youth mobility will be the main focus.Burnham has also saidhe wants a public debate on how the UK could move to a closer relationship with the EUafter the next election. At a meeting of European defence ministers in Paris this week, the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said that they were “united and unwavering” in support for Ukraine in the face of Russian hostility.Starmer said: “We need to build up pan-European cooperation and coordination on defence and security – a common security framework as much as a common market. The EU is changing to respond to that, but it cannot be the EU alone when Europe’s periphery is core to its defence.“Britain must be central to that project. We are one of two nuclear powers. We are a leadingNatomember. We have a viable next-generation fighter jet programme. And we are pledged to work alongside European allies to guarantee security in Ukraine.“Ireland and the UK stand side by side in the coalition of the willing and with Ukraine, working together to guarantee and shape the security of our continent. I hope and believe that Britain’s relationship with its friends and allies can and should be strengthened by this urgent and common security project.”Explore more on these topicsKeir StarmerEuropeEuropean UnionDonald TrumpForeign policyDefence policyNatonewsShareReuse this content

title: Florid language and long silences: five things we learned from week three of Russell Brand’s rape trial | UK news | The Guardian
description: The former comedian and his wife gave evidence in the case in which he denies all charges against him
Author: Emine Sinmaz
Headline: The former comedian and his wife gave evidence in the case in which he denies all charges against him
Content: Russell and Laura Brand arriving at court for the start of the third week of his trial.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAView image in fullscreenRussell and Laura Brand arriving at court for the start of the third week of his trial.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAUK newsFlorid language and long silences: five things we learned from week three of Russell Brand’s rape trialThe former comedian and his wife gave evidence in the case in which he denies all charges against himEmine SinmazSat 31 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 04.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRussell Brand’s trial at Southwark crown court began with widespread media coverage on 12 October. The former comedian and presenter faces three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of attempted indecent assault against six women, in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999. He denies all the charges. Here are five things we learned in the third week of his trial.1.Russell Brand’s evidenceBrand, 51, who wasin the witness boxfor four hours on Wednesday, told the jury the criminal case had been a “deeply traumatic episode” in his life.He blamed his public fall from grace on 2023 media reports, including a Channel 4 Dispatches documentary, about his alleged sexual misconduct. He said he had achieved “staggering fame” after his marriage to the US pop star Katy Perry but that now nobody would “touch [him] with a bargepole”.The prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones KC, suggested he hadn’t been “abandoned” by everyone he knows, and noted he had millions of followers online. “This is not the case of poor Mr Brand being taken apart by the media,” she said.Brand denied her suggestion that consent had not been “uppermost” in his mind between 1999 and 2009, telling the court: “Consent is absolutely non-negotiable.” He said he was “innocent” of all the charges and added: “Consent is fundamental, essential, necessary and, indeed, in many ways more important than sex itself.”Brand admitted he waswrong to have used his fameand success to “facilitate” sexual activity with women. “I think I was in a position of fame, a successful person who was admired, and I misused that commodity very selfishly,” he said.2.Laura Brand’s evidenceBrand’s wife, Laura, began her evidence on Thursday by confirming she is the TV presenter Kirsty Gallacher’s sister, and that they are the daughters of the Ryder Cup-winning golfer Bernard Gallacher.She told the court she and Brand fell in love after meeting in 2006 but that the comedian had cheated on her early in their relationship.“I wasn’t interested in having a relationship with him if he was sleeping with other people. I was invested, we both had told each other we loved each other, but it was clear it was difficult for him to be monogamous,” Laura Brand said.They broke up in February 2007 but restarted their relationship in 2015 and married two years later. Laura Brand insisted he was a “wonderful father” and an “amazingly attentive husband”. “We have a very frank, honest and clear relationship and marriage,” she said.During cross-examination by Karmy-Jones, Laura agreed that Brand has a channel on the video-sharing platform Rumble, presents at political conferences and was baptised in early 2024 after the sexual misconduct allegations emerged.3.Brand’s demeanour in courtBrand has remained still during the trial, but he was animated during his wife’s evidence, and could be seen smiling and laughing at times. He appeared to be mouthing words towards her as she talked about his 2024 baptism and nodding when she spoke of their friendship.He also showed more emotion during his evidence. With his hands behind his back, he began by giving confident answers in a booming voice to his barrister, Ian Winter KC. “Mr Brand, that is nice and loud,” the judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, said. Brand also used florid language such as “badinage”, “loquacious” and “coquettishness”.But there was a marked shift in the comedian’s demeanour during cross-examination, which was punctuated with pauses and long spells of silence. There was a long pause after the prosecution’s first question: “You blame Dispatches, don’t you?”, and again when Karmy-Jones repeated the question.4.Confronted by his own contentBrand was confronted with extracts from his 2007 book, My Booky Wook, and his comments in media appearances.The first alleged rape victim had told the court she believed Brand was gay and effeminate when they first met at a 1999 Labour party conference fringe event, leading to her agreeing for him to come to her hotel room.The prosecutor pointed out that in his book, Brand used a picture of himself as a seven-year-old and wrote the caption: “This is the exact moment when I decided to act gay to attract girls. It took 15 years to produce results.”Karmy-Jones read out another in which Brand wrote: “My egotism and the single-mindedness with which I pursued potentially sexual conquests could often make me uneasy company.”In another he set out: “Now if I want something – whether it’s a job or a woman – I will determinedly, resolutely, remove anything that’s in the way, until I possess the object of my desire.”In the book, Brand referred to himself as a “fervid, febrile mass of sexual energy” towards the end of sex, adding: “I’ll do anything. I’m demonically sexy.”5.Closing speeches and next weekThe prosecutor gave her closing speech on Friday, telling jurors that the six women who had come forward to accuse Brand did not know one another and had nothing to gain.“There is no benefit to them, apart from perhaps some closure by coming before you and telling you their accounts of what happened to them so long ago,” Karmy-Jones told the jury.“What’s happened, we suggest, is these women have realised they’re not alone and they’ve bravely come before you to tell you the truth. The truth of what happened to them so many years ago. The truth they have lived with, which in some cases has haunted them for years.”Brand’s barrister is expected to make his closing speech when the trial resumes on Monday.Explore more on these topicsUK newsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: How ‘sin bin’ for red light jumpers saves cyclists from being saddled with a fine | Cycling | The Guardian
description: Police scheme in City of London offers errant cyclists a choice – watch a roadside safety video or pay a £50 penalty
Author: George Francis Lee
Headline: Police scheme in City of London offers errant cyclists a choice – watch a roadside safety video or pay a £50 penalty
Content: Cyclists in the 'sin bin' after jumping a red light.Photograph: City of London policeView image in fullscreenCyclists in the 'sin bin' after jumping a red light.Photograph: City of London policeCyclingHow ‘sin bin’ for red light jumpers saves cyclists from being saddled with a finePolice scheme in City of London offers errant cyclists a choice – watch a roadside safety video or pay a £50 penaltyGeorge Francis LeeSat 31 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 11.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Aman cycled through a red light in the City ofLondonthis week, he was surprised when the police pulled him over. He was positively shocked when, instead of giving him a fine, officers took him into a gazebo to watch a bike safety film.Aman was one of 30 cyclists caught in the first 20 minutes that morning, as part of a new scheme by City of London police to dissuade cyclists from running red lights.Many concerned pedestrians have celebrated the time-out zone and, perhaps more surprisingly, cyclists have too.The new pop-up scheme, called “stop, look, listen, change”, gives offending riders the chance to view an educational film about the dangers of red light jumping. Those caught by police who do not want to pay a £50 fine are taken to a “sin bin” by the roadside, where they watch testimonies from visually impaired road users.“It is about taking that time away,” said Rob McTaggart, media and engagement manager at City of London police. “Time they didn’t stay waiting for the light is now the time they’re having to spend watching the video. It’s a bit of instant justice in that regard.”As cyclists continued to be corralled into the time-out zone, McTaggart said the police team had noticed no difference between the numbers of red light runners on hired e-bikes versus those on regular bicycles.When the sin bin was first launched two weeks ago, roughly 70 people were brought in within 90 minutes, McTaggart said. None of the halted riders opted to take the fine.Watching the safety film, McTaggart said, was useful for spreading road education.“Right now you can jump on a bike without any training whatsoever,” he said. “It’s about that understanding that just because you can go, it doesn’t mean you should go. We’re not going to enforce our way out of it.”View image in fullscreenCity of London police officers monitoring cyclists.Photograph: City of London policeSgt Stuart Ford, who helped create the scheme, said it was inspired by theExchanging Places initiative, where cyclists are brought into large goods vehicles to understand risks like blind spots and difficulties in manoeuvring.Ford said he was sympathetic to cyclists – “You can quote me: I like bikes” – but added that police “get more complaints than anything else in the city around cyclists jumping lights and their behaviour”. He added: “I’m afraid to say it but a lot of the time, the cyclist is the protagonist here.”Ford collaborated with theNational Federation of the Blind UK (NFBUK)to understand how vulnerable road users are affected by riders skipping lights or riding on the pavement.Hyacinth Malcolm, who is fully blind, said: “I’m just lost for words as to why they [cyclists] are behaving the way they’re behaving.”Malcolm said she had to rethink before going out for a daily coffee because of the risk of cyclists colliding with her.Sarah Leadbetter, a disability activist with visual impairments, also said the footways were not safe for disabled people and that things were getting worse.She said she relied on a cane, her guide dog and the rotating cone at pedestrian crossings – a small, unassuming plastic or metal cone which is attached to the underside of the push-button unit.But, she said, she could not be certain of her safety because cyclists “suddenly come through the red light and go straight into you”.McTaggart said the scheme had sparked discussions across the country and that there was a “huge appetite for what we’re doing here”. In the last week, pedestrians have complained of cyclists riding through the recently pedestrianised Oxford Street.Sarah Gayton, street access campaign coordinator from NFBUK, commended the new education scheme, but hoped to see the fine increased to £300 and further action taken by the government. “Something has got to give,” she said. “We need designs that work for everybody.”While some have pitted cyclists and pedestrians against each other, Tom Fyans, CEO of the charity LondonCyclingCampaign, said he also wanted to see more changes in London’s road designs to better suit all road users.View image in fullscreenTom Fyans, CEO of London Cycling Campaign: ‘London isn’t designed for cycling.’Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianStanding at the busy junction of Old Street roundabout in the east of the capital, he said: “London isn’t designed for cycling, it’s getting better, but it’s designed for cars. What we need to see is far more cycle-friendly, pedestrian-friendly designs where the car is less important. Then you’ll see a much safer environment for everybody.”On the new scheme, Fyans said his charity supported the measures over what he believed to be ineffective monetary penalties. He said: “Punishing cyclists with fines and criminal prosecutions, it doesn’t really work. But getting them to think about their impact on other road users – hearts and minds – is much better.”Fyans said most cyclists do follow the Highway Code, but that a focus on bicycle users was “disproportionate” and a result of the rising number of bike users on London’s roads.“I think there’s double standards quite often,” he said. “We’re not the biggest danger. It’s cars and speeding and drivers not paying attention that kill people on our roads. That’s the biggest challenge that needs addressing.”Fyans, who works with Wheels for Wellbeing – a cycling disability group – said he understood the dangers for visually impaired pedestrians and wheelchair users.But can relations between cyclists and pedestrians be improved? “Let’s address it, but let’s be proportionate about what the real problem is,” he said. “Cyclists are not really the main problem on the road when it comes to danger.”Explore more on these topicsCyclingRoad safetyLondonBlindness and visual impairmentDisabilityfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Healey to veto new offshore wind projects if they will not lower bills | Renewable energy | The Guardian
description: UK chancellor’s plans add to concerns government is moving away from pro-renewables agenda
Author: Sammy Gecsoyler
Headline: UK chancellor’s plans add to concerns government is moving away from pro-renewables agenda
Content: The shift towards renewable energy ‘has to come at the right pace, in the right places, with the grid to carry it’, Healey said.Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAView image in fullscreenThe shift towards renewable energy ‘has to come at the right pace, in the right places, with the grid to carry it’, Healey said.Photograph: Ben Birchall/PARenewable energyHealey to veto new offshore wind projects if they will not lower billsUK chancellor’s plans add to concerns government is moving away from pro-renewables agendaSammy GecsoylerSat 31 Oct 2026 07.48 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 08.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJohn Healey has said he will veto new offshore wind projects if they will not lower bills, adding to concerns that the government is moving away from the pro-renewables agenda.Announcing his plans, the chancellor said clean power is “how we break the grip of international gas prices on our bills”, but added the shift towards it “has to come at the right pace, in the right places, with the grid to carry it”.New offshore wind projects lodging bids for subsidy contracts will only get signed off by ministers if they believe that all the power generated could be accommodated by Britain’s electricity grid without pushing up costs for consumers.Writing in the Times, he said: “There’s no sense building power that can’t connect and then paying to switch it off. We will take that approach into our next renewables auction, only buying projects that can lower bills while strengthening our energy security.”The move appears to be a further shift away from Labour’s target of having clean power by 2030, afterHealey revealed more than £3bn worth of cuts to the energy department’s budgetin the budget, much of which will pay for higher defence spending.The cuts caused alarm among renewables experts, who warned they meant that Britain was unlikely to hit its targets on green heating, and were seen as a dismantling of former energy secretary Ed Miliband’s green agenda.There is concern in government that wasted wind charges could add to energy bills, with the NationalEnergySystem Operator (Neso), which is funded through energy bills, being forced to pay wind turbines to switch off when there is not sufficient cabling capacity to transmit their power to consumers.A National Audit Office report in September warned that homes and businesses could be faced with a potential annual bill of £7.8bn by 2030 to deal with the issue.Healey appeared to preemptively address criticism of the plans. He said: “This is not a retreat from clean power. It is the credible route to it. Cheaper electricity will make it easier for businesses and households to electrify, strengthening our energy security and helping us decarbonise the wider economy.”He added that “without the renewable generation added in recent years”, this year’s gas price shock “would have hit families and firms even harder.“Those who want to rip up renewables would leave Britain more exposed to volatile markets and the dictators who exploit them.”One casualty of the cuts announced in the budget was a reduction in the amount of money available for the government’sscheme to subsidise heat pumps, leading to warnings that clean heating ambitions were being undermined.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUnder the scheme, a typical household can claim £7,500 towards a heat pump, with about 60,000 a year being fitted in existing homes. The government has a target to raise that to 250,000 a year by 2030, andwas planningto increase the scheme’s funding from £400m this year to just over £700m by 2029-30.Some believe the cuts, much of which will pay for higher defence spending, are evidence of a broader shift away from the pro-renewables agenda pushed by Miliband and his successor,Miatta Fahnbulleh. Allies of Miliband and Fahnbulleh insisted the government’s green agenda remained as strong as ever, pointing out that Healey also announced a long-term move to shift green costs away from bills and on to taxpayers – something the two energy secretaries have both championed.Healey announced on Wednesday that the government would fund the defence investment plan in part through cuts to other departments.Much of that will come from the energy department, including £741m from the boiler upgrade scheme, the government’s plan to incentivise people to replace their gas boilers with electric heat pumps.Explore more on these topicsRenewable energyJohn HealeyWind powerEnergynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘This is a robust recipe’: the experimental farm bucking the decline in UK birds | Birds | The Guardian
description: Allerton Project attracts abundant wildlife and its success can offers clues to reversing the sharp drop in populations
Author: Matthew Pearce
Headline: Allerton Project attracts abundant wildlife and its success can offers clues to reversing the sharp drop in populations
Content: The Allerton Project director, Alastair Leake, among the wildlife seed mix, which encourages birds to feed and nest.Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe Allerton Project director, Alastair Leake, among the wildlife seed mix, which encourages birds to feed and nest.Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The GuardianBirds‘This is a robust recipe’: the experimental farm bucking the decline in UK birdsAllerton Project attracts abundant wildlife and its success can offers clues to reversing the sharp drop in populationsMatthew PearceSat 31 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFarmer Alastair Leake is standing in a field of sprouting winter wheat, pointing at his experiment. One side was ploughed before planting, with green shoots breaking through neat rows of upturned soil. On the other, the crop was drilled directly into the earth, emerging through a messy carpet of “trash” – stems, stubble and crop residue from previous harvests.“When we’re watching to see where the birds are landing to feed, none of them are going on to the ploughed side,” says Leake, the director of the Allerton Project farm, standing on the trashy side. “They’re all coming and feeding down here.View image in fullscreenAlastair Leake stands on the ‘beetle bank’ where 1,300 beetles per sq metre make their home.Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The Guardian“That’s because that’s where the seeds, the earthworms and the insects are. On the ploughed side, they’re all buried.”It is experiments such as these that have enabled the Allerton Project to buck thedecline in farm bird populations across the UK. Farm bird abundance at Allerton has risen 145% since 1992 when monitoring began, compared with a 23% decline nationally over the same period.“This is not some study that’s been done overnight,” Leake says. “We can be fairly confident that this is a robust recipe that we’ve got here.”‘Shocking and sobering’: UK bird populations fall to lowest level on recordRead moreThe Allerton Project is a working farm and research centre on the Leicestershire-Rutland border, where farmers and scientists have spent more than three decades testing how farming can produce food while supporting wildlife.Frequently hosting farmers, policymakers and businesses, the 320-hectare “demonstration farm” uses a range of sustainable agriculture, habitat creation and landscape management methods to show how agriculture can be a part of environmental action.“I don’t want people to come here and say: ‘Oh, that’s a nice nature reserve they’ve got going there’,” Leake says of his guests. “I want them to go back on to their farms and say: ‘Do you know what, I can do that.’”View image in fullscreenThe winter feeding station helps birds through the ‘hungry gap’ of January, February and March.Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The GuardianChanges in farming practices across the UK have devastated farmland bird populations. An increase in pesticide use and a loss of suitable habitats have driven some species to extinction, according to the RSPB. But at Allerton, farm bird numbers are at their highest level since records began, with song thrush, blackbirds and linnets in particular on the rise.Leake points to a “bird table”, a channel of dedicated wildlife seed mix that splits the field. In these unkempt strips found all over the farm, kale, teasel, sorghum and millet are grown to supply seeds to birds through winter.View image in fullscreenA sign at Allerton explaining its research into sustainable farming methods, biodiversity and habitat creation.Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The Guardian“That is probably the most important thing we’ve done, [making] sure that there is food in the landscape for those birds to go and feed on,” he says. “If they manage to survive what we call the ‘hungry gap’, which is January, February, March, that means they’re ready to breed again.” Goldfinches love the teasel, he adds.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenLeake holds some of the dried wildlife seed pods that the birds feed on.Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The GuardianAdjoining the bird table is the “beetle bank”, a strip of uncultivated land planted with long, tussock-forming perennial grasses. As the grass dies down year after year, it falls over and builds a thick, fibrous blanket of dead plant material, where beetles move to hibernate.“When it warms up in the spring, they go out into the crops and they eat the pests that attack the crops,” says Leake, adding that the beetles mean the crops do not need to be sprayed with pesticides. “But also they provide insect food for birds.”View image in fullscreenThe plough field on one side and the carpet of ‘trash’ – stems, stubble and crop residue from previous harvests – on the other.Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The GuardianIn a nearby field, Leake showcases an innovation found in gardens all over the country: bird feeders. “We fill the barrel up with wheat and the birds come and feed off it in the wintertime,” says Leake. “It’s just what people do in the gardens, feeding birds and things, but we’re doing it for farmland birds instead.”The less-discussed aspect of wild bird protection is predator control. Foxes and crows, for example, can prey on eggs and chicks, sometimes holding back the recovery of vulnerable ground-nesting birds.Killing predators can be contentious.Leake says Allerton’s approach is as humane as possible, targeting predators only during nesting season, the most vulnerable time for birds. “Our approach is a much more managed one,” he says. “So we are just reducing the pressure at the critical point.”He says these measures prove it is possible to reverse the decline in wild bird populations. “We have reached the highest number [of birds] against the backdrop of the national figure continuing to go down,” he says. “This is because we’re learning how to manage the whole estate better for nature as time moves on. We come up with new ideas, we put them in place, and that is bringing nature recovery.“There’s no reason why this couldn’t be done across the whole country. No reason at all, given the right incentives for people to do it.”Explore more on these topicsBirdsAnimalsWildlifeConservationBiodiversityRural affairsLeicestershirefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Bunch of baloney’: calls grow for Cop summit reforms as countries on track to fail nature targets | Cop17 biodiversity summit | The Guardian
description: Cop17, focused on protecting nature and restoring ecosystems, concludes on Saturday with critics saying system allows ‘one idiot’ to stall progress
Author: Patrick Greenfield
Headline: Cop17, focused on protecting nature and restoring ecosystems, concludes on Saturday with critics saying system allows ‘one idiot’ to stall progress
Content: A baby orangutan is rescued after a wildfire in East Kalimantan, Indonesia. Governments are likely on track to continue their record of never having met a target in the 34-year history of the Cop convention.Photograph: Jamartin Sihite/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA baby orangutan is rescued after a wildfire in East Kalimantan, Indonesia. Governments are likely on track to continue their record of never having met a target in the 34-year history of the Cop convention.Photograph: Jamartin Sihite/AFP/Getty ImagesThe age of extinctionCop17 biodiversity summit‘Bunch of baloney’: calls grow for Cop summit reforms as countries on track to fail nature targetsCop17, focused on protecting nature and restoring ecosystems, concludes on Saturday with critics saying system allows ‘one idiot’ to stall progressSupported byAbout this contentPatrick GreenfieldSat 31 Oct 2026 08.30 EDTFirst published on Sat 31 Oct 2026 04.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCalls are growing for major reforms to UN biodiversity summits as countries fail to deliver on their promises to halt the destruction of the natural world, with governments likely on track to continue their record of never having met a target in the 34-year history of the convention.Two weeks of negotiations at biodiversity Cop17 in Yerevan, Armenia, concluded on Saturday morning with countries vowing to redouble their efforts to meet this decade’s targets, which include commitments to protect 30% of the planet for nature, restore nearly a third of Earth’s degraded ecosystems and reform $500bn (£410bn) ofenvironmentally damaging subsidies.Agreed just four years ago by nearly every government on the planet, they aim to transformhumanity’s relationship with nature. Despite progress in some areas, governments are way off track on meeting almost all of the targets.
