The UK is set to meetjust threeof the 23.After talks that ran overnight from Friday into Saturday morning, countries signed off several measures, including acommitmentto ramp up action on meeting existing targets and reaffirming a goal to increase biodiversity finance to $30bn a year by the end of the decade.During the conference, environment ministers, activists and officials appealed for significant changes to the way the summits function to ensure governments follow through with meaningful action on the drivers of biodiversity loss.Panama’s environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, a veteran conservationist, said the Cop process had been “designed to fail”, arguing that decisions should be taken by a majority as the consensus-based process allows “one idiot” to prevent agreement.“A lot of what’s going on out here at the Cop is just a bunch of baloney and beautiful speeches and BS,” he told AFP earlier this week. “We cannot have – we cannot expect – a consensus between every nation on Earth on every topic. That’s ridiculous. Cops have been designed to fail, and they are not disappointing.”He also argued that the UN should host a single environmental Cop each year to tackle the climate, biodiversity, plastics and other issues in one go.“This just makes my blood boil, because while we fiddle, Rome burns,” he said.View image in fullscreenCountries agreed measures at Cop17 including a commitment to ramp up action on meeting existing targets.Photograph: Karen Minasyan/AFP/Getty ImagesThe negotiations in the Armenian capital have seen Argentina, Saudi Arabia and Russia water down language on environmental ambition in the final agreement, while wealthier governments were divided on who would contribute more financial resources.European nations would like to see additions to the list of donor states, as China and several of the Gulf states are still classified as developing countries in the UN process despite decades of rapid economic development. The final agreement in Yerevan left this issue open.Key decisions ona fund to mobilise resourcesfrom firms that make money from digital forms of biodiversity, such as pharmaceutical companies, were postponed to the next summit in Ecuador in two years’ time. It had been hoped that the fund would generate £1bn a year for nature conservation, with a significant share going to Indigenous communities, but it has so far raised just over $10,000.Big pharma accused of ‘free-riding on nature’ as global fund attracts just $7,000Read moreThe calls for changes to the biodiversity Cop process echo anintervention by leading policy expertsduring climate Cop29 in Azerbaijan in 2024 who said the summit was “no longer fit for purpose” and needed to shift to focus on implementation.Ruth Davis, the UK’s nature envoy, said she recognised that the meetings could be “extremely frustratiing”, but a huge amount of implementation was happening around the world.“We’ve got to make the system actually deliver outcomes for people, otherwise they’ll lose confidence in it,” she said. “In the end, this is a process that is owned by governments who are parties to it. But I know we are going to find friends and allies in making the process work for the citizens of countries for whom this is really important, not least because they are the ones facing the impacts.”Efforts to reform the UN’s sprawling environmental agenda are already under way. Inger Andersen, the executive director of the UN environment programme, said that the current systems were driving change, but they were moving too slowly.“Right now, the environmental agenda is very cluttered. There are lots of meetings, important as each one is. Let’s begin with the easy stuff, like programmatic overlap between conventions, which has an energy-sapping effect,” said Andersen. “We identified the illegal wildlife trade back in the 70s as a problem, then we identified migratory species, then broader biodiversity, then wetlands.“Each of these conventions came along at the right time, but we now have a plethora of them. Maybe we should think about that.”Explore more on these topicsCop17 biodiversity summitThe age of extinctionClimate crisisGreenhouse gas emissionsBiodiversityUnited NationsWildlifeConservationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump boosted half of US coal plants with taxpayer dollars and ‘free passes to pollute’, report says | Coal | The Guardian
description: Environmental Defense Fund analysis shows administration handed out $950m and Clean Air Act exemptions
Author: Hilary Beaumont
Headline: Environmental Defense Fund analysis shows administration handed out $950m and Clean Air Act exemptions
Content: Emissions rise from a coal-burning power plant in Colstrip, Montana, on 1 July 2013.Photograph: Matt Brown/APView image in fullscreenEmissions rise from a coal-burning power plant in Colstrip, Montana, on 1 July 2013.Photograph: Matt Brown/APDemocracy, climate and justiceCoalTrump boosted half of US coal plants with taxpayer dollars and ‘free passes to pollute’, report saysEnvironmental Defense Fund analysis shows administration handed out $950m and Clean Air Act exemptionsDemocracy, climate and justice is supported byAbout this contentHilary BeaumontSat 31 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 09.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s a good time to be a coal plant in the US. The Trump administration has given support to almost half of the nation’s coal plants, helping them to continue operating despite economic and regulatory headwinds, according to a newanalysisby the Environmental Defense Fund.The analysis, which looked at the 184 operating coal plants that are connected to the grid, found that 90 received support from theTrump administrationthrough “cash handouts, free passes to pollute, and requirements to stay online past their retirement dates”.The administration provided $950m in taxpayer dollars to 24 coal plants and handed Clean Air Act exemptions from toxic pollution limits to 70 coal plants, according to the EDF analysis.“It’s extending the life of these coal plants,” said Surbhi Sarang, director and senior attorney at the Environmental Defense Fund. “The administration has leveraged a multitude of tools to prop up coal plants, and ultimately all of that is harming Americans even more by increasing electricity costs, by increasing pollution – it’s like Americans are getting hit twice.”In 2015, the EPA’s Mercury and Air Toxics Standards first took effect, driving down dangerous pollution from power plants by more than 90%. In 2024, the EPAupdated the standardsto further reduce harmful pollution from coal-fired power plants. In the early days of the second Trump term,companies were invitedto email the administration to request an exemption from the 2024 standards. According to emails obtained by the EDF through Freedom of Information Act requests, companies expressed concern that the standards would cost them too much money.The Colstrip plant in Montana has operated for more than 40 years,affecting nearby communitieslike the Northern Cheyenne reservation by releasing toxic chemicals like mercury, arsenic, lead and nickel. “That’s one of thedirtiest coal plantsthat’s still operating in the nation,” Sarang said.In 2024, the Mercury and Air Toxics Standards for coal-fired power plants was strengthened in several ways. For example, the standard for fine particulate matter, or fPM, reduced allowable emissions of nickel, arsenic, lead and other toxic metals from coal plants by two-thirds. According to the EDF, NorthWestern Energy and Talen Energy, which own and operate the Colstrip plant,requested an exemptionfrom the fPM requirement.View image in fullscreenThe WA parish generating station in Thompsons, Texas, on 16 February 2017.Photograph: Luke Sharrett/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesBrian Bird, president and CEO of NorthWestern, wrote an email to the Department of Energy in March 2025 asking for a 15-minute chat about the standards with administrator Lee Zeldin. In theemail, obtained by EDF, he argued that it would cost $500m to comply with the new rule: “It is ludicrous that our customers would have to cover the costs of a $500m investment for such a slight improvement to particulate matter capture,” he wrote.The Trump administration gave NorthWestern anexemptionfrom complying with the 2024 updated standards, which the administration went on to repeal in February.Sarang said the Colstrip plant had not installed modern pollution controls that could reduce emissions. If it had been required to comply with the 2024 updated standards, it would have had to upgrade its equipment, she said: “It would have had pretty significant impacts on air pollution.”NorthWestern, which became Colstrip’s majority owner earlier this year,describes the coal plantas a “dependable bridge to a cleaner energy future” that supplies reliable energy “until viable, equivalent, carbon-free energy resources are commercially available”.Asked to comment on EDF’s report, NorthWestern said its technology at the Colstrip plant is “state of the art” for removing sulphur dioxide, and is 99.6% efficient in removing filterable particulate emissions. The company said if the updated 2024 federal standards had taken effect, it would have required it to become 99.8% efficient by 2028, costing hundreds of millions of dollars. The company said its mercury emission control at the Colstrip plant meets current state and federal requirements.Another coal plant that received a pass from the Trump administration is the WA parish coal plant outside of Houston, Texas. Community members living nearby have called for it to beshut downdue to its planet-heating CO2 emissions and what they say are ‘hazardous’ levels of particulate matter.The plant’s owner, NRG, asked the Department of Energy for an exemption for all of its coal-fired facilities including the WA parish plant, arguing that its facilities wouldn’t be able to comply with the new standards and would need to “derate in order to comply”, taking megawatts off the grid in “critical areas”, according to anemailobtained by EDF. NRG wrote that complying with the regulations “with razor thin margins” would risk the affordability and reliability of the grid.A 2018 Rice University study found that the plant is responsible foras many as 177 premature deathseach year from PM 2.5, which are particles small enough to enter the bloodstream through the lungs, causingincreased ratesof respiratory diseases, heart attacks and strokes. “Our research has shown that WA parish is the deadliest power plant in Texas,” explained Rice professor Daniel Cohan.NRG did not respond to a request to comment.Five reasons why the US midterms matter for the climate – and your energy billRead moreCohan said plants across the country were supposed to meet the 2024 updated standards. “Trump is letting them off the hook from the more stringent version of the standard,” he said.“It lets them stay open longer,” Cohan explained. “Many coal plants in this country are barely on the edge of breaking even, and so any regulations that force them to spend more money to clean up their pollution is likely to cause some of them to choose to retire and be replaced by cheaper and cleaner sources.”The administration defended its support for the coal industry in a statement. “The Democrats’ energy-subtraction policies shuttered American coal plants that provided reliable, affordable power to families and businesses when they needed it most. President Trump promised to revive America’s coal industry, and the Trump Administration has backed and saved more than 100 coal plants this term. By championing beautiful, clean coal, President Trump has prevented the retirement of more than 17 gigawatts of power andsaved livesduring heightened demand periods,” White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers wrote in a statement.Explore more on these topicsCoalDemocracy, climate and justiceTrump administrationAir pollutionClimate crisisFossil fuelsPollutionUS politicsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We’re looking at a 30-year run’: UK pair aim to complete world’s most complex board game | Board games | The Guardian
description: Decades from now, friends may become first people known to have finished The Campaign for North Africa
Author: Mark Brown
Headline: Decades from now, friends may become first people known to have finished The Campaign for North Africa
Content: Andy Taeger (left) and James Purcell about to embark on a long strategic endeavour.Photograph: Mark Pinder/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAndy Taeger (left) and James Purcell about to embark on a long strategic endeavour.Photograph: Mark Pinder/The GuardianBoard games‘We’re looking at a 30-year run’: UK pair aim to complete world’s most complex board gameDecades from now, friends may become first people known to have finished The Campaign for North AfricaMark BrownNorth of England correspondentSat 31 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 19.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“We have had a six-turn practice run. It took about 18 months,” said Andy Taeger, with what seemed like a chuckle as he contemplated playing the world’s most complicated board game.“Based on that, we are looking at a 20- to 30-year run for the full game,” said his gaming partner James Purcell. “We’ve come to terms with it.”The Guardian joined the pair in aNewcastlefront room on Friday as they prepared to start an insane odyssey, playing the legendarily knotty war game The Campaign for North Africa.If they finish it – and that, subject to the events of the next two to three decades, is the intention – they will become the first people known to have completed a game so vast, detailed and time-consuming that it has achieved mythical status in board gaming communities. It is a holy grail.Purcell, 29, is a mental health worker from Wallsend, Taeger, 30, a software developer from Gosforth. They’re happy to be called geeks. They met about 10 years ago and realised straight away that they had a connection.“We were at a house party with a mutual friend and I was singingJames Blunt’s Wisemenin one of the bedrooms, quite drunk,” said Purcell. “Andy happened to pass by the bedroom door, heard me singing and decided to join in. So we became fast friends from there.”View image in fullscreenA practice run of the most complicated board game ever devised.Photograph: Mark Pinder/The GuardianTheir shared love of Dungeons & Dragons and phases playing Yu-Gi-Oh!, a trading card game, and Carcassonne, a board game, have kept the friendship going. When another friend mentioned The Campaign for North Africa, a 1979 game designed by Richard Berg simulating the desert war of 1940-43, they set out to discover more.They watched a few videos, read up about it and went to the pub. “We both realised that we’d been thinking about the game for two weeks. By the end of the night, we were committed to giving it a try,” said Purcell.Along with buying the game – £970 from eBay – they decided to chronicle their journey on a weekly podcast,War With a Mate. “We knew there was no reason to keep playing unless we’re held accountable,” said Purcell. “Otherwise we knew we’d buy the game, we’d give up inside two weeks and we’d have a thousand-pound board game that we can do nothing with.“With a podcast, people can follow along and if we back out we’ve got the shame of everyone calling us out on it.”The pair have spent 99 podcast episodes chronicling their prep and practice for the game before starting it at 7.30pm on Friday for episode 100. It could take 20 years, but “originally it was looking like 50,” said Purcell, not wanting to contemplate the idea of still playing as they approached 80.View image in fullscreen‘We haven’t punched the German pieces out yet because we won’t need them for about five years.’Photograph: Mark Pinder/The GuardianOn Friday afternoon, they were setting up in a friend’s house because they will livestream day one. It will normally be played at Taeger’s flat.The game comes with a 10ft map, which they have divided up into five picture frames and 1,600 pieces, which they will magnetise. “We haven’t punched the German pieces out yet because we won’t need them for about five years,” said Purcell.They will have to keep track of aircraft, truck convoys, land units, supply dumps, water use, fuel evaporation and so, so much more, including not to do anything that could be deemed a war crime.It comes with a history book as well as seven rule books with a dizzying list. One of the best known is the “pasta rule” about Italian forces needing more water in order to boil their pasta rations. It’s assumed to be a joke – but who knows?‘A gaming success story’: how Warhammer became one of Britain’s biggest companiesRead moreBerg does seem to be “poking fun” at the players, said Purcell. At the same time, he clearly also has a thorough knowledge of the campaign. “The amount of research behind this must have been insane,” said Taeger.Purcell is playing as the Axis forces and Taeger as the Commonwealth. It remains to be seen if the game will be so historically accurate that Purcell is destined to lose. He doesn’t think so.“I think we’ve seen already, through the practice run, you can very much change the fate of the campaign through better decision-making,” he said.Both think the game could very well end up a draw, which would be gutting. “I think, honestly, a loss might even be better than a draw because at least it’s a definitive result,” said Taeger. There is also the chance they’ll find that the game is simply not finishable, but thanks to the podcast, they will have plenty of people cheering them on.“The reaction has been surprisingly positive,” said Purcell, with many boardgamers thankful that someone is doing it so they don’t have to. “We’ve not really had many people decry it as the stupid thing that it is, which would be the natural reaction.”The players are determined, but they also intend to take it seriously – and tread very carefully.“You don’t want to make a mistake because you were in a bit of a rush,” said Taeger, definitely laughing now. “You might have to be dealing with it for the next 10 years.”Explore more on these topicsBoard gamesNorth of EnglandNewcastlefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Andy Burnham open to calls for formal apology for Britain’s role in slave trade | Commonwealth of Nations | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: UK PM to launch drive to restructure debt of poorest Commonwealth countries but rejects demands for reparations
Author: Pippa Crerar
Headline: Exclusive: UK PM to launch drive to restructure debt of poorest Commonwealth countries but rejects demands for reparations
Content: Andy Burnham said he wanted to share his ‘sorrow and regret’ for the pain and suffering of millions of people due to slave trade.Photograph: Russell Cheyne/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham said he wanted to share his ‘sorrow and regret’ for the pain and suffering of millions of people due to slave trade.Photograph: Russell Cheyne/AFP/Getty ImagesCommonwealth of NationsAndy Burnham open to calls for formal apology for Britain’s role in slave tradeExclusive: UK PM to launch drive to restructure debt of poorest Commonwealth countries but rejects demands for reparationsBritish people can’t be made to pay for the wrongs of slavery – but we must confront our complicated history | Andy BurnhamPippa CrerarandNatricia DuncanFri 30 Oct 2026 21.47 EDTFirst published on Fri 30 Oct 2026 18.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has gone further than any previous prime minister towards offering a formal apology for Britain’s role in the transatlantic slave trade, in a Guardian article ahead of a Commonwealth leaders’ summit where the subject is expected to dominate.As he prepares to fly to theCaribbeannext week, the prime minister said he was open to calls for an official apology on behalf of the state and offered formal talks to those affected, including individual countries and campaign groups at home and abroad.Burnham wrote: “The Britain I believe in is confident, decent and brave. We led the world in abolishing slavery – and we can show leadership again today.”While any formal statement will depend on that dialogue, Burnham gave what amounted to a personal apology, saying he wanted to share his “sorrow and regret” for the pain and suffering of millions of people, and to recognise the way the slave trade still shapes the world now.The royal crown branded on enslaved Africans: Britain’s monarchy and the slave tradeRead moreHowever, he rejected demands from Caribbean countries and campaigners for the UK to pay financial reparations for its role in the slave trade, maintaining the position of successive governments that British people today could not be held liable for the past.He wrote that reparations were not the “right answer”, adding: “I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, which happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part.”Instead, Burnham said he would launch a new drive to restructure debt for the poorest Commonwealth countries – led by former prime minister Gordon Brown and expected to eventually include organisations such as the IMF – helping them repay debt over a longer period and with better interest rates.Debt servicing costs for the poorest and most vulnerable Commonwealth countries are at their highest in more than 25 years, he added, with more than 40% of those spending more on interest repayments than on health.Burnham’s intervention follows years of pressure from Caribbean states, backed by some African countries, for European nations including the UK, France and Spain tooffer reparations– including monetary compensation, a full formal apology, support for health and education and debt cancellation.As recently as last week, the Commonwealth secretary general, Shirley Ayorkor Botchwey,said a formal apology for slaveryfrom King Charles, who will attend the heads of government summit, “wouldn’t hurt” and the “time has come” for a serious conversation on reparations.Writing for the Guardian, Burnham said: “The transatlantic slave trade was a brutal and barbaric violation of those people. They were denied their humanity. They were separated from their families, treated as property and worked to their deaths.“I want to express my sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering of so many millions and to recognise the way it still shapes our world today.”View image in fullscreenA protester from the Guyana reparations committee holds a placard as people demonstrate on the day King Charles visited Georgetown, during a tour of Caribbean nations that will also take him to Antigua and Barbuda for the Commonwealth heads of government meeting.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersHe added: “We are offering a structured dialogue with those affected by the transatlantic slave trade. Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process and I am open to them.”Burnham’s intervention received a cautious welcome from leading figures in the Caribbean. Dorbrene O’Marde, the chair of the Antigua and Barbuda reparations support commission, said his organisation welcomed the statement as “a movement in the correct direction in the interest of reparatory justice and humanity generally”.But, he added: “We reject the decision that financial reparations will not be on the table.”‘We want a full apology for slavery’: Commonwealth at a crossroads as king heads to the CaribbeanRead moreRalph Gonsalves, former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines and a senior figure inthe Repair campaign, told the Guardian that an apology was the first point in the Caribbean community’s 10-point reparations plan but “though necessary, is insufficient”.He added: “We are pleased to hear that [the UK] comes into a conversation. But it can’t be a conversation about nothing. It has to be a conversation about something. If they are not going to entertain reparations, what is the conversation about? Nothing.”Sir Hilary Beckles, the chair of the Caricom reparations commission, said he believed Burnham “is carrying the broad middle of British opinion on this matter”.He said the call for financial reparations need not be a stumbling block to progress: “There are much broader issues that can occupy that dialogue. So you don’t know what you will emerge out until you have a conversation of decency.“I think the prime minister will find that Caribbean leaders are very reasonable people on the matter of developing a new Anglo-Caribbean bond … words are important, but the spirit of collaboration is more important.”Caribbean leaders have been reacting to Bunham’s announcement. In a statement, the prime minister of Barbados, Mia Mottley thanked Burnham for “breaking new ground” but said she and the UK government “are not yet on the same page on every element”.“On reparations in particular, our views differ, and we will say so plainly and respectfully. Honest disagreement on some questions should not hold back progress on the many others where we can readily agree.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“An apology, a commitment to eradicate a mindset that is anchored in Afrophobia and against all things “black”, investment in health and education, development partnership that fights systemic poverty and institutionalised inequality, and fairer terms on debt for vulnerable states, as called for by the Bridgetown Initiative, are a few of the areas where we believe understanding can be reached and settled,” her statement said.“I thank prime minister Burnham and his foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, for breaking new ground and recognising that this is the right thing, and the moral thing, to do by ensuring that we move to the next stage of engagement on this difficult and emotional issue,” it added.Antigua and Barbuda’s prime minister Gaston Browne, who is hosting this year’s CHOGM, welcomed particularly Burnham’s offer to assist with debt restructuring and a transition to renewable energy.“The Caribbean’s longstanding position on reparatory justice remains unchanged. Differences over financial compensation should be addressed through dialogue, but they need not prevent progress in areas where agreement is possible,” he said in a statement.Jamaica’s prime minister, Andrew Holness, also welcomed Burnham’s willingness to discuss a formal apology. In September, Jamaican officialslodged a landmark petitionto the king seeking legal advice on its claim for slavery reparations, which will be heard by the privy council in March.“We have always been open to having full and meaningful dialogue on this important issue. We welcome this development, coming in the wake of our legal petition which is now before the privy council,” Holness said in a statement.Similarly, the Bahamas prime minister, Philip Davis, commended Burnham’s decision to agree to a dialogue and consider an apology. “The Bahamas approaches this dialogue with a clear understanding that the issue is not simply one of historical remembrance. It concerns the enduring consequences of slavery and the importance of justice, acknowledgment and meaningful redress for the generations of Africans and their descendants who continue to live with its legacy,” he said.The UK government has taken a cautious approach to the issue amidpressure from leftwingMPs to offer a formal apology and engage in reparatory justice, alongside concerns over the potential fiscal and electoral impact, withpolls suggesting most voters are opposedto financial compensation.The Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm), which King Charles will also attend, runs from Sunday 1 November until Wednesday 4 November.At the previous Chogm summit in Samoa two years ago, Britain’s former colonies agreed “the time has come” for a dialogue about reparations – even though then-prime minister Keir Starmer said it would not be on the agenda.Some inside the UK government had questioned whether Burnham should even attend after the reparations row dominated the 2024 gathering. But his decision to address the issue head-on is likely to be welcomed in Antigua and Barbuda.Campaigners see the summit as the culmination of decades of advocacy from Caribbean leaders for a deeper acknowledgment of the UK’s historic responsibility for the enslavement of millions of Africans.Advocates say the UK had been under increasing pressure to act after a UN resolution in March which described the trafficking and racialised chattel enslavement of Africans as the gravest crime against humanity.The UK was among the 52 countries that abstained, saying that while it recognised the gravity of the issue, it disagreed with thefundamental propositionof the text which it said risked creating a hierarchy of historical atrocities.In June, Mottley,announced a new manifestofrom Caribbean leaders asserting the “moral, ethical and legal case” for reparations over damage caused by hundreds of years of enslavement.The 10-point plan argued that repair could include international debt cancellation and that climate justice and slavery reparations were “inextricably linked”.Burnham also referred to the history of Manchester as “the cotton capital of the world” which grew in part thanks to cotton picked by enslaved people.In 2023 the owner of the Guardian apologised for the role the newspaper’s founders had in the transatlantic slave trade, and launchedthe Cotton Capital seriesand a 10-year programme of restorative justice.Explore more on these topicsCommonwealth of NationsAndy BurnhamReparations and reparative justiceCommonwealth summitSlaveryBritish empireColonialismShareReuse this content

title: Is time up for backyard fireworks? UK ministers weigh partial ban over noise concerns | Bonfire Night | The Guardian
description: Consultation follows growing calls from campaigners, vets and National Farmers’ Union for tighter regulation
Author: Nicola Davis
Headline: Consultation follows growing calls from campaigners, vets and National Farmers’ Union for tighter regulation
Content: Government proposals include expanding the list of fireworks banned for general sale.Photograph: David Tramontan/Sopa Images/Rex/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenGovernment proposals include expanding the list of fireworks banned for general sale.Photograph: David Tramontan/Sopa Images/Rex/ShutterstockBonfire NightIs time up for backyard fireworks? UK ministers weigh partial ban over noise concernsConsultation follows growing calls from campaigners, vets and National Farmers’ Union for tighter regulationNicola DavisScience correspondentSat 31 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs the nights draw in, the season of sparklers begins, with Diwali,Bonfire Nightand New Year’s Eve among the occasions typically celebrated with fireworks. But if campaigners get their way, this could be the last blast for bangers in the back yard.In January concerns about the noise and availability of fireworks wereaired in a parliamentary debate, with two petitions clocking up more than 180,000 signatures each, while earlier this month the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade closed aconsultationon proposals including making louder fireworks only available to professional users.Harriet Main, a public affairs manager at the RSPCA, said the charity was thrilled by the consultation: “For too long, pets, wildlife, and livestock have suffered from stress, fright and severe injury caused by loud unregulated back-yard DIY displays.“Public appetite for change is overwhelming: the RSPCA hosted its own online action to help supporters submit their views to the consultation, and this generated over 51,000 responses eager to speak up for animals. This extraordinary turnout demonstrates just how deeply people across Britain care about protecting animals from the devastating impacts of unnecessarily loud fireworks.”In recent years there have been reports of a host of animal fatalities linked to fireworks, from the death ofa baby red pandaat Edinburgh zoo toa dachshundin North Yorkshire.Ministers have ruled out a complete ban on the public buying fireworks. Instead, their proposals include expanding the list of fireworks banned for general sale and reducing the permitted decibel level of consumer fireworks from 120dB to 110dB, meaning their loudness would be approximately halved.Dr Gwen Rees, the president of the British Veterinary Association, said vets were acutely aware of the fear, distress, injury and lasting anxiety fireworks caused to animals in the UK each year. “Lower noise limits would reduce one of the main causes of firework-related distress while allowing celebrations to continue,” she said. “But quieter fireworks are not a complete solution. Flashes and unpredictable timing can still affect animals, so clearer labelling, responsible use, tighter controls on sales and private use, and better public awareness are also essential to protect animal welfare.”A tightening of regulations has been backed by organisations including the National Farmers’ Union, which has cited animal welfare concerns and fire risks in relation to private firework displays. “One member reported losing around four acres of wheat after a firework landed in a standing crop during harvest,” the NFUnoted.View image in fullscreenLower noise limits would reduce firework-related distress to animals while allowing celebrations to continue, the British Veterinary Association said.Photograph: Alamy/PAChanges to pyrotechnics and fireworks regulations will be made as soon as parliamentary time allows after analysis of the feedback from the consultation, the government said, adding that there would be a six-month “transitional period” after the law was changed.However, the British Fireworks Assocationhas pushed back, noting that many of the behaviours that frustrate communities – such as setting off fireworks in a public place or after 1am – are already illegal, and that removing large numbers of legal and regulated products from the consumer market might push people towards finding hidden-market fireworks and pyrotechnics.Recent efforts to tacklethe use of fireworks and pyrotechnics in Scotland – including the introduction of “firework control zones” where the devices are banned – have had a mixed reception.Helen Whitelegg, the campaigns manager at the charity Redwings Horse Sanctuary, said: “We believe the zones create a two-tier system of protection where they are put in place and risk pushing more use of fireworks to the surrounding areas.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionShe added: “We are aware that the widely anticipated step of introducing a licencing requirement for anyone using fireworks has been shelved due to lack of resources and there is no indication when this part of the legislation is likely to be brought in.”But it is not only the UK where firework fervour has cooled. In the Netherlands a countrywide ban on most consumer fireworks came into effect in August, while Czechia has also tightened its regulations. On 29 November, Swiss citzens will have their say on proposals to ban noisy fireworks.In Germany, there is already a limited window in which fireworks can be bought or used, while there are also bans on fireworks in some zones and near certain facilities. Even then, there are calls for stronger regulations, with one survey suggesting almost half of those polled were in favour of a total ban, with exceptions only for very small fireworks such as sparklers.Whitelegg said that among other measures, Redwings backed a reduction in the maximum loudness of fireworks to 90dB, as is the casein New Zealand,noting that while a Dutch-style ban would be preferable, the use of low-noise fireworks presented a practical compromise.“I think the direction of travel does suggest that change is inevitable,” she said. “And because of what we’re seeing in other countries, it’s not unique to the UK by any stretch of the imagination.”Explore more on these topicsBonfire NightAnimal welfareDiwaliNew yearAnimalsWildlifePetsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘You need the power of all your votes’: Bedouin women secure success for Arab parties in Israeli election | Israel | The Guardian
description: With 180,000 eligible voters, Bedouin turnout was key in Palestinian-led parties winning unprecedented 19 seats
Author: Emma Graham-Harrison
Headline: With 180,000 eligible voters, Bedouin turnout was key in Palestinian-led parties winning unprecedented 19 seats
Content: Hanan Alsanah and Amira Habdoubi from Abu Talul at a meeting of the women’s group Alashniat.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianView image in fullscreenHanan Alsanah and Amira Habdoubi from Abu Talul at a meeting of the women’s group Alashniat.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianIsrael‘You need the power of all your votes’: Bedouin women secure success for Arab parties in Israeli electionWith 180,000 eligible voters, Bedouin turnout was key in Palestinian-led parties winning unprecedented 19 seatsEmma Graham-Harrisonin AzzarnugSat 31 Oct 2026 13.16 EDTFirst published on Sat 31 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLast year, Umm Khaled Fatoun returned from volunteering in a Jewish-Arab support centre for victims of war to find bulldozers tearing into her son’s house in the Bedouin village of Azzarnug.The demolition crew, who arrived under police escort, did not even allow them to remove furniture or solar panels before reducing the home and its contents to a pile of rubble.This week, she took action of her own at the ballot box, targeting the extremist national security minister who ordered – andboastsabout – the mass destruction of Palestinian and Arab homes.“I had one goal, to send [Itamar] Ben-Gvir home,” Fatoun said. “There isn’t a single family in the Bedouin community that hasn’t been hurt by his campaign against us.”In the weeks before election day, she joined a grassroots campaign to educate other Bedouin women about their rights and potential power.It had spectacular results, with voting rates tripling in some Bedouin villages in the southern Negev region in Tuesday’s election, amid a broader surge in turnout among Bedouin voters.Graphic of projected seats in the KnessetYears of violent, racist government opened the door for change in conservative communities, said lawyer Hanan Alsanah, who founded the Alnashmiat network that led the grassroots programme.“We said that even if all the men go to vote, it is only half the community. You need the power of all your votes, because Ben-Gvir has a lot of power,” she said. Alsanah is also co-director of Itach-Ma’aki, female lawyers for social justice.The rise in Bedouin votes came amid a historically high turnout among Arab citizens of Israel. Their votessecured an unprecedented 19 seatsin the Knesset for Palestinian-led parties and were critical to stripping the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and his allies of their governing majority.This year, the lowest turnout in any Bedouin community was 62%. The highest was more than 93%. With an estimated 180,000 eligible voters, their turnout was key to the Islamist Ra’am party beating polling expectations.View image in fullscreenHanan Alsanah, Amira Habdoubi, Fatmeh Abu Khweder, Umm Khaled Fatoun and Mayada Abu Khweida.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianNetanyahu has repeatedly used racist fearmongering to try to boost voter turnout among his own base. This year, his attacks included anAI-generated imagepurporting to show a crowded polling station in a Palestinian area and Bedouin female voters.In an apparent attempt to undermine the surge in votes for Palestinian-led parties, Netanyahu accused them of fraud and foreign support.“The increase in voter turnout in the Bedouin community in particular, and the Arab community in general, is unprecedented in the history of the state,” said Amit Segal, a pundit and close confidant of the prime minister.The allegations have been rejected by opposition leaders, election organisers and the activists in the Negev.“I am very proud of our turnout. They are talking about ‘corruption’ [as the reason for high voter turnout]. The correct word is ‘awareness’,” said Amira Habdoubi, an organiser from the village of Abu Talul.View image in fullscreenAmira Habdoubi from Abu Talul serves coffee for the women at a meeting.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianFor a community whose civil rights are policed by racist authorities, the election was a rare opportunity for political expression, she added. “We can’t protest, because they will arrest us. Voting is the only opportunity we have to make a political protest.”The Muslim Bedouin are part of a marginalised minority insideIsrael. Before the state was created, they roamed widely across the Negev desert.Now, although their villages take up only 2.5% of the land in the region, many are deemed “unrecognised”, targeted by the state for demolition and left without basic services including electricity and water supplies. The majority of the Negev has been designated as military training grounds and firing ranges.More than 100,000 people live in about 30 unrecognised communities in the Negev. Another 200,000 live in official towns, or places with some level of recognition.Netanyahu’s pursuit of open-ended regional conflicts also drove Bedouin turnout. War is particularly terrifying in unrecognised villages because the state does not provide them with bomb shelters or warning sirens before rocket, drone and missile attacks.Rockets that hit Bedouin villages without shelters killed six of the 36 child victims of the 7 October attacks. Several adults were also killed that day in the villages and at least four people have been seriously injured by Iranian missiles.Organised crime is another concern, rising almost unchecked under the current government.“We had clear goals. Stop the home demolitions, stop the hatred, stop the war. Ben-Gvir talks all the time about security, but we feel no security and no one cares about us,” said Mayada Abu Khweida.View image in fullscreen‘Stop the hatred, stop the war’: Mayada Abu Khweida prepares breakfast for a meeting.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianThe activists worked to help women understand their rights and tackle logistical and practical obstacles to voting, as well as cultural ones.“Because [residents of unrecognised villages] can’t vote in the municipal elections, a lot of women don’t know they have a right to vote in national elections,” said Abu Khweida. “We told them: ‘There is a legal way to express your anger and raise your voice.’”For similar bureaucratic reasons, there are no polling stations in unrecognised villages, so voters have to travel to nearby towns. Men went any way they could, including on camel, horse, donkey and bike, on journeys that took up to an hour in each direction.Jewish women offered lifts to Bedouin women, but because in 2019 Israel’s election committee ruled that organising transport volunteers was illegal, voters and drivers connected individually.“Hundreds of women volunteers went to help Bedouin women to access the polls, and at the same time about 150 men went to do protective presence at the polling stations,” said Raluca Ganea, the founding executive director of the Jewish-Arab community action group Zazim.“We wanted to have Jewish men standing there to de-escalate, in case there was a rightwing provocation of some kind. So it would not be the Bedouin men in front of the provocateurs, because if the police come or there is violence, they are much more likely to be arrested or worse.”View image in fullscreenMohammed Abu Khweida outside his cousin’s demolished house in the unrecognised village of Azzarnug.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianNetanyahu’s racist get-out-the-vote campaign on social media included photos of Bedouin women with their faces covered.Some of these women covered their faces to avoid being seen by strangers from outside their own community. In recognised towns, where women could vote in their communities, most did not cover their faces, Alsanah said.Others hid themselves to avoid becoming fodder for Ben-Gvir’s extremist social media feed, which regularly features humiliation of Arab citizens.“The women were worried the extremists would take photos at the polling stations and covered their faces to protect themselves from being exploited on social media,” Abu Khweida said, adding that his campaign of humiliation has affected all of Bedouin society.The grassroots mobilisation of Bedouin voters aimed in part to give children back their dreams, one reason why women responded so strongly.“In the last election in 2022, turnout among women was around 20%. Now in the unrecognised villages, informal data shows more than 60% turnout among women,” Alsanah said, adding that Israel does not break down voting statistics by gender.The project built on more than a decade of work with Alnashmiat, based in Arab and Jewish solidarity, that could set an example for a new government, Alsanah said.“We learned an important lesson from this election campaign. We should work together, men and women, Arab and Jewish citizens, and we should bring this approach to the Israeli parliament to rebuild the state.”Explore more on these topicsIsraelWomenMiddle East and north AfricaBenjamin NetanyahufeaturesShareReuse this content

title: US cancels G20 ‘family photo’ after Australia, UK and others refuse to appear with Russia | G20 | The Guardian
description: Marco Rubio pulls plug on traditional photo op at meeting of foreign ministers after about one-third of countries threaten boycott
Author: Ben Doherty
Headline: Marco Rubio pulls plug on traditional photo op at meeting of foreign ministers after about one-third of countries threaten boycott
Content: US secretary of state Marco Rubio speaks at the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta, Georgia.Photograph: Megan Varner/Pool Reuters/APView image in fullscreenUS secretary of state Marco Rubio speaks at the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta, Georgia.Photograph: Megan Varner/Pool Reuters/APG20US cancels G20 ‘family photo’ after Australia, UK and others refuse to appear with RussiaMarco Rubio pulls plug on traditional photo op at meeting of foreign ministers after about one-third of countries threaten boycottBen Dohertyand Associated PressFri 30 Oct 2026 20.29 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 22.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe traditional “family photo” to open the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting has been abruptly cancelled in the US after a host of nations – including Australia and the UK – refused to appear beside the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov.The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, pulled the plug after several European officials, the UK and Australia made it known they would boycott or walk out of the snapshot that often kicks off such international gatherings.Rubio still opened the talks in Atlanta with an appeal for unity on the issues that threaten international security and trade.“We are in a critical moment,” Rubio told his colleagues. “We are facing a series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises.”‘We hope he’ll accept’: US invites Putin to G20 summit at Trump golf clubRead moreAbout one-third of countries at the talks made it known they would not appear beside any Russian representatives.European Union nations had made clear they would boycott any photo with the Russians. “In no case will there be a family photo with European partners and Mr Lavrov together because … there is no normality with Russia,” Germany’s foreign affairs minister, Johann Wadephul, warned ahead of Friday’s session.The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, promised similar. “We do not engage in that way with the Russians and have not for a number of years,” he said.During the meeting’s opening session, Australia’s foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, condemned Russia’s invasion of Ukraine as brutal and unjustified - in front of Lavrov - saying Russia’s illegal war had affected international markets and worsened global food security.A spokesperson for Wong said Australia supported the US decision to cancel the group photo. “Australia has been clear and consistent: we will not normalise Russia’s brutal and illegal invasion of Ukraine.“Our focus at theG20remains on the important work before us and addressing the challenges facing the global economy.”The schism in Atlanta is yet further evidence of the rupture caused by the Trump administration’s attempt to reintegrate Russia and its isolated president, Vladimir Putin, into the international community despite Putin’s ongoing war against Ukraine.Diplomats who attended the opening session described it as cordial but said Russia’s position on Ukraine is unyielding – as is its opposition to Poland’s membership in the G20.Those disagreements, which also include the Trump administration’s not inviting G20 member South Africa over the objections of others, will probably prevent the foreign ministers from producing a joint communique when the meetings wrap up on Saturday, participants said.That did not surprise the Polish deputy prime minister and foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, representing his country at its first time as a guest at a G20 meeting.“We have wars going on and we have participants in those wars around the table, so it’s very difficult to agree a common line,” he told reporters.Several participants, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to discuss the closed-door talks, said all had agreed to try to overcome their differences despite the long odds and to work to make next month’s G20 leaders’ summit hosted by the president, Donald Trump, in Florida a success.Ukraine, which is not a G20 member but was invited to attend previous meetings, was not invited this year, with US officials saying it was a deliberate choice to include only formal members of the group. Poland, not a member, is seeking formal membership with US support.But missing from the invitation list was South Africa, a G20 founding member and the only African country in the group. South Africa is embroiled in several bitter disputes with the Trump administration, and when it chaired the G20 last year, top US officials, including Trump and Rubio, shunned the meetings it hosted.“We have consistently maintained that our nonparticipation is not voluntary,” Phindile Kunene, a spokesperson for the South African international relations minister, Ronald Lamola, said.Explore more on these topicsG20Australian foreign policyRussiaAustralian politicsUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Plantation tourism’: court victory signals hope in Jamaica’s fight to keep beaches public | Jamaica | The Guardian
description: A temporary injunction in the coastline battle for beaches to be publicly accessible, not sealed off for private developments, is just a step in fighting what islanders call a tourism model that disadvantages Jamaicans
Author: Natricia Duncan
Headline: A temporary injunction in the coastline battle for beaches to be publicly accessible, not sealed off for private developments, is just a step in fighting what islanders call a tourism model that disadvantages Jamaicans
Content: Environmental activists, supporters and families gather on the rocks at One Man Beach in Montego Bay during Eva Buzo’s 34km protest swim. Photograph: Ina Sotirova/The GuardianA temporary injunction in the coastline battle for beaches to be publicly accessible, not sealed off for private developments, is just a step in fighting what islanders call a tourism model that disadvantages JamaicansByNatricia Duncanin Montego Bay andAnthony Lugg; photographs by Ina SotirovaSat 31 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen the Australian human rights lawyer Eva Buzo emerged from the sea on to the shores of One Man Beach in Montego Bay on Sunday after her gruelling, nearly 11-hour-long swim, the thunderous pulse of welcome drums was drowned out by the chants of “free beach” from jubilant supporters.Here in Jamaica’s tourism capital, against a backdrop of jagged mountains and sunset-tinted clouds, Buzo – a celebrated marathon swimmer – said she was pleased to help support the important work of theJamaicaBeach Birthright Environmental Movement (Jabbem) and others fighting for free public access to Jamaica’s beaches.View image in fullscreenEva Buzo emerges from the sea at One Man Beach in Montego Bay after completing her 34km protest swim.Photograph: Ina Sotirova/The Guardian“People’s rights are more important these days than ever, and people keep on trying to encroach on our fundamental freedoms,” she said, calling the privatisation of beaches a colonial legacy. But for Jabbem, her swim was not the most significant milestone this month in its fight for public access.That came earlier in October, when Jabbem celebrateda rare victoryin one of several court cases to end the1956 Beach Control Actthat had given the state ownership of the island’s foreshore and seabed. The act has allowed successive administrations to restrict access to beaches and sell off coastlines to wealthy luxury hoteliers.8:57Why Jamaicans can’t access their own beachesIn October, however, the court issued an injunction preventing the government from continuing to restrict access to Little Dunn’s River in St Ann while the case continues.“This victory means a lot for the Jamaican people. It means that our case is strong,” said Dr Devon Taylor, an immunologist with a PhD in biochemistry, who founded Jabbem in 2020.View image in fullscreenDr Devon Taylor, a founding member of Jabbem says recent court victory meant campaigners’ case is ‘strong’.Photograph: Ina Sotirova/The GuardianWilbourn Carr, 73, who is involved in another fight for beach access in Portland parish, in Jamaica, said the temporary injunction offered hope for other cases.“The matter of beach access is right across Jamaica. And we just had some success at Little Dunn’s River with that injunction. It gives us hope. Because the fact is that one judge now believes thatJamaicans should have access,” he said.The Jamaican government has said it will appeal. In an interview, the environment minister, Matthew Samuda, said there was no basis for protest. He said the government was safeguarding critical tourism investment and protecting communities from crime, while improving beach access through updated legislation requiring future developments to create access points and investment in community leisure spaces.In the case of Little Dunn’s River, Samuda said access had been restricted after a murder.View image in fullscreen‘The matter of beach access is right across Jamaica.’ Wilbourn Carr with other supporters.Photograph: Ina Sotirova/The Guardian“Because of the cultural sensitivity and the love that certain residents of St Ann and those who travel far and wide to come to the facility have for the space, the government intervened and said it would put up appropriate security structures and would facilitate free access to this area on a weekend basis, Friday, Saturday and Sunday,” he said, describing this as “structured management” that also provided benefits such as lifeguards.Describing tourism as the “largest foreign exchange earner” and the main source of income for nearly 200,000 Jamaicans, Samuda accused activists of portraying the industry as “the enemy”.He said: “176,000 people aren’t protesting anything to do with beach access, but 176,000 people are feeding their families because of our tourism product … Let’s not put their needs and their concerns on one side.”View image in fullscreenEva Buzo during her swim.Photograph: Ina Sotirova/The GuardianTaylor, however, rejected crime prevention as justification for beach closures, pointing out that “the Beach Control Act of 1956 predates the level of crime seen in Jamaica and was never a tool to control crime”. He referred to the Little Dunn’s River restrictions as an illegal “collective punishment of the Jamaican people” that had nothing to do with solving an alleged murder.“So you could close it until forever, until you solve this murder, which you have not solved,” he said. “You present no evidence that this place was still under threat … So we refute Little Dunn’s River was closed to solve some murder or to stop more from happening, because four years later you only allow the people to use it on Saturdays and Sundays. We deserve leisure seven days a week.”Paul Roberts, a British architect living in Jamaica and Jabbem’s St Ann community coordinator, argued that the government is creating a false impression that Jamaicans cannot be trusted.View image in fullscreenPaul Roberts, a British architect living in Jamaica, is Jabbem’s community coordinator for St Ann.Photograph: Ina Sotirova/The Guardian“It’s a load of rubbish,” he said. “I’ve been coming here for 15 years now and I’ve never had any trouble. I’ve never been robbed, I’ve never been mugged and I’ve never faced any issues.”Campaigners did not oppose hotels, Taylor said, but rather a “plantation tourism” model that disadvantaged Jamaicans.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Long WaveNesrine Malik, Micha Frazer-Carroll and the team guide you through the biggest Black stories from around the worldEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Cheap labour of the Jamaican people, degradation of the environment, exclusion of the Jamaican people from the foreshore, plantation tourism, untenable working conditions. Lock us out using colonial-era law. The industry is guilty of that,” he said.“We the people do not want to be treated as second-class citizens in our country … we want fairness, equality and equity.”View image in fullscreenA beachfront resort under construction along Jamaica’s north coast, where public access to the beach remains restricted.Photograph: Ina Sotirova/The GuardianBuzo described access to shared public spaces as a human rights issue, pointing to countries such as Australia, where she is from, and Barbados in the Caribbeanthat maintain public beach access alongside thriving tourism industries.“There’s no reason why hotels can’t have beachfront properties that then front on to a public beach. It’s just this kind of exclusivity and segregation that small amounts of people think they need,” she said.Samuda argued Jamaica was different because, although the country had “conquered our crime monster”, it had “spent 30 years being in the top three most murderous countries on the planet”.View image in fullscreenCommunities have been denied access to spaces because successive governments have failed to address colonial inequities, say campaigners.Photograph: Ina Sotirova/The GuardianMuch of Jamaica’s coastline was also rocky, he said, with only a fraction considered “beach”. He argued that most of the “beachy” areas remained publicly accessible, although some carried restrictions or charges.Jabbem is campaigning for full, free and unfettered beach access, arguing that many families are priced out by high entrance fees and forced to buy expensive on-site food and drinks owing to outside-food bans. The group’s western Jamaica community coordinator, Monique Christie, said tourists also lost out when separated from local communities.“The product that is Jamaica is not the hotel. It’s definitely not the rooms. It’s definitely not the name of the resort. It has always been us, the people. It has always been our warmth and the desire of everyone to just come and meet us.”View image in fullscreenTheresa Rodriguez-Moodie (left) the chief executive of the Jamaica Environment Trust.Photograph: Ina Sotirova/The GuardianDr Theresa Rodriguez-Moodie, the chief executive of the Jamaica Environment Trust, said questions over what constitutes publicly owned space had become increasingly complex, leaving many Jamaicans feeling disenfranchised.Two years on from our first newsletter … how has the Long Wave evolved?Read more“I think that we need to be paying attention to what the Jamaican people are asking for, they’re talking about, and find a way to address that through changes to the law, changes to the policies.”In March, Jamaica’s prime minister, Andrew Holness, proposed a beach access and management policy supposedly intended to modernise legislation and increase access. Campaigners say it still permits unacceptable restrictions.“The 2026 policy that was published in March was supposed to try and address some of the issues, but it really didn’t,” Rodriguez-Moodie said.For Taylor, the fight will continue. “The people are crying out. We need a fundamental change. And they must listen to the people because we won’t stop until this law is abolished and we have fundamental rights and workers’ rights in this country. That is what our ancestors fought for,” he said.Explore more on these topicsJamaicaAmericasCaribbeanLand rightsCoastlinesEnvironmental activismfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Riot police deployed to Poland’s constitutional court after judge suspended | Poland | The Guardian
description: President Karol Nawrocki seen struggling to gain entry to court building in Warsaw amid long-running row over the court’s legitimacy
Author: Jakub Krupa
Headline: President Karol Nawrocki seen struggling to gain entry to court building in Warsaw amid long-running row over the court’s legitimacy
Content: Police are seen around the premises of Poland's constitutional court after its head was suspended in Warsaw, Poland, on Friday.Photograph: Agata Grzybowska/Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPolice are seen around the premises of Poland's constitutional court after its head was suspended in Warsaw, Poland, on Friday.Photograph: Agata Grzybowska/Anadolu/Getty ImagesPolandRiot police deployed to Poland’s constitutional court after judge suspendedPresident Karol Nawrocki seen struggling to gain entry to court building in Warsaw amid long-running row over the court’s legitimacyJakub KrupaSat 31 Oct 2026 00.27 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 02.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRiot police were locked in a tense standoff with protesters outside Poland’s constitutional court on Friday night after its top judge was suspended in the latest escalation in a decade-long dispute over the court’s legal status.The clashes followed a controversial decision by a group of government-appointed judges to suspend the court’s contested president, Bogdan Święczkowski, and his deputy, Bartłomiej Sochański, amid disagreements over the bench’s legitimacy.The move prompted a furious reaction from the rightwing opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party, with its leader, Jarosław Kaczyński, condemning what he claimed was an “assault” on the court.The court frequently ruled in favour of Polish legislation over EU law and the European Union accused Poland’s highest court of being too close to the nationalist political power of the time.Poland’s ascent from communist state to top 20 economy reverses the brain drainRead moreThe PiS-backed conservative president, Karol Nawrocki,a close ally of Donald Trump,turned his plane around en route to a state visit in Senegal to return to Warsaw and intervene at the court on Friday night.Hundreds of protesters – including opposition MPs – gathered outside the building to show their support for the suspended judges. Police said they detained three people after some protesters breached the tribunal’s fence and others threw objects at officers.Shortly before 1am on Saturday, Nawrocki appeared outside the court andmade his way through the police cordon, withone video showing the president tussling with securityand other judges to force his entry into the building. As of 4am local time,the president remained inside the building.In aclip posted online, Nawrocki was heard saying the government appointees “were not judges of the constitutional court”.In a statement read out on his behalf outside the court at 5am, Nawrocki criticised “a violation of Poland’s constitutional order”, saying “a constitutional body was seized by force”. He called for security forces to leave the premises.The latest clash is likely to further polarise the country, setting the scene for a dramatic showdown in next year’s parliamentary election, with polls showing the populist-right with a chance to return to power.View image in fullscreenPolice are seen around the premises of Poland’s top court amid protests over its head’s suspension in Warsaw, Poland.Photograph: Agata Grzybowska/Anadolu/Getty ImagesThe court has been at the centre of a dispute dating back to 2015, when the outgoing centrist and the incoming rightwing governments moved in quick succession with legally questionable moves to stack the bench with their appointees.The dispute over the appointmentsparalysed the court, followed byfurther attempts to cripple itduring the PiS’s eight years ofilliberal rulemarred byclashes with the EUover the rule of law.Since returning to power in 2023, Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk,has repeatedly pledged to reverse controversial reformsashe sought to mend relations with Brussels, while refusing to recognise the court’s legitimacy in the current form.However, his efforts have been thwarted by opposition-aligned presidents who used their veto powers and expansive interpretations of their powers to block reforms.In the latest twist this year, Nawrocki,who unexpectedly won last year’s presidential election against Tusk’s candidate,refused to swear in five judges elected by the current parliament, further complicating the legal situation.Earlier this month, the Council of Europe’s advisory body on the rule of law, the Venice Commission,saidthe president’s refusal should not prevent judges from taking up their posts.On Friday night, a group of judges elected by the current majority moved to suspend Święczkowski, a former minister under PiS, and seize procedural control of the court. Anna Korwin-Piotrowska – who is one of the five judges not accepted by Nawrocki – said she had assumed the top position, citing the longest experience in the judiciary.View image in fullscreenDisputed chief justice Bogdan Swięczkowski presents his judicial document to reporters in front of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal in Warsaw, Poland.Photograph: Radek Pietruszka/EPAExperts are deeply divided in their opinion on the legality of the judge’s suspension. Marcin Matczak, a prominent law expert and outspoken critic of PiS, said he “did not think he would ever end up defending” Święczkowski, but believed the legal basis for his suspension was “non-existent”.Separately, justice minister Waldemar Żurek said he had asked for Święczkowski and deputy chief Sochański to be stripped of their legal immunity to face prosecution for obstructing the court’s work.View image in fullscreenPolish president Karol Nawrocki arrives at the constitutional tribunal in Warsaw, Poland.Photograph: Dawid Żuchowicz/Agencja Wyborcza.pl/ReutersDespite criticism, Tusk insisted that “restoring the rule of law is our duty.”“After years of PiS’s lawlessness, this is a difficult process, sometimes painful, and it requires decisive action. There is no other way,” he argued.Earlier this month, he pledged “the court will begin its work in accordance with the constitution, whether people like it or not.”Poland’s foreign minister Radosław Sikorski told reporters on the margins of a G20 meeting in Atlanta that “the constitutional tribunal was politicised under the previous government.”“What is happening has the purpose of allowing the majority of duly elected judges to make the tribunal function again,” he said.Opposition leaders and the court’s social media account accused the government of carrying out a judicial “a coup d’état”. Several European far-right figures, including Britain’s Nigel Farage, Liz Truss and the Netherlands’ Geert Wilders, also condemned the move.US ambassador to Poland Tom Rose said in a post on X: “The events unfolding tonight … are very serious.”“Both sides offer sharply different accounts of what happened and why,” he said. “Whatever the facts ultimately establish, thousands gathering outside the tribunal make an already dangerous situation more combustible. The last thing Poland needs is a confrontation that spirals into something far worse.”Explore more on these topicsPolandEuropeDonald TuskKarol NawrockinewsShareReuse this content

title: Eight in 10 homes in London’s poshest postcodes now sell below asking price, Coutts finds | House prices | The Guardian
description: Sellers in areas such as Belgravia and Mayfair face hundreds of thousands of pounds in losses as property prices fall
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: Sellers in areas such as Belgravia and Mayfair face hundreds of thousands of pounds in losses as property prices fall
Content: Properties in Belgravia have fallen 30.8% below their peaks.Photograph: Mike Kemp/In Pictures/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenProperties in Belgravia have fallen 30.8% below their peaks.Photograph: Mike Kemp/In Pictures/Getty ImagesHouse pricesEight in 10 homes in London’s poshest postcodes now sell below asking price, Coutts findsSellers in areas such as Belgravia and Mayfair face hundreds of thousands of pounds in losses as property prices fallLauren AlmeidaSat 31 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEight out of 10 properties in London’s most exclusive neighbourhoods – such as Mayfair, Belgravia and Knightsbridge – now sell below asking price, according to research by Coutts, which provides private banking services to wealthy clients.Property prices in “prime central London”, which covers the city’s most expensive postcodes, have dropped 5% in the third quarter of 2026, as theslowdown in the UK’s property markethits its wealthiest residents.It means some affluent people are facing hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of pounds in losses to the value of their homes, with properties selling at an average 10% discount to their asking price, Coutts found.Prices in the highest end of London’s property market are now 14% below their peak in 2014, having been hit hard by Brexit, the Covid pandemic, higher property taxes and a surge in borrowing costs. Buying and selling agents in the capital have also reported a slowdown in interest from foreign-born buyers after theabolition of the non-dom tax regime.Exclusive areas such as Knightsbridge and Belgravia, and South Kensington have been hit the hardest, Coutts said, with prices 30.8% and 26.9% below their peaks respectively.View image in fullscreenOne of west London’s mews, where properties have long been sought-after.Photograph: Sunpix Travel/AlamyAlex Webster, head of lending at the bank, said buyers and sellers at the top end of the market were taking a more cautious approach, even before the chancellor, John Healey’s, first budget this week.Sellers will now be watching to see if the budget “encourages some of that delayed activity to return”, she said. “But financing conditions and the wider economic environment will continue to influence the market.”There has been no change in the Bank of England base rate since last December but volatility in the bond market has driven up the swap rates that influence the pricing of fixed-rate mortgages.View image in fullscreenLondon’s Belgravia.Photograph: Ian West/PAWhile the Bank of England has kept its key interest rate on hold at 3.75%, expectations are growing that next week its monetary policy committee will vote to increase the rate for the first time in three years to 4%.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn the meantime, sellers in prime central London are increasingly shying away, Coutts found, with new listings down 14% compared with the previous quarter and available stock down by 6% year-on-year.Transactions were 9.1% lower in the third quarter of this year, it said, with the biggest slowdown in the £2m-£5m band, where transactions were down 22.3%.However, separate research from the estate agent Savills found that buyers at the very top end of the market are driving activity, with 26 transactions above £10m in the third quarter of this year, taking the total to 127 over the past year. Together, these sales were worth £2.88bn, it found.Explore more on these topicsHouse pricesLondonPropertyHousingHousing marketnewsShareReuse this content

title: Avanti West Coast paid out £20m in ‘delay repay’ passenger refunds this summer | Rail industry | The Guardian
description: Intercity train operator’s compensation bill likely to top £70m this financial year amid rise in claims across network
Author: Gwyn Topham
Headline: Intercity train operator’s compensation bill likely to top £70m this financial year amid rise in claims across network
Content: Avanti West Coast paid out more than £50m in refunds in 2025-26.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAvanti West Coast paid out more than £50m in refunds in 2025-26.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianRail industryAvanti West Coast paid out £20m in ‘delay repay’ passenger refunds this summerIntercity train operator’s compensation bill likely to top £70m this financial year amid rise in claims across networkGwyn TophamTransport correspondentSat 31 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAvanti West Coast paid out more than £20m to passengers in just three months this summer in refunds for disrupted journeys on Britain’s main intercity rail network.The intercity operator paid out almost as much in a four-week period to 25 July – £9.3m – as its annual profits for each of the past two years. It repaid a further £12.2m in the subsequent eight weeks.The “delay repay” compensation bill for slow-running or cancelled services has been spiralling upwards across the railway network in recent years, according to official figures, with Avanti the biggest payer – although never before at this scale.Most train operators are yet to publish this year’s payouts. According to the most recentpublished financial figuresfrom the Department for Transport (DfT), covering all operators, the total passenger compensation for delays rose to £150m across the railway in 2024-25, up 8% compared with the previous year, of which about 27% was Avanti’s payouts (£40.5m).Fare inflation and efforts to make passengers aware of their rights have contributed to the industry’s soaring bill, as well as the delays themselves. Compensation has become increasingly automated and some operators now proactively repay passengers who have been delayed.Under the contracts that replaced the franchising system since the pandemic, train operators’ income comes from fees paid by the DfT instead of depending on fare revenue, with the taxpayer instead taking any profit or loss from ticketing income or refunds.Avanti, which is due to be takeninto public ownership next yearas part of Great British Railways, paid out more than £50m in 2025-26, and is expected to pay out more than £70m this financial year.Asheatwaves hit the railway, fewer than half of Avanti trains ran on time in July with passengers delayed by an average 19 minutes, according to figures from the Office of Rail and Road. Its peak payout period also covered theincursion of a large herd of cowson the tracks for several hours one Tuesday.View image in fullscreenGWR (Great Western Railway) paid back £29.7m to customers last year.Photograph: Ian Dewar/AlamyLong-distance operators typically pay out the largest sums, with customers more likely to claim owing to the expense and the chance of delays reaching the 60-minute threshold where fares are refunded in full.Avanti and GWR are unusually generous among long-distance operators in paying compensation for delays after 15 minutes, when passengers are eligible for refunds of 25% of the fare paid.GWR, which runs trains from Wales and the south-west to London, and LNER, which runs London-Scotland trains on the east coast mainline, were the next highest refunders in 2025, paying back £29.7m and £28m respectively.The number of compensation claims filed by passengers across Great Britain’s railway reached 9.1m in 2026, up almost 10% year on year, with 80% of the claims approved, according to data from the Office of Rail and Road.An Avanti West Coast spokesperson said: “We apologise to customers affected by train delays. A range of factors can impact service performance, and we are working closely with our industry partners to improve punctuality and reliability across the network.“To make it as easy as possible for customers to claim compensation when things don’t go to plan, we are committed to ensuring that customers are able to promptly receive any compensation for delays and offer automatic delay repay for journeys delayed by 15 minutes or more.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAccording to Avanti, between May to August this year it was directly responsible for only 23% of those delays, with Network Rail or other operators responsible for the majority, as well as external factors such as trespassers on the line.GWR said the increase in its delay repay payments this year was “driven largely by repeated heatwaves, with prolonged periods of unprecedented temperatures affecting both trains and railway infrastructure”, including track defects, points failures, speed restrictions and train cooling issues.The operator said the payments recognised “the impact of disruption and helping maintain confidence in rail travel”, adding: “We’ve recently made efforts to increase publicity of the scheme, with clearer, more frequent announcements onboard delayed trains and on social media disruption updates.”View image in fullscreenLNER, which compensates customers only after 30-minute delays, nonetheless paid out £28m in 2025.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianLNER, which compensates customers only after 30-minute delays, did not provide updated financial data.According toDfT research, about half of disrupted passengers claim compensation, but an increasing number are satisfied with the process and results.Most train operators now resolve more than 99% of claims within 20 days, according to data from the rail regulator.A DfT spokesperson said it was “acting to tackle the root causes of disruption” and making it easier for passengers to get refunds, adding: “Under Great British Railways, we will make it quicker and easier to claim compensation through an easy-to-use service, which will also be available wherever passengers purchase their tickets.”Explore more on
