title: Jump scares, leather gloves and squeaking moth noises: theatre horror masters on how they make their shows so scary | Stage | The Guardian
description: Whether in the immersive haunted horror show Blackout or the campily satisfying 2:22: A Ghost Story, ‘tis the season to be scared witless. Meet the theatre-makers who are putting the horror into Halloween
Author: Kate Wyver
Headline: Whether in the immersive haunted horror show Blackout or the campily satisfying 2:22: A Ghost Story, ‘tis the season to be scared witless. Meet the theatre-makers who are putting the horror into Halloween
Content: Devil in the details … Ami Okumura Jones and Ty Fanning in Paranormal Activity.Photograph: Matt CrockettView image in fullscreenDevil in the details … Ami Okumura Jones and Ty Fanning in Paranormal Activity.Photograph: Matt CrockettStageJump scares, leather gloves and squeaking moth noises: theatre horror masters on how they make their shows so scaryWhether it’s immersive chiller Blackout or the campily scary 2:22: A Ghost Story, ‘tis the season to be scared witless at the theatre. But what’s the secret to making an audience gasp in terror?Kate WyverSat 31 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 08.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was 1am. Total darkness. Locking up a wedding venue, Sam Beech’s car sensor went off: there was something behind him. “It went on for half an hour,” the writer and director recalls, “on the front bumper, then round the back. But every time I looked, there was nothing.” It kept going, snuffling around the car. So he stopped looking. “I thought: ‘If I don’t look behind me, it won’t get me.’” Since then, Beech, the creator of one of a plethora of horror shows currently haunting the stage, admits, “I don’t like driving in the dark”.Beech’s experience was eerily similar to a scene in Andy Nyman’s hit 2010 playGhost Stories, which Beech had seen four times, so the gnarly end the character had met on stage filled his mind when the sensor went off in the dark. Now, the uncanny experience has fed into his own new horror showBlackout(touring the UK to 27 February), which uses everything that made him so scared that night: the quiet, the absence, the idea of something lurking in the shadows. “It’s the Jaws effect,” says Chris Fisher, the illusions designer behind the stage show ofParanormal Activity(at London Ambassador’s theatre to 27 February, and touring the UK), which had me sheepishly checking under my bed for several nights and stopped just short of nightmares. “It’s scarier to see the fin and hear the music,” Fisher says, “than it is to see the mechanical head of the shark.”On stages across the country, theatre-makers are hoping to make their audiences grab the arms of strangers next to them. But it’s easy to go wrong with horror, Fisher says: “It often goes too far, too hammy. Too – and I say this affectionately – Blithe Spirit.” But when you get it right, he says, discounting Noël Coward’s farce about an eccentric clairvoyant, “people leave with a newfound understanding of what theatre can do”.View image in fullscreenFear factor … Blackout.Photograph: Craig FullerFor years, 1987’s The Woman in Black was the reigning champion of achieving a proper nail-biting scare on stage. On a sparse set, the show invited the audience to imagine a pony and trap as the story set off, priming them, like Beech’s stalking shadow and Fisher’s Jaws theory, to fill in the gaps for themselves. It was unrivalled for years, but recently, perhaps kicked off by the success of Ghost Stories, there’s been an increasing flood of shows trying to eke out new ideas of horror plays. The campily satisfying haunted house thriller2:22: A Ghost Storyis ever-touring and the hallucinatoryStranger Things: The First Shadow(which also features Fisher’s illusions) is going strong in London’s West End. Farther west in the city, at the Bush theatre, Mei Leng Yew’s recent debutThe Hungry Ghostplayed with Chinese traditions and queer obsession to create a nightmarish story of possession. Going down the route of psychological horror, the immersive touring experienceSinsuses audience participation to determine what happens on stage. This Halloween season, the ghosts and ghouls have busy schedules.double quotation markIt only takes one mistimed moment for your brain to go: I didn’t believe that“Maybe 2.22 was so successful that it just initiated a cascade,” says comedian Kirsty Mann, who tests her audience’s belief in ghosts with a true tale of her haunted house in the comedy-horrorCorpse, which is coming to London’sSoho theatrein February after an Edinburgh fringe run. “These things come in cycles,” she says. “But people go to the theatre for escapism and horror is the ultimate escapism. There’s so much awfulness in the world right now, people are turning more to the fantastic, and with horror, you’re not just following the story. You’re totally separated from reality.” Now, finding the scariest night out possible has become “almost a drug”, Fisher says, for audiences chasing the high of the collective fright. “It’s like being on a rollercoaster,” says Mann, who saw Paranormal Activity three times in one month.The line between successful scare and unimpressed shrug is a fine one. “It’s a bit like comedy,” says Carolyn Downing, sound designer onThe Silence of the Lambs, the stage adaptation of the psycho-killer movie that is touring the UK to 26 June. “It has to be super-precise. It only takes a mistimed or misaligned moment, and your brain’s quick enough to go: ‘I didn’t believe that.’” The success of that minuscule moment relies on the atmosphere created by dozens of people backstage. “It’s all about the buildup,” Downing says. Achieving the perfect jump scare requires the increase in tension, the wrongfooting, and the offbeat fright just as you’ve relaxed. “It won’t scare you if you’re half expecting it,” she says.View image in fullscreenPhantom of the theatre … Sophie Lenglinger and Robin Morrissey in The Haunting of Hill House.Photograph: Pamela RaithHorror works best, set designer Ti Green believes, “when your understanding of the rules are pulled apart”. For the stage adaptation of Shirley Jackon’s 1959 gothic novelThe Haunting of Hill House, Green wanted to build a world that looked solid and dependable. “That’s the first step,” she says. “The second is to dismantle everyone’s sense of safety.” Jackson’s story is a quintessential haunted house, with a group of ghost seekers wandering around a decrepit mansion. Paying homage to Jackson’s description of “Hill House, not sane”, much of Green’s set is made of translucent gauze, so depth and vision can play with the idea that everything is constantly in flux, making it feel, she says, “as if the house is doing it, not as if the theatre is doing it”.In Blackout, Beech aims for the opposite effect: he wants the theatre itself to feel haunted. Having created the award-winning Statfold Scream Park, he is moving his experience in horror events on stage with this touring show that plays in each venue for just one night. “Five hundred people walk into a theatre and choose to accept something they know isn’t real,” he says, setting up the show, which is framed as a rehearsal. With the audience as ghosts to the action, Blackout aims to dissect and strengthen the classic tropes of horror: “darkness, silence, negative space”. As in The Woman in Black, the agreement to suspend disbelief allows the paranormal to take a step closer.double quotation markThe juiciness of horror is that you can zoom in on sound, make it feel visceral and intenseThese conventions of horror on stage are not cheat codes. “Anyone can go and buy a magic trick and try to perform it,” Fisher says, “but they’re not actually doing real magic. It’s all about how you present it, what story you put with it. It’s the same with horror.” Many of the principles of good illusion – and good horror – have remained largely unchanged over time. “For Paranormal Activity, I went back to the ways that Victorian magicians or spiritualists would have done it,” Fisher says. “The majority of the illusions could have been used for hundreds of years.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIllusions such as Fisher’s have become a significant selling point for modern horror on stage, perhaps, as Mann suggests, because they give a “wow factor” that is hard to recreate on screen with the ubiquitous powers of AI and CGI. “In live theatre, if you pull off an amazing trick,” she says, “you can have that moment of, ‘Holy shit, how did they do that?’”View image in fullscreenCell mates … Mollie Gallagher and John Partridge in The Silence of the Lambs.Photograph: Marc BrennerMaximising the bodily experience of sharing the space, theatre has the opportunity to be even scarier than film, allowing the fear to slip off the stage and follow you home. “The really scary stuff is when it taps into a deep fear you have,” says Mann. In Corpse, which uses minimal set and choice illusions by John Bulleid, she pushes on the bruise of the feeling: this could happen to me.Other shows have the challenge of a direct comparison with their originals; that Paranormal Activity, The Silence of the Lambs and The Haunting of Hill House, which is touring the UK to 21 November, are all adaptations says something of the endurance of spooky stories. For The Silence of the Lambs, Downing felt a responsibility to achieve the iconic sound of moths, which marks a significant turning point in the story. Using foley techniques, she’s previously made the sound of birds with flapping leather gloves, but the moths needed to be smaller and finer. Her list of moth-making ingredients includes rustling leaves, swooshing paper, rubbed hands and the real recorded squeaking of death’s-head hawkmoths. “The juiciness of horror is that you can zoom in on sound,” she says, “make it feel visceral and intense.”This is key; a horror play has to be felt. So much of that feeling being handed over to the audience, Fisher says, is down to the actors. “Like with illusion, when you see something again and again, you become a bit jaded with it. It’s the same thing with horror scares. It’s so important to keep those reactions as if they are experiencing it for the first time, because that’s what we’re doing.”Halloween in the UK is growing. “We’re about 10 or 15 years behind America,” says Beech. “I think that’s probably the same with horror shows and audience appetite.” As demand grows, so do these theatre-makers’ ambitions. “I want to keep pushing it,” says Fisher. When the Paranormal Activity team recently locked the show in New York, he says, “we all sat down for dinner, together for the first time in months, and were like, ‘What shall we do next?’” He nods to me: “Make sure you have those nightmares.”Explore more on these topicsStageHalloweenTheatrefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Yaga: chicken bones? Saltburn parties? This folk horror is so debauched, it’s hilarious | Television | The Guardian
description: Heated Rivalry’s Hudson Williams and Carrie-Anne Moss star in this audacious mystery about a Slavic witch. There’s supernatural weirdness, detective work … and a hero who looks a lot like Tim Key dressed in leather
Author: Rhik Samadder
Headline: Heated Rivalry’s Hudson Williams and Carrie-Anne Moss star in this audacious mystery about a Slavic witch. There’s supernatural weirdness, detective work … and a hero who looks a lot like Tim Key dressed in leather
Content: Chilled to the bone … Carrie-Anne Moss as osteo-academic Katherine in Yaga.Photograph: Bell Media/SkyView image in fullscreenChilled to the bone … Carrie-Anne Moss as osteo-academic Katherine in Yaga.Photograph: Bell Media/SkyThe watcherTelevisionYaga: chicken bones? Saltburn parties? This folk horror is so debauched, it’s hilariousHeated Rivalry’s Hudson Williams and Carrie-Anne Moss star in this audacious mystery about a Slavic witch. There’s supernatural weirdness, detective work … and a hero who looks a lot like Tim Key dressed in leatherRhik SamadderSat 31 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHalloween was once a simpler time, when neighbourhood kids would dress up as mythical serial killers, the undead or bedsheet-wearing ghosts. At some point, following America’s lead, it became sexy and cat-forward. It has now become a sort of conceptual art show. I’ve heard people this year planning to go to parties dressed as Erling Haaland, Prom Carrie (Prime Video edition) and Bad Bunny’s half-time Super Bowl show. It’s horrifying.The perception of witches has evolved, too. Once understood to be a malignant version of the crone archetype, sympathy for witches has grown. They have been embraced as a feminist image of the older woman, free of patriarchal command and possessed of a powerful rage. In recent years, Maleficent, Elphaba from Wicked and Marvel’s Scarlet Witch have given witches a pop edge. Some of my most intense friends proudly wear slogan T-shirts proclaiming themselves descended from the witches whom society failed to burn.Now, in swoops Yaga (Sat, 9pm, Sky Atlantic), a quasi-horror mystery series from Canadian streamer Crave. They are known for making Heated Rivalry (matching oversized jerseys? Huge Halloween outfit this year). Yaga is another genre-bender. It opens with a cocky detective, Charlie Rapp, arriving in the quiet fishing town of Whittock, present day. He’s investigating the disappearance of Henry Park, son of a wealthy local family. As the case grows violent, it brings evidence of cult activity to light, and increasingly hints at the existence of a dark, supernatural figure behind events.To those unfamiliar with Slavic folklore, Baba Yaga is a forest-dwelling hag who lives in a hut on chicken’s feet, flies around in a pestle and mortar, and eats children. It is her voice that bookends every episode in a taunting monologue, though her exact involvement with Henry’s disappearance is a grisly little puzzle. I’m a few episodes in, and it’s still unclear if she is a literal character in the play or the embodiment of its theme: women being sick of men’s shit.The men are certainly a rum bunch. Charlie Rapp is our hero – yet his credentials are questionable, and he flirts with every woman in town, including his police partner Carson. Henry Park – played by Heated Rivalry’s Hudson Williams – is vain, adulterous and given to druggy parties. Williams also plays Henry’s slippery roommate Logan. The show has fun with the unlikely physical resemblance between them, as when Logan answers the door to the surprised detectives. “I have brown eyes and glasses,” he explains with a straight face. He’s also naked under his overalls, FYI.The women are formidable, including Clark Backo’s drily unimpressed take on police detective Carson. She’s introduced as a fan of romantasy (or what her superior officer describes as “fairy smut”). Carson is unenthusiastic about pursuing the case of the missing rich kid. “Billionaires aren’t real people,” she shrugs. Even more no-nonsense is Carrie-Anne Moss as an older, morally ambiguous osteo-academic. When Charlie sits beside her at a bar and asks what excites her, she replies: “Sex. And bones.”Given the bones, and the overalls, you may be thinking: “Stuff the spooky business, are there hella sexy shenanigans?” Yes and no … The theme of Henry’s parties, which take place Gatsby-like in his absence, is Dark Solstice. Expect masked ball eroticism, fetish wear and debauchery and, elsewhere, an erotic encounter that had me laughing at the audacity. But it’s never wholesome fun. There are chicken bones in unexpected places, and Rapp in particular is haunted by horror imagery. While sex is on the menu, the male gaze is under the microscope.Playwright-creator Kat Sandler has, so far, found room on the broom to make Yaga pointed but playful, and fun while tackling the darkest of subject matter. There are Ukrainian covers of pop songs, a hero who looks like a leather-trouser version of Tim Key, and Saltburn-esque parties. But what I really want, whisper it, is for an actual witch to appear, rather than the political idea of one. I’m basic, and like pointy hats. Will this be another Blair Witch situation? How far will the witch-tease go? I’m crossing my fingers and burying the hair of a bat.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionThe watcherfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Guide #267: Robert Pattinson embraced his inner lowlife and became one of the best actors of his era | Culture | The Guardian
description: In this week’s newsletter: Sandra Hüller and Anne Hathaway might have been in more films this year – but Pattinson’s remarkable run confirms him as one of the best performers of his generation
Author: Gwilym Mumford
Headline: In this week’s newsletter: Sandra Hüller and Anne Hathaway might have been in more films this year – but Pattinson’s remarkable run confirms him as one of the best performers of his generation
Content: Rogues gallery .. Robert Pattinson in (clockwise from top left) The Odyssey, Dune: Part Three, Primetime and The Drama.Composite: Universal/Warner Brothers/AP/A24View image in fullscreenRogues gallery .. Robert Pattinson in (clockwise from top left) The Odyssey, Dune: Part Three, Primetime and The Drama.Composite: Universal/Warner Brothers/AP/A24The Guide newsletterCultureThe Guide #267: Robert Pattinson embraced his inner lowlife and became one of the best actors of his eraIn this week’s newsletter: Sandra Hüller and Anne Hathaway might have been in more films this year – but Pattinson’s remarkable run confirms him as one of the best performers of his generationGwilym MumfordSat 31 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 04.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor prolific actors, 2026 has been a banner year. The roles have kept piling up for a small cohort of stars, the roles have kept piling up, to the point where you wonder how they found the time to do vital things like sleep, shower or scarf down nuclear-fallout-covered chicken wings on YouTube interview shows.Just look at Sandra Hüller, who by the time December ends will have racked up six projects in 2026, ranging from austere cold war road-trip movies to migraine-inducing Marvel blockbusters. Anne Hathaway, meanwhile, has since January appeared as – deep breath – a psychologically tormentedfading pop star, a catatonicpopular novelist, a suburbanitefending off hungry dinosaurs, anIthacan queenfending off hungry suitors and reluctant fashion journo Andy in the belatedDevil Wears Prada sequel. (Hathawaydidalso have time to go on thenuclear chicken wings show, but was unable to partake, due to being heavily pregnant.)Robert Pattinson’s 2026 output looks almost leisurely compared to Hüller and Hathaway’s, though by normal standards the four films that he will have starred in by the end of year is an impressive haul. More impressive still is the quality of work, a remarkable run of roles that cements his status as one of the best performers of his era. And most certainly the best player of lowlifes: his 2026 has been a true rogues’ gallery, with every shade of scumbag accounted for.This malcontent tendency is magnificently on display inPrimetime, in UK and Irish cinemas now. Directed by Lance Oppenheim – film-maker wunderkind also behind the much-talked-about You Can See Everything – this clammy, queasy drama recalls the heyday (and ultimate demise) of To Catch a Predator, the US network reality show notorious for its stings on putative paedophiles. Pattinson plays the show’s preening host Chris Hansen, famous for his habit of sidling into the middle of an operation and casually confronting his target. Hansen’s slick, nightly news exterior disguises a grubby desire to bend the show’s ethics to breaking point, his motivations complicated by a trauma-inducing incident early in his career, and Pattinson does a great job at showing glimpses of the frayed, angry, fearful figure behind the squeaky-clean veneer. (Hansen, it should be noted, has declared the film “a completely made-up work of fiction” and “an insult to the thousands of men and women who work hard every day to protect children from predators”.)Before Primetime came The Odyssey, and another oleaginous figure for Pattinson to ooze into. His alpha-suitor Antinous was, by design, a more two-dimensional character than Hansen; a crawling, craven antagonist primarily present for audiences to bristle at and Odysseus to dispatch with extreme prejudice. Still, Pattinson nails the assignment, with a performance that some critics saw as “stealing the show” – some achievement in a gargantuan three-hour epic featuring giants, men transforming into pigs and the like.Compared to the lowlifes of Primetime and the Odyssey, Pattinson’s character in gleefully black comedyThe Dramais positively well adjusted. Indeed, initially gentle art historian Charlie is the recipient of no little sympathy in the early stages of the movie, having been broadsided by a horrifying detail – which, six months after the film’s release, I’m still wary of revealing – from the past of his bride to be (played by Zendaya, another prolific 2026 star, and one who now shares three films with Pattinson). But as Charlie unravels, his cracked decision-making and general brittleness becomes deeply unlikeable. By the day of the wedding itself, you’re half-rooting him to fail miserably – a remarkable turnaround, and testament to Pattinson’s gift for unlikability.There is of course one more performance to come this year and it’s a big onein Dune: Part Three. Pattinson plays Scytale, a shape-shifting manipulator set on usurping Timothée Chalamet’s space-messiah Paul Atreides. Another antagonist then – though Atreides’ slide into antihero-dom at the end of the previous Dune might complicate things. Still, with his dead eyes and general air of quiet menace in the film’s trailers, it’s hard to imagine Pattinson’s character will be handing out cupcakes and kittens.But what is it that makes Pattinson so adept at playing sleazeballs? Certainly his playing against type, a former Twilight heart-throb gone to seed, seems effective. It helps too that he picks roles better than just about anyone, often working with auteurs who seem to understand his magnetic/repellent duality. It’s a shame that this sort of role tends to get sidelined for worthier, more outwardly heroic parts when it comes to awards season: no one seems to be including Pattinson in their Oscar best actor prognostications.Perhaps that suits him fine – his choice of role hardly seems to be an impediment at the box office.The Odysseyis one of the highest-grossing films of the year, Dune: Part Three will probably join that bracket when it arrives in December, and both The Drama and Primetime have massively punched above their indie-film weight. And if you have had enough of him on the dark side, next year he reprises his role as the Dark Knight in the second of the latest Batman films. In the meantime, though, if you want a wrong’un played right, just call for R-Patz.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTo read the complete version of this newsletterplease subscribeto receive The Guide in your inbox every FridayExplore more on these topicsCultureThe Guide newsletterRobert PattinsonThe OdysseynewslettersShareReuse this content

title: ‘Being hated is very bracing’: Helen Garner on surviving three marriages and being called a ‘rotten feminist’  | Helen Garner | The Guardian
description: Her unsparing fiction and true crime writing have made her one of Australia’s most controversial and celebrated authors. The author discusses relationships, resilience – and finding global recognition five decades into her career
Author: Emma Brockes
Headline: Her unsparing fiction and true crime writing have made her one of Australia’s most controversial and celebrated authors. The author discusses relationships, resilience – and finding global recognition five decades into her career
Content: Helen Garner.Photograph: Jillian FreyerView image in fullscreenHelen Garner.Photograph: Jillian FreyerHelen GarnerInterview‘Being hated is very bracing’: Helen Garner on surviving three marriages and being called a ‘rotten feminist’Emma BrockesHer unsparing fiction and true crime writing have made her one of Australia’s most controversial and celebrated authors. The author discusses relationships, resilience – and finding global recognition five decades into her careerSat 31 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 18.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfew years ago, whenHelen Garnerhad an idea to write a book about Australian rules football, her heart soared then immediately sank. The impetus was Ambrose, her teenage grandson, who played for a local team. Garner enjoyed watching them and wanted to put this into writing. Then the dreary thought: “I’ll have to swot, read the rulebook.” People to whom she mentioned the idea assumed she’d be writing a polemic, “like what it means in society and how terrible it is and what violence means. And I’m going: ‘What a bore.’”As anyone familiar with Garner’s almost 50-year writing career will know, there is nothing more igniting to the 83-year-old than the invitation to outrun boredom by going off in an unauthorised direction. Garner, who is speaking to me via video call from her home in Melbourne, occupies that tiny category of writers famous enough to be recognised in public. Stopped by strangers in the street, she’s often treated to their strong views about her work. As a result, perhaps, she has perfected a very Garnerian obstinacy, enabling her to resist other people’s bossy opinions which, in the case ofThe Season, meant no tedious explainers about the rules, history or sociology of Aussie rules football. Instead, says Garner, she envisaged following a single season of Ambrose’s U16s team, the Flemington Colts, as “a nanna’s book”. During publicity, she’d turn up to an event at a library to find “the first five rows packed with nannas; all these white-haired women with hankies in their hands. And I feel nobody writes about nannas. I mean, sentimentally, yes; but I want to say what they’rereallylike.”To say what something is really like is the ethos behind all of Garner’s books and it has, on occasion, landed her in spectacular trouble. It has also won levels of devotion from readers who have turned her into an almost guru-like figure in her 80s, turbocharged by the publication last year of her wisdom-heavydiaries– which won the Baillie Gifford prize – and helped, one suspects, by her ability to combine insight and erudition of the highest literary order with a style that is at times comically down to earth. (A classic example: referring to the controversy around The First Stone, the 1995 book she wrote about feminism, Garner says: “I gave a lot of people the shits.” It’s not a line one can imagine, say, Marilynne Robinson delivering.)The current mania around Garner is a long-overdue correction for a writer who, outside Australia, was ignored and condescended to for decades. In 1987, in a typically sniffy reference to Garner in the TLS, her work was referred to as “Mills& Boon for bohemians”, yet she is now credibly hailed as a contender for the Nobel prize, can fill 900-seat venues in New York, and has seen practically her entire back catalogue reissued in the US. (Carrie Bradshaw was shown carrying a copy of Garner’s 2014 book, This House of Grief, in a scene from And Just Like That … and Dua Lipa interviewed her on her podcast.) All of which Garner shrugs off, referring to herself as an “old kind of warhorse” who was never interested in prizes in the first place, not least, she says, because “you have to put on that look that you’re pleased for the other person”, even when – a typically bracing admission – “their book was not as good as mine”.View image in fullscreenNoni Hazlehurst and Colin Friels in the 1982 film of Monkey Grip.Photograph: RGR Collection/AlamyThe fact is that Garner has always cut through the flab and waffle of so much literary culture in pursuit of something more honest. In her first novel,Monkey Grip, published in 1977 and based on her rackety life at the time, Garner told the story of Nora, a woman with a young child living in a bohemian shared house in Melbourne and on-off dating a heroin addict called Javo. Garner had arrived at this point in her own life partly as a result of fleeing a rigid, repressed childhood in the town of Geelong near Melbourne. As the oldest of six kids, she had frequently clashed with her father, a wool merchant and “a rather domineering person”, she says, who bullied her meek stay-at-home mother and kept no books in the house. After attending an Anglican girls’ school, Garner won a place at the University of Melbourne, where she spent the best part of three years in the pub. “It was a strange time. Once you get estranged from your parents, you go galumphing across the landscape seizing this and throwing out that. I look back and I see a lot of damage. We trampled through each other’s lives.”This sense of damage would become more profound in Garner’s late 20s after a short-lived marriage to Bill Garner, whom she’d met at college and with whom she had a daughter, Alice. The pair split up when Alice was two and Garner moved into a series of hippy shared houses. It was an unstable life that had what Garner now calls a “kind of berserk quality to it – there was a lot of smashing and breaking that went on”, and only became more precarious when Garner, who had been working as a teacher, “opened my big mouth” and was fired from a school in Victoria for giving an impromptu and explicit sex education lesson. At the same time, she fell in love with a heroin addict and, a few years later, looking back over her diaries from that period, realised she wanted to write about it, embarking on Monkey Grip with the modest ambitions that enabled its fresh, uncontrived voice. “It was a private thing, writing down in a notebook what I thought about what was happening in my life,” she says. “So, I didn’t compare what I had written with anything great or mighty. I thought I’d just tell the story of what  happened.”Looking back now, she finds the novel “rather naive and undefended”.But it thrills her, 50 years on, that Monkey Grip is not only still in print, but highly popular. She was in a shop, recently, “and there was a young bloke who said: ‘Aren’t you Helen Garner? I’m reading Monkey Grip, and we’re living the life!’” She laughs and assumes a look of mock horror. “And I thought: ‘Ooh, don’t do that.’” I’d always assumed Javo had died way back, but fans of the book may be interested to know the real-life Javo is alive and well and living in Hobart, Tasmania, where he has a wife and grandchildren. After offering his spare room to Garner’s own 25-year-old grandchild who was visiting that part of the world recently, he wrote to Garner, “to say how marvellous it was to see our two grandchildren together”.double quotation markI did feel sad. I thought: God, everyone hates me, this is terrible. But I didn’t regret it for a minuteMonkey Grip, which was written with the electric, offhand energy of a young writer yet to grow self-conscious, caused a sensation in Australia and was followed by a series of short, brilliant novels, includingThe Children’s BachandCosmo Cosmolino, before Garner pivoted to nonfiction in the mid-1990s. (She’d return to fiction in 2008 withThe Spare Room, based on Garner’s experience of nursing her close friend through cancer. The book has recently enjoyed an operatic adaptation in Melbourne.) And in the background, always, Garner maintained her diaries, recording her second marriage to Jean-Jacques Portail, a journalist whom she met in Paris, where she moved for a couple of years in the late 1970s while living on a writer’s grant and trying to write her second novel. Portail moved back to Melbourne with Garner, and they split up in 1985. A few years later, Garner moved to Sydney to be nearer to the writer Murray Bail, the man who would become her third and (to date) final husband, and who dominates the last volume of her diaries.Alongside entries about fashion, art, friendship, nature and the end of her marriage to Bail, the diaries offer readers a chance to witness the epic battle between Garner’s extremely robust writer’s ego and its near-constant collapse. A typical entry, from 1997, reads: “I have to admit to myself that I feel irrelevant, small, hollow, untalented, worthless – and frightened. The energy required to maintain self-command is so great that I am always tired. How repellent one is. If only I were writing something.”I’m curious about how Garner reconciles these two things – confidence and self-doubt – particularly in the wake of The First Stone, her first nonfiction book, in which she interrogated the case of two female students at the University of Melbourne who accused the master of their college of groping them. A mid-90s cause celebre in Australia, Garner foreshadowed culture wars to come by presenting the story as a possible overreaction on the part of the women, putting the boot in, she says, “to what I thought was a rather punitive form of feminism. I got into a hell of a lot of trouble. Really, it was quite astonishing, the amount of hostility I copped. I was thought to be a rotten feminist; a heretic. I heard that someone on a judging panel said: ‘If this book by Helen Garner even gets on the long list, I will’ … thunderous threats …’” Garner says: “I just laughed. Because I think it’s a sort of compliment.”The First Stone was much more subtle and ambivalent than its detractors allowed, being a real intellectual reckoning with a complicated subject. Given the response, I’ve always wondered how Garner came back from it. “I had the shit kicked out of me! People savaged me. And it took me a while, but when I got over it, I thought: ‘Well, I survived that, and now I’m free. I can write what I really want. And I won’t have to see if it comes out pure.’ Being hated is very bracing. It’s not destructive. Well, it could be; if I’d published that book now … but the internet didn’t exist then. I did feel miserable and sad and I thought: ‘God, everyone hates me, this is terrible.’ But I didn’t regret it for a minute.”Because it was the book you wanted to write? “Yeah. And I made mistakes in it; but I got a lot of amazing letters. I reckon I got about 800 and I answered every one. It was quite an exercise; someone would cover me with loathsome abuse and I’d write back: ‘Thank you for your kind letter …’ And the good letters I got were long and thoughtful, saying: ‘I read your book and I’d like to tell you something that happened to me.’ And that made me think I opened up the subject for people to talk about calmly.” It can’t have hurt that thebook was a huge bestseller.“Yeah, and thatreallygave them the shits. And they’d go around saying: ‘Oh, yes, of course Helen’s motivation was purely commercial.’”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markIt’s the hardest thing people ever do, being married. Harder than having kidsIt helped that Garner had a career in freelance journalism to fall back on, particularly when she got stuck on a book,This House of Grief, which told the story of the trial and conviction of Robert Farquharson, who murdered his three children to get back at their mother, and which took eight years to finish while the various appeals played out. After the success of Monkey Grip, Garner dashed off a second novel, “and it was crap, and my publisher correctly bounced it back. That was a nasty moment, but they were right. Justbecause you’ve written one book doesn’t mean you know how to write the next one.” But while better novels followed, including The Children’s Bach, published in 1984 and widely considered her masterpiece, she moved permanently to nonfiction after The First Stone, coming to specialise in a kind of literary true crime with a series of devastating books built around high-profile murder trials.That shift was brought about in part by her marriage to fellow novelist Murray Bail. Garner’s account of the collapse of that marriage appears in How to End a Story, her third volume of diaries, and it’s quite something; at one point, in a fury at the insidious, unfaithful Bail, she throws cups, an espresso machine and a saucepan full of beetroot soup across the kitchen. Garner writes that Bail belittled and gaslit her, and dismissed her work as inferior to his. “I thought my marriage was the worst marriage in the world and I was the world’s biggest wimp for going along with it,” she says. Since the diaries came out, however, a lot of people have said to her “‘that book is my marriage.’ And that sort of shocks me – they’re talking about a marriage they’re still in. But it can be terribly difficult. I reckon it’s the hardest thing people ever do, being married. Harder than having kids.”She regards having her only child, Alice – at the age of 26 and without any great planning – as the greatest good fortune of her life. And the happiest she has ever been, she says, has been during these past decades of living next door to Alice and her husband and three children. Bail, meanwhile, comes out of the diaries looking very bad indeed. Any feedback from him since publication? “The answer to that is no. And either he hasn’t read it or he’s saying he hasn’t read it. I haven’t had any contact with him now since long before I published the diaries. We parted badly and painfully and it’s never been mended.” She sighs. “He also published a memoir in which he summed up my part in his life in about three sentences. I was roundly dismissed. And I went on like it was the collapse of civilisation. But. You know. Bless him.”Given the relative literary reputations of Helen Garner and Murray Bail these days, she can afford to be generous. And, of course, one of the delights of the diaries is the schadenfreude of watching a man flex his superiority over a woman who will, in time, be regarded as one of the great writers of our age. Splitting up gave her just the impetus she needed, she says. “I felt very liberated by no longer living in close companionship with someone who had ideas about literature which were too severe and didn’t suit my work. He had this hierarchy of forms, and I subscribed to them for a long time because I’d been educated to think that as well.But after I split up with him, I relaxed into being a nonfiction writer. And I stopped doing it defensively. I thought: ‘Actually, this is my natural form.’ And I still feel that very strongly: I’m out here, and I’m good at this, and it’s really fun to do, and it gets you out of the house, rather than stewing in your own self-hatred.”View image in fullscreenJudy Davis and Elizabeth Alexander in the stage adaptation of The Spare Room.Photograph: Brett Boardman/The GuardianSo it was with The Season, in which for the space of winter training Garner showed up every week at the football ground to watch her grandson and his cohorts play. Garner went through her customary period of thinking it was all a mistake, that the book was a terrible idea and she’d never be able to drag it over the line. The toughest experience she ever had with this kind of self-doubt was during the writing of Joe Cinque’s Consolation, her deeply affecting 2004 book about the killing of Joe Cinque, a young engineer from New South Wales whose girlfriend injected him with ‘Get in there and do it!’ heroin and was later convicted of manslaughter. “I actually told Maria Cinque, his mother, that I wasn’t going to write the book. I wrote her a letter and said I’m really sorry, I’m going to have to give up, I can’t do this. And she rang me up and said: ‘What do you mean you can’t do it? We gave you our story, you said you were going to do it, you’ll do it! Do it!’ God, I nearly died of shame. I look back on that and think you need someone who’s going to kick you right up the arse. Don’t you think? You don’t want someone who’s going to say: ‘Oh, darling, it must be so hard, I really feel for you.’ You want someone to say: ”This is Garner’s circuit, from idea to execution via collapse, shame and eventual, dogged persistence. A few days before our conversation,Anne Carsonwas announced as the winner of the Nobel Prize in literature, a decision thoroughly approved of by her Australian peer. Taped up on the wall of her office, Garner has a poem of Carson’s, which she looks at in times of dire need. “If I ever had a tattoo, I’d have that last line tattooed on me,” she says. “I just think it’s so marvellous.” The poem describes a stormy night at sea, fraught with peril, existential and otherwise. “And the last line is: ‘Nothing for it just row.’”The Season by Helen Garner is published in the UK on 5 November by W&N. title: What we’re reading: Ian Rankin, Louise Kennedy and Guardian readers on the books they enjoyed in October | Books | The Guardian
description: Writers and Guardian readers discuss the titles they have read over the last month. Join the conversation in the comments
Author: Ian Rankin
Headline: Writers and Guardian readers discuss the titles they have read over the last month. Join the conversation in the comments
Content: View image in fullscreenWhat we're readingBooksWhat we’re reading: Ian Rankin, Louise Kennedy and Guardian readers on the books they enjoyed in OctoberWriters and Guardian readers discuss the titles they have read over the last month. Join the conversation in the commentsIan Rankin, Louise Kennedy andGuardian readersSat 31 Oct 2026 05.04 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 05.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIan Rankin, authorI’m a huge fan of Muriel Spark, but wasn’t sure I needed another biography of her, yet James Bailey’sLike a Cat Loves a Birdwas a winning blend of detail and readability.A Bad, Bad Placeby Frances Crawford is a prize-winning debut crime novel set in 1970s Glasgow. It’s clever, authentic and humane with unforgettable protagonists and pitch-black humour.The Heights by Ian Rankin is published by Orion (£25). To support the Guardian order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.David, Guardian readerI’ve loved (most of) China Miéville’s books (I think that he and Alan Moore are the real doyens of “weird” fiction) – butThe Rouseis surely his opus: sometimes prose-poetry, sometimes stream-of-consciousness, with shades (literally) of Lovecraft and MR James running through a bleak, unsettling yet compelling tale. I strongly suggest you take a very deep breath and launch into an adventure (lasting more than 1,200 pages) that will leave you dazed and amazed!Louise Kennedy, authorI normally read one book at a time but, perhaps because I am on the road at the moment, I have three on the go. Emma Cline’s short story Arcadia almost killed me, and I’ve been a devotee ever since.Switzy,her new novel, accompanies on his final journey a man whose wealth and privilege offer no protection from the dementia that has begun to addle his poor brain. Edith Wharton’sThe House of Mirth: so far, charming, pretty Lily Bart is in charge of her story, but an encounter with a man who appears not to wish her well suggests there may be trouble ahead. John McGahern’sMemoiralready has my heart rent in twain, to paraphrase an old Irish ballad, and he hasn’t even finished primary school.Stations by Louise Kennedy is published by Bloomsbury (£20). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Sophie, Guardian readerAlmost Lifeby Kiran Millwood Hargrave is a beautiful and heartbreaking love story that transported me back in time to Paris in the late 1970s and 80s. The main characters, Laure and Erica, as well as the other characters, soon feel like friends – friends who are human and imperfect, and who sometimes make frustrating decisions, but who are all the more lovable for it. It’s elegantly and smartly written, and paints such vivid pictures – I rarely read past my bedtime these days, but I stayed up late for this one, torn between wanting to finish and never wanting the book to end. It captures the feeling of love and being in love so well.Mark, Guardian readerThis year, I’ve set myself the challenge of only reading books by writers who aren’t part of the Anglosphere, with each writer being from a different country. It’s certainly forced me to read stuff outside my comfort zone – which is how, this month, I’ve ended up readingIndependent Peopleby Halldór Laxness, a 500+ page novel about an Icelandic farming family. Over the course of about 20 years in the early 20th century, we follow the hardships and privations of a stubborn farmer who insists he fend for himself to maintain independence on his own land.I expected this book to be unrelentingly grim reading – and in parts it is, especially in the almost indifference to death. But it’s also very humorous in its characters’ cynicism towards one another. It’s beautifully atmospheric in its prose, particularly the changing of the seasons and their effect on the dramatic landscape of the farm. Reading so much literature in translation has given me an appreciation of when it’s done well (without ever knowing the original text), and the translation by JA Thompson, in collaboration with Laxness, is sublime.Explore more on these topicsBooksWhat we're readingIan RankinEdith WhartonEmma ClineChina MiévilleShareReuse this content

title: ‘They cheer like it’s football’: Celebrity Traitors fans hit bars to watch climax | The Traitors | The Guardian
description: One south London bar provided Claudia Winkleman-themed cocktails and its very own banishment ceremony
Author: George Francis Lee
Headline: One south London bar provided Claudia Winkleman-themed cocktails and its very own banishment ceremony
Content: Shock in Arch Clapham as comedian James Acaster revealed he was a reluctant traitor.Photograph: Andy Hall/The GuardianView image in fullscreenShock in Arch Clapham as comedian James Acaster revealed he was a reluctant traitor.Photograph: Andy Hall/The GuardianThe Traitors‘They cheer like it’s football’: Celebrity Traitors fans hit bars to watch climaxOne south London bar provided Claudia Winkleman-themed cocktails and its very own banishment ceremonyGeorge Francis LeeSat 31 Oct 2026 07.53 EDTFirst published on Sat 31 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCries, cheers and boos emanating from pubs across the country on Friday night were less likely to be linked to any sports fixture than the nation coming together for the dramatic climax of the BBC’s The Celebrity Traitors.The cloak and dagger reality show, in which contestants attempt to deceive or deduce who among them are “Faithfuls” and “Traitors” for a charity cash prize, drew inmore than half of the UK’s TV audiencein its debut episode earlier this month.The popularity of the Claudia Winkleman-hosted programme was so great that fans left their living rooms and flocked to public venues to watch the second series of the show.The series’s psychological mind games are what appealed to Calum, a regular viewer and account manager from Edinburgh who was waiting to watch Thursday’s semi-final at a bar in Clapham. “For me, it’s how good people are at lying and then how that translates into normal life. You can almost second-guess anyone you’re around,” he said.The intensity from fans had not only caused venues to screen each episode of the hit show, but offer an entire night of entertainment inspired by the programme. In south London bar Arch Clapham, attenders sipped Claudia Winkleman-themed cocktails, ate “100% Traitor” chocolate coins and twice took part in their very own banishment ceremony. Banishment, in which contestants vote out a peer they suspect to be a Traitor near the end of each episode, provokes some of the most visceral reactions from fans.View image in fullscreenPunters at Arch Clapham participating in a Celebrity Traitors game during the semi-final screening on Thursday.Photograph: Andy Hall/The GuardianCalum and his friend Ali had previously “stumbled” into Arch Clapham’s watch party for the first series’s finale of The Celebrity Traitors last year, and they were captivated by the crowd’s excitement. “There were people cheering like it was football,” Ali said. “I’m not personally too into sports, but I like having the atmosphere.”This year’s run of treacherous celebrity TV had 3 million more viewers than the previous year’s iteration. Ali explained that the programme had encouraged friends, co-workers and even strangers to discuss each episode, with many seeking to avoid spoilers at all costs.He said: “I think back in the day, everybody was watching X Factor. There’s not really been anything since then that everyone’s been watching, so it’s quite nice. You can probably pick out a random person and they’ve probably been watching.”Brandon Bolland, a supervisor at Arch Clapham, said the bar had screened every episode of the latest series after the previous two finales of The Traitors’s standard and celebrity versions drew in a lot of punters. “We were packed. It was really, really popular,” he said.During Thursday’s semi-final, those attending the Traitors-themed night were equally jubilant and appalled when comedian James Acaster shocked audiences by revealing he was a reluctant traitor.It was these bombshell TV moments – such as when actor Richard E Grant made the unexpected decision to reveal he was a Traitor in the game’s first episode – that made the act of watching the show together more enjoyable, Bolland said.He added: “It’s like watching the World Cup when this is on. People are jeering and shouting like they’re watching a football game.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBlue Planet III features cloudier footage to prove authenticity amid AI boomRead moreAnother notable moment for fans that caused loud scenes was when fan favourite Miranda Hart was murdered earlier in the series, he added.This year’s highly anticipated finale saw stars such as comedian Romesh Ranganathan and actor Michael Sheen attempt to uncover the two remaining traitors: TV personality Maya Jama and content creator Kenny Oghenovo Ojuederie (known as King Kenny).For Siobhan, an IT account manager, the social manipulation and subterfuge in these sections are the show’s biggest draw. “That whole psychology aspect and how they can play that is super interesting to me,” she said.Siobhan’s love for the Traitors led her to introduce her parents to the show, and has led to a number of vocal outbursts. She added: “I’m talking to the TV when I’m watching it!”Despite players being required to manipulate one another, some find the show’s format to be a comforting watch. Ziad, who attended the watch party with his husband, said the programme stood out “in a day and age where reality TV is solely about fights and political divide”.“It’s the closest you get to a feelgood show,” he added.While viewers were united by their Traitors fervour, they also shared a love of the game’s cut-throat rules. This was made clear when the Clapham bar hosted its own roundtable discussion once the semi-final had finished, and the only Guardian journalist present was deemed a Traitor and banished.This article was amended on 31 October 2026. Miranda Hart was murdered in the game, not banished as an earlier version said.Explore more on these topicsThe TraitorsBBC OneBBCfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Selma Blair says she is ‘so sorry’ to those she alarmed following alleged air incident  | Selma Blair | The Guardian
description: Actor pleaded not guilty to allegedly kicking a nurse and a police officer after an incident on flight from Los Angeles to New York
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Actor pleaded not guilty to allegedly kicking a nurse and a police officer after an incident on flight from Los Angeles to New York
Content: Selma Blair said in her statement that she has never intended to hurt or frighten anyone.Photograph: Ryan Murphy/APView image in fullscreenSelma Blair said in her statement that she has never intended to hurt or frighten anyone.Photograph: Ryan Murphy/APSelma BlairSelma Blair says she is ‘so sorry’ to those she alarmed following alleged air incidentActor pleaded not guilty to allegedly kicking a nurse and a police officer after an incident on flight from Los Angeles to New YorkPress AssociationSat 31 Oct 2026 01.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSelma Blair has spoken for the first time since being charged with assault after a mid-air assault incident, saying she is “so sorry” to anyone “that I hurt, I frightened, that I alarmed”.Blair pleaded not guilty to state assault charges over allegations she kicked a nurse and a police officer after an incident involving crew members on a flight from Los Angeles to New York earlier this month.At the time, her representatives said her alleged behaviour had been brought on by a severe medical emergency.Selma Blair charged with assault of police officer and nurse after allegedly attacking flight attendantsRead moreIn a videopostedto Instagram, Blair said: “I know I’ve been quiet for a couple weeks since October 11. And you deserve to hear from me directly, and I’m sorry that it’s taken this long.“There is a legal matter going on, and my lawyers have asked me to not say anything about that day, and I’m listening to them.”The actor said she took the matter “very seriously” and that the “very simple and the truest thing I know about myself is that not one day ever have I intended to hurt or frighten anyone”.“And so to the people that I disappointed, that I hurt, I frightened, that I alarmed, I am so sorry,” she said, adding that she appreciated everyone who had reached out to her in support since the incidents.Blair then assured fans that her service dog Scout, who accompanied her on the flight, was doing well. She was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in 2018 and got the Labrador as a service dog five years ago.The actor concluded: “So, right now I’m going to be taking care of my health. And my son. And thinking of you all with my gratitude and love.”Blair, 54, was detained by police when the Delta flight landed in New York and was taken to hospital for evaluation.A police officer taking her to Jamaica hospital medical centre alleged in charging documents that while securing Blair to a stretcher, the actor pulled one of her legs from the straps and kicked her repeatedly around the face, neck and chest, causing serious pain and substantial swelling.Later, a nurse moving Blair said the actor kicked her in the chest.She was arraigned on two counts of second-degree assault late the following day at a court in Queens, where a judge set her bail at $20,000 (£15,141) cash or $60,000 dollars bond and set the next hearing for January.Her lawyer Shawn Barnes told the judge that her actions were not intentional.He said the actor missed several doses of “a powerful medication that controls severe neurological symptoms,” according to the New York Daily News and New York Post.Mr Barnes said she boarded the flight in Los Angeles amid a heavy workload and hit her head during the flight.He said these factors, along with the altitude, led to “a state of severe confusion and disorientation”.Explore more on these topicsSelma BlairShareReuse this content

title: Unseen Harry Houdini writing published on 100th anniversary of his death | Books | The Guardian
description: Strand magazine to feature never-before-seen article from Hungarian-born escapologist who was also a prolific author
Author: Richard Luscombe
Headline: Strand magazine to feature never-before-seen article from Hungarian-born escapologist who was also a prolific author
Content: Harry Houdini chains himself to a locomotive wheel for an escape attempt, circa 1910.Photograph: Transcendental Graphics/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHarry Houdini chains himself to a locomotive wheel for an escape attempt, circa 1910.Photograph: Transcendental Graphics/Getty ImagesBooksUnseen Harry Houdini writing published on 100th anniversary of his deathStrand magazine to feature never-before-seen article from Hungarian-born escapologist who was also a prolific authorRichard LuscombeSat 31 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUnseen writing byHarry Houdini, the world’s most renowned escapologist and illusionist, is being published in the US on Saturday, the 100th anniversary of his death.As well as being famous for his magic acts and quest to expose fake mediums and spiritualists before he died in 1926 at the age of 52, Houdini, whose real name was Eric Weisz, was aprolific author, with more than two dozen books, short stories and plays to his name.One of them, an article titled An Interesting Scrapbook, was never published, and appears for the first time in print Saturday inStrand magazine, a literary publication that specializes in presenting lost or hidden works by prominent writers and historical figures.It is a detailed look at some of the performers who shaped the early days of magic as a stage production, and inspired the path of Houdini, a Hungarian immigrant to the US as a child, into the best-known, and one of the most creative and popular entertainers of his day in Europe and America.It features images of numerous theater bills from an era of growing public fascination with the supernatural blended with an increasing appetite for unusual or fanciful acts. Houdini explores advertised performances including “necromantic miracles”, “magical delusions”, and “the greatest living wizard”.“What makes the article remarkable is it reveals a side of Houdini that has largely been overshadowed by his extraordinary fame as an escape artist,” said Andrew Gulli, Strand’s editor-in-chief.“Here we have Houdini the historian, painstakingly documenting forgotten magicians, theatrical performers, old playbills, and the remarkable world of 19th-century entertainment.“There’s something rather poignant about the world’s most famous magician devoting so much attention to entertainers whose names have largely disappeared from history.”The article was preserved among many of the artist’s other papers in theHoudini Libraryat the Harry Ransom Center at the University of Texas at Austin, where a curated tour will mark the anniversary of his death on Saturday.Houdini experts at the University of Michigan, and the online fan site Wild About Harry, told Gulli they believed it has never previously been in the public domain.“[Finding] a published version of An Interesting Scrapbook turned out to be as elusive as the man himself, which raises an interesting mystery of why,” he said.“Houdini was an accomplished author and an extraordinarily effective self-publicist. He was also fiercely competitive and protective of his professional knowledge. Could he have deliberately withheld this material because he feared rival magicians might benefit from his research? Or was it simply a project he never completed?“We don’t know the answer, but the question itself adds another dimension to the discovery.”Houdini was known to despise spiritualism being presented as anything other than entertainment, and dedicated increasing time in the years before his death from peritonitis debunking performers he called “charlatans” for claiming to be mind readers, or possess supernatural powers.Several commemorations are planned globally on Saturday to mark the anniversary, including a gala and public eventsin Budapest, where he was born in 1874; anda séanceat his former home in New York.Explore more on these topicsBooksHarry HoudiniShareReuse this content

title: ‘A gust of wind blowing back her hair added something special’: Mark McEvoy’s best phone picture | Photography | The Guardian
description: It was very cold and the young smoker was barelegged, barefoot and wearing a fur coat … How could the photographer resist?
Author: Grace Holliday
Headline: It was very cold and the young smoker was barelegged, barefoot and wearing a fur coat … How could the photographer resist?
Content: Cigarette break in Margate Old Town, 2014, shot on iPhone 4S.Photograph: Mark McEvoyView image in fullscreenCigarette break in Margate Old Town, 2014, shot on iPhone 4S.Photograph: Mark McEvoySmart shotPhotography‘A gust of wind blowing back her hair added something special’: Mark McEvoy’s best phone pictureIt was very cold and the young smoker was barelegged, barefoot and wearing a fur coat … How could the photographer resist?Grace HollidaySat 31 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis Margate shop is now an ice-cream parlour, but back in 2014 it was a vintage clothes store. Mark McEvoy, who had relocated from London the previous year with his partner and baby daughter, approached the young woman to ask permission to take this shot.“I remember it being a very cold October day, so I was surprised she was barelegged and barefoot,” he says. “My guess is that she was working in the shop, or maybe a friend of someone working there. The fur coat may even have been for sale inside, just something she put on to keep warm during a cigarette break.”‘They looked like two curtain-twitchers, though not very subtle ones’: Peter Crome’s best phone pictureRead moreMcEvoy didn’t notice the blond-haired, barelegged mannequin in the window until he stepped back. “A gust of wind blowing back her hair and her pose added something special,” he notes.In more recent years, McEvoy has been scanning and collating his 40-year archive of photographs, and reflecting on his work across various devices and formats; a range of iPhone models but also analogue cameras, both 35mm and medium format. “I am a bit of a purist, inspired by the documentary tradition of cropping in the frame when you take the photo. So, rather than say to myself, ‘I can crop that out in post’, I’ll move physically closer to the subject instead,” McEvoy says.It’s an approach he would recommend to any aspiring photographer. “These days, with AI and advanced editing software, it’s too easy to manipulate a photo, and the line between fact and fiction becomes more and more blurred.”Explore more on these topicsPhotographySmart shotArtfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Blind date: ‘He said: “If heaven is real, you’ll definitely be going there”, which might be the nicest thing anyone’s ever said to me’ | Dating | The Guardian
description: Nelson, 41, who works in legal services, meets Louise, 37, who works in marketing
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Nelson, 41, who works in legal services, meets Louise, 37, who works in marketing
Content:
Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianBlind dateDatingBlind date: ‘He said: “If heaven is real, you’ll definitely be going there”, which might be the nicest thing anyone’s ever said to me’Nelson, 41, who works in legal services, meets Louise, 37, who works in marketingSat 31 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleView image in fullscreenNelson on LouiseWhat were you hoping for?Great company and wonderful conversation.First impressions?Louise is such a sweet, sincere person. With very interesting hobbies!What did you talk about?All sorts of funny things, from feeding monkeys to the worst theatre shows and wooden toys.Most awkward moment?When we met, I wanted to greet her with a friendly hug but she was seated and had to get up.Good table manners?Impeccable, and she had amazing taco-eating skills.Best thing about Louise?She will laugh and think I’m taking the mick but I’m not: her dedication to the things she loves. So admirable! Passion and commitment. It’s infectious.Would you introduce Louise to your friends?Yes.Q&AFancy a blind date?ShowBlind date is Saturday’s dating column: every week, two 
strangers are paired up for dinner and drinks, and then spill the beans 
to us, answering a set of questions. This runs, with a photograph we 
take of each dater before the date, in Saturday magazine (in the
 UK) and online attheguardian.comevery Saturday. It’s been running since 2009 – you canread all about how we put it together here.What questions will I be asked?We
 ask about age, location, occupation, hobbies, interests and the type of
 person you are looking to meet. If you do not think these questions 
cover everything you would like to know, tell us what’s on your mind.Can I choose who I match with?No,
 it’s a blind date! But we do ask you a bit about your interests, 
preferences, etc – the more you tell us, the better the match is likely 
to be.Can I pick the photograph?No, but don't worry: we'll choose the nicest ones.What personal details will appear?Your first name, job and age.How should I answer?Honestly
 but respectfully. Be mindful of how it will read to your date, and that
 Blind date reaches a large audience, in print and online.Will I see the other person’s answers?No. We may edit yours and theirs for a range of reasons, including length, and we may ask you for more details.Will you find me The One?We’ll try! Marriage! Babies!Can I do it in my home town?Only if it’s in the UK. Many of our applicants live in London, but we would love to hear from people living elsewhere.How to applyEmailblind.date@theguardian.comWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Describe Louise in three wordsEnergetic, passionate, excellent conversationalist (four I know!).What do you think Louise made of you?An oddball with similar interests?Did you go on somewhere?It was a work night so we remained sensible.And … did you kiss?It was a work night.If you could change one thing about the date, what would it be?I wouldn’t change a thing! It was a very pleasant date overall.Marks out of 10?9 out of 10. A really pleasant evening!Would you meet again?Yes, I would.View image in fullscreenNelson and Louise on their dateView image in fullscreenLouise on NelsonWhat were you hoping for?Fun conversation with an interesting person and to discover a new restaurant.First impressions?A gentleman, very polite, laughs very loudly (in a good way).What did you talk about?London zoo volunteering – a typical day. Nelson growing up in Singapore. Covid – how I was in Singapore and Bali just as it started kicking off. Theatre shows we’ve been to – how perfect Oliver! is (this was mainly me). How we both go and see all the Oscar-nominated films every awards season. Nelson’s new startup.Most awkward moment?The waitress thought a photographer would be joining us and we needed a table for three.Good table manners?I was more conscious of my own, as I ate the tacos with my hands while he used cutlery.Best thing about Nelson?He’s a very interesting and interested person – so many hobbies and passions. I liked that he shared my enthusiasm for all things cultural.Would you introduce Nelson to your friends?Can’t think why not, he’s very interesting and sweet!Blind date: ‘Most awkward moment? When she squished an insect that was on my forehead’Read moreDescribe Nelson inthree wordsPerceptive, warm, bright.What do you think Nelson made of you?He said: “If heaven is real, you’ll definitely be going there”, which might just be the nicest thing anyone’s ever said to me. He also laughed very heartily all the way through so hopefully he thought I was funny.Did you go on somewhere?No, but we were the last to leave on a Tuesday night, so pretty good going.And … Did you kiss?No.If you could change one thing about the evening, what would it be?The pineapple/lime/cinnamon ice-cream was incredible, we should’ve got one each.Marks out of 10?8 (the date, not Nelson as a person!).Would you meet again?I think as friends – maybe at the cinema as Oscar season is approaching!Nelson and Louise ate atMirtala, London W4. Fancy a blind date? Emailblind.date@theguardian.comExplore more on these topicsDatingBlind dateRelationshipsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Don’t make sugar a treat – or hide the broccoli: top chefs on how to make your kids happy eaters | Food | The Guardian
description: Tom Kerridge, Helen Goh and other foodies on what they feed their children
Author: Mina Holland
Headline: Tom Kerridge, Helen Goh and other foodies on what they feed their children
Content: Photographs: Louise Hagger/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPhotographs: Louise Hagger/The GuardianChefs' family mealsFoodDon’t make sugar a treat – or hide the broccoli: top chefs on how to make your kids happy eatersTom Kerridge, Helen Goh and other foodies on what they feed their childrenMina HollandSat 31 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 04.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTom KerridgeAcey,10I’m fairly certain every child is a picky eater. People who tell you their kids happily tuck into beetroot and feta salads? I don’t buy it. The majority of children are selective, and you just have to navigate it. If they see you eating vegetables often enough, eventually they come round.Acey is 10, lifts weights and is seriously into rugby; he’s already training with boys older than him. He’s constantly burning energy, so my job is to get food into him before he realises he’s hungry. If I wait for him to ask, all he’ll want is whatever comes in the brightest wrapper.double quotation markIf he’s involved, he’s more likely to eat itHe eats loads of meat and fish, loves cheese and salami, and we’ll make omelettes, burgers or cheese toasties with cured meat. He’s started making his own smoothies, too, blitzing frozen mango and pineapple with a mixture of coconut and cow’s milk. He’d never choose fruit, but if I put a chopped apple in front of him, he’ll eat it. This is also true of breakfast; he’ll say he’s not hungry, but if I put yoghurt, honey and granola in front of him, it’ll disappear.Vegetables are still a work in progress. Sweetcorn, peas and carrots are fine, but anything greener needs a bit of encouragement. That’s where the old chef’s tricks come in. A tomato sauce packed with blended vegetables, a bolognese or stew cooked low and slow, or getting him to thread peppers on to kebabs or build his own pizza. If he’s involved, he’s more likely to eat it.We don’t eat together enough during the week because of my work hours, but weekends are different. The barbecue goes on, everything gets dumped in the middle of the table – burgers, chicken, pitta, hummus, salad – and everyone helps themselves. He dodges the salad, but he’ll happily mop up the olive oil with warm bread, and that’s a start.Tom Kerridge is a TV chef and founder of five restaurants includingThe Hand & Flowersin Marlow, Buckinghamshire.Meera SodhaArya, 9, andYogi, 6As a mixed-race family, we cook boldly and eat widely. I cook from everywhere east of India and my husband, Hugh, loves Nigel Slater. That said, our children don’t automatically eat boldly, although they did both choose to be vegetarian.Our eldest, Arya, only ate beige food until she was about six. Now she’ll out-eat all of us on the chilli front and that’s become her thing, it’s almost an identity. She even has a T-shirt with a bottle of sriracha on it (she first tried it age seven with some tofu nuggets I was experimenting with). Meanwhile, Yogi is becoming more open-minded; six to 12 months ago, she’d sometimes burst into tears if I put something new on the table. Now she eats most things, but I tend to have a backup – like fried eggs or bread and cheese.View image in fullscreendouble quotation markI’ve always found it works to introduce something new alongside something familiarFalafelis one of our go-to meals – I always keep some ready-made in the freezer. Everyone customises their own – with gherkins, pickled beetroot and chillies, hummus, cucumber, cherry tomatoes, grated carrot, mayonnaise, sriracha, cabbage, tahini and even mango chutney – which they find empowering. Egg fried rice was one of the first things we ate together and remains a favourite. We all love katsu curry, most dals, paneer in any form, and tofu, either in nuggets, or in a homespun poke bowl or, surprisingly, the silken kind with rice and a sweet and salty sesame sauce.I’ve always found it works to introduce something new alongside something familiar. When I first made them my sticky mango and lime paneer naans, I explained they both loved all its ingredients – paneer, mango, naan. I’ve introduced spices gradually, too, making mild versions and then adding a quarter of a teaspoon more each time I make it.I was labelled a fussy eater as a child, but I think I just had incredibly sensitive taste buds. We underestimate how differently kids experience flavour; a cumin seed can seem explosively bitter, and something like kimchi can be overwhelming. The biggest lesson for me has been not to label children. If you keep calling them fussy, they start believing that’s who they are. I used to tell Arya, “Just try one cherry tomato every year and see what happens.” The other day, she ate not one, but three.Meera Sodhais a cook, author of four cookbooks and Guardian Feast columnist.Helen GohSam, 15, andJude, 11I’ve got two very different children, in temperament and in the way they eat. I’ve realised over time that the best way to tackle it is to find different ways to prepare the same thing.Sam says he hates roast chicken, but what he actually doesn’t like is the fatty, “slimy” skin. If I slice up the breast and wrap it in a flour tortilla, he’s delighted. Jude, meanwhile, wants the chicken leg, skin and all. The same goes for broccoli. Sam likes it crisp and crunchy; Jude likes it cooked a minute longer until it’s soft. Once I started askingwhythey didn’t like something, instead of writing it off, feeding them became much easier.View image in fullscreendouble quotation markI’m wary of hiding vegetables – I don’t want food to become a trickThey’ve always loved tuna macaroni, which I originally made with lots of sweetcorn. Over time, I’ve slowly built in more flavours – I’ll cook down onions, carrots and celery into a really delicious base, then grate in courgette until it melts away like butter, or finely slice green beans so they disappear into noodles. I’m wary of hiding vegetables, though. I tell them what’s in there because I don’t want food to become a trick. I’d rather they thought, “Actually, grated courgette is what makes this taste so good.”When the boys were little, I couldn’t work out why they devoured my mum’s congee and omelettes but barely touched mine. Mum laughed and said, “Salt and sugar”, each of which she adds a pinch of when she cooks. As a new mother I was so focused on doing everything “right”, whereas she was focused on making it delicious.They love chilli con carne and poke bowls. For the poke, I briefly marinate cubed salmon in mayo, soy, maple syrup, lemon and, more recently, wasabi. Grill it for two minutes and then put that on top of a rice bowl with edamame, corn and, if I’m feeling fancy, a pineapple and mango salsa. We also love ants climbing a tree, a Sichuan Chinese dish with glass noodles and minced pork.Sometimes I think we put too much pressure on ourselves to produce the perfect balanced plate. The other night I was rushing out and just put prosciutto, halloumi, avocado and cucumber on the table. Sam texted me afterwards saying, “More of this, please.” It made me realise that a meal doesn’t have to look worthy to be balanced.Helen Gohis a pastry chef and the author ofBaking and the Meaning of Life. She co-writes theSweet Spot columnin Guardian Feast.Anna JonesDylan, 10, andEsca, 3My eldest, Dylan, is 10 now and a brilliant eater, but it took a long time to get here. He always liked fruit and raw vegetables, which reassured me, but meals with sauces or lots of mixed flavours just weren’t his thing.The big shift came when he was about six or seven and became obsessed with ninjas. All the stories featured ramen shops, gyoza and bowls of noodles, and I realised that food had become part of his imagination. We started making ramen at home, recreating the little trays of udon, vegetables and tofu he’d seen. Once Japanese food felt familiar through stories, it gave him the confidence to try other flavours, too.View image in fullscreendouble quotation markI think about protein in small ways, adding extra eggs and ground almonds to pancakesOur younger son, Esca, is three, and he’s in his buttered toast and plain pasta era. We offer him a little of whatever we’re eating every night and most evenings he ignores it. I’ve tried not making alternatives, but I spend my life cooking to nourish people. I can’t send my child to bed hungry!Having two boys at such different ages has made me much more relaxed. I know tastes change because I’ve watched it happen. In the meantime, I look for small wins. Smoothies packed with yoghurt, nut butter and seeds frozen into ice lollies have been a life-saver this summer. I think about protein in small ways, too, adding extra eggs and ground almonds to pancakes.More than anything, I think children need ownership. Dylan loves tasting recipes I’ve been working on and giving me a verdict, but he’s just as inspired by seeing other children cook. He loves the Buddy Oliver and What’s Cooking Omari? shows on TV, and has been enjoying some of my old childhood recipe books – vintage Jane Asher and Jenny Chandler. It’s become a genuine interest.Anna Jonesis an award-winning food writer, author of four books about vegetarian home cooking.Easy family ramenView image in fullscreenAnna Jones’s easy family ramenThis is a very long way from authentic ramen and is something I make with staple ingredients that my kids like to eat.I cook the noodles separately as I find cooking them in the broth does not work. If you are using ready-to-cook noodles you can pop them straight in, though. I often use coconut aminos instead of soy sauce here as it adds umami with less salt; you can buy it from most supermarkets. I use a range of green veg, whatever I have to hand: broccoli, peas, edamame and sugar snaps all seem to go down well. I get extra points if I roast the broccoli.Serves 2, small(ish) kids and 2 adultsFor the quick brothA couple of coins of gingerA bunch of spring onions1-2 tbsp white miso1-2 tbsp veg stock powder1 tsp soy sauce or coconut aminos200g pack of udon noodles(you can also use ramen noodles or the straight-to-wok, ready-to-eat kind)For the tofuOil400g block of firm tofu, chopped2 tbsp sesame seeds1 tbsp maple syrup1 tbsp soy sauce or coconut aminos4 big handfuls of green veg(broccoli, greens, sugar snaps, peas, edamame)To serve (add as desired)Crumbled-up seaweed snacks,gomashio,furikakePut the ginger and the green tops of the spring onions into a deep pan and add a litre of cold water and bring to boil and simmer for a few minutes. Finely slice the white part of the spring onions.In a separate pan, cook your noodles in boiling water according to packet instructions then drain and run under cold water. If any of your veg needs cooking (broccoli, frozen peas etc) you can add it for the relevant number of minutes with the noodles.
