Then drain and cool the lot.Put a frying pan on the heat, add a little oil and the chopped tofu, and cook for a few minutes until it’s crisp and golden on all edges. Add the sesame seeds and cook for another few minutes until the seeds are toasted, turn off the heat and add the tablespoon of soy or coconut aminos and the tablespoon of maple syrup, and toss in the pan to coat.Stir the miso and stock into the broth.Put the noodles into the bottom of four bowls, with enough room for your veg, tofu and broth. Put the broth into a jug and the tofu, vegetables and toppings into little bowls on the table so everyone can help themselves – little ones may need help with the warm broth. Slurp.Marie MitchellMarcie,5Weaning was such fun because Marcie ate everything. I probably drove myself mad trying to expose her to as much variety as possible. She’d be having adventurous home-cooked food while we were eating takeaway. Then she started nursery and the fussiness crept in.I’ve never put pressure on what she has to eat. We decide what goes on the table, but once it’s there it’s up to her. If we give her agency, she’s more likely to try things. We’re quite strict about not making alternatives, though we always make sure there’s something she’ll enjoy. Usually that’s fruit.double quotation markWe eat together almost every night because it’s an important pause in the dayI don’t like creating hierarchies around food. I don’t want food to become about rewards and punishments. I’m also not a fan of hiding vegetables. If she doesn’t know she’s eating something, she won’t know it’s something that she likes.Family dinner isn’t always relaxing. But we still eat together almost every night because it’s an important pause in the day. Our classic meal is a slow‑cooked tomato sauce with lots of garlic, paprika and a little bit of sugar – that can go on pasta but I’ll often serve it with prawns. She’ll also eat tofu in any form – loves the stuff – and corn on the cob, crispy kale and any fish that isn’t breaded, which I serve with homemade chips. We get her involved, too – setting the table or perhaps rolling her own roti, if that’s what we’re having. I think children respond well when you don’t infantilise them. They’ll often surprise you.Marie Mitchell is a cook and the author of the award‑winning Caribbean cookbook,Kin.Ravneet GillDonnie,2.5, andRoman,newbornPeople are always telling me what a good eater Donnie is, but he’s only two and a half, so I know that could all change. I was such a fussy eater as a child – eating Indian food at home was non-negotiable, but I’d eat chips and a KitKat at school for lunch every day. Then I snapped out of it; when you learn about food and try some of the best produce, you can’t not love it. That’s what I’m trying to do for Donnie.When we started weaning, I bought baby food pouches, probably out of fear of getting it wrong. Then I remember looking at them in the supermarket and thinking, “Hang on, I know how to cook.” So I started giving him bits of whatever we were eating – a lamb chop, a piece of salmon, a spoonful of rice. I’ve never really skimped on seasoning, either. He grew up eating cumin, coriander and proper home cooking; it’s only chilli he isn’t keen on.double quotation markI’ve tried not to frame sugar as a treat – he knows he’s allowed it, so he doesn’t pine for itWe don’t make separate meals or “healthy” snacks. If we’re eating steak and chips, beef shin ragu or rotis, that’s what he’ll have. If we’re at the restaurant, I’ll let him have ice-cream or chocolate cake. I’ve tried not to frame sugar as a treat because I think that’s where things went wrong for me. Donnie knows he’s allowed it, so he doesn’t pine for it.Of course, there are days when he barely touches a vegetable, and then the next he’ll eat a bowl of prawns or happily munch asparagus. I don’t fixate on it. The important thing is that food is around, we eat together, and he sees us enjoying it, too. That’s how I learned to love food, and I hope it’ll be the same for him.Ravneet Gillis a pastry chef, food broadcaster and co‑owner ofGina restaurantin Chingford, London E4.Jackson BoxerRoma, 13,Ruscha, 9,Marlowe,6, and Ilya, 3The difficulty with feeding four children is that there aren’t many points on the Venn diagram where all of their likes overlap. Just when you discover something they all eat, one of them decides they no longer like it. There are a few constants, though. A good ragu bolognese can usually carry the week. I’ll make a huge batch, then serve it with pasta one night, folded into tacos the next, over rice after that. I’m forever making chicken stock, too. Pasta is cooked in it, rice is cooked in it. It’s the easiest way I know to smuggle a bit of vitality into food in a form they find irresistible.double quotation markI used to take it personally. Eventually I realised that refusing food is one of the few forms of power children haveBeyond that, feeding children is much less a culinary challenge than a psychological one. They each cultivate their own impossible preferences. Breakfast is a perfect example: two insist on thick American-style pancakes, the other two will only eat crepes. I make one batter, then dilute half of it.I used to take it personally. Eventually I realised that refusing food is one of the few forms of power children have. In a family where cooking matters, they understand that saying “Mum’s a better cook than you” lands exactly where it hurts.I grew up surrounded by wonderful cooks and didn’t appreciate any of it because it was all I knew. That’s the great misfortune of childhood: you don’t value your parents’ cooking until you’re deprived of it. So I try not to take the ingratitude too seriously; it’s almost a happy inheritance.Jackson Boxeris chef/owner ofBrunswick House,VesperandDove, all in London, and culinary director ofCowley Manornear Cheltenham and Henri in London.Rosie BirkettAurelie,4,andEdwyn,2I don’t think of my kids as fussy eaters – but that wasn’t always the case. With my eldest, Aurelie, I took every rejection personally. I’d put something in front of her that she’d happily eaten a fortnight earlier and suddenly she’d refuse it. By the time Edwyn came along, I knew that if you keep exposing them to things, they often come back around. Pickiness is almost always a phase.Being afood writerprobably made it harder. I was trying to apply everything I know about making food exciting, when children often want the opposite: simple things. I’ll spend hours making something complex, only for them to reject it in favour of buttered pasta. I’ve had to separate my ego from what they’re asking for.double quotation markIf I’m introducing a new pasta dish, I hold back a plain portion, to serve with butter or olive oilWe’ve learned what meals work for us. They love slow-cooked food: chicken noodle soup, braised beef shin, lamb, pasta cooked in chicken stock, smoked fish chowder with sweetcorn, dal with spinach and cauliflower chopped up small. I usually try to introduce new things alongside foods they know, say aubergine or mushrooms with chicken and roast potatoes. We ask them to try it, applaud them for doing so, and offer it again another day if they don’t like it. If I’m introducing a new rice or pasta dish, I will usually hold back a couple of plain portions, to serve with butter or olive oil. The backup plan is always carbs and fat! Sometimes on holiday they’ll try something from my plate in a restaurant because it feels like a privilege rather than an obligation.My expectations were too high in the beginning. Now I know it’s the pattern over weeks and months that counts. If all else fails, there’s always Greek yoghurt with fruit after dinner – and a glass of milk before bed.Rosie Birkettis a food writer and cookbook author. She has a weekly Substack newsletter,A Lot on Her Plate.Margot HendersonHector,33,Owen,30, andFrances,27I’ve been thinking a lot about the meals my kids grew up on recently – I’m working on a project about family food. The three of them always seemed to be eating, so I took the approach that if they didn’t eat one meal they weren’t going to starve.We mostly gave them what we were eating. They loved pasta, roast chicken, brown rice, stir‑fries with broccoli, chard and Chinese vegetables, which they were used to because in those days we lived near Chinatown. We’d make rice balls, frittatas full of vegetables, tortellini with spinach, roast pumpkin. Apart from giving them the odd chicken bone to suck on, I kept them vegetarian until they were about two because I wanted to encourage a love of vegetables and for them to eat widely. It mostly worked, although none of them ever really took to fennel!double quotation markThe important thing was that food was always enjoyableView image in fullscreenBut they weren’t angels about food. Green vegetables were usually tricky, although they always loved peas. There was plenty of tomato pasta – I often say they were virtually made of the stuff – and we gave them fish fingers, too, which I’m rather against now, given the state of the oceans. I also used to make them “crusties”, just like my mum made for me. When our brown loaves were a few days old, I’d slice them thinly, spread them with butter and honey or Marmite, then pop them in a low oven until crisp. Perfect for packed lunches, and intriguing to the other kids.The important thing was that food was always enjoyable. They grew up in restaurants – as babies they’d sleep under the tables, or join us in high chairs. Ours was a social house, people always coming for lunch or supper, so they were in an environment where food was a joyous, social thing. I don’t underestimate the power of that.Margot Henderson is chef-patron of Rochelle Canteen, London E2.Brown rice and pumpkin ballsView image in fullscreenMargot Henderson’s brown rice and pumpkin balls. Photographer’s assistant: Sam Reeves; food styling: Nicole Herft; prop styling: Sandy SuffieldI once had a business making rice balls, and when I became a mum they became a go-to snack for my kids.Makes about 14 balls220g short-grain brown rice500ml water100g pumpkin, chopped up into 2cm pieces1 tbsp wholemeal flour(optional)2 tbsp sunflower seeds2 tbsp sesame seeds¼ cup flat parsley, roughly chopped¼ cup coriander, leaves roughly chopped, stalks finely chopped2 bunches of spring onions, finely choppedA pinch sea salt1 tbsp soy sauce or tamari1.5 litres of plain oil(rapeseed or sunflower)Wash the rice several times until the water runs clear, cover in water and leave to soak for 30 minutes. Drain. You will need a saucepan big enough to hold the rice and water, with a tight-fitting lid. To this, add the rice, water and salt, and cover with the lid.Place the pot over a high heat and bring to the boil; when you see steam coming out the side or hear the pan bubbling, turn the heat right down to very low and then cook for 45 minutes. Don’t take the lid off. Set aside for at least 15 minutes.While the rice is cooking, prepare the other ingredients. The rice should have absorbed all the water and come together into a lovely sticky consistency. You should be able to squish it flat easily.Once the rice has cooled down, mix in the rest of the ingredients with the exception of the oil. It should be a good sticky consistency and come together when squeezed. You can add the flour to help with the binding if needed. Roll into ping‑pong-sized balls.In another deep pan, heat the oil to 180C. Drop the balls in and fry for three to five minutes, until golden brown. Once cooked, place on a plate lined with kitchen paper. Cook in batches so the oil temperature doesn’t drop too low.There you have it! They can be eaten hot or cold. A minty yoghurt dip would be nice alongside.Explore more on these topicsFoodChefs' family mealsChefsParents and parentingTom KerridgeFamilyChildrenfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Dark green dust’: the best (and worst) supermarket green teabags, tested and rated | Tea | The Guardian
description: Green tea can be a mixed bag – we sipped our way through the supermarket shelves to find the ones worth boiling the kettle for
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: Green tea can be a mixed bag – we sipped our way through the supermarket shelves to find the ones worth boiling the kettle for
Content: The quality of green tea varies considerably.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Robert BillingtonView image in fullscreenThe quality of green tea varies considerably.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Robert BillingtonThe FilterTeaReview‘Dark green dust’: the best (and worst) supermarket green teabags, tested and ratedGreen tea can be a mixed bag – we sipped our way through the supermarket shelves to find the ones worth boiling the kettle forThe best (and worst) supermarket teabagsTom HuntSat 31 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy mother-in-law has a mug that reads: “By replacing your morning coffee with green tea, you can lose up to 87% of what little joy you still have left in your life.” Some people will never like green tea, while others will probably have tried only poor-quality, over-brewed bags filled with the dust and fannings left over from the production of whole leaf tea. Only one of today’s teas contains whole leaves, and the difference is hugely noticeable, though that’s not to say the more economical bags are undrinkable. Some are single-origin or organic, and are certainly satisfactory, so long as you brew them properly.Due to the large surface area of these tiny broken leaves, you need to be careful not to over-brew them. To stand the best chance of making a half-decent cup, use water at 80C – you can achieve that temperature by quarter-filling a cup with cold water, topping it up with just-boiled water and leaving it to brew for about 90 seconds. You’ll end up with a much sweeter cup, with nuanced kelp, edamame and toasted-straw flavours (all of which are, admittedly, acquired tastes).The best supermarket green teabagsBest overall:Clearspring organic Japanese senchaView image in fullscreen£3.99 for 20 sachets at Victoria Health (20p/sachet)£4.10 for 20 sachets at Ocado (21p/sachet)★★★★☆Small, individually wrapped bags of green fannings and brown stems with a classic umami, earthy aroma. Chamomile-yellow in colour with a distinct, savoury scent alongside a sweet, brothy tone. Quite astringent, so I’d recommend a shorter brew time. Bags free from plastic.Best bargain:Duchy Organic green teaView image in fullscreen£2.50 for 50 bags at Waitrose (5p/bag)★★★☆☆Dark green dust fannings and brown stems with a seaweedy aroma, from a single estate (Korakundah in the Nilgiri mountains, southern India). A clear, buttercup-yellow brew that holds a bright and complex flavour with a sweet start, an astringent finish and a full mouthfeel. Organic and Fairtrade.And the rest …Pukka organic supreme matcha green teaView image in fullscreen£4.74 for 20 sachets at Asda (24p/sachet)£5 for 20 sachets at Tesco (25p/sachet)★★★★☆A small, individually wrapped bag of organic dark green fannings and brown stems made from a blend of sencha, Vietnamese and Indian green teas, plus 2% South Korean matcha. A sweet, oceanic aroma, a golden-yellow colour and a honeyed, floral and grassy flavour with hints of citrus. Bright and sharp, with a mild astringency.Teapigs Mao Feng green teaView image in fullscreen£3.50 for 15 bags at Waitrose (23p/bag)£5 for 15 bags at Amazon (33p/bag)★★★★☆The only whole tea leaf in the test comes in a plant starch pyramid teabag full of large, broken dark green leaves with a kelpy scent. A light and clear green-lemon colour and complex, brothy, seaweed aroma. Bright and crisp with an earthy-umami depth, bright, fruity quality and mild astringency. One star Great Taste award in 2025, industrially compostable bags, and this week’s best splurge.Tesco green teaView image in fullscreen85p for 20 bags at Tesco (4p/bag)★★★☆☆Dark green fannings with brown flecks produce a chamomile-yellow cup with clarity, toasted straw aroma, vegetal notes and a strong, astringent finish. Good tannic structure, too. Rainforest Alliance-certified, and plant-based, compostable bags.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCo-op Fairtrade green tea infusionView image in fullscreen£1.05 for 20 bags at Co-op (5p/bag)★★★☆☆Faded green fannings and brown stems make a sienna-coloured cup with a toasted straw aroma, a savoury, toasted-rice broth flavour and an astringent finish. Fairtrade, plus the bags can go in food or garden waste bins.M&S pure green teaView image in fullscreen£1.50 for 20 bags at Ocado (8p/bag)★★★☆☆Green fannings and brown stems with an umami-seaweed aroma. A yellow-ochre cup with a sweet, toasty aroma of autumn leaves, a savoury broth flavour with a hint of jasmine and a rounded texture. Fairtrade.Diplomat pure green teaView image in fullscreen65p for 40 bags at Aldi (2p/bag), in-store only★★☆☆☆Khaki and brown stem dust and low-grade fannings that are clear and yellow-ochre in the cup. A roasted twig aroma and a sweet but sharp, tannic, textural and full-bodied flavour. Rainforest Alliance logo on pack.Knightsbridge green teaView image in fullscreen65p for 40 bags at Lidl (2p/bag), in-store only★★☆☆☆Faded olive green and brown fannings that create a bright, amber cup with good clarity and a straw-like, umami aroma. Deep in flavour with a sweet, grassy edge, notes of seaweed and an astringent finish. Texturally smooth and satisfying. Rainforest Alliance logo on pack, and biodegradable bags made from plant-based fibres.Sainsbury’s green teaView image in fullscreen90p for 20 bags at Sainsbury’s (5p/bag)★★☆☆☆Dark green fannings with some brown stems combine to make a sienna-coloured cup with clarity and a toasted rice and kelp aroma. Astringent but sweet, with a spinach broth quality and a faint floral note. Rainforest Alliance-certified and compostable bags.For more, readthe best (and worst) supermarket coffeeExplore more on these topicsTeaThe FilterFoodfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘The last fortress’: historic Athens cafe closes as countercultural area gentrifies | Greece | The Guardian
description: Mouria coffeehouse unable to renew lease in Exarchia, known for leftwing solidarity, resistance and radicalism
Author: Helena Smith
Headline: Mouria coffeehouse unable to renew lease in Exarchia, known for leftwing solidarity, resistance and radicalism
Content: A tourist reads his book outside Mouria, one of the oldest cafes in Athens, in the Exarchia neighbourhood.Photograph: Panagiotis Moschandreou/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA tourist reads his book outside Mouria, one of the oldest cafes in Athens, in the Exarchia neighbourhood.Photograph: Panagiotis Moschandreou/The GuardianGreece‘The last fortress’: historic Athens cafe closes as countercultural area gentrifiesMouria coffeehouse unable to renew lease in Exarchia, known for leftwing solidarity, resistance and radicalismHelena Smithin AthensSat 31 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 04.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt has been the hangout of writers, artists, poets and politicians, doctors and lawyers, radicals and revolutionaries for as long as anyone can remember. And for 44 years, Christos Vanas, the proprietor of Mouria, has let them all in.Every day at 7am, the taciturn former waiter has been the first man to step inside the historic cafe in Exarchia,the heart of leftwing Athens. It is a ritual he has kept punctiliously, opening up the famous gathering place before he himself has had his first coffee.View image in fullscreenChristos Vanas and his daughter Areti will close Mouria on Sunday.“Only Saturdays are different,” says his daughter Areti, drawing on a Karelia, the aromatic Greek cigarette that, like Mouria, has been around for more than a century. “By 5am, he is here serving tsipouro and other [alcoholic] spirits to warm up the stallholders of the street market outside.”But this weekend will be Vanas’s last. After a send-off expected to last into the small hours, the cafe’s large, iron-framed doors will shut forever on Sunday when patrons walk out of the mosaic-floored institution. It will be the closing act in a drama that began with the expiry of the premises’ lease last summer.View image in fullscreen‘It will be as if a friend died,’ says Nontas Papayiannis, a retired lawyer who has visited Mouria almost every day for 20 years.Photograph: Panagiotis Moschandreou/The Guardian“It will be as if a friend died,” sighs Nontas Papayannis, a retired barrister who has frequented the cafe for the past 20 years. “Another change to Exarchia, but also another loss in aGreecethat is dying before our eyes.”Born and bred in the neighbourhood long viewed as the nerve centre of Athens’ counterculture scene, the blue-eyed septuagenarian has also kept to a regime, rocking up at his favourite watering hole “at least four times a week” within an hour of the clock striking noon.View image in fullscreen‘A visit here is the route to relaxation,’ said Stelios Goutis, a retired actor.Photograph: Panagiotis Moschandreou/The GuardianStelios Goutis, 83, is an actor who trod the boards for more than six decades before his fame broadened playing Papa Triantafyllos, a priest with a penchant for a tipple or two in the TV seriesHara’s Cafe. He waxes lyrical about“the calming effect” of traditional eateries that have had such an outsized role in the lives of Greeks.“A visit here is the route to relaxation,” Goutis says with thespian flair at one of Mouria’s marble-topped tables. “You stop by after work. You down a tsipouro or two, you meet friends you may or may not have arranged to meet, and all the pressures of daily life slip away. It’s a form of psychotherapy. When it goes, we’ll look back at it as a memory of good times even if it is a loss, too.”Both men were among the 7,500 signatories of an online campaign that urged the Greek culture ministry to have the cafe declared a protected heritage site when the building’s owners announced they would not be renewing its tenancy in an area fast undergoing gentrification. The culture ministry failed to intervene.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreen‘So much has changed’ in Exarchia, said Areti. ‘You could be anywhere.’Photograph: Panagiotis Moschandreou/The GuardianFew districts in downtown Athens are more redolent of resistance, leftwing solidarity, radicalism and anarchist foment than Exarchia. Itsspirit of anti-authoritarianismdates back to the uprising at the nearby Athens Polytechnic, an event that led to the death of dozens of students but is credited with the collapse of rightwing military rule in 1974, barely 35 years after the nation’s bitter civil war.‘No influencers’: the hotels, restaurants and beauty spots restricting photoshootsRead moreBut with tourist numbers in the Greek capital more than doubling over the last decade, the neighbourhood of narrow, graffiti-daubed streets has also been discovered by investors, catering to the tastes and needs of foreign visitors.“We were like the last fortress here,” says Areti, dressed in a black leather jacket and Dr Martens boots, the garb favoured by the area’s more youthful residents. “We didn’t change our menu, we didn’t raise our prices or serve Aperol spritzes and cafe lattes. It’s about nostalgia and we’ll leave with our heads held high.”For Greeks raised in Exarchia, it was an unnerving experience to walk streets that were no longer recognisable, she lamented. “So much has changed. Everywhere you look there are new shops with signs in English and buildings turned into suites and short-term rentals. You could be anywhere.”For many, the last straw had come when travel platforms began advertising tours of the hangouts in Exarchia patronised by hardened leftists. “There have been groups outside the cafe,” says Areti, her eyes firmly focused on her footwear. “What to say?”Mouria is not alone. Its closure is emblematic of the decline of traditional coffee houses across Greece, even if the proliferation of third-wave and Italian-style cafes in more recent years has earned the country the reputation of having “a cafe economy”.View image in fullscreen‘We were like the last fortress here,’ Areti said.Photograph: Panagiotis Moschandreou/The GuardianIn villages far and wide,kafeneiaonce considered the life and soul of communities are vanishing, turbocharging depopulation.But in Exarchia, among local people so fervently opposed to corporate culture, the end of the landmark coffeeshop on the corner of Charilaou Trikoupi and Kallidromiou streets is also part of a concerted effort to alter the neighbourhood’s traditional leftwing identity. Anger has similarly mountedover the construction of a metro stationin Exarchia’s main square, championed by the centre-right government as a way of cleaning up a district that many conservatives regard as an affront to their own ideology. The public work, which has resulted in increased policing, has deprived residents of their one open space to gather.“Exarchia is perhaps the only neighbourhood in Athens where the leftwing concept of the ‘revanchist city’ is applicable,” notes Nicos Souliotis, a sociologist at the National Centre for Social Research. “State policies are clearly aimed at imposing social discipline and control. The activism we have seen around Mouria is about defending the neighbourhood’s identity and established way of life.”View image in fullscreenMouria’s closure is emblematic of the decline of traditional coffee houses across Greece.Photograph: Panagiotis Moschandreou/The GuardianFor Maria Tsampra, another longtime veteran of the cafe and a former employee of the defunct leftwing daily newspaperEleftherotypia,the sociologist is spot on.Enjoying what will be one of her last platters of mezedes at Mouria, she says the cafe’s closure is as much about “erasing memory” – because that, she adds, is also part of the neighbourhood’s “all for profit” transformation – as it is shutting down a leftwing stronghold in the heart of Athens.“There’s this attempt at revisionism, of controlling us through the rewriting of history,” Tsampra says before breaking into a smile: “It won’t work. In Mouria we found a haven and we won’t be forgetting it anytime soon.”Explore more on these topicsGreeceGentrificationHospitality industryEuropeOvertourismnewsShareReuse this content

title: Jackson Boxer’s recipe for roast apples with toffee sauce and soured cream | Food | The Guardian
description: Autumn on a plate: come in from the fireworks and warm up with this sweet, rich caramelised apple treat
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Autumn on a plate: come in from the fireworks and warm up with this sweet, rich caramelised apple treat
Content: Jackson Boxer’s roast apples with walnuts and soured cream.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Eden Owen-Jones.View image in fullscreenJackson Boxer’s roast apples with walnuts and soured cream.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Eden Owen-Jones.FoodJackson Boxer’s recipe for roast apples with toffee sauce and soured creamAutumn on a plate: come in from the fireworks and warm up with this sweet, rich caramelised apple treatJackson BoxerSat 31 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIlove a tarte tatin: it’s one of those perfect recipes that contains only a few key ingredients at its core – in this case, butter, sugar, apples and pastry – yet it brings out the absolute best qualities from each: the sugar dark, bittersweet, caramelised, and tempered by the acidity of the apples, the texture softened but held by the combination of butter and fruit pectin. The only problem is that the whole thing happens behind a screen of puff pastry, meaning that tarte tatin takes a great deal of practice and repetition to reach the right level of caramelisation blind. So, here, I’ve dispensed with the pastry altogether, making it a much easier preparation. For the intrepid, this is delicious cooked over a bonfire, where the smoke adds an incredible extra dimension; it also functions as a warming treat after a chilly evening out watching the fireworks.Roast apples with walnuts and soured creamThis basically follows my method for making tarte tatin, but without the need for pastry – nor to turn out a pan of seething caramel at significant danger to the skin on your wrists. The butter and sugar in the presence of the apples produce a beautiful and slightly acidic toffee sauce, while the fruit retains enough bite to stand up for itself and avoid disintegrating into mush. By drying out the quartered fruit in the fridge first, you ensure a nice, even caramelisation of the sugar and helps the apples maintain their shape and integrity. That said, you can also dry them in an oven set to 80C (60C fan)/gas very low for 30 minutes.Prep5 minDry2 hrCook45 minServes46 apples– braeburn or discovery, for preference100g unsalted butter, softened100g caster sugar500gsoured cream, to serveA few pinches ground cinnamon, to serve100g toasted walnuts, to servePeel the apples, cut them in half and then into quarters, then cut out and discard the cores. Put the apple pieces on a tray and leave uncovered in the fridge for two hours to dry out.Heat the oven to 210C (190C fan)/410F/gas 6½. Press the butter all over the base of an ovenproof nonstick pan, so it covers the entire flat surface, then scatter the sugar evenly over the top. Arrange the apples cut-side up on top (I like to shape them into a fan), then put the pan on a medium heat to melt the butter and caramelise the sugar for five to 10 minutes, gently shaking the pan every few minutes, until the sugar has melted to a dark caramel. Transfer to the oven and bake for 30 minutes, until everything is deliciously brown and bubbling.Remove, leave to cool for 10 minutes, then divide between warmed bowls and serve with a generous spoon of soured cream, a dusting of cinnamon and some toasted walnuts.Jackson Boxer is chef/owner ofBrunswick House,VesperandDove, all in London, and culinary director ofCowley Manornear Cheltenham andthe Henriettain LondonExplore more on these topicsFoodBonfire NightFruitDessertBakingBritish food and drinkNuts and seedsrecipesShareReuse this content

title: ‘We were mortgage-free at 45, here’s how you can do it too’ | Mortgages | The Guardian
description: Even modest overpayments can save you a fortune. We look at the best ways to pay off your biggest debt early
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Even modest overpayments can save you a fortune. We look at the best ways to pay off your biggest debt early
Content: Adrian and Tulay Massey. ‘I have been able to invest in myself and the life I want to lead,’ said Adrian.Photograph: Adrian and Tulay MasseyView image in fullscreenAdrian and Tulay Massey. ‘I have been able to invest in myself and the life I want to lead,’ said Adrian.Photograph: Adrian and Tulay MasseyMortgages‘We were mortgage-free at 45, here’s how you can do it too’Even modest overpayments can save you a fortune. We look at the best ways to pay off your biggest debt earlyHolly MeadSat 31 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 08.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Adrian Massey was made redundant from his job as a food developer in 2010, the bill that worried him the most was the mortgage. Just over a decade later he and his wife, Tulay, had cleared their debt early, saving themselves £30,000 and freeing up some money to start their own business.The couple had bought their six-bedroom home in Banbury, Oxfordshire, for £280,000 two years before he lost his job.With an interest rate on their mortgage of 6.1%, the couple’s monthly payment was about £1,400. “It felt like a burden; a chain around my neck,” says Adrian, 50. “I started thinking about the best way to pay it down.“It dawned on me what could happen if you overpay even a relatively modest amount. You can really start to make a difference.”When he started his next job he set up a standing order to overpay the mortgage. “We looked at our current income and outgoings, and then, based on our spare cash, we decided how much did we want to put into clearing the mortgage without overstretching ourselves,” he says.They decided they could afford £500 a month. After that, any pay rises they received were funnelled into the mortgage, and the couple would sometimes add a lump sum of up to £2,000 from savings.View image in fullscreenAnalysis of household incomings and outgoings can help gauge how much you can afford to overpay your mortgage.Photograph: AlamyWhen their five-year, fixed rate deal ended in 2013, they remortgaged to a rate of 2.5%, choosing a tracker deal that had no limits on overpayments.The extra they paid each month started to make an even bigger difference. By 2021, Adrian and Tulay were mortgage-free – seven years ahead of schedule.“I know that, purely from a financial point of view, there are advantages to investing more in the stock market because of the returns you get, but the freedom was more important to me,” he says. “It has meant I have been able to invest in myself and the life I want to lead, rather than being shackled to this payment.”The money that used to go into repayments has been used to set up a business, ATM Food Innovations, and Adrian has also upped his pension contributions.“Making the final payment felt really good; it’s a real sense of relief and liberation,” he says. “You know that whatever happens, no one can take your house away.”Every bit helpsWith interest rates rising, it is no wonder that achieving mortgage-free status is a goal for so many.Andrew Hagger, finance expert at Moneycomms, says: “For most people, repaying the mortgage means getting rid of the biggest financial commitment hanging around your neck.“They dream of what they could do with all the extra disposable income: holidays, update the car, home improvements, or retire early. The list is endless.”Clearing your mortgage not only means removing what is likely to be your largest monthly expense, it can also save you thousands of pounds in interest that would have been paid over the full term.And even small overpayments can make a big difference. On a 25-year mortgage of £200,000, with an interest rate of 5%, overpaying by just £20 a month could save you £5,700 in interest and clear your debt nine months early, according to Moneycomms.Overpaying by £50 a month on the same loan would save you £13,400 in interest, and clear the mortgage almost two years early. A £100-a-month overpayment would save £24,530 and clear the debt three years and six months ahead of schedule.Overpayments don’t have to be on a regular basis. You could pay off a lump sums when you come to the end of your deal, or switch to a new lender, or part-way through if the terms of your loan allow it.In the above example, a one-off overpayment of £10,000 could save £11,870 in interest and pay off the mortgage one year and two months early.To make an overpayment, contact your lender. Often it is as simple as making a transfer to the account.View image in fullscreenMost mortgages let you overpay up to 10% of the outstanding balance each year without charges.Photograph: Rosemary Roberts/AlamyAs your overpayments start to make an impact, you will typically be offered the option to reduce either your monthly payments, or the mortgage term. If repayments are comfortable, choose the latter. This means that more of your money goes towards paying off the debt and you’ll clear the balance sooner.One downside to overpaying is that you can’t easily get the money back if you need it, so ensure you have a savings buffer in case of an emergency; typically three to six months’ of essential outgoings is recommended.“It’s tempting to try to throw every spare penny at the mortgage, but find a balance between making progress towards being mortgage-free and retaining enough flexibility to deal with life’s unexpected costs,” says David Hollingworth, director at the mortgage broker L&C.Understand the terms of your mortgage: most let you overpay up to 10% of the outstanding balance each year without charges. Hollingworth says: “It’s worth checking as early repayment charges can be substantial, often 3-5% of your overpayment, which can erode, or remove, the benefit of the overpayment.”Offset mortgages: the best of both worlds?If you want to overpay without locking away your money, an offset mortgage can be a good alternative to a standard deal. These let you link a savings account to your mortgage. The savings balance is deducted from the amount you owe, reducing the amount of interest you are charged. For example, on a £200,000 mortgage with a savings balance of £10,000, you would be charged interest on £190,000 of the loan.The trade-off is that you don’t earn interest on your savings, but they are accessible if you need them; any money withdrawn from the account is simply no longer offset from the mortgage balance. So, in the above example, if you withdrew £2,000 from the savings account, you would then be charged interest on £192,000 of the mortgage loan.View image in fullscreenOffset mortgages can help you become mortgage-free with more flexibility.Photograph: Chris Dorney/AlamyDavid Hollingworth, director at the mortgage broker L&C, says: “An offset can suit those with substantial cash savings or who receive lump sum bonuses. It allows your cash to work harder without limiting your ability to draw on it when required.”A 25-year, £200,000 offset mortgage at a rate of 5.46%, with a £10,000 savings balance, could save £28,550 in interest costs and clear the debt one year and nine months early, Moneycomms says.It’s worth noting that the choice of offset deals is more limited than for standard mortgages, and typically they have a higher interest rate. L&C currently lists more than 7,500 mortgage products but just 150 of them are offset deals. They are typically about 0.4-0.5 percentage points more expensive than a standard mortgage, says Hollingworth.Explore more on these topicsMortgagesPropertyMortgage ratesBanks and building societiesSavingsBorrowing & debtfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Budget 2026: how to beat the new savings tax rates | Savings | The Guardian
description: The budget offered a ‘sting in the tail’ for savers by raising tax rates but there are ways to ease the pain
Author: Hilary Osborne
Headline: The budget offered a ‘sting in the tail’ for savers by raising tax rates but there are ways to ease the pain
Content: The levels of tax rates, which will apply to savers across the UK, will be 24% for basic-rate taxpayers, 44% for higher-rate taxpayers and 49% for those on the additional rate. They will come into effect on 6 April.Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PAView image in fullscreenThe levels of tax rates, which will apply to savers across the UK, will be 24% for basic-rate taxpayers, 44% for higher-rate taxpayers and 49% for those on the additional rate. They will come into effect on 6 April.Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PASavingsBudget 2026: how to beat the new savings tax ratesJohn Healey’s budget offered a ‘sting in the tail’ for savers by raising tax rates but there are ways to ease the painHilary OsborneandRupert JonesSat 31 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSavers were bothwinners and losersinWednesday’s budget. In his first outing as chancellor, John Healey dropped a plan to cut the cash Isa limit for under-65s but surprised everyone with an extra tax charge on savings and property income. His predecessor, Rachel Reeves, had already announceda plan to increase the income tax rates for savers and landlordsthat was due to take effect in April 2027. But Healey went further, adding an additional two percentage points to each of the rates.Jason Hollands, managing director at wealth manager Evelyn Partners, describes the higher rates as a “sting in the tail” for savers.However, he says: “There are practical steps savers can consider to mitigate this interest tax crunch, although the right approach will depend on their circumstances.”The new taxesThe levels of tax, which will apply to savers across the UK, will be 24% for basic-rate taxpayers, 44% for higher-rate taxpayers and 49% for those on the additional rate. They come into effect on 6 April.This means it will get harder to find savings accounts that beat inflation – especially if, as expected, that stays high next year.View image in fullscreenThe new tax rates mean it will be harder to find savings accounts which beat the rate of inflation.Photograph: David-Prado/Getty Images/iStockphotoAnna Bowes, personal finance expert at advice firm The Private Office, says if inflation hits 3.5%, with the new tax to pay, a saver who pays basic-rate tax will need to earn 4.61% gross interest to retain the value of their money.A higher-rate payer will need 6.25% gross, and an additional-rate taxpayer will need 6.86%. Currently, she says, these higher two rates “are impossible as far as I am aware” to find on a standard savings account.There are, however, allowances you can use that will protect some savings, meaning you can beat inflation with a lower-paying account.Your tax-free allowancesMost people can earn a chunk of interest from their savings without facing any tax bill. You don’t have to pay tax on anything earned on money held in cashIsas, and the maximum amount you can put into one in each tax year is going to stay at £20,000.This was set to be slashed to £12,000 for anyone aged under 65 from April 2027. But Healey has ditched that plan.Aside from Isas, other things come into play that reduce the tax you pay on savings, or mean you don’t pay any tax at all.View image in fullscreenIf you’re saving for a child’s future, consider putting it in their name instead of holding it yourself. Pay into their child trust fund, or junior Isa if they already have one, or set up a junior IsaPhotograph: JGI/Jamie Grill/Getty Images/Blend ImagesYour tax-free personal allowance covers all of your income, and for the 2026-27 tax year, this is £12,570.If your personal allowance isn’t fully used up by your wages, pension or other income, HM Revenue and Customs will apply it to your savings interest.And there are two more savings allowances that people can benefit from.There’s the personal savings allowance (PSA), which means basic-rate taxpayers can receive £1,000 of interest each financial year without paying any tax, and higher-rate taxpayers can receive up to £500. Additional-rate taxpayers don’t get any PSA.Until a few years ago, you would usually have needed to have a huge amount saved before exceeding the £500 or £1,000 threshold, but with accounts currently paying 5%-plus, it is much easier to get caught out.There’s also the “starting rate for savings,” which some people on a low income can get on top of the PSA, where you can earn up to £5,000 of interest without paying tax on it. To benefit, the rest of your income (for example, wages or pension) has to be less than £17,570 a year.What the higher taxes meanThe Isa allowance governs how much you put in each year while the PSA is based on how much you get back.How quickly you use up the PSA depends on your tax position. A basic-rate taxpayer who puts £20,000 cash into a non-Isa savings account paying 5% interest will earn annual interest of exactly £1,000 – so will use up their entire PSA. If they found a higher paying account, they would face 24% tax on all the interest over £1,000, so they’d hand over 24p of every £1.For a higher-rate taxpayer it would only take £10,000 in the same account to wipe out their £500 PSA. They would pay a rate of 44% on everything they earned over £500 – 44p in the £1.Happy birthday! What deals and discounts does your age unlock?Read moreWhen it comes to Isas you can put in up to £20,000 every tax year, as long as you are over 18. Once money is in a cash Isa it is protected from tax forever, so over time you can build up a huge amount of savings that don’t attract tax, as long as you don’t withdraw them.You do not have to leave it with the same provider. You can move around to get better rates – subject to individual account rules – so it is wise to make the most of this shelter.How to beat the riseIf you have a substantial savings nest egg you might want to review where they are held. Experts always recommend that you have emergency funds that are easy to access, so do not let a small tax bill deter you from doing that.But Hollands says it is worth checking that you are not holding too much in savings. “Holding more cash than you need for several years can mean missing out on the potential for longer-term investment growth,” he says.View image in fullscreenHolland and Coates both suggest low coupon short-dated gilts as an alternative place to put cash.Photograph: Peter Dazeley/Getty ImagesLook at your family situation. Hollandssays couples who are married, or in a civil partnership, should look at their savings and allowances together.If you have both used your Isa and personal savings allowances, but one partner pays tax at a lower rate, he says transferring cash to them could reduce an overall family tax bill.“But this needs to be a genuine transfer: the money becomes theirs, legally and in practice, and they must be free to decide what to do with it, so trust is key,” he says.If you’re saving for a child’s future, consider putting it in their name instead of holding it yourself. Pay into their child trust fund, or junior Isa if they already have one, or set up a junior Isa. You can pay up to £9,000 a year into a junior Isa, and all the returns are tax-free.Outside the Isa wrapper there will still be a potential tax bill if you are the child’s parent. If the child earns more than £100 in interest from money you have put in their account, you will be taxed on the returns. This isn’t the case if you are a grandparent.Check whether you could make your money work harder by overpaying on your mortgage (see right), or putting more into your pension. Money paid into your pension won’t just avoid the savings tax, it will also attract a nice tax break and, possibly, cut the rate you would need to pay on savings.Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, says: “When you pay into your pension, you can get tax relief at your highest marginal rate and lower your ‘adjusted net income’.View image in fullscreenIsas can help you beat the new tax rates.Photograph: 57stock/Alamy“Not only does it mean you pay less tax on your income, but it could also help bring you back below other tax thresholds, while helping boost your prospects for retirement at the same time.”If you do that, the cash will be locked in. For money that you need access to, there are options. Premium bonds are one. There’s no interest and prizes are all tax-free. Each person in the UK can hold up to £50,000, and they are government-backed so are a safe place for your cash.The prize fund recently increasedso each bond has a 21,000-1 chance of winning.Holland and Coates both suggest low coupon short-dated gilts as an alternative place to put cash. These are UK government bonds, paying a small annual interest rate, and set to mature within the next couple of years. When they mature the return you get will not be liable for capital gains tax (CGT).This type of investment can be bought via an investment platform, and can be held in your stocks and shares Isa, or outside it. You will face some kind of fees for running the account. Most of the return comes from the CGT saving at the end, and this can make them very attractive in terms of the after-tax returns, when compared to the post-tax interest on a cash savings account, says Holland.“This is especially the case for people subject to the higher and additional rates of tax,” he says.Explore more on these topicsSavingsSavings ratesBanks and building societiesBudgetBudget 2026John HealeyPensionsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: 10 spine-chilling places to visit in Britain for Halloween | Travel | The Guardian
description: Ghostly shipwrecks, an abandoned nuclear bunker, a haunted folly … we dare you to visit these weird and ghoulishly eerie sites
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Ghostly shipwrecks, an abandoned nuclear bunker, a haunted folly … we dare you to visit these weird and ghoulishly eerie sites
Content: Racton Monument is said to be one of the most haunted places in Sussex.Photograph: Stuart C Clarke/AlamyView image in fullscreenRacton Monument is said to be one of the most haunted places in Sussex.Photograph: Stuart C Clarke/AlamyTravel10 spine-chilling places to visit in Britain for HalloweenGhostly shipwrecks, an abandoned nuclear bunker, a haunted folly … we dare you to visit these weird and ghoulishly eerie sitesDave HamiltonSat 31 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 04.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWest Sussex’s haunted follyA derelict, 24-metre tall redbrick and flint folly outside Chichester,Racton Monument(known locally as Racton Ruin) is said to be one of the most haunted places in Sussex and has been the site of many paranormal investigations. George Montagu Dunk, the second Earl of Halifax, commissioned the folly, but there is no conclusive account as to why he had it built. Some say it was as a summerhouse, others a viewing point to watch ships come in from the Solent. A ghostly woman walking in the grounds and eerie sounds such as sudden manic laughter are among reported spooky happenings. Now completely gutted and roofless, it’s on private land and unsafe to enter, but still easily seen from nearbyfootpaths.‘The event horizon of a black hole’in Bannau BrycheiniogView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Margaret Clavell/AlamyCompleted in 1927, thePontsticill reservoirin the Bannau Brycheiniog (Brecon Beacons) national park supplies water for much of south Wales, holding up to 15.5 billion litres (3,400 million gallons). Like other reservoirs of its time, such as Ladybower in Derbyshire, Pontsticill was built with a bell-mouth spillway, which looks like an eerie giant plughole – or the event horizon of a black hole. Created by flooding a valley, ghostly remains of the submerged village, including a 15th-century church, can resurface during droughts when water levels drop. Richard Ayoade used its terrifying presence with great effect in his 2010 film, Submarine.Shipwrecks inthe KentmarshesView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Tony Watson/AlamyWith place names such as Deadman’s Island, Slaughterhouse Point and Bedlam’s Bottom,Chetney Marshesneeds no introduction. This forgotten, marshy outpost on the fringes of north Kent, with a limited palette of greens and greys, is home to a collection of slowly decaying, old barges and boats. Such is their level of deterioration, it can be hard to distinguish between the rotten hulks and the marsh itself. Information on the wrecked vessels is hard to come by and contradictory, with Historic England claiming they are former Thames barges. Yet on older maps, they are marked as the more tantalising Victorian prisoner transport ships. An atmospheric place for an otherworldly wander.A nuclear bunker in EssexView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jon D/AlamyGrowing up on terrifying visions of nuclear war, such as 1980s films Threads and Where the Wind Blows, bunkers have always held a certain macabre mystique.Kelvedon Hatchwas one such bunker, built in the early 1950s to house up to 600 military personnel and civilians, as well as the prime minister. In this worst-case scenario, it would have become the seat of power in a post-apocalyptic Britain. Above the surface, it looks like an unremarkable bungalow, but, like a Bond villain’s lair, this leads to a three-storey underground shelter equivalent in size to 25 average British homes. Today, the bunker is home to one of the world’s largest cold war museums.A wailing, windswept tree on the Lancashire moorsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Yorkshire Pics/AlamyOn a Pennine hill overlooking Burnley, theSinging Ringing Treeis an eerie sound sculpture created by architects Mike Tonkin and Anna Liu. It is three metres tall and designed to look like a brutalist windswept tree. The sculpture comprises a series of galvanised steel pipes tuned to various pitches over a range of different octaves. On a gusty day, as the wind blows through the pipes, it creates a weird, somewhat discordant harmonic. The artwork is one of fourPanopticons, but rather than embodying the original concept – a circular prison with a single guard at its centre – they are far more benign, designed to be seen by many rather than as a symbol of oppressive surveillance.The Lake District’s ‘skull cave’View image in fullscreenPhotograph: North News and Pictures/AlamyTucked away in the Tilberthwaite valley, between Coniston and Langdale,Hodge Closeis an abandoned slate quarry on National Trust land. In the right conditions, its cave tunnel openings and dark pool resemble a skull, which fans of the hit Netflix series The Witcher will recognise – though it’s much harder to see in real life than in the scenes starring Henry Cavill (Geralt of Rivia) and Kim Bodnia (Vesemir). Abandoned in the 1960s, industrial remains litter the site, giving it an edgy, post-civilisation feel.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLondon’s paupers’ graveyardView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jim Monk/AlamyCrossbonesgraveyard, just south of the River Thames near Shakespeare’s Globe theatre and the Shard, was once outside the city’s boundaries (and laws) in an area known as “The Liberty of the Clink”. A pauper’s graveyard, it was the final resting place of medieval sex workers and souls not deemed suitable for Christian burial. More than 15,000 people are estimated to have been unceremoniously buried here. Today, it’s been reclaimed as a garden of remembrance, both mystical and macabre with its own special beauty, and is open to the public at certain times for guided walks and talks.A smugglers’ cave inNorthumberlandView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Peter Reed/AlamyHundreds of years ago,Cateran Holewas used by bandits to hide smuggled contraband. Found in the middle of Bewick Moor, about four miles north of Eglingham, it feels as far away from civilisation as you can get, and the steps leading down to its 35 metre-long, dark underground chamber are notoriously difficult to find – making it all the more thrilling when you finally do. You can walk into increasing darkness if you’re brave enough, before the tunnel tapers to a narrow point, but be cautious: there are no safety barriers, lighting or warning signs.Stony stares from a drystone wall inDumfries and GallowayView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Marsh/AlamyWe all know that strange feeling of being watched – then turning round to find nobody there. If you wander just off theOld Edinburgh Roadin a beautiful, isolated corner of the Galloway Hills, not far from Newton Stewart, you’ll find a whole bunch of faces staring out at you from the confines of a drystone wall. Artist Matt Baker carvedQuorum – the Stone Facesin 1997 as part of a residency in the Galloway Forest. The heads have since become part of the landscape and have even formed new eyebrows out of lichen. The artwork is a stone’s throw away from another impressive piece calledThe Eye, a 10-metre tall cone sculpture on the banks of Black Loch.The church ‘floating’ on Rutland WaterView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alex Hannam/AlamyArrive on a cold morning as the mist shroudsSt Matthew’s church in Normanton, and it appears as if it is rising up from the depths of a lake. Normanton Church, as it is also known, stands on a small, boulder-strewn promontory on the vast expanse of Rutland Water. Built in the 1820s on the site of a medieval chapel, the church was scheduled for demolition when the man-made lake/reservoir was built in the 1970s. Thankfully, a last-minute public campaign saved it from this watery fate. Easy to view from the shoreline, it is open on scheduled days and for private events.Dave Hamilton is the author ofWeird GuideandWild Ruins, published byWild Things PublishingExplore more on these topicsTravelHalloweenfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Apologies for any confusion!’: how to write the perfect passive-aggressive email | Email | The Guardian
description: In a survey, ‘just to be clear’ came out as the most loathed phrase. But I think I can do better
Author: Emma Beddington
Headline: In a survey, ‘just to be clear’ came out as the most loathed phrase. But I think I can do better
Content: ‘I think we’d all be happier taking a deep breath.’Photograph: Posed by model; Francesco Carta fotografo/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘I think we’d all be happier taking a deep breath.’Photograph: Posed by model; Francesco Carta fotografo/Getty ImagesEmail‘Apologies for any confusion!’: how to write the perfect passive-aggressive emailIn a survey, ‘just to be clear’ came out as the most loathed phrase. But I think I can do betterEmma BeddingtonSat 31 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 01.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnew contender for the most passive-aggressive email phrase has emerged. “Just to be clear” was chosen by 52% of desk jockeys in a survey by email verification company ZeroBounce, closely followed by the perennial pass-ag fave, “per my last email” (40%), which tied with the identical-in-intent “as previously discussed”. Further down the list came “for future reference” and “kindly note”.If you ask me, these all verge onactualaggressive. Imagine saying “just to be clear” out loud to another person: that’s a conversational poke in the ribs, isn’t it? It’s the kind of thing you unleash 10 minutes into an ill-tempered wrangle with your home insurance company about inflated renewal premiums. “Kindly note” is even worse – it’s a phrase from an angry message on the office kitchen wall about microwave abuse.No, we can do better than that, or at least I – a person whose own spouse frequently describes her as unpleasantly passive-aggressive – can. Let me explain: an exchange of professional passive-aggressive emails is a ritual as intricately coded as a Belle Epoque duel and it demands the appearance of great politeness. Your message needs to read, on its surface, as exquisitely helpful and friendly, while leaving every cc and bcc on the thread in no doubt as to it what it really is: an epistolary shanking.A good pass-agg email starts with a simulacrum of warmth and gratitude. I can usually generate the appearance of warmth by harnessing the dizzying rush of anger generated by whatever stupid message has prompted me to press “reply all”. “Hi X!” I usually start perkily, then I pause to hold up both middle fingers to the screen. Next comes gratitude: “Great to hear from you,” (it wasn’t) “and thank you so much for your message”. Thanks, that is, for giving me a chance to show everyone you’re out of line. I say “everyone”, because I like to deploy a cc on this kind of email.I follow this Trojan Shetland pony of an intro with a selection of my preferred zingers:“My understanding was … apologies if this was incorrect?”I understood perfectly. I am correct. I am sorry for nothing. The question mark is a mere disingenuous flourish.“As agreed,”The import of this little phrase is clear: I have kept the receipts and I want you to know that. This email will be followed near-instantaneously by a second email, forwarding the evidence that I am right. The body of that second email will just read “FYI”, which is passive-aggressive for “checkmate, loser”.“Apologies for any confusion”or“apologies if this was unclear”It, and I, was entirely clear. I am only sorry you are a dolt. Some pass-ag practitioners drop in a bland, smiling emoji here, but I am a purist.Hope this helps!I hope this leaves you seething with the same fury your message inspired in me.“No response required”By saying I don’t expect you to respond it will make you look petty when you do; it also subtly implies you’ve already gone home. Your move.Warm regards,Warm like the fires of hell.Still, as much as I get satisfaction from the perfect turn of passive-aggressive phrase, I always realise later that it’s a hollow pleasure. What am I doing fighting, albeit with elegant restraint, a fellow worker when the real enemy is capitalism? Why are we emailing at all when we could be contemplating the beauty of a sunset, shoulder to shoulder? For future reference: I think we’d all be happier taking a deep breath, pressing backspace, and walking away.Explore more on these topicsEmailWork & careersfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Tim Dowling: having a tortoise reminds you that life is long | Family | The Guardian
description: My wife got ours when she was eight, and he came to live with us soon after we got married. I don’t remember anything about that in the vows
Author: Tim Dowling
Headline: My wife got ours when she was eight, and he came to live with us soon after we got married. I don’t remember anything about that in the vows
Content: Illustration: Selman Hosgor/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Selman Hosgor/The GuardianThe Tim Dowling columnFamilyTim Dowling: having a tortoise reminds you that life is longMy wife got ours when she was eight, and he came to live with us soon after we got married. I don’t remember anything about that in the vowsTim DowlingSat 31 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 15.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is the first truly bleak day of autumn – the sky is a deep grey and a steady drizzle is falling. Sitting in the unflattering light of a kitchen downlight and looking out the window, I think: this is it now, until spring.Except it isn’t, quite, as a few hours later the cloud begins to break up and a shaft of watery sunlight reaches the brick step just outside my office shed. When I open the door to let in the warm afternoon air, I find the tortoise sitting there.“Oh, hey,” I say. “It’s you.”There aren’t many pets that allow you to forget their existence for any length of time. The cat reminds me that I have a cat twice a day. The dog will not let me forget I have a dog for half an hour. But it has been at least a week since it even occurred to me that I have a tortoise.double quotation markThe tortoise has outlived two dogs and three cats. On occasion, when he was in a dormant period, I used him to prop open the kitchen door“All good?” I say. The tortoise winds its neck anticlockwise, so it can fix me with its right eye.Certain experiences – raising children, say, or stepping into the path of a bus – remind you that life is short. But many other experiences remind you that it’s long – mostly things breaking, and then breaking again. I have measured out my life in dual-function push-button kitchen tap spray head replacements – they last, on average, about three years, and according to my order history, I’m on my fourth one.Having a tortoise is definitely the latter sort of experience.My wife got ours when she was eight years old. At some point he escaped for a whole year, was found, went to live on a farm for 20 more years and then, when the farm was sold, was suddenly returned to us. By that point we’d been married for six years. There had been nothing about a tortoise in our wedding vows.That was almost 30 years ago. Since then, the tortoise has outlived two dogs and three cats. Over the decades, I’ve spent countless hours searching the garden beds for him after dark. I’vediscovered him on his backand set him right about a dozen times. He’s bitten me at least as often. On occasion, when he was in a dormant period of reduced metabolic activity, I used him to prop open the kitchen door. And there were many years when I had to fish him out from the gap under the washing machine to tell him that spring was here.double quotation markThe tortoise could spend another night outside, but I won’t find him again. I carry him into the kitchen. He looks miserable, but that’s really his only lookI consult a weather app. “You know what?” I say. “I think it’s about that time.” According to the forecast, the tortoise could spend another night outside, but I will not find him this easily again.I pick him up and carry him into the kitchen. He looks miserable, but that’s really his only look. I open the fridge, peel off a lettuce leaf and set it down in front of him. He sniffs it and then looks away disdainfully. When I check again an hour later, both the tortoise and the lettuce are in the same spot. An hour after that, both have disappeared.That evening, a friend’s grown son drops by. As he looks around, I can see it dawn on him that he hasn’t been in our house since he was a child. In fact, the last time he was in our house, we lived somewhere else.“Do you still have that tortoise?” he says.“Yeah, look, he’s right there,” I say, pointing to the spot next to the dog’s bed where the tortoise sits, legs and head withdrawn.“Whoa,” says the friend’s son.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTim Dowling: could the new dog’s tricks make her into a star?Read moreThe dog comes running into the kitchen, to remind everyone that there is a dog in the house. The cat, a coward, hides somewhere until all non-family members have left the building. Many friends who visit our house regularly have never seen him. Some don’t believe we even have a cat, but we have pictures.The next morning, the tortoise is standing in the middle of the square of sun coming through the skylight, awaiting more lettuce.“I was just thinking about him,” my wife says.“Having not thought about him at all?”“Yeah, exactly,” she says. “How did you find him?”“He found me,” I say.The morning after that I wake early, in the dark, oppressed by a heavy weight. The dog is standing on my chest, looking down at me. The cat is also there, squatting on the pillow alongside my head.“What?” I say. The dog yawns theatrically. The cat presses a paw to my lips.All this reminds me that I have a tortoise and that, thankfully, he doesn’t do stairs.Explore more on these topicsFamilyThe Tim Dowling columnfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Country diary: An impromptu birding trip with a total stranger – and it was magical | Birds | The Guardian
description: Slimbridge, Gloucestershire: A chance meeting led me and my partner into an afternoon of discovery and generosity that is nothing like a certain YouTube documentary on birding
Author: Eben Muse
Headline: Slimbridge, Gloucestershire: A chance meeting led me and my partner into an afternoon of discovery and generosity that is nothing like a certain YouTube documentary on birding
Content: Birdwatching on the River Severn.Photograph: Eben MuseView image in fullscreenBirdwatching on the River Severn.Photograph: Eben MuseCountry diaryBirdsCountry diary: An impromptu birding trip with a total stranger – and it was magicalSlimbridge, Gloucestershire:A chance meeting led me and my partner into an afternoon of discovery and generosity that is nothing like a certain YouTube documentary on birdingEben MuseSat 31 Oct 2026 01.30 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 05.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“What did you just see?” a bearded man asked, through the open window of his old Mini Cooper.“Just some crows in that tree.”“Slimbridge Wetland Centre is closed. I just missed it!”We too had been greeted at Slimbridge by a shut door at the visitor centre, dashing our hopes of some late-afternoon birdwatching. “I’m gonna find another way to the estuary. Want to hop in?”Before I had a chance to contemplate this stranger’s offer, my partner, Beth, had jumped into the back seat of the Mini, and we motored away into the unknown.View image in fullscreenSunset and waders.Photograph: Eben MuseWe set off on foot down a promising track, following our new friend, Phil. With each step towards the shore he became more alive, extolling the weather, the ancient churches on the hills, and our fortuitous meeting.I’m not an expert birdwatcher, but Phil has a lifetime of honed skill – he cupped his ear to the curlew’s cry, pointed to long-tailed tits, shelducks, dunlins and a medley of geese. We learned that he’s a composer, and helps to run a museum in the mid-Wales town where my sister lives.View image in fullscreenRoe deer near the sea wall.Photograph: Eben MuseAs we approached the Severn seawall, roe deer with glowing antlers stared at us. I couldn’t help but think ofListers, a rip-roaring YouTube documentaryabout two young men who enter the cut-throat world of competitive birdwatching, spending a year chasing glory and rare birds across the US. They found that an ostensibly nature-based activity can become a Pokémon-style “Gotta catch ’em all” exercise, in which underhand strategy and toxic behaviour can be hard to avoid. Not so here, as we followed our excited leader’s stream of identifications and free-flowing observations.The moment we mounted the seawall, we saw a horizon ablaze with a sunburst of burnished copper. The mudflats were dotted with countless waders and gulls, and the Severn’s mighty tide was already starting to rush in. “See the marsh harrier? Incredible, incredible,” Phil murmured. We watched as the harrier glided over, sublime, sending ripples through the assembly. And there wasn’t a whiff of competition.Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now at guardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsBirdsCountry diaryRural affairsWildlifefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Disquiet grows in Albanese’s back yard as Grayndler artists unite against ‘insane’ AI proposal | Sydney | The Guardian
description: Inner west Sydney seat has long been safely held by the PM – but potential changes to copyright laws are angering its large creative community
Author: Caitlin Cassidy
Headline: Inner west Sydney seat has long been safely held by the PM – but potential changes to copyright laws are angering its large creative community
Content: ‘Artists are the first to be thrown under the bus’ … H Morgan-Harris (right) and Ran Stanton at Tortuga Studios in St Peters, in Anthony Albanese’s electorate.Photograph: Liz Ham/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Artists are the first to be thrown under the bus’ … H Morgan-Harris (right) and Ran Stanton at Tortuga Studios in St Peters, in Anthony Albanese’s electorate.Photograph: Liz Ham/The GuardianSydneyDisquiet grows in Albanese’s back yard as Grayndler artists unite against ‘insane’ AI proposalInner west Sydney seat has long been safely held by the PM – but potential changes to copyright laws are angering its large creative communityGet ourdaily political email,free appordaily news podcastCaitlin CassidySat 31 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 21.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe prime minister is facing growing discontent within his own electorate as creatives push back against the federal government’s proposal to allow AI companies to scrape everything Australians create online.Anthony Albanese’sseat of Grayndlerin Sydney’s inner west is home to more than 3,000 cultural and creative businesses, and 10% of its workers are employed in cultural and creative fields – compared with 4.2% nationally.He has held it on a safe margin for three decades, and has spoken of its high representation of live music, theatre and artist spaceswith pride.But now, as Labor considers givingAI companies accessto Australian creatives’ worksby defaultas it pursues a compromise with US tech giants, locals are reacting with dismay.In a rush to lure AI companies, the Australian government risks undoing a creative ecosystem that has taken decades to build | Dan GuthrieRead moreLabor is mulling over the copyright changes in a suite of reforms surrounding AI, including datacentres, energy and the economy. While Albanese has promised “the strongest possible protection”, warning it would be “theft” if creatives weren’t paid for their work, creative industries are alarmed that AI companies have requested a weakening of copyright law to train their models using Australian material.Some AI companies have said making licensing agreements under existing copyright law would be too difficult, while Anthropic has suggested an “opt-out” model which would allow it to scrape content unless a rights holder objected, prompting warnings from Coalition senators and the recording industry that thiscould amount to an acquisition of property by the government.The federal government’s draft laws are expected by the end of the year, with consideration in parliament due in 2027.View image in fullscreenPete Strong says AI is ‘the wild west and we really need to push back’.Photograph: Liz Ham/The GuardianPete Strong is a screenprinter and Greens councillor for Bayside. His business is based in Grayndler, with his solar-powered wheelie bin sound systems a fixture around the inner west.He said AI could be “good for humanity” but is now an “extraction industry mining for profit for the few”.“I’m completely against [the federal government’s proposal],” he said.“There’s obviously an AI gold rush at the moment, it’s the wild west and we really need to push back. It’s hard enough being a starving artist these days without having all your work taken and used in these nefarious ways.”Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter hereThis year Strong curated a show called “overthrow the algorithm”. He has also been a vocal critic of a proposed datacentre at Cooks Cove.“I’ve seen a backlash [to the government] already,” he said. “It started with the datacentre uprising.”Labor’s proposalswere leakedin September as senior personnel from OpenAI, the creator ofChatGPT, met Labor ministers and warned that Australia’s copyright laws were preventing the company from training models locally.For the inner west designer and artist Lu Campbell-Smith, AI has been useful in her practice. But she said having to opt out was “outrageous”.“It just really pinpoints how Australia’s [a] test market and they’re happy for us to just be a little resource to be exploited,” she said.“Why would anyone want to make anything and post anything online if … you’re creating free content for an AI machine?”View image in fullscreenLu Campbell-Smith at her desk in Tortuga Studio’s co-working space called the aerie.Photograph: Liz Ham/The GuardianGrayndler has always been an ultra-safe Labor seat. Albanese’s face as a much younger man is plastered on to cans of Albo Pale Ale at Willie the Boatman brewery in St Peters. For the past few elections, he has won on first preferences alone.But at the next federal election, he will be challenged by 28-year-oldHannah Ferguson, the co-founder of Cheek Media, who willrun as an independent.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNo sitting member has lost their seat from such a margin at a federal election. Were it not for the longstanding popularity of Albanese, Grayndler would have been a prime target for the Greens and progressive independents.Now, Ferguson is betting that his popularity is waning. And polling indicates the same. Guardian Australia’slatest Essential pollshows Albanese’s disapproval rating at 56%, the equal highest since he took office.View image in fullscreenA moss-covered computer artwork by Morgan-Harris sits beside the entry to the aerie.Photograph: Liz Ham/The GuardianAt Tortuga Studios and the aerie, one of the longest-running artist-led spaces inSydneywhich operates out of an old brick factory in St Peters, the frustration is palpable.H Morgan-Harris, an author, curator and director of the space, said there was a risk the Australian creative ecosystem could be “decimated”.Labor and the Coalition are poised to take a reckless gamble on AI. Haven’t they realised community support has collapsed? | Edward Santow and Sarah SacherRead more“This whole conversation always comes back to money,” she said, adding: “The artistic ecosystem is the bedrock of human interaction and human connection. And you risk our societal value by threatening it.”Morgan-Harris’s copywriting industry has already been “heavily impacted” by AI, she said. Asked what her response was to the federal government’s latest proposal, she said it wasn’t “one you can print”.“I just feel like artists are the first to be thrown under the bus,” she said.“I think a lot of people were really excited when [Albanese] got into government, but there’s a yawning chasm in terms of the recognition, consideration and protection of the value of this sector. This honestly feels like the end of times to a lot of us.”View image in fullscreenTortuga Studios has been running for 19 years and provides a hub for artists, designers and craftspeople in Sydney’s inner west.Photograph: Liz Ham/The GuardianJason Zoidberg, a co-founder of Monster Mouse Studios in Marrickville, said the AI industry had already “without consequence” stolen the “collective labour” uploaded by artists. He said it was “utterly crazy” that the government was considering giving companies the green light to do so.“It just feels insane that they’re like, ‘Yeah, please come and we want to invest in you,’ when we’ve seen all these horrible things that they’re doing,” he said.If there is a flipside, Zoidberg said, he is witnessing a surge in interest in traditional, hands-on art forms.“There’s a backlash in the inner west against social media and AI,” Zoidberg said. “So our workshops are actually getting more participants. But it is also just a niche, a little inner west bubble.”Explore more on these topicsSydneyAnthony AlbaneseNew South WalesAI (artificial intelligence)Datacentres - AustraliaAustralian politicsAustralian artnewsShareReuse this content

title: Storm warnings for Melbourne, Canberra, Sydney and Brisbane as cold front ‘packs a punch’ | Australia weather | The Guardian
description: BoM predicts hail, damaging winds and possible flash flooding across Victoria, NSW and parts of Queensland into Sunday
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: BoM predicts hail, damaging winds and possible flash flooding across Victoria, NSW and parts of Queensland into Sunday
Content: The BoM is warning storms could bring hail, strong winds and possible flash flooding across Victoria, NSW and parts of Queensland.Photograph: James Ross/AAPView image in fullscreenThe BoM is warning storms could bring hail, strong winds and possible flash flooding across Victoria, NSW and parts of Queensland.Photograph: James Ross/AAPAustralia weatherStorm warnings for Melbourne,
