Canberra, Sydney and Brisbane as cold front ‘packs a punch’BoM predicts hail, damaging winds and possible flash flooding across Victoria, NSW and parts of Queensland into SundayGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastAustralian Associated PressSat 31 Oct 2026 02.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStorm warnings are in place for multiple capital cities across Australia’s east and south-east as a severe weather front sweeps across the country.Heavy rain, winds and thunderstorms are forecast to hitMelbourneand eastern Victoria throughout Saturday afternoon as a cold front meets warm, humid air.The storm front is then expected to travel further east, impacting Canberra and inland NSW before reaching the east coast on Sunday, stretching as far as southernQueensland.Cloudy with a chance of moths: bogong swarms are bamboozling weather radars across NSWRead moreThe Bureau of Meteorology warned of possible flash flooding in some areas and potentially destructive winds of over 125km/h that could bring down large trees or damage property.Melbourne and parts ofVictoriarecorded moderate rainfall and some lightning on Saturday morning, with a more intense band of thunderstorms forecast into the afternoon.“It’s this follow-up band of storms which could pack a punch,” BoM meteorologist Angus Hines said on Saturday.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe storms are expected to impact Melbourne, parts of Gippsland, the north-eastern ranges, and north-central Victoria, with damaging winds the greatest risk.The risk area will extend further north through inland NSW into the evening – up to Queensland’s southern interior and along the NSW coast south ofSydneyaround Wollongong and the Illawarra.The forecast in these areas includes possible damaging winds, heavy rainfall and large hailstones.“Expecting some very active storms here a little bit later on in the day, mid to late afternoon for many of these areas, and potentially not until the evening hours by the time we’re looking at storms getting out towards the east coast,” Hines said.The focus of concern will shift further north on Sunday, with heavy rain and storms aroundBrisbaneduring the afternoon and early evening.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSevere thunderstorms were most likely for parts of the NSW mid-north coast, the northern rivers, parts of the tablelands and the Hunter region, with possible hail, heavy rainfall, flash flooding and destructive winds of more than 125km/h.Areas that had recorded heightened rainfall in the past fortnight were also at risk of flash flooding, Hines said.“If you do live through this area, tomorrow is definitely a day you’ll want to keep a watch on the radar to see if any big storms are headed your way,” he said.A broader area of potential concern for Sunday stretches from Newcastle, north of Sydney, up to Gympie on the Sunshine Coast.A severe wind warning is also in place across the mountains of northern Victoria and southern NSW, with wind gusts of more than 100km/h recorded on Saturday morning.Explore more on these topicsAustralia weatherMelbourneVictoriaNew South WalesSydneyCanberraQueenslandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Albanese looks for reset on world stage as ‘spot fires burn’ domestically and likely interest rate hike looms | Australian politics | The Guardian
description: The prime minister will speak with King Charles and others at the Commonwealth heads of government meeting in Antigua and Barbuda
Author: Ben Doherty
Headline: The prime minister will speak with King Charles and others at the Commonwealth heads of government meeting in Antigua and Barbuda
Content: Anthony Albanese is attending Chogm and will be away when the RBA delivers its interest rate decision on Tuesday.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPView image in fullscreenAnthony Albanese is attending Chogm and will be away when the RBA delivers its interest rate decision on Tuesday.Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAPAustralian politicsAlbanese looks for reset on world stage as ‘spot fires burn’ domestically and likely interest rate hike loomsThe prime minister will speak with King Charles and others at the Commonwealth heads of government meeting in Antigua and BarbudaGet ourdaily political email,free appordaily news podcastBen Dohertyand AAPFri 30 Oct 2026 22.24 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 23.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs “summit season” begins, reaffirming ties with fellow leaders on the world stage could be a circuit breaker forAnthony Albaneseamid domestic and economic woes, analysts have said.But alikely interest rate hike, triggered byhigher-than-expected inflation, while the prime minister is overseas will make his job – and the treasurer’s – even harder.Albanese is attending the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda from Saturday.He will hold talks with King Charles III and allies including the UK and Canadian prime ministers, Andy Burnham and Mark Carney, at the biennial meeting.Labor is losing control of the economic narrative as cash-strapped households look for someone to blame | Tom McIlroyRead moreThe discussions will constitute a well-needed reset after controversies overgrant fundingandpressures on inflation, according to Dr Zareh Ghazarian, an associate professor of politics at Monash University.“It is a strategically important time for him,” Ghazarian said.“He’s got a lot of spot fires burning domestically but this is going to be an opportunity for him to present himself to be much more on the front foot.“There’s a lot of pressure, so this trip could just be a moment to reset the political debate for people … this is a critical moment to present himself as a world leader amongst other world leaders.”Albanese will be away when the Reserve Bank hands down its next interest rate decision on Tuesday, with markets tipping a rise to 4.85%.It would be the fifth interest rate hike in 2026 and a challenging situation for the government to navigate, amid continuing cost-of-living pressures.Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter hereAlbanese emphasised the value of attending Chogm before his departure on Saturday morning. In a crowded international calendar, the Commonwealth is occasionally dismissed as irrelevant, ananachronistic relicof a former imperial era.“The Commonwealth heads of government meeting is an important forum,” Albanese said.“[It provides] an opportunity to work with some of our closest partners on shared challenges, including climate change, the preservation of our oceans, trade and investment and the rise of AI.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBack to Back Barries: Is inflation driving Chalmers and Albanese apart? – podcastRead moreThe issue of historical slavery, and its ongoing legacy, is likely to be a key point of contention at Chogm.Burnham,writing in the Guardian, said having “difficult conversations to safeguard the Commonwealth for the future” was the right thing to do.“Not just because it is in our interests, but because the Britain I believe in is confident, decent and brave. We led the world in abolishing slavery – and we can show leadership again today.”He called the transatlantic slave trade a “brutal and barbaric violation” of people “treated as property and worked to their deaths”.“I want to express my sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering of so many millions of people, and to recognise the way it still shapes our world today,” he wrote.Caribbean nations have made renewed calls for Britain to apologise for its role in selling enslaved people for profit, and for reparations, as the King toured the Caribbean.Burnham said: “Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process and I am open to them.” But he said he did not believe reparations for slavery was the “right answer”.Australia would not be a bystander to any debate about slavery and the slave trade.Across the 19th and early 20th centuries, Australian agriculturerelied heavily on “blackbirding”: the use of coercion, trickery, bribery and kidnapping to bring more than 60,000 Pacific Islanders to work as indentured labourers in Australia, primarily on Queensland’s sugar and cotton plantations.The Chogm meeting will kick off a busy end to the year overseas for Albanese, with international summits in Turkey, the Philippines, China and the US in coming weeks.The foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, is currently in Atlanta, Georgia for the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting. The start of that conference has been overshadowed by the presence of Russia, with about one-third of the countries attending vowing toboycott the customary “family photo”if the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, was involved.Explore more on these topicsAustralian politicsAnthony AlbaneseAustralian foreign policyJim ChalmersInterest ratesCommonwealth of NationsCommonwealth summitnewsShareReuse this content

title: US cancels G20 ‘family photo’ after Australia, UK and others refuse to appear with Russia | G20 | The Guardian
description: Marco Rubio pulls plug on traditional photo op at meeting of foreign ministers after about one-third of countries threaten boycott
Author: Ben Doherty
Headline: Marco Rubio pulls plug on traditional photo op at meeting of foreign ministers after about one-third of countries threaten boycott
Content: US secretary of state Marco Rubio speaks at the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta, Georgia.Photograph: Megan Varner/Pool Reuters/APView image in fullscreenUS secretary of state Marco Rubio speaks at the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta, Georgia.Photograph: Megan Varner/Pool Reuters/APG20US cancels G20 ‘family photo’ after Australia, UK and others refuse to appear with RussiaMarco Rubio pulls plug on traditional photo op at meeting of foreign ministers after about one-third of countries threaten boycottBen Dohertyand Associated PressFri 30 Oct 2026 20.29 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 22.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe traditional “family photo” to open the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting has been abruptly cancelled in the US after a host of nations – including Australia and the UK – refused to appear beside the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov.The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, pulled the plug after several European officials, the UK and Australia made it known they would boycott or walk out of the snapshot that often kicks off such international gatherings.Rubio still opened the talks in Atlanta with an appeal for unity on the issues that threaten international security and trade.“We are in a critical moment,” Rubio told his colleagues. “We are facing a series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises.”‘We hope he’ll accept’: US invites Putin to G20 summit at Trump golf clubRead moreAbout one-third of countries at the talks made it known they would not appear beside any Russian representatives.European Union nations had made clear they would boycott any photo with the Russians. “In no case will there be a family photo with European partners and Mr Lavrov together because … there is no normality with Russia,” Germany’s foreign affairs minister, Johann Wadephul, warned ahead of Friday’s session.The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, promised similar. “We do not engage in that way with the Russians and have not for a number of years,” he said.During the meeting’s opening session, Australia’s foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, condemned Russia’s invasion of Ukraine as brutal and unjustified - in front of Lavrov - saying Russia’s illegal war had affected international markets and worsened global food security.A spokesperson for Wong said Australia supported the US decision to cancel the group photo. “Australia has been clear and consistent: we will not normalise Russia’s brutal and illegal invasion of Ukraine.“Our focus at theG20remains on the important work before us and addressing the challenges facing the global economy.”The schism in Atlanta is yet further evidence of the rupture caused by the Trump administration’s attempt to reintegrate Russia and its isolated president, Vladimir Putin, into the international community despite Putin’s ongoing war against Ukraine.Diplomats who attended the opening session described it as cordial but said Russia’s position on Ukraine is unyielding – as is its opposition to Poland’s membership in the G20.Those disagreements, which also include the Trump administration’s not inviting G20 member South Africa over the objections of others, will probably prevent the foreign ministers from producing a joint communique when the meetings wrap up on Saturday, participants said.That did not surprise the Polish deputy prime minister and foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, representing his country at its first time as a guest at a G20 meeting.“We have wars going on and we have participants in those wars around the table, so it’s very difficult to agree a common line,” he told reporters.Several participants, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to discuss the closed-door talks, said all had agreed to try to overcome their differences despite the long odds and to work to make next month’s G20 leaders’ summit hosted by the president, Donald Trump, in Florida a success.Ukraine, which is not a G20 member but was invited to attend previous meetings, was not invited this year, with US officials saying it was a deliberate choice to include only formal members of the group. Poland, not a member, is seeking formal membership with US support.But missing from the invitation list was South Africa, a G20 founding member and the only African country in the group. South Africa is embroiled in several bitter disputes with the Trump administration, and when it chaired the G20 last year, top US officials, including Trump and Rubio, shunned the meetings it hosted.“We have consistently maintained that our nonparticipation is not voluntary,” Phindile Kunene, a spokesperson for the South African international relations minister, Ronald Lamola, said.Explore more on these topicsG20Australian foreign policyRussiaAustralian politicsUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: A top-secret spy mission, a decades-old scandal – and the Austin Powers-esque saga to lift the lid | Australian politics | The Guardian
description: Rex Patrick’s latest transparency fight is over what he calls ‘most open secret in the history of Australian spying’ – maybe even the world
Author: Sarah Basford Canales
Headline: Rex Patrick’s latest transparency fight is over what he calls ‘most open secret in the history of Australian spying’ – maybe even the world
Content: Rex Patrick’s latest push to reveal historical documents related to the Timor-Leste bugging scandal comes after years of attempts.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPView image in fullscreenRex Patrick’s latest push to reveal historical documents related to the Timor-Leste bugging scandal comes after years of attempts.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPAustralian politicsA top-secret spy mission, a decades-old scandal – and the Austin Powers-esque saga to lift the lidRex Patrick’s latest transparency fight is over what he calls ‘most open secret in the history of Australian spying’ – maybe even the worldGet ourdaily political email,free appordaily news podcastSarah Basford CanalesFri 30 Oct 2026 20.04 EDTLast modified on Fri 30 Oct 2026 20.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA campaign to uncover any documents relating to whetherAustralian spies bugged Timor-Lesteto gain the upper hand in sensitive oil and gas negotiations will be a little less secret after a critical win by the former senator Rex Patrick.The politician turned transparency advocate is trying to finally lift the lid on the top-secret mission in 2004 that became a public scandal years later after an ex-spy and a former attorney generalattempted to mount a case in The Hague.But the Australian government stands by its Glomar response – to neither confirm nor deny first that the bugging took place and second that any relevant documents exist.Witness K and the ‘outrageous’ spy scandal that failed to shame AustraliaRead moreOn Friday, the administrative review tribunal (ART) ruled in Patrick’s favour, forcing the commonwealth to hold unclassified parts of the three-day hearing in late November in public.Government lawyers argued the whole saga is so sensitive that even sections of the hearing open to the public should remain behind closed doors in case someone accidentally says something they shouldn’t.Patrick told Guardian Australia the situation was a farce, arguing the bugging scandal is the “most open secret in the history of Australian spying”, maybe even the world.A ‘very high-stakes’ gamePatrick’s bid to gain further insight into the affair began with a request for cabinet documents from 2004 held by the National Archives of Australia.The Australian government’s position, along with the responsible agency, the Australian Secret Intelligence Service (Asis), remains that any such documents cannot be publicly confirmed or denied.Asis contends that alone the records could undermine national security and Australia’s standings with other countries.The documents would relate to Australia’s strategy forsettling how much of the Timor Sea it could maintain control over after Timor-Lesteofficially gained independence from Indonesia in 2002.Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter hereThe negotiations determined the countries’ shared control over the Greater Sunrise gasfields, which hold resources estimated to be worth more than $50bn.Patrick’s win on Friday means at least some of the government’s defence over why it cannot publicly reveal details of the 2004 bugging – which preceded to a commercially favourable agreement for Australia against the impoverished nation – will be heard in public.At a preliminary ART hearing last week to rule on whether part of the hearings should remain open, lawyers for the archives argued the matter is so sensitive that even sections of the hearing open to the public should remain behind closed doors in case someone accidentally says something they shouldn’t.Parts of the hearing will already remain closed so top-secret details can be debated, but the commonwealth had argued the open hearings should also be debated in secret.The commonwealth unsuccessfully proposed the media and the public should be barred from the open hearings but would be able to view a transcript after careful review by the nation’s foreign intelligence agency.The deputy chief solicitor, Justin Davidson, argued last Thursday the stakes are “very high” and it would be nearly impossible to mitigate the risk of an intelligence official revealing something they shouldn’t.“I’m not, frankly, beyond making a mistake,” Davidson said.Ewan McMillan, an Asis deputy director general, and Michelle Chan, a deputy secretary at the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (Dfat), will offer their testimonies in late November when the case is heard in full.Davidson had argued the unclassified details they share in an open hearing might be “interesting to the public” but not necessarily in the public interest.On Friday, the ART deputy president Peter Britten-Jones ruled against the commonwealth, noting officials were “highly qualified and experienced” enough not to let national secrets slip in an open forum.“The risk of an inadvertent disclosure of certificated material is negligible,” he wrote in his ruling.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPatrick said the whole administrative saga felt like a replay of an Austin Powers movie.“Only Asis and Dfat think the operation is still a secret,” Patrick said.“It’d be funny if it wasn’t so serious, or if the taxpayer wasn’t paying for the silk, barristers and lawyers arguing the government’s case.”A decades-long international affairPatrick’s latest push to reveal historical documents, or at least the existence of them, comes after years of attempts.In 2021, the former senator took the archives to the tribunal for heavily redacting a cabinet submission from 2000 outlining Australia’s negotiating strategy forbartering with its impoverished allyon the Timor Sea maritime boundary and a related minute.Thenegotiations, which predated the bugging scandal by four years, were criticalfor Timor-Leste and Australia, because they dictated access to the Greater Sunrise gasfields.The tribunal later released the document with fewer redactions, which showed cabinet in 2000 was concerned that Timor-Leste’s independence process may disrupt access to the oil and gas reserves in the Timor Sea, because Australia’s prior agreement with Indonesia for a 50/50 revenue split would be void.Sailor, spy, whistleblower, grandfather: the life of Witness K revealed in court documentsRead moreThe bugging operation occurred in 2004 when Asis operatives planted listening devices in key Timor-Leste government offices to uncover Timor-Leste’s bottom line, its negotiating tactics and the competing views of cabinet members.In 2006, Australia ended upsecuring a 50/50 splitof the Greater Sunrise fields, positioned 450km north-west of Darwin and 150km south of Timor-Leste. The deal was a boon for thejoint venture of multinationals, led by Woodside, seeking to exploit the Timor Sea.The bugging operation was later revealed after a former Asis officer, known as Witness K, approached the lawyer and former ACT attorney general Bernard Collaery, who was also acting for Timor-Leste, in 2013 about his knowledge of the operation.Together, the two attempted to help Timor-Leste’s dispute against the maritime boundary agreement in The Hague, the international permanent court of arbitration, before Collaery’s office was raided and Witness K’s passport seized.Timor-Lestewithdrew its Australian espionage claimsin The Hague in 2017 as a “confidence-building measure”, and a new maritime border was signed in 2018.In a 2019 affidavit for the proceedings against Collaery, which were dropped in 2022, the Timor-Leste president, Jose Ramos-Horta, said he believed the disclosure of further details of the operation would not create any new or additional problems for Australia.“I believe the relationship between Timor-Leste and Australia would benefit from, rather than be prejudiced by, a full and open disclosure in this of what may or may not have occurred in 2004,” he said.Explore more on these topicsAustralian politicsAustralian intelligence agenciesWitness K caseAustralian foreign policyTimor-LestenewsShareReuse this content

title: Tusk defends overhaul of Poland’s constitutional court despite protests | Poland | The Guardian
description: Prime minister says shake-up is vital to restore tribunal crippled by years of political disputes
Author: Jakub Krupa
Headline: Prime minister says shake-up is vital to restore tribunal crippled by years of political disputes
Content: Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, said the court ‘in the form imposed by PiS was not a genuine court’.Photograph: Marcin Gadomski/EPAView image in fullscreenPoland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, said the court ‘in the form imposed by PiS was not a genuine court’.Photograph: Marcin Gadomski/EPAPolandTusk defends overhaul of Poland’s constitutional court despite protestsPrime minister says shake-up is vital to restore tribunal crippled by years of political disputesJakub KrupaSat 31 Oct 2026 18.43 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 18.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePoland’s prime minister,Donald Tusk, has vowed to see through a contested overhaul of the country’s constitutional court, declaring that “in certain matters, there can be no compromise”.Ina prime-time television address on Saturday night, Tusk was defiant, despite overnight protests that saw riot police drafted to protect the court’s building, saying the shake-up was vital to restore a tribunal crippled by years of political disputes.Riot police deployed to Poland’s constitutional court after judge suspendedRead moreParalysed for more than a decade, the courtsat at the coreof rule of law clashesbetween the rightwing Law and Justice (PiS) party and the EU during the party’s eight-year rule.Since returning to office in 2023, the centre-right Tusk hassought to unwind those judicial changes, but his agenda has beenfrustrated by opposition-aligned presidents with extensive veto powers. Earlier this year, president Karol Nawrocki refused to swear in five judges approved by parliament.The crisis flared again on Friday when a group of government-backed judges attempted to seize procedural control of the tribunal, suspending the PiS-appointed chief judge and deputy and prompting street protests.View image in fullscreenConservative supporters assemble outside the constitutional court in Warsaw.Photograph: Agata Grzybowska/Anadolu/Getty ImagesDefending the action, Tusk said “there was never any doubt that the court in the form imposed by PiS was not a genuine court”, citing adverse rulings from European tribunals.He compared the opposition outrage to “a thief snatching an elderly woman’s handbag, running off, and when he is caught, he screams that he is subjected to violence”.Tusk said: “Let’s call things for what they are: for years, there have been organisations and politicians inPolandwho seek to destroy democracy and the rule of law. It is no coincidence they find support among pro-Russian forces globally.”He later highlighted that Russia’s former president Dmitry Medvedevhad joinedthe opposition in an outcry over the changes, accusing Warsaw of “a constitutional coup” and “hounding the conservatives”. “And everything is clear,” Tusk said.He also criticised opposition-aligned Nawrocki for joining the protests on Friday night and forcing his entry into the court’s building to intervene. “In a democratic state, no politician can enter a court to issue orders or intimidate judges – not even the president,” Tusk said. “We Poles have succeeded too well in building a strong state to surrender now.”He said it was the government’s duty to ensure its security and the conditions necessary for the court to operate. “And I intend to fulfil that duty,” he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe confrontation sets the battle lines before next year’s parliamentary election, with polls pointing to a close race between Tusk’s broad coalition and the nationalist right.However, experts remain divided over whether the government’s procedural gambit at the court is lawful.Poland’s Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights said on Saturdaythe legal basis for the temporary suspension was “questionable”, warning it would “not contribute” to restoring the court.The foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, conceded thatthe events outside the court were “not elegant”, but insisted: “The alternative was to concede an unconstitutional transformation of Poland into a presidential republic.”Nawrocki held some cross-party political talks on Saturday, with no apparent breakthrough. His senior aide, Zbigniew Bogucki, responded to Tusk’s address, calling the prime minister “a pathological liar, who is setting Poland ablaze”.Explore more on these topicsPolandDonald TuskEuropeProtestKarol NawrockinewsShareReuse this content

title: Oleshky evacuees reunite with families after truce allows crossing back into Ukraine | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Residents of nearby villages line highway waving flags to greet the evacuees’ convoy from the Russian-occupied city
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Residents of nearby villages line highway waving flags to greet the evacuees’ convoy from the Russian-occupied city
Content: People evacuated from the Russian-controlled city of Oleshky arrive in Ukraine at an undisclosed location.Photograph: EPAView image in fullscreenPeople evacuated from the Russian-controlled city of Oleshky arrive in Ukraine at an undisclosed location.Photograph: EPAUkraineOleshky evacuees reunite with families after truce allows crossing back into UkraineResidents of nearby villages line highway waving flags to greet the evacuees’ convoy from the Russian-occupied cityAssociated PressSat 31 Oct 2026 15.17 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 15.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEvacuees from Russian-occupied Oleshky have been reunited with their families after crossing into Ukrainian-held territory on Saturday.The major rescue operationbegan on Fridayand was carried out under the most significant truce since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine four and a half years ago.Evacuees wrapped in Ukrainian flags stepped off buses at the Ukrainian-Belarusian border to be reunited with family members. Volunteers with hand-drawn welcome signs handed coffee to the weary people who had travelled by bus and plane through Russia and Belarus. Residents of nearby villages lined the highway waving flags and torches to greet the convoy.Evacuation of civilians begins in besieged Ukrainian city of OleshkyRead moreTetiana Leonidivna, 71, thanked the Ukrainian soldiers who helped her to flee. “We love them, we love them,” she said through tears. “We know that they are protecting us. And a deep bow to them, and a deep bow to their parents, for having such children. I am proud, I am simply proud.”The ceasefire in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region began early on Tuesday and was expected to continue through Sunday evening. The White House said the first lady Melania Trump helped broker the localised deal, while Pope Leo XIV pressed Russia andUkraineto allow aid deliveries and evacuations.Relatives and volunteers with the Red Cross, Médecins Sans Frontières and World Central Kitchen welcomed the evacuees as they arrived at the border, ready to provide aid and food, including for their pets.View image in fullscreenDmytro and Larysa were delighted to return to Ukrainian-controlled territory.Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/ReutersHolding a cigarette between shaking fingers, 48-year-old Ivan Yevhenovych described his last months in Oleshky. “It was very difficult. There were a lot of drones. It was hard to move around the streets,” he said. “Since spring, there hasn’t really been any staple food left. People had a little bit of their own reserves. We are thrifty people.”He said landmines or drone strikes were killing residents every day.An estimated 2,000 people remained in Oleshky when the temporary truce took hold. They were offered the choice of being evacuated to Ukrainian- or Russian-held territory, or remaining in the city with replenished food and medical supplies.“Many people stayed behind and didn’t want to leave,” Yevhenovych said. “Some for their houses, some for their animals.”View image in fullscreenRelatives and volunteers welcomed the evacuees at the border, ready to provide aid and food, including for their pets.Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/ReutersUkrainian authorities, seeking to protect those who remained and safeguard future humanitarian missions, have not said how many residents evacuated Oleshky and have restricted details of their route. Melania Trump posted on social media on Friday that the humanitarian convoy could safely evacuate more than 750 people.Liza Paliy, 19, waited at the border for her father, whom she last saw more than two and a half years earlier when she fled the occupied city with her mother and sister. “We thought at that time that it would be a month, two maximum, and we would return, but unfortunately two years have already passed,” she said.Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, hailed the humanitarian mission as a win.“This is an extremely important moment. Behind us are difficult negotiations, agreements, preparations, and an enormous amount of work. But most importantly, the people who waited so long to be rescued are finally safe,” he said in an online post.Lubinets said evacuees ranged in age from just over one year old to 94, and they brought pets, including dogs, cats, a parrot and a raccoon. He said he hoped the Oleshky truce could be replicated elsewhere, saying it “could form the basis of a new mechanism for responding to the most difficult humanitarian crises”.View image in fullscreenEvacuees ranged in age from just over one year old to 94.Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/ReutersYana Lantratova, Russia’s human rights commissioner, said both sides have agreed to conduct regular humanitarian missions in and around Oleshky. Lubinets did not mention this development.“The mission has concluded, but, unfortunately, living conditions in Oleshky remain extremely difficult,” she said. “We will make every effort to support those residents who have made the decision to stay.”Some Oleshky evacuees who chose to move to Russian-occupied territory were taken to a temporary shelter in Simferopol, Lantratova said. The city is in Ukraine’s Crimean peninsula, which Moscow annexed in 2014.“After everything they have endured and a long journey, it is essential for these people to rest, recover and feel cared for. However, support should not be limited to just a roof over their heads and a hot meal,” she said in a social media post.View image in fullscreenPets, including dogs, cats, a parrot and a raccoon, were also evacuated.Photograph: Danylo Antoniuk/Anadolu/Getty ImagesA Ukrainian drone attack killed a 30-year-old woman and a 41-year-old man in Russia’s western Bryansk region, the local governor, Yegor Kovalchuk, said on Saturday. Five others were wounded, he said.Local officials also reported Ukrainian drone attacks in the Russian republic of Bashkortostan. Russian media outlets said there was a fire in the region’s capital, Ufa, home to several oil refineries.The Russian defence ministry said on Saturday its forces had shot down 433 Ukrainian drones overnight.The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said Moscow launched drone attacks on energy and railway infrastructure across Ukraine overnight, leaving 280,000 households in Dnipro and Kyiv regions without power.Explore more on these topicsUkraineRussia (Football)EuropeRussia (World news)newsShareReuse this content

title: Protests under way in Germany and France as minister warns against use of Halloween masks – as it happened | Europe | The Guardian
description: France’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, has warned protesters that covering their faces with Halloween costumes could result in fines
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: France’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, has warned protesters that covering their faces with Halloween costumes could result in fines
Content: 09.59 EDTProtesters begin marching in French citiesProtesters inParishave begun marching from Porte de Bagnolet, with demonstrations also taking place inLilleandLyon.Leftist party La France Insoumise (LFI) candidate in France’s 2027 presidential election Jean-Luc Melenchon and French-Palestinian member of the European Parliament Rima Hassan take part in a nationwide demonstrations over the rising cost of living and inequality in Paris.Photograph: Ed Jones/AFP/Getty ImagesA person in an inflatable costume taking part in the demonstration in Paris.Photograph: Pedro Nunes/ReutersA protester gives a flower to a gendarmerie officer.Photograph: Abdul Saboor/ReutersA protester dressed up as a ghost holds a placard reading “A ghost more visible than Bardella in the European Parliament”, in reference to Jordan Bardella, the president of the far-right National Rally.Photograph: Sameer Al-Doumy/AFP/Getty ImagesProtesters wearing Halloween masks pose with placards during demonstrations in Lille, northern France.Photograph: François Lo Presti/AFP/Getty ImagesA protester in Lyon holds a sign reading ‘We’re just one finger away from revolt’.Photograph: Jeff Pachoud/AFP/Getty ImagesShareUpdated at10.20 EDT

title: Police clash with masked rioters after largely peaceful protests across France | France | The Guardian
description: Demonstrations also taking place in Germany, where officers fire teargas to disperse crowds as evening falls
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: Demonstrations also taking place in Germany, where officers fire teargas to disperse crowds as evening falls
Content: A protester uses a firework during a demonstration organised by labour unions as part of nationwide demonstrations.Photograph: Pedro Nunes/ReutersView image in fullscreenA protester uses a firework during a demonstration organised by labour unions as part of nationwide demonstrations.Photograph: Pedro Nunes/ReutersFrancePolice clash with masked rioters after largely peaceful protests across FranceDemonstrations also taking place in Germany, where officers fire teargas to disperse crowds as evening fallsJon HenleyEurope correspondentSat 31 Oct 2026 14.23 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 17.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleClashes have erupted in Paris, Marseille and other cities after tens of thousands of demonstrators, some in Halloween fancy dress, marched acrossFrancein a third wave of protests over the cost of living and deteriorating public services.The interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said about 150 planned demonstrations around the country had passed off peacefully, but police had encountered an “extraordinary” level of violence from some rioters as the rallies ended.One riot police officer had been hit by a molotov cocktail inParis, he said, describing the incident as an “attempted murder” and adding that the night was not yet over. “We are fully prepared for those looking for confrontation tonight,” he said.About 320,000 people – down from an estimated 410,000 last weekend – took part in rallies around the country, the interior ministry said, including 70,000 in Paris who marched along boulevards on the south-eastern outskirts, avoiding the city centre.As evening approached and the largely peaceful demonstrations came to an end, police in several cities fired teargas and stun grenades to disperse crowds joined – as on the previous Saturday – by groups of masked rioters. Police carried out 511 arrests.View image in fullscreenA protester wearing a Marie Antoinette costume holds a placard reading ‘Give them brioche’ flanked by a protester dressed as a wizard holding a placard reading ‘A potion for the revolution’ during a demonstration in Lyon, France on 31 October 2026.Photograph: Jeff Pachoud/AFP/Getty ImagesNuñez said earlier this week that 70,000 police and gendarmes, including elite units, would be deployed in an effort to quell violence on the protests’ sidelines, warning that Saturday looked like “a very high risk” day.The Paris protesters set off peacefully from the Porte de Bagnolet near the ring road, holding placards with slogans including “No need for teargas to make our future look bleak” and “Disguised as an angry citizen for Halloween”, as a helicopter flew overheadOn and around its destination, the Porte de Charenton, dozens of masked people dressed in black used hammers to pry up paving stones and hurl them at police, and at least one incendiary device was thrown at security forces.Police responded with teargas and baton charges. “A hardcore of several hundred rioters” had attacked police with projectiles, the Paris police prefecture said. Officers had “manoeuvred to restore public order”, it added.In Lyon protesters threw projectiles at police, prompting officers to fire teargas, and in Toulouse police used water cannon against an unauthorised protest that drew several thousand people, mostly young demonstrators.From teargas in Paris to gen Z in Germany: protests across Europe – in picturesRead moreThe marches brought together school students, who have been calling for better conditions for a month, trade unions and gilets jaune (yellow vests) protesters united in anger at the cost of living, widening inequalities and Emmanuel Macron’s ⁠government.“The French economy is doing badly no matter what happens, because today we’re being run by a group of incompetents who juggle billions while families are struggling with a few cents,” said one protester on the Paris march, Jérôme Rodrigues. “That’s why we’re here, to keep shouting our demands louder and ‌louder.”View image in fullscreenProtesters wearing Halloween costumes pose in front of the French national flag during a demonstration in Lyon, 31 October 2026.Photograph: Jeff Pachoud/AFP/Getty ImagesA protester in Nantes, Camille Guérin, said: “We say no to the cost of living, no to the far right, yes to high school students’ demands, yes to giving citizens a voice.”Saturday’s rallies came two weeks after widespread street violence and looting rocked numerous French cities during a firstwave of mass protest on 17 Octoberthat became one of the worst days of civil unrest in the country’s recent history.Student protesters vowed to stage new high school and university blockades on Tuesday and Thursday. “Then we will join the 5 November demonstration called by workers and trade unions,” said Sabrine Kharbach of the Union Étudiante, a student organisation.View image in fullscreenProtesters light smoke flares after a demonstration organised by ‘GenZ regelt!’ (Gen Z has got this!) in Berlin on 31 October 2026.Photograph: Ralf Hirschberger/AFP/Getty ImagesProtests also took place elsewhere in Europe. InGermany, police fired water cannon to disperse protesters who hurled firework and other projectiles at the end of youth-led protests organised by a group called “Gen Z regelt!” (Gen Z will sort this).Thousands of police were deployed across the country, with tensions rising as evening fell after mostly peaceful demonstrations for “for education, health, the climate and an affordable life” in dozens of cities.In Frankfurt, Germany’s financial hub, at least two stores were looted as protests turned violent, with several more damaged and police ⁠trying to gain control of the situation, according to a Reuters witness. A march was also temporarily halted in the city after protesters set off fireworks.In the western city of Cologne, police fired water cannon to disperse a crowd after saying protesters had targeted officers with fireworks.In Berlin, protesters hurled bottles and eggs while protesters set barricades ablaze in Hamburg, and police were using pepper spray on demonstrators in some places, the newspaper Bild reported.Police were also on alert in Barcelona after an anonymous TikTok network called Blocus urged new gatherings, and in Italy after recent clashes with protesters in Milan, Turin and Bologna.Explore more on these topicsFranceProtestParisGermanyEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Starmer says UK must get closer to Europe as US relationship changes | Keir Starmer | The Guardian
description: Shift in dealings with Washington not likely to reset once Trump leaves Oval Office, former PM says
Author: Kevin Rawlinson
Headline: Shift in dealings with Washington not likely to reset once Trump leaves Oval Office, former PM says
Content: ‘A stronger Europe is vital and the UK must be at the heart of it,’ Starmer said.Photograph: ITV via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘A stronger Europe is vital and the UK must be at the heart of it,’ Starmer said.Photograph: ITV via Getty ImagesKeir StarmerStarmer says UK must get closer to Europe as US relationship changesShift in dealings with Washington not likely to reset once Trump leaves Oval Office, former PM saysKevin RawlinsonSat 31 Oct 2026 09.32 EDTFirst published on Sat 31 Oct 2026 09.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK and other European nations must draw closer together as the US becomes a less-reliable partner,Keir Starmerhas said in his first significant political intervention since leaving No 10.The former prime minister warned European leaders of the threat posed by Russia, among others, and said the shift in relations with Washington during Donald Trump’s presidency was not likely to reset once he leaves the Oval Office. He accused them of being caught out by these new realities twice already.“A strongerEuropeis vital and the UK must be at the heart of it,” Starmer told an audience at the British Irish Chamber of Commerce on Friday. “Europe has twice been caught asleep, failing to anticipate and prepare for predictable events.“First, whenRussia’s attack on Ukraineexposed longstanding European weaknesses on defence and security, and second, when President Trump made clear, once and for all, that the US will no longer bankroll our European security. We have to catch up.”Starmer had called for closer European ties beforestepping down as prime ministerin July. Three months earlier, amid Trump’s war with Iran and his threats to withdraw from Nato, Starmer said Europe represented a “partnership for a dangerous world we must navigate together”.He said those ties should go further than just defence, adding that Brexit had done “deep damage” to the UK economy, and that he wanted to be “more ambitious”, including pursuing “closer economic cooperation [and] closer security cooperation”.View image in fullscreenKeir Starmer alongside the US president, Donald Trump, at the Nato leaders’ summit in Ankara, Turkey in July.Photograph: Yves Herman/ReutersStarmer spoke after spending time in Dublin meeting senior business leaders and politicians, including the taoiseach, Micheál Martin, with whom he established the annual UK-Ireland summit.“I will say here what I have said to European leaders. This is about responding to a permanent change of affairs, not an aberration of the Trump presidency. Things will not go back to the way they were before.“That doesn’t mean the US relationship is no longer important. On the contrary, the military, security and intelligence alliance is far too strong for that. But it does mean enabling Europe to take on far more responsibility for its own defence and security.”His comments reflect a growing consensus on the left of UK politics that closer ties with Europe are essential to ensure economic and military security. Soon after taking office as Starmer’s successor,Andy Burnhamsaid that he intended to be “bolder” about closer ties with the EU.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAs Trump fans the flames of a world on fire, can diplomacy take back control?Read moreNext month,Burnham will attend a crucial EU-UK summitwhere new agreements on food standards, energy and youth mobility will be the main focus.Burnham has also saidhe wants a public debate on how the UK could move to a closer relationship with the EUafter the next election. At a meeting of European defence ministers in Paris this week, the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said that they were “united and unwavering” in support for Ukraine in the face of Russian hostility.Starmer said: “We need to build up pan-European cooperation and coordination on defence and security – a common security framework as much as a common market. The EU is changing to respond to that, but it cannot be the EU alone when Europe’s periphery is core to its defence.“Britain must be central to that project. We are one of two nuclear powers. We are a leadingNatomember. We have a viable next-generation fighter jet programme. And we are pledged to work alongside European allies to guarantee security in Ukraine.“Ireland and the UK stand side by side in the coalition of the willing and with Ukraine, working together to guarantee and shape the security of our continent. I hope and believe that Britain’s relationship with its friends and allies can and should be strengthened by this urgent and common security project.”Explore more on these topicsKeir StarmerEuropeEuropean UnionDonald TrumpForeign policyDefence policyNatonewsShareReuse this content

title: Man in Belfast charged with possessing explosives and firearms | Belfast | The Guardian
description: The 35-year-old was charged after police searched properties in Shankill Road and Edwina Street areas
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: The 35-year-old was charged after police searched properties in Shankill Road and Edwina Street areas
Content: Police and army during a security operation on Riga Street off the Shankill Road in north Belfast, 30 October 2026.Photograph: Rebecca Black/PAView image in fullscreenPolice and army during a security operation on Riga Street off the Shankill Road in north Belfast, 30 October 2026.Photograph: Rebecca Black/PABelfastMan in Belfast charged with possessing explosives and firearmsThe 35-year-old was charged after police searched properties in Shankill Road and Edwina Street areasNadeem BadshahSat 31 Oct 2026 16.21 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 16.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA man has been charged under the Explosives Act and Firearms Order after police searched properties in Belfast.The 35-year-old was charged with offences including two counts of possessing explosives under suspicious circumstances, and possession of a prohibited weapon (discharge of electricity or noxious gas).He is due to appear before Belfast magistrates court on Monday, the Police Service of Northern Ireland said.The charges follow searches at properties in the Shankill Road and Edwina Street areas of north Belfast on Friday and Saturday.DCI McCallum said: “Following these searches a number of suspicious devices, along with other items, were located and seized by officers for forensic examination.“Local residents who were evacuated as a precaution have now been allowed to return home following the public safety operation conducted alongside ammunition technical officers.“All cordons have now been lifted from the area, and we thank local residents for their patience as inquiries were conducted yesterday and into today.”McCallum added: “As we continue to investigate the circumstances surrounding this incident, we would appeal to anyone who may have information that could assist with inquiries to contact us on 101, quoting reference number 261 30/10/26.”Explore more on these topicsBelfastNorthern IrelandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Almost 140 arrested at protest against Palestine Action ban outside US embassy in London | UK news | The Guardian
description: Met alleges demonstrators ‘meeting to purposefully commit a crime’ in largest such gathering under Burnham
Author: Sammy Gecsoyler
Headline: Met alleges demonstrators ‘meeting to purposefully commit a crime’ in largest such gathering under Burnham
Content: A demonstrator is removed by police during a protest in support of Palestine Action outside the US embassy in London on Sunday.Photograph: Carlos Jasso/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA demonstrator is removed by police during a protest in support of Palestine Action outside the US embassy in London on Sunday.Photograph: Carlos Jasso/AFP/Getty ImagesUK newsAlmost 140 arrested at protest against Palestine Action ban outside US embassy in LondonMet alleges demonstrators ‘meeting to purposefully commit a crime’ in largest such gathering under BurnhamSammy GecsoylerSat 31 Oct 2026 14.28 EDTFirst published on Sat 31 Oct 2026 10.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlmost 140 people have been arrested at the largest mass demonstrations under Andy Burnham’s premiership opposing the proscription of Palestine Action.Hundreds of people gathered outside the US embassy in Battersea, south London, holding signs that read: “I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action.” Demonstrators also held a vigil in support of the group outside the US consulate in Edinburgh.Before the London gathering, the Metropolitan police warned those taking part “that they face arrest as part of a robust policing operation” and that anyone “playing a key role in organising the event, giving instructions to others and/or providing logistical support” would probably be committing an offence.In a statement on X, the Metropolitan police said: “139 people have now been arrested. Officers remain on scene and are continuing to make arrests.”Commander Adam Slonecki, who is leading the policing operation, said: “All those intending on coming to this event know that supporting a proscribed organisation is unlawful – they are essentially meeting to purposefully commit a crime.Defend Our Juries, the group behind the demonstrations, said the Met was “terrified of facilitating US embarrassment” andestimatedthat “around 400 people” gathered to take part.More than 4,000 arrests have been made for supporting Palestine Action since the ban came into effect, Defend Our Juries said, representing the vast majority of terror arrests since last July.Among those sitting outside the US embassy, holding a sign that appeared to express support for Palestine Action, was Sue Morhall. “The USA is complicit in most of the wars that are going on. I just feel the leaders of this world, including Trump, need to know that people are so against what’s happening in Gaza,” said the 79-year-old retiree.View image in fullscreenSue Morhall takes part in the demonstration outside the US embassy in London.Morhall believes there is a chance Burnham could rescind the proscription. “I think it’s early days. I’m hopeful, though pigs might fly,” she said. “I think he’s going to perhaps wait until the midterm elections in America. It’s a terrible shame that people who are trying to stop a genocide are being arrested.”She has been arrested “five or six” times at previous demonstrations and feels “OK” about being hauled into a police van again. “It’s the principle, and this is one that I feel very strongly about,” she said.The Rev Bill White, 72, who also held a sign that read: “I oppose genocide. I support Palestine Action,” said: “I’m appalled that Britain is helping facilitate the genocide that is happening in Palestine. We supply weapons that are being used on Palestinians.”View image in fullscreenRev Bill White also took part in the demonstration.He said he had “hoped for better” from Burnham and resigned from the Labour party after Palestine Action was proscribed as a terrorist group.As a faith leader, he said there was “no choice” other than to take part in the demonstration. “This is the right thing to do. There’s a bad law and it is wrong to criminalise people that are trying to prevent genocide,” he said. “How can I not be here?”A Defend Our Juries spokesperson said: “The Met police overzealous response outside the US embassy today only serves to further expose how far authorities in the UK will go to appease American interests. Israel’s war crimes that have caused death and injury to thousands could not happen without the US’s approval.”The protests come before an appeal at the UK supreme court against Palestine Action’s designation as a terror group on 4 November.Last month, more than 160 people were arrested or reported for summons at a similar demonstration in support of Palestine Action staged outside the Labour party conference in Liverpool.The new government has come under pressure to rescind the ban, though Shabana Mahmood, who has stood firm in favour of the group’s proscription, remained in post as home secretary.The journalist and author Sarah Helm, the wife of the prime minister’s national security adviser, Jonathan Powell, was accused of supporting Palestine Actionafter posting on X: “God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action.” Her post came in response to news that the Irish authorSally Rooneycan no longer sell her books in the UK because of her support for the group.During the Labour party conference, two activists confronted the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, during a meal at Pizza Express in the city centre where he was challenged about the arrests. Videoof the incidentshowed one of the protesters urging Miliband to declare a genocide in Gaza and de-proscribe Palestine Action.Miliband said he was happy to discuss the issue but at another time, before the protesters were ushered out.One woman, who held a sign that, bar swapping the word “authors” to “retirees”, replicated the X post by Sarah Helm, was among thosearrestedin London, despite the Met ultimatelyassessingthat Helm’s post “did not meet the criminal threshold”.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK charity shop profits plummet amid shift in secondhand clothes market | Charities | The Guardian
description: British Heart Foundation describes ‘exceptionally challenging’ trading after retail profit reportedly fell 23% amid rise of platforms such as Vinted
Author: Harry Cockburn
Headline: British Heart Foundation describes ‘exceptionally challenging’ trading after retail profit reportedly fell 23% amid rise of platforms such as Vinted
Content: An Oxfam shop in London. Oxfam’s retail head said the shift had been ‘challenging …  and it is going to be painful for the sector’.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAn Oxfam shop in London. Oxfam’s retail head said the shift had been ‘challenging …  and it is going to be painful for the sector’.Photograph: Jill Mead/The GuardianCharitiesUK charity shop profits plummet amid shift in secondhand clothes marketBritish Heart Foundation describes ‘exceptionally challenging’ trading after Oxfam’s retail profit reportedly fell 23% amid rise of platforms such as VintedHarry CockburnSat 31 Oct 2026 11.10 EDTFirst published on Sat 31 Oct 2026 10.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleProfits at some of the UK’s best-known charity shops have plummeted as they face a number of pressures, including from online secondhand clothes platforms, prompting claims that a key part of the sector’s fundraising model could be under threat.According to unpublished accountsseen by the Financial Times, Oxfam’s retail profit fell 23% to £4.9m in the last financial year, compared with £6.4m in the previous year.The British Heart Foundation (BHF), which has the biggest high street presence of any charity in the country,has announced plansto close 150 stores after they made a £3.3m loss in the last financial year. Cancer Research UK and Scope have also closed, or are closing, some of their shops.But these losses come despite UK spending on secondhand clothing having quadrupled over the past decade, rising to £8.8bn a year, according to GlobalData.The shift has come alongside the rise of websites such as Vinted and Depop, suggesting that people who might previously have donated clothes to charity shops are instead selling them directly to other consumers and profiting themselves.View image in fullscreenThe British Heart Foundation, which has the biggest high street presence of any charity in the country, has announced plans to close 150 stores.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianAlongside this change, Chinese companies are selling more clothes in developing countries, particularly in Africa, which has long been a major market for unwanted secondhand clothing.“It has been challenging … and it is going to be painful for the sector,” Lorna Fallon, the head of Oxfam’s retail operation, told the Financial Times.Oxfam’s latest filings reveal that for every £100 people spend in its shops, just £6 now goes towards the charity’s work on alleviating global poverty. As recently as 2022, the figure was £22, the FT reports. However, the organisation’s focus on books and music means it has no plans to reduce its number of shops.In June, BHF carried out a major review of its retail arm, which employs almost 3,700 staff, after profits from its shopsplungedfrom £18.8m in 2024 to £3.6m in the year to 31 March 2025.The charity cited “an exceptionally challenging trading environment”, and said it was aiming to close 90 stores by the end of March 2027 and another 60 by the following March.The rapid change in fortunes for charity shops also highlights their limitations in the face of greater competition. Whereas Vinted and Depop directly connect sellers with buyers, charity shops remain at the mercy of high street and warehouse rents and other associated costs and inefficiencies, including collecting, sorting, pricing and storing clothes.Another issue hampering high street charity shops is that the clothes being donated are increasingly substandard. Speaking to the Guardian earlier this month, Tansy Hoskins, the author of Charity Shop World,describedthe sector as dealing with “avalanches” of poor-quality clothes across the country, as people use charity shops as convenient dumping grounds for unwanted purchases.“Quality is the big change marker – it’s gone through the floor. You’re just fighting against the waste,” Hoskins said.Robin Osterley, the chief executive of the Charity Retail Association, said: “Fast fashion has had an impact on donations quality, there’s no question about that.”View image in fullscreenOxfam’s focus on books and music means it has no plans to reduce its number of shops.Photograph: Vuk Valcic/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockBut he added: “We don’t see Vinted or any of the other online platforms as an issue at all. It might be having a little bit of an effect – where people have one bag for charity shop donations and one for Vinted – but we believe these effects are significantly mitigated by two things.“The first is that Vinted and other platforms are having a very positive effect on people’s attitudes towards secondhand shopping, and creating an environment where it’s much more normalised. A rising tide floats all ships.“The second factor is that there are a lot of people who buy things from charity shops to sell on the online platforms. Our members get a significant income from them.”Bafta trustees may have broken charity law by accepting free guest ticketsRead moreOsterley instead suggested theNovember 2024 budgethad had a much larger impact on bricks and mortar charity shops, in which national insurance increases and the lowering of the national insurance threshold – affecting more part-time staff – has had a “really significant” effect on the costs charity shops face, as well as inflationary pressures across the economy.Richard Hawkes, Oxfam GB’s chief executive, said: “Whilst there is no getting away from the fact that the charity retail sector has been impacted by the cost-of-living crisis, like the rest of the high street, there is still much to be hopeful and positive about for the future.“The growth of secondhand presents real opportunities for the whole sector, but it also means we need to think differently about the traditional charity retail model.He added: “Our shops also offer much more than just an income. They give us a presence in communities where we might not otherwise be, while providing opportunities to engage with more than 20,000 volunteers. This wider role remains a vital part of what makes charity retail so valuable.”Explore more on these topicsCharitiesRetail industryOxfamVoluntary sectornewsShareReuse this content

title: A world-first focus on long-term outcomes could transform UK government – or create new spending fights | Economic policy | The Guardian
description: Tucked away in John Healey’s budget is decision to ringfence preventative projects where future savings outweigh initial cost
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: Tucked away in John Healey’s budget is decision to ringfence preventative projects where future savings outweigh initial cost
Content: The chancellor, John Healey, pictured in the Commons with Andy Burnham after delivering the budget. The new measure is being billed as a way to tackle neglected long-term issue such as rough sleeping.Photograph: House of Commons/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe chancellor, John Healey, pictured in the Commons with Andy Burnham after delivering the budget. The new measure is being billed as a way to tackle neglected long-term issue such as rough sleeping.Photograph: House of Commons/ReutersEconomic policyAnalysisA world-first focus on long-term outcomes could transform UK government – or create new spending fightsPeter WalkerSenior political correspondentTucked away in John Healey’s budget is decision to ringfence preventative projects where future savings outweigh initial costSat 31 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 11.02 EDTShareIt merited the briefest of mentions in John Healey’s speech and just one paragraph in the 166-pagebudget document, but some believe it could revolutionise not just public spending but the very process of government itself: a new focus on long-term outcomes.The idea in the broad sense is very simple. Any spending deemed to be “preventative” – that is, the initial outlay will be more than made up for by future savings – will from now on be ringfenced, meaning it cannot be raided for more immediate needs.This might sound uncontroversial, but it follows many years of long-term spending being pillaged to plug day-to-day gaps, particularly so during and after the austerity measures of the 2010 coalition government, which slashed numerous prevention-based services, not least the Sure Start programme for families with young children.But now, starting from the upcoming spending review, which kicks off next year, projects that can be shown to bring down costs in the future will be protected via a new piece of jargon – a preventative departmental expenditure limit, or PDEL.“It could end up being quite a major change in how the government runs spending reviews, and the entire spending framework,” said Stuart Hoddinott, at the Institute for Government thinktank, which had called for such a system to be implemented. Officials in the Treasury agree, with one calling it an “important reform”.That is, however, about as straightforward as it gets. The budget document uses Andy Burnham’s new spending toprevent rough sleepingas an example of the sort of thing that would qualify. A few other areas would seem likely: for example, public health programmes to prevent future illness, and Sure Start-type early years schemes.View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham’s new rough-sleeping prevention plan is the type of project that would qualify to be protected under the PDEL.Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty ImagesBut beyond that, no one really knows what might or might not qualify for PDEL status. Departments say they are waiting for Treasury guidance, which has not yet been drawn up. “A lot depends on the definition,” Hoddinott said. “While it sounds simple, it becomes quite difficult when you think about how it will work in practice, as you could make any argument that almost all types of spending are preventative.”Government officials agree, with one making the point that, in theory, the Ministry of Defence could argue all its spending is preventive, given the very obvious costs to the country of fighting a war, let alone losing one.There is therefore the potential for a new variant of the endless spending-review tussles between departments and the Treasury, as ministers try to protect their pet projects from future plunder.But what is perhaps just as important is the symbolism. Some other governments around the world protect specific preventative budgets – public health, for example – but this is believed to be the first time one has introduced this as a blanket policy.Government officials are billing the decision as part of a wider focus under Burnham to try to deal with knotty and neglected issues that have longer-term costs and repercussions, including rough sleeping and adult social care.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOne said: “Too often government departments have ended up raiding these types of budgets to fund short-term measures. This is an attempt to combat that as part of a wider push to transform the way the state operates.”Those whose work revolves around trying to generate long-term benefits to the public are cautiously delighted.“This does feel like a really good thing,” said Greg Fell, Sheffield city council’s director of public health and the president of the Association of Directors of Public Health.“There are a lot of questions about how it will work. Is it about preventing future acute demand, or creating the conditions for communities to thrive? Those are different things and they require a different mindset and way of operating. And with some spending, it might take decades to realise the benefits.“But as a country we have never been very good at this sort of thing, so it’s up to all of us to make sure it works.”Explore more on these topicsEconomic policyBudget 2026John HealeyAndy BurnhamLabourBudgetTax and spendinganalysisShareReuse this content

title: UK police should not have let US force take over airbase trial, MoD documents show | UK news | The Guardian
description: According to documents obtained by the Guardian, officials accused Cambridgeshire force of breaching US-UK deal by handing over case of woman strangled by US pilot
Author: Rob Evans
Headline: According to documents obtained by the Guardian, officials accused Cambridgeshire force of breaching US-UK deal by handing over case of woman strangled by US pilot
Content: The Guardian uncovered a series of cases showing how US military personnel are not being brought to justice in British courts.Photograph: Kathy images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe Guardian uncovered a series of cases showing how US military personnel are not being brought to justice in British courts.Photograph: Kathy images/ShutterstockBase justiceUK newsUK police should not have let US force take over airbase trial, MoD documents showAccording to documents obtained by the Guardian, officials accused Cambridgeshire force of breaching US-UK deal by handing over case of woman strangled by US pilotRob Evans,Harry Davies,Louisa LoveluckandEmine SinmazSat 31 Oct 2026 09.30 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 09.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMinistry of Defence officials have privately accused a UK police force of wrongly handing over the investigation of an American fighter pilot who strangled a British woman to the US military, according to documents obtained by the Guardian.Cambridgeshire police allowed the US military police to quickly take control of the investigation into Capt Jacob Wulfson after he had been accused of sexuallyassaulting Sarah Steele in his Cambridge flat.The decision meant Wulfson was not tried in an English criminal court. Instead he wasprosecuted in a military tribunal on a US airbasein neighbouring Suffolk.View image in fullscreenAn all-male jury of Capt Jacob Wulfson’s fellow air force officers convicted him of strangling an intimate partner but acquitted him of sexual assault.Photograph: United States Air Forces CentralMinistry of Defence officials said the Cambridgeshire force should “absolutely” not have let theUS militarypolice take over the investigation in a clear breach of a long-established agreement with the US.The disclosure of the case by the Guardian in June provokedimmediate criticism from Downing Street, which said it was “deeply distressing” and “very concerning” that the UK authorities were not involved in prosecuting Wulfson.‘Degrading’: why did a US fighter pilot avoid British trial after strangling a woman in England?Read moreThe government to set up a high-level inquiry to examine how and why police forces have been transferring investigations into serious crimes to the US military police.The Ministry of Defence, which is responsible for handling the military relationship with the US, is one of the key departments taking part in the inquiry.A batch of documents, disclosed via the Freedom of Information Act, revealed the private views of MoD officials about the Steele case, which centres on an obscure agreementsigned bythe US and the UK decades ago.Under the terms of the agreement, police in the UK have the primary right to investigate alleged crimes byAmericans stationed in the country.The MoD officials made it clear the agreement was “pretty unambiguous” and only permitted the US militaryto acquire jurisdiction over investigationsin a “narrow set of circumstances”. These circumstances are: if the offences were committed while the Americans were on duty, or if they were committed against another member of their armed forces or property.In a memo written on 8 July, MoD officials based in Washington wrote: “The Steele case does not, on the surface, appear to meet the bar for a visiting force to be awarded jurisdiction.” In the agreement, the US military is formally known as a visiting force.Four days earlier, the MoD officials had referred to the Steele case in an email to colleagues, saying: “The decision-making on this specific case seemed at odds with what is very clear” in the agreement.Another MoD official agreed that “as best as we understand the facts, this should absolutely have been for the UK courts”.An unidentified Greater Manchester police officer wrote in an email to MoD officials on 6 July that Cambridgeshire police had “wrongly, in my view” handed over the Wulfson investigation to the US military.Cambridgeshire police said they were conducting a review of the case with what they called “the assistance of material provided” by US Air Force lawyers. The force said it “remained engaged with the victim”.“We are working with government, wider policing and criminal justice partners to ensure greater clarity of jurisdictional decision making,” they added.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHow the US bypasses British courts to try its military over crimes in the UKRead moreThe US military aims to prosecute as many of its personnel as possible within the boundaries of its agreement with the UK.The Americans often ask police in the UK if they can take over the prosecution of their military personnel – requests the police agree to, even when they have primary responsibility for investigating them.A series of cases uncovered this year by the Guardian have highlighted concerns that British victims are required to give evidence in US courts martial, an unfamiliar legal system that often does not afford the same protections as that of a court in the UK.Wulfson was off-duty when he assaulted Steele in his Cambridge flat in December 2023 after the pair talked on the Tinder dating app.Steele testified at Wulfson’s court martial, which was held on his airbase at Lakenheath, Suffolk in April, that her experiencewas “degrading and distressing”.The verdict and sentence were decided by an all-male jury of Wulfson’s fellow air force officers. All the lawyers were American. Steele was subjected to invasive and aggressive questioning by Wulfson’s lawyer.Wulfson was convicted of strangling an intimate partner but acquitted of sexual assault. He was dismissed from the US Air Force and confined to a military jail on Lakenheath for six months.Thecross-government inquiry, which includesofficials from the Home Office, Ministry of Justice and Foreign Office, is looking at how US military personnel are not being brought to justice in British courts.The inquiry, which also involves police chiefs, is scrutinising a series of cases uncovered by the Guardian this year.In each case, police handed over the investigations to US military police even though the American perpetrators were off-duty and the British victims had no connection to the armed forces.They were tried in US courts martial on American bases.Tyrion Davis allegedly rapedtwo women in Suffolk. He was convicted of one charge of sexual assault, but cleared of 10 further counts of sexual assault and abusive sexual contact.Hannes Marschalekallegedly exposed himself to a 16-year-old girland four young women in Littleport, Cambridgeshire. He negotiated a plea bargain at a court martial and admitted a charge of indecent conduct. He won an appeal in a US military court that quashed his conviction on technical grounds. This ruling is now being challenged.The US has more than 12,000US militarypersonnel in the UK, stationed in at least 15 bases and facilities. The two biggest bases are at Lakenheath and Mildenhall, in Suffolk. Significant numbers of American military personnel live in East Anglia.Explore more on these topicsUK newsBase justicePoliceUS militaryCrimeMilitaryMinistry of DefenceCambridgeshirenewsShareReuse this content

title: Abdul El-Sayed’s campaign disinvites Haley Stevens from events to limit ‘distractions’ | Michigan | The Guardian
description: A public spat has cast Democratic tensions in the spotlight as the close US Senate race draws to a head
Author: Roque Planas
Headline: A public spat has cast Democratic tensions in the spotlight as the close US Senate race draws to a head
Content: Democrats Abdul El-Sayed (left) and Haley Stevens have been feudingComposite: Robin Buckson/The Detroit News via APView image in fullscreenDemocrats Abdul El-Sayed (left) and Haley Stevens have been feudingComposite: Robin Buckson/The Detroit News via APMichiganAbdul El-Sayed’s campaign disinvites Haley Stevens from events to limit ‘distractions’A public spat has cast Democratic tensions in the spotlight as the close US Senate race draws to a headRoque PlanasSat 31 Oct 2026 19.58 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 20.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAbdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Michigan’s tightly fought US Senate race, has asked Democratic congresswoman Haley Stevensto stay awayfrom his campaign events.“I don’t want any distractions,” El-Sayed told reporters after a campaign rally,according to the New York Times. “It seems as though other folks are more interested in making this race about things that it’s not about.”The two had planned to appear together on Sunday at a church service in Detroit.The public rupture between the progressive El-Sayed and the more moderate Stevens, whom he defeated in a bitter primary, has cast Democratic tensions into the spotlight in one of the most consequential elections in the party’s campaign to retake control of the Senate.Stevens endorsed El-Sayed shortly after he won the primary election in August, and planned to campaign with him on Sunday.But Stevens had until now avoided appearing publicly with her former opponent, whom she has criticized publicly for weeks.
