Her fiance, Jason Turkish, hascampaigned on behalfof Republican candidate Mike Rogers.And just two days before they were scheduled to campaign together this weekend, Stevens demanded that El-Sayed denounce an outside group’s political ad that blamed higher prices on US support for Israel’s war in Gaza.“Congresswoman Stevens seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago,” El-Sayed shot back in a statement, which noted that the American Israel Public Affairs Committee spent heavily to defeat him in the primary.“Let’s all focus on the task at hand: that’s beating Mike Rogers, holding Trump accountable, and getting money out of politics, putting money in pockets, and passing Medicare for All,” the statement said.The open feuding worries manyDemocrats, who see the tight race as a must-win for the party to win back the Senate.“I have no idea what the hell Haley Stevens is doing,”Michiganstate senator Mallory McMorrow told CNN Friday. “This is a moment where we have to recognize the stakes. People are not talking about ads. They are not talking about Haley Stevens. They are talking about the price of gas and groceries.”Explore more on these topicsMichiganDemocratsUS politicsUS SenatenewsShareReuse this content

title: Virginia and DC sue to stop Trump’s arch as government looks to start construction | Washington DC | The Guardian
description: Legal challenges to Donald Trump’s proposed memorial arch are mounting even as its construction is imminent
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Legal challenges to Donald Trump’s proposed memorial arch are mounting even as its construction is imminent
Content: Donald Trump holds up a model for his proposed at the White House on 15 October 2025.Photograph: Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump holds up a model for his proposed at the White House on 15 October 2025.Photograph: Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP/Getty ImagesWashington DCVirginia and DC sue to stop Trump’s arch as government looks to start constructionLegal challenges to Donald Trump’s proposed memorial arch are mounting even as its construction is imminentAssociated PressSat 31 Oct 2026 13.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe legal challenges toDonald Trump’s proposed memorial arch are mounting, with theDistrict of ColumbiaandVirginiasuing in federal court on Saturday as the administration says construction could begin as early as next week.There are now three lawsuits calling for a halt to potential work on a monument that would rise 250ft (76 meters) on a patch of grass off the bridge that spans the Potomac River, connecting the city with the Arlington national cemetery. That would make the arch 100ft taller (30 meters) than the Statue of Liberty is from its base to the top of the torch.The US district judge Tanya Chutkan is already considering issuing an order to halt the project until the original lawsuit against theTrump administrationby three Vietnam war veterans and an architectural historian is resolved. She held a hearing on Friday but did not immediately act, though she said she would move expeditiously.Trump plans to begin DC golf course renovation in defiance of judge’s orderRead moreIn the latest lawsuit, two attorneys general, Brian Schwalb ofWashington DCand Jay Jones of Virginia, argue that “as soon as defendants break ground on this project, they will inflict irreparable harm on both the District and Virginia. The arch site sits at the center of a major traffic artery between the District and Virginia, in the monumental core of the capital, on an island that straddles the Potomac River. During the three-year period of construction, the arch project will inevitably snarl traffic between the jurisdictions, produce pollution and storm water runoff in the Potomac, interfere with emergency services, and pose numerous other challenges.”As the original plaintiffs have, they also are seeking a temporary restraining order that would slow the administration’s plans to move ahead imminently with construction.The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.The lawsuit raises concerns about how the traffic interruption would affect emergency responses in a region where joint operations are the norm, and where a January 2025 midair collision between a US military helicopter and passenger airliner killed 67 people.The Republican administration, in a recent court filing, said it had plans to seek final approval of the project, a Trump favorite, at Thursday’s meeting of the Capital National Planning Commission and possibly begin construction the same day, despite the two pending lawsuits.On Friday, the government submitted a 106-page plan for the arch that envisions a massive structure more than 12 stories high that includes a huge bronze statue of Lady Liberty with wings and carrying a torch with an eternal flame. The structure would include an observation deck with views to the east and west, an “occupied roof” and two mezzanines.Inside the arch are rooms for program space, offices, a staff lounge, circular staircases, multiple elevators and a “fire command center”. The project proposes significant traffic changes in the area, including rerouting traffic on nearby roads. Administration officials have said the arch also will have a national security function.Explore more on these topicsWashington DCVirginiaArchitectureInjunctionsDonald TrumpTrump administrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: More than 50m Americans cast ballots in early voting with three days to go before midterms | US midterm elections 2026 | The Guardian
description: Record number of early votes cast, with Democrats outnumbering Republicans in states which collect that information
Author: Oliver Milman
Headline: Record number of early votes cast, with Democrats outnumbering Republicans in states which collect that information
Content: A man in Fairfax, Virginia, casts an early vote on 31 October 2026.Photograph: Jim Lo Scalzo/EPAView image in fullscreenA man in Fairfax, Virginia, casts an early vote on 31 October 2026.Photograph: Jim Lo Scalzo/EPAUS midterm elections 2026More than 50m Americans cast ballots in early voting with three days to go before midtermsRecord number of early votes cast, with Democrats outnumbering Republicans in states which collect that informationOliver Milmanand agenciesSat 31 Oct 2026 12.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere has been a surge of early voting for the US midterm elections, with millions more Americans going to the polls compared with the last such election amid a series of tight contests that will determine control of Congress.More than 50.5m early votes have been cast across the US as of Saturday morning,according to an analysis by the University of Florida. This is already nearly 5m more votes than the total number of early votes made in the last midterm elections, in 2022.Voter enthusiasm for Tuesday’s election appears to be strongest among Democrats, with 10.7 million registered Democrats having voted so far, according to the states that collate such information, compared with 7.8 million registeredRepublicans.Affordability, AI and Iran: Americans on the key issues guiding their midterm votesRead moreThese party affiliations are not indicative of actual votes cast but polling has shown widespread unhappiness with the presidency of Donald Trump and unusually close races in states usually won comfortably by Republicans.Republicans are defending a 53-47 Senate majority in a midterm election in which the battleground map has expanded significantly, withDemocratsaiming to pull off victories in traditionally conservative-leaning states such as Texas, Alaska and even Kansas that could allow them to take control of the Senate.In Texas, a state central to Democratic ambitions, more than 7 million people have already voted early, University of Florida data shows. This is already 1.5 million more people than the number who voted early in the state during the 2022 midterms.In Harris county, which includes Houston, 862,700 people had voted as of Wednesday,an Associated Press analysis found, compared with 564,500 at the same point in 2022.The surge comes in a county that has reliably voted Democratic in recent elections, though by varying margins. In 2024, Kamala Harris defeated Trump there by nearly 6% in the presidential contest, while Democratic Senate candidate Colin Allred carried the county by roughly 11% over the Republican incumbent senator Ted Cruz.This year, the state’s Republican attorney general, Ken Paxton, faces Democrat James Talarico ina closely watched Senate race, while the Republican governor, Greg Abbott, is seeking re-election against Democrat Gina Hinojosa.Hundreds of millions of dollars have poured into the Senate race as Republicans fight to defend a state where Democrats have not won a statewide election in more than three decades. Trumpvisited Texasearlier this week, his third trip there in a month.In other close-fought Senate races, early voting has also increased in these midterms, according to the AP. In South Carolina, which Trump won by nearly 18% in the 2024 president election, early voting is up 83% compared with the 2022 midterms.In Kansas, where another unusually tight Senate battle is under way in a normally reliable Republican state, early voting is up 34%, while in Maine early voting is up 44%. In Michigan, the site of another key Senate race, early voting is up 32%.The midterms will decide the composition of the US House of Representatives and Senate for the final two years of Trump’s second term, with the rising costs of food, gasoline and other essentials, as well as the Iran war and concern over government corruption, forming the backdrop to the voting.Trump, weighed down by deep unpopularity among voters, has sought to boost struggling Republican candidates with rallies held across various previously safe states. This effort has included the US president commenting repeatedly on the physical appearance of candidates and dismissing alarm over rising gasoline costs as secondary to the profits of fossil fuel companies.Trump hinted at the toil of this effort at a rally in Florida on Friday night. “I thought this was it,” he said. “I thought I could relax. Twenty-eight days of this crap in a row is a lot. It’s a lot.”Explore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026DemocratsRepublicansUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ads accusing Republican candidates of protecting Epstein fill airwaves in final midterm push | US midterm elections 2026 | The Guardian
description: But select Democrats, too, are being accused of having ties to the late sex offender as country prepares to vote
Author: Ariana Baio
Headline: But select Democrats, too, are being accused of having ties to the late sex offender as country prepares to vote
Content: Politicians of all stripes appear eager to associate their opponents with the late sex offender.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenPoliticians of all stripes appear eager to associate their opponents with the late sex offender.Photograph: ReutersUS midterm elections 2026Ads accusing Republican candidates of protecting Epstein fill airwaves in final midterm pushBut select Democrats, too, are being accused of having ties to the late sex offender as country prepares to voteAriana BaioSat 31 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 11.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn races across the country, Democratic candidates or groups that support them have released ads accusingRepublicansof protecting pedophiles by voting against legislation to release files related toJeffrey Epstein.The ads appear intended toevoke an emotional responseby accusing candidates of “protecting” Epstein, a notorious pedophile accused of running a sex-trafficking ring involving minors.Ananalysis from CNNfound that candidates and outside groups have spent more than $35m on Epstein-related ads. Anotherfrom the Washington Postfound that Democrats spent more than $40m on Epstein-related ads across six key Senate races.The Epstein files are a sledgehammer for the US midterms | Katie PhangRead moreIn Colorado,ads targeting Republican Jeff Cranknote that the lawmaker voted against releasing the Epstein files.In one, the family members of Virginia Giuffre, a woman who survived abuse at the hands of Epstein and died by suicide last year, claim Crank “covered up Epstein’s crimes to protect Donald Trump”.Ashley Hinson, a Senate candidate in Iowa,was accusedof voting to “protect her donors” by refusing to vote to release the Epstein files.“This week I had to explain to my boys, ‘No, Mom does not protect pedophiles,’” Hinsonsaid in a campaign adresponding to attacks over the Epstein files.Anad targeting Mike Collins, the Republican running for a Georgia Senate seat, says “Mike Collins voted against releasing the Epstein files even after he knew Epstein’s sex-trafficking operation exploited 14-year-old girls for sex”.Florida Republican Jimmy Patronisfaced an attackfrom his Democratic opponent, claiming he called investigating Epstein “a waste of his time”.A spokesperson for Crank’s campaign accused the Epstein-related ad of being “intentionally vague”, in a statement tothe Washington Post,because his position was that he would vote against the file’s release until he could be confident that victim information was properly redacted. The campaign also said it was “unfortunate” that his opponent, Jessica Killin, was “preying on a grieving family with the help of the Washington Democrats”.Crank’s staff invited and met with Giuffre’s family, though Crank himself did not meet with them in person, theNew York Times reported.Crank’s campaign also said it offered to meet with Epstein victims before the vote on the legislation.Last year, Democrats and a select few HouseRepublicanstried to force a vote on the Epstein files through a discharge petition – a procedure used in Congress to bypass the traditional steps of legislation and force a vote on the House floor.Donald Trump,who knew Epstein in the 1990sand early 2000s, opposed the discharge petition for the files,reversing his campaign promiseto increase government transparency. House Republicans largely aligned themselves with him, prompting anger from high-profile Trump voters.Eventually, under pressure from allies, Trump supported the legislation, giving Republican lawmakers the go-ahead to vote for it. All but one House Republican voted for the Epstein Files Transparency Act.Many of the ads omit the fact that nearly every House Republican voted to release the Epstein files when the Epstein Files Transparency Act came to the floor, although at that point Trump had agreed to sign the legislation and release the files. Instead, the ads refer to Republicans opposing early attempts to force the legislation to the floor.Republicans have pointed to this fact when disputing the attack ads.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Of course I voted to release the Epstein files,” Hinson said in a direct-to-camera ad, accusing her opponent, Josh Turek, of lying. While Hinson voted for the final Epstein Files Transparency Act, she did not sign on to the discharge petition.Patronis, meanwhile, never called the investigation a “waste of time”, buttold a local radio stationthat while he had “no problem getting everything all released”, the issue was a “massive energy and time suck at the end of the day”.Melissa Stone, a spokesperson for Patronis’s campaign, highlighted his work with Trump to obtain disaster funding after Hurricane Isaias and said his opponent, Gay Valimont, was “still talking about a dead pedophile in a sad web video than helping the people of [the first congressional district] recover.”Some Republicans and groups supporting the GOP have sought to flip the script, accusingDemocratsof taking money from donors who had ties to Epstein.During a Georgia Senate debate, Collins accused his opponent, Jon Ossoff, of accepting campaign donations from Reid Hoffman, a tech billionaire who had ties to Epstein. Hoffman hassaidhe only knew Epstein through fundraising relationships and regrets it.“You can claim to fight against the Epstein class, but I’m going to tell you, this call is coming from inside the house and the Epstein class is on stage right now and it’s you,”Collins said.In New Mexico’s gubernatorial race, an outside groupreleased an adaccusing Democratic candidate Deb Haaland of accepting a ride on Epstein’s private jet and taking “tens of thousands of dollars from Epstein businesses” and then “asking for more”.Haaland did not fly on Epstein’s jet, but did take a flight booked by one of Epstein’s companies in 2014.Haaland has saidshe was unaware the chartered flight was owned by an Epstein-owned company.Explore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026Jeffrey EpsteinRepublicansDemocratsUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Maurene Comey ruling offers hope of check on Trump’s assault on rule of law | US news | The Guardian
description: Legal experts welcome judge’s rejection of firing of James Comey’s daughter prosecutor but warn an appeal is likely
Author: Victoria Bekiempis
Headline: Legal experts welcome judge’s rejection of firing of James Comey’s daughter prosecutor but warn an appeal is likely
Content: Maurene Comey pictured in 2019 while prosecuting the case against Jeffrey Epstein.Photograph: Peter Foley/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMaurene Comey pictured in 2019 while prosecuting the case against Jeffrey Epstein.Photograph: Peter Foley/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesUS newsAnalysisMaurene Comey ruling offers hope of check on Trump’s assault on rule of lawVictoria Bekiempisin New YorkLegal experts welcome judge’s rejection of firing of James Comey’s daughter prosecutor but warn an appeal is likelySat 31 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 11.02 EDTShareA recent legal ruling against an effort to fire the star-prosecutor daughter of a former FBI chief targeted by Donald Trump could send a strong message about politicized firings – and influence other judges weighing similar cases, legal veterans said.Judge Jesse Furman ruled this week that the Department of Justice’s firing of assistant US attorney Maurene Comey without cause was unlawful. Comey, the daughter of former FBI director James Comey, successfully litigated numerous high-profile cases during her tenure at the southern district of New York, including guilty verdicts against Ghislaine Maxwell and Sean “Diddy” Combs.“It looks as if Judge Furman has completely vindicated her and rejected just about all of the arguments made by the government,” said Carl Tobias, Williams chair at the University of Richmond School of Law. “And so it’s really important to have this because of the way she was essentially summarily fired, and so it sets a valuable precedent.”Maurene Comey was illegally fired as federal prosecutor, judge rulesRead moreThe Department of Justice, which fired her without cause, had argued thatarticle II of the US constitution, which defines presidential power, imbued Trump and his attorney general with a right to fire line prosecutors – who are not political appointees.But Furman this week rejected the department’s position, ruling Comey’s firing was not greenlighted under any law and in fact, violated the Civil Service Reform Act.View image in fullscreenMaurene Comey, then an assistant US attorney, points at Ghislaine Maxwell, far left, while she presents the rebuttal for the prosecution during Maxwell’s sex-trafficking trial in New York in 2021.Photograph: Elizabeth Williams/APThe justice department’s claim “flies in the face of nearly two centuries of Supreme Court precedent”, Furman said. “It is also without merit. Indeed, to accept Defendants’ argument would be to unsettle the very equilibrium established by this Nation’s constitutional system.”For legal observers, Furman’s decision is cause for optimism – even if optimism of the cautious sort – amid the Trump administration’s alleged repeated attacks on the rule of law. While one judicial opinion does not a panacea make, they said, such a ruling can send a strong message and be considered by other judges weighing similar cases.“One thing I would caution is that it’s very clear the government will appeal this,” Tobias said. The justice department would do this via the second circuit court of appeals.“I expect that Furman would be affirmed by that court, and then I assume the administration would then appeal to the US supreme court,” he added.Then, it would up to the US supreme court to decide whether they even want to hear the case – and if they decline, the lower appeals court decision would stand.“You are seeing the courts step up and stop and prevent the administration when they are violating the rule of law,” said Neama Rahmani, founder of West Coast Trial Lawyers and a former federal prosecutor. Just this Monday, Los Angeles federal court judge David CarterrejectedTrump’s attempt to set aside 20,000 ballots in California, Rahmani noted.“Whether it’s the supreme court and birthright citizenship, or even individual cases like this, there have been limited, I would say, rulings by the court that have limited what President Trump can do.”Like Tobias, Rahmani said the justice department can fight federal district and appeals court decisions. And, this kind of case does contain legal issues that might pique the supreme court’s interest – especially if different federal appeals courts were to reach different conclusions.If the supreme court did decide to hear arguments on Comey’s case, it would by no means guarantee a check on Trump’s power.“There are a lot of the justices on the supreme court that really don’t believe there should be much of any restrictions on what the president can do,” Rahmani said. “So this is far from the silver bullet.”For now, though, Furman’s decision can prove influential.“The decision can be used by other folks who do believe that they were terminated lawfully,” Rahmani said, adding, “It is not binding at all, but it’s certainly something that judges look to with similar or exact same facts.”Elizabeth Wolstein, a partner at Schlam Stone & Dolan LLP and former Manhattan federal prosecutor in the civil division, said that a judge’s decision in one case could potentially affect how other judges’ weigh similar issues.“It doesn’t have any binding effect on another judge, even in the same district, as opposed to how a second circuit or US supreme court case would be binding,” Wolstein said. But, “if it’s well reasoned and persuasive, it is definitely going to be persuasive to another judge faced with a similar issue.”Comey filed suit over her ouster in September 2025. Comey said she neither received notice nor explanation of her firing. Instead, Comey on 16 July 2025 got a letter that stated “your employment with the Department of Justice is hereby terminated, and you are removed from federal service effective immediately.”When Comey asked the then Manhattan US attorney, Jay Clayton, about this notice, he allegedly said “all I can say is it came from Washington. I can’t tell you anything else,” per court papers.The Department of Justice has said Comey’s firing was directed by the former US attorney general Pam Bondi and subsequently “ratified” by her successor, Todd Blanche.Comey’s lawyers and critics of the US president have claimed that she was fired because her father is longtime Trump foe James Comey. Trump’s justice department has repeatedly tried prosecuting James Comey, this week making public its third case against him; one prior proceeding was dismissed, another is pending.The department had defended the idea that someone’s familial relations could be considered in termination proceedings.Maurene Comey’s legal team viewed Furman’s ruling as a positive development in protecting the rule of law. Comey’s attorneys are Ellen Blain, Nicole Gueron and Deepa Vanamali at Clarick Gueron Reisbaum, as well as Margaret Donovan at Koskoff Koskoff & Bieder.“The Court’s decision is a complete rejection of this administration’s sweeping claim to unchecked executive power, and it demonstrates that our constitutional system of checks and balances is alive and well,” the team said in a statement.The justice department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Furman’s decision or claims of politically driven firings. In a statement, the White House rejected allegations that Trump’s justice department is trying to punish opponents.“Unlike Joe Biden, President Trump has not weaponized the Department of Justice against his political foes. The Department is focused on restoring law and order and keeping Americans safe,” Lauren Bis, a White House spokesperson, said in a statement. “The results speak for themselves: Under President Trump, we have seen thelargest decrease in violent crimein American history.”Explore more on these topicsUS newsTrump administrationUS justice systemanalysisShareReuse this content

title: The staggering $446m Elon Musk has spent on the US midterms – visualized | US midterm elections 2026 | The Guardian
description: The tech mogul’s midterm donations backing Republicans have made him the largest single-cycle political donor in modern US history
Author: Nick Robins-Early
Headline: The tech mogul’s midterm donations backing Republicans have made him the largest single-cycle political donor in modern US history
Content: LoadingUS midterm elections 2026The staggering $446m Elon Musk has spent on the US midterms – visualizedThe tech mogul’s midterm donations backing Republicans have made him the largest single-cycle political donor in modern US historyNick Robins-Early,Andrew Witherspoon,Will Craft, Alvaro Dominguez, andDaniel WolfeSat 31 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 06.01 EDTShareElon Musk has poured so much money into US politics this midterms election cycle that his donations could fund half a dozen SpaceX rocket launches or buy thousands of Tesla Cybertrucks. At theTesla Diner in Los Angeles, Musk could order more than 31.9m cheeseburgers with the money he has spent on the midterms.Musk, the world’s richest person, has funnelled at least $445.77m into Republican-aligned political action committees (Pacs) and groups since last year, according to US Federal Election Commission data as of 29 October. The contributions have made him the Republicans’ most prominent financial backer and the largest single-cycle political donor in modern US history.Musk’s spending is a staggering example of the SpaceX and Tesla CEO’s political influence, as he seeks to help Donald Trump’s administration retain control of Congress in the upcoming midterm elections, though currentpolls predict Democratsachieving a majority. The contributions are at a scale that is difficult to fathom and dwarf efforts from big name megadonors like George Soros or Michael Bloomberg, setting a new precedent for how the rich and powerful attempt to shape politics.a diagram shows Elon Musk’s $446m flowing to midterms campaigns across US statesView image in fullscreenPhotograph: The GuardianOnly last year, Musk claimed he would step away from making large scale political donations after putting nearly $300m towards Trump’s 2024 presidential election campaign. FEC data since then shows he has not only leaned back into financing campaigns, but that his spending has dramatically ramped up as election day approaches, increasing by about $200m in the final two months of campaigning.Musk’s money has primarily flowed into several Republican-alignedSuper Pacs, with his largest contribution of $216m going intohis own America Pac. The Pac has targeted 43 House and Senate races across the US, blanketting voters with television commercials, digital ads, text messages and mailers.America Pac made 839 independent expenditures in House races and 623 in Senate races in 17 states across the country.The spending varies greatly depending on the state, however, with campaigns in battlegrounds such as Michigan and Arizona receiving more of the Pac’s support.Musk’s Pac has spent the most in his home state of Texas, where a closely fought Senate contest between Democratic candidate James Talarico and RepublicanKen Paxtonhas turned into the most expensive race of the midterms. America Pac has overall poured more than $33m into efforts toelect Paxton, while Musk also made a $168m contribution to the Senate Leadership Fund which supports the Paxton campaign.A large portion of America Pac’s output focuses on attack ads against Democratic candidates such as Talarico, often accusing them of being radical socialists or targeting them over supporting transgender rights. The Pac has spent $28m on anti-Talarico content, including between $300,000 and 350,000 in October on a single Google ad targeting the Texas Senate candidate.“James Talarico supports parents being charged with child abuse if they do not support transitioning their children,” stated the ad, which was shown more than 10m times over an eight day period.Musk has also reposted America Pac’s content to his more than 200m followers on X, the social media platform he owns. One of Musk’s posts in October amplified an America Pac attack ad and claimed: “Talarico wants to trans your kids and destroy the border.”The nearly $446mthat Musk has donated this election cycle far exceeds his contributions in the 2024 presidential race, when the tech mogul also held rallies and appeared on stage next to Trump during the campaign. While Musk has been a less visible presence in the midterms, potentially reflecting theUS public’s dislike of him, behind the scenes he has greatly upped his financial support for Republicans.Musk’s spending far outpaces all other donors in the elections, including fellow tech and finance moguls like Marc Andreessen, who also started his own Super Pac. Musk has put more money into this election cycle than what every top Silicon Valley donor, including himself, spent on the 2024 presidential election combined.Area circle chart shows Elon Musk’s 2026 political contributions surpass top tech donors, including himself, from the 2024 general election.View image in fullscreenThe stakes of the midterm elections are potentially high for Musk, who has closely aligned himself with the Trump administration and benefited from its lax policies toward regulating tech and artificial intelligence. SpaceX has also intertwined itself into the government more extensively, landing lucrative contracts this year for Trump’s missile defense program and the use of Musk’s Grok AI chatbot in the Pentagon.Despite the immense and unprecedented scale of Musk’s political spending, his contributions this election are still only a tiny fraction of the centibillionaire’s overall assets.A closing line to the story. It says: Musk’s net worth is hovering around $924bn —meaning that his $445.8m in political donations account for less than 0.05% of his total wealth. Alongside it is a cutout of Elon Musk sitting on a pile of cash.View image in fullscreenExplore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026US politicsElon MuskUS political financingThe super-richRepublicansSuper PacsShare

title: Canelo Álvarez wins back world title as Houthi attacks cast shadow over Riyadh | Boxing | The Guardian
description: Canelo Álvarez regained the WBC super-middleweight title with a unanimous-decision win over Christian Mbilli in Riyadh despite regional security concerns
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Canelo Álvarez regained the WBC super-middleweight title with a unanimous-decision win over Christian Mbilli in Riyadh despite regional security concerns
Content: Canelo Álvarez (right) exchanges punches with Christian Mbilli during their WBC super-middleweight title fight in Riyadh early on Sunday.Photograph: Fayez Nureldine/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCanelo Álvarez (right) exchanges punches with Christian Mbilli during their WBC super-middleweight title fight in Riyadh early on Sunday.Photograph: Fayez Nureldine/AFP/Getty ImagesBoxingCanelo Álvarez wins back world title as Houthi attacks cast shadow over RiyadhMexican star wins unanimous decision over MbilliÁlvarez, 36, regains WBC title after Crawford defeatRead Bryan Armen Graham’s round-by-round reportGuardian sportand agenciesSat 31 Oct 2026 19.26 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 19.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMexico’s Saúl “Canelo” Álvarez reclaimed the WBC super-middleweight title with a unanimous-decision victory over the previously unbeaten Christian Mbilli in Riyadh on Saturday night.The fight went ahead at Kingdom Arena despite a week of heightened security concerns in the Saudi capital, where the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted missiles and drones launched by Iran-aligned Houthi forces. Several events in the kingdom were cancelled or postponed, including the Six Kings Slam tennis exhibition.Canelo Álvarez defeats Christian Mbilli for WBC super-middleweight championship – live reactionRead moreÁlvarez, 36, fighting for the first time in more than a year, relied on his trademark counter-punching and precise body shots to overcome the aggressive French champion and re-establish himself among boxing’s elite.The judges scored the contest 115-112, 116-111 and 117-110 in favor of the Mexican. (The Guardianhad it 117-110.)“It’s something unbelievable. It feels like my first title. Now, after 21 years as a professional, 16 years ago I won my first title. Now I won that title again. I’m so proud of my team,” ‌Canelo said in English.“I love boxing. That’s why I’m here, because I still love boxing and I enjoy it a lot.”Mbilli, who entered the fight with a record of 29 wins and one draw, sought to unsettle Álvarez with relentless pressure and a higher volume of punches. But the challenger landed the cleaner blows, including a sharp uppercut that staggered Mbilli in the seventh round.View image in fullscreenÁlvarez evades a right hand from Mbilli during Saturday’s fight.Photograph: Fayez Nureldine/AFP/Getty ImagesThe victory marked a significant comeback for Álvarez, who suffered only the third defeat of his professional career when Terence Crawfordoutpointed him by unanimous decisionin September 2025.That losscost Álvarez his undisputed super-middleweight crown, ending his reign as holder of the division’s four major titles.The contest took place three weeks aftera missile strike on King Khalid International Airportin Riyadh killed at least 12 people and wounded more than 300. A second projectile struck a passenger terminal the following day, according to the Saudi-led military coalition, while several international airlines suspended flights to the kingdom amid the mounting threat to civilian aviation.Turki al-Sheikh, the chairman of Saudi Arabia’s General Entertainment Authority and one of boxing’s most influential power brokers, saidearlier this monththat Álvarez had personally assured him he would go ahead with the fight regardless of the security situation. “Canelo reached out and told me he’ll still fight in Riyadh this October, no matter what happens,” Al-Sheikh wrote on social media. “He fears nothing.”View image in fullscreenÁlvarez celebrates after Saturday’s win in Riyadh.Photograph: Fayez Nureldine/AFP/Getty ImagesThe escalation threatened Saudi Arabia’s ambitions to establish itself as a global destination for major sporting events. The kingdom has become a dominant force in professional boxing under Al-Sheikh, using its considerable financial resources to attract some of the sport’s biggest names, even as its expanding sporting footprint has drawn scrutiny over its human rights record and accusations of sportswashing.Álvarez made a brief, apparently oblique reference to the circumstances surrounding the fight during his post-fight remarks, thanking family members who were watching from afar rather than ringside.“I also want to thank my family, who are watching me from afar today for the first time,” he said in Spanish. “My siblings, my parents, my daughters, my son, and my wife – who also couldn’t make it due to certain circumstances.”Álvarez did not elaborate on those circumstances or explicitly link their absence to the security situation.Mbilli, 31, had been elevated to full WBC champion followingCrawford’s departure from the division, having previously held the interim title.The Cameroon-born boxer fought to a split draw against Lester Martínez on the undercard of the Álvarez-Crawford showdown, ending a run of 29 consecutive professional victories.Saturday’s result improved Álvarez’s record to 64 wins, three defeats and two draws and handed Mbilli the first loss of his professional career.Explore more on these topicsBoxingCanelo ÁlvarezMexicoSaudi Arabia and sportTurki al-SheikhTerence CrawfordShareReuse this content

title: Breeders’ Cup 2026, day two: Moore’s ‘one bullet’ hits the target in Turf – as it happened | Breeders' Cup | The Guardian
description: Benvenuto Cellini and Ryan Moore quickened clear to win the $5m Breeders’ Cup Turf
Author: Greg Wood
Headline: Benvenuto Cellini and Ryan Moore quickened clear to win the $5m Breeders’ Cup Turf
Content: 3h ago18.53 EDTMOORE'S "ONE BULLET" HITS THE TARGET IN BREEDERS' CUP TURFA series of strongly-fancied European-trained runners failed to deliver at the Breeders’ Cup meeting at Keeneland on Saturday but the visitors finally notched a victory asBenvenuto CelliniandRyan Moorequickened clear to win the $5m Turf.Moore was initially expected to rideDiamond Necklace,a stable companion of the winner at the Aidan O’Brien yard, in Saturday’s race, but switched toBenvenuto Celliniafter he drew an inside stall.It proved to be an inspired decision, and Moore found a charmed path to the lead from a position on the inside rail turning in, hitting the front well inside the final furlong on the way to a three-quarter length success.The win was Aidan O’Brien’s 28thvictory atGroup OneorGrade Onelevel in 2026, equalling his own record, which was set in 2017. The International meeting in Hong Kong in December will offer him a chance to set a new mark.“Ryan was calm and relaxed on him and let it happen,” O’Brien said. “He was brilliant on him. He did it again, he had to come out and come round. Time after time he produces on the day. He accepted early he let them go, but he had one bullet to fire which he executed perfectly.”Benvenuto Celliniis a possible runner in Hong Kong, and will stay in training as a four-year-old next season.Sovereignty, the 2025 Kentucky Derby winner, was a convincing winner of the most valuable race on the card, the $7mClassic, with Japan’s Forever Young, successful in the race last year, only fifth.Bill Mott’s four-year-old was a firstClassicwinner for the Godolphin racing and breeding operation, having also supplied Godolphin’s first win in the Kentucky Derby in 2025.Earlier on the card, several big names from the European circuit came up short, including Charlie Appleby’sNotable Speech, who finished fast into second place behindDeterministicin his attempt to win theMilefor the second year running.Blue Bolt, a multiple Group One winner this year, and O’Brien’s fillyPrecise, the Irish 1,000 Guineas winner, both finished unplaced behindKathynmarissain theFilly & Mare Turf,while Wesley Ward’sBacio,who is trained next to the track, comfortably beat Donnacha O’Brien’sComanche Brave,the July Cup winner, in theTurf Sprint.Share

title: Lewis Hamilton storms to his first Ferrari pole at F1 Mexican GP with Antonelli fourth | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: Lewis Hamilton took pole position at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez, his first for Ferrari, while Kimi Antonelli is well placed as he nears title confirmation
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Lewis Hamilton took pole position at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez, his first for Ferrari, while Kimi Antonelli is well placed as he nears title confirmation
Content: Lewis Hamilton competes during qualifying at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez.Photograph: Simon Galloway/LAT ImagesView image in fullscreenLewis Hamilton competes during qualifying at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez.Photograph: Simon Galloway/LAT ImagesFormula One 2026Lewis Hamilton storms to his first Ferrari pole at F1 Mexican GP with Antonelli fourthGeorge Russell second on grid after qualifyingAntonelli well placed as he nears title confirmationGiles Richardsat the Autódromo Hermanos RodríguezSat 31 Oct 2026 19.03 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 20.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEven as Formula One’s young gunKimi Antonelliremains on course to claim his first world championship on Sunday it was the veteran, seven-time champion Lewis Hamilton who gave a salutary reminder that there is very much fight left in the old dog yet as he claimed a spectacular pole position for the Mexico City Grand Prix.Hamilton delivered a superb lap for Ferrari to secure his first pole for the team and just beat Mercedes’ George Russell into second. World championin waiting Antonelli was in fourth placebut remains in position to close out the title on Sunday, although Hamilton and Russell, who must win the race to have any hope of keeping the fight alive, have at least locked out the front row.Mexican Grand Prix qualifying: Lewis Hamilton takes pole – liveRead moreIt was clearly a hugely emotional moment for Hamilton at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez to finally nail the top spot forFerrariin his second season with the team, with the 41-year-old’s 105th pole also his first since 2023.“Thank you so much, that’s been such a long time coming,” he said. “That feels good. I’m lost for words. My first pole with Ferrari. 105 poles, I like that number.“Where there’s a will, there’s a way. It’s all in the mind. For sure, you might feel aches and pains, luckily I don’t, I do all those different things to keep myself young and fit. But I love what I do, and love is not gone.”The title is all but in Antonelli’s hands but the day belonged assuredly to Hamilton who brought the crowd to their feet and earned a rapturous reception with an exemplary lap against very tough competition. His advantage over Russell was ultimately just nine-thousandths of a second.It is an extraordinary feat for Hamilton, coming after hisdebut win for Ferrari in Barcelonaand having endured a very difficult opening season with the team, showing that he has lost none of his edge when he has the right machinery beneath him.View image in fullscreenLewis Hamilton enjoys the acclaim after taking pole in Mexico.Photograph: DPPI/ShutterstockHis sheer joy in the moment was unsurprising given it had been such a long wait for the British driver. The pole is Hamilton’s first since the Hungarian GP in 2023 and Ferrari’s first since Budapest last year. It is only his second in Mexico, having last taken the top spot a decade ago in 2016.He will, of course, be looking for the win but that alone would not be enough to deny Antonelli the crown. The Italian is 123 points ahead of Russell and 124 in front of Hamilton. If he is 100 ahead after the Mexican GP he will take the title. Russell or Hamilton have to win the race to stay in the fight but even should one of them do so, Antonelli will still be champion if he finishes in ninth place or higher.Anything less than a win for Russell or Hamilton and Antonelli would still be champion even if he failed to finish. Having secured fourth place on the grid, just staying out of trouble would surely be enough for the Italian. If he seals it on Sunday he will become F1’s youngest world champion at just 20 years old and the first Italian to claim the crown since Alberto Ascari in 1953.View image in fullscreenKimi Antonelli only needs to finish ninth to clinch the title.Photograph: Florent Gooden/DPPI/ShutterstockCharles Leclerc was third for Ferrari and Max Verstappen in fourth on track but has a one-place grid penalty for a clash with Liam Lawson in practice on Friday. The New Zealander who finished in eighth also has a one-place penalty. Lando Norris was in sixth for McLaren.For the opening runs in Q3 it was close at the front of the field with no driver holding a clear advantage. The Ferraris set the pace on the opening salvoes, with Leclerc setting a very strong time of 1min 16.647sec. The two Mercedes could not match him, with Antonelli having to really work the car and managing only seventh on his opening run but Norris came close, one-tenth back. Verstappen, however, was showing great pace and came within four-hundredths of a second of Leclerc.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFor the final laps Russell found his best form of the weekend to take the top spot only for Hamilton to pip him. Leclerc could not better his teammate, while Antonelli followed them through – he improved but could not match the leaders. Verstappen had a minor lockup in the final sector, costing him his shot and with it the British driver had sealed the place.Oscar Piastri was knocked out unusually early for McLaren. Failing to make it out of Q2, he finished in 13th complaining of a lack of rear grip.Esteban Ocon, meanwhile, has denied reports of a violent altercation with his team after the Frenchman was dropped by Haas from competing in the race weekend. Haas made the shock announcement on Saturday morning that Ocon had been replaced for the rest of the weekend by Ryo Hirakawa, but offered no explanation as to why. The 32-year-old Japanese driver, who has won two World Endurance Championships and the Le Mans 24 Hours, will make his F1 race debut on Sunday.View image in fullscreenHaas staff remove the name and number of Esteban Ocon from the garage after he was dropped from competing in the race weekend.Photograph: Bryn Lennon/Formula 1/Getty ImagesOcon is set to be replaced next season by the Ferrari junior Rafael Câmara and his sudden removal from competition in Mexico suggests relations between him and the team have broken down. He had an angry exchange with his race engineer Laura Müller during FP2 on Friday, after which he returned to the Haas garage without removing his helmet.Reports followed that a disagreement between Ocon and team staff had surfaced. While Ocon admits the disagreement, he rubbished suggestions that the exchange of views turned physical.“Following the recent decision from Haas F1 Team confirming that I will not be participating in this weekend’s Mexico City Grand Prix, I wish to formally address some media reports and speculation surrounding the situation,” a statement from Ocon read. “Last night, a difference in viewpoints led to a discussion with the parties involved. Whilst I acknowledge that this took place, I categorically reject any reports or allegations suggesting that any form of physical violence was used to resolve any differences of any nature.“I strongly condemn violence in all its forms and firmly believe that disagreements should always be handled with professionalism, respect, and mutual understanding. I kindly ask that speculation be avoided while the matter is being addressed. Further updates will be communicated in due course.”Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Lewis HamiltonFormula OneKimi AntonelliFerrariMercedes GPMotor sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Spurs see off Crystal Palace after Mateta’s early red to pile pressure on Sage | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Tottenham moved into the top half of the Premier League table after a comfortable 2-0 win over strugglers Crystal Palace
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: Tottenham moved into the top half of the Premier League table after a comfortable 2-0 win over strugglers Crystal Palace
Content: Jan Paul van Hecke scored Tottenham’s second goal to earn their third Premier League win in a row.Photograph: John Sibley/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenJan Paul van Hecke scored Tottenham’s second goal to earn their third Premier League win in a row.Photograph: John Sibley/Action Images/ReutersPremier LeagueSpurs see off Crystal Palace after Mateta’s early red to pile pressure on SageEd Aaronsat Tottenham Hotspur StadiumSat 31 Oct 2026 15.42 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 18.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFortune is not favouring Pierre Sage. Just when theCrystal Palacemanager needed a positive result, Jean-Philippe Mateta’s early red card condemned his side to a third straight defeat in the league, leaving their manager’s position hanging by a thread.Goals from Archie Gray and Jan Paul van Hecke ensured that Tottenham recorded a third successive victory for the first time in 616 days as they moved into the top half of the table. To put that into context, Spurs have had three full-time managers since then, so it was no wonder that Roberto De Zerbi looked so pleased at full time.Tottenham v Crystal Palace: Premier League – liveRead moreBy contrast, Sage’s future is in doubt, given that there was an expectation he could be sacked if they lost this game. While Mateta’s reckless red card did him no favours and Palace managed to stay in the game until Van Hecke’s innovative finish 17 minutes from full time, they now find themselves in the bottom three. Only the chair, Steve Parish, will decide his fate with Liverpool up next at home before the international break. Sean Dyche and Thomas Frank are waiting in the wings.“I told the players I want to be the first on pitch on Monday. I will do the best session I can. Now I have the rage to train more, because the game I saw this evening is not in line with my conviction,” said a defiant Sage. “It’s not me to decide this thing, but if I have one hour, I will give my best during one hour, and if I have 10 years, I will give my best during 10 years. I am responsible for the situation, and I am the guy who will find the solution for the situation.”View image in fullscreenJan Paul van Hecke uses his head to double Spurs’ lead.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PAHaving won only twice at home in the league all year, Tottenham’s supporters had reason to be optimistic after successive victories over Coventry and Chelsea. But while De Zerbi used his programme notes to urge his players not to get complacent, there is no mistaking the signs of momentum, and the Italian singled out the performance of his compatriot – £100m summer signing Sandro Tonali – in midfield. “We played with two players more,” said De Zerbi. “We can’t forget where we were before the last international break. But now we are playing as a team.”Tottenham’s cause was certainly aided when Mateta was sent off after only 13 minutes. The France striker was never going to get to the ball before Micky van de Ven as he passed it back to Antonin Kinsky, and Mateta’s studs caught the Tottenham defender on the back of his heel. The referee, Michael Oliver, initially showed a yellow card but the outcome was inevitable when the VAR directed him upstairs. Some of the home supporters gasped when they saw a slow-motion replay on the giant screens, although that made it look much worse.View image in fullscreenJean-Philippe Mateta’s reckless challenge on Micky van de Ven (left) resulted in a red card for the Crystal Palace player.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PASage shook his head as Mateta trudged down the tunnel. Not for the first time this season, after Axel Disasi’s red card against Ipswich last month, Palace found themselves down to 10 men with most of the game still to play. They kept Tottenham at bay for a while but played a part in their own downfall again. No one was picking up Gray – who scored his first Spurs goal against Palace in a rare win under Thomas Frank last year – at the back post from a deep Mohammed Kudus corner, and he headed in unopposed. The television cameras cut to Parish in the stand looking less than impressed.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenArchie Gray (right) heads home to open the scoring for Tottenham against Crystal Palace.Photograph: Jed Leicester/Tottenham Hotspur FC/ShutterstockDe Zerbi replaced Gray, on a yellow card, at the break with Pedro Porro. Palace retreated even further and Van Hecke should have done better from close range after another corner but ballooned into the crowd. In an attempt to relieve some of the pressure, Sage threw on former Arsenal striker Eddie Nketiah to jeers from the Spurs fans. Dwight McNeil had a rare sight of goal that was blocked but Palace almost paid the price as Tottenham broke downfield.Any hopes Palace had of snatching something ended when Fernandes picked out Van Hecke and the Dutchman, on the ground, cleverly nodded the ball over the line after Henderson had pushed his initial header on to the bar. Had Kudus scored after being set up by 18-year-old Luca Williams-Barnett,it would have rounded off the perfect afternoon for De Zerbi, who is the latest example of how quickly things can change in football.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueTottenham HotspurCrystal Palacematch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Packers’ Josh Jacobs faces fresh abuse allegations from three women in police records | Green Bay Packers | The Guardian
description: Three women detailed alleged incidents involving the Packers running back dating to 2021 as the NFL continues its investigation into his battery case
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Three women detailed alleged incidents involving the Packers running back dating to 2021 as the NFL continues its investigation into his battery case
Content: Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs faces fresh allegations of physical abuse.Photograph: Kayla Wolf/APView image in fullscreenGreen Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs faces fresh allegations of physical abuse.Photograph: Kayla Wolf/APGreen Bay PackersPackers’ Josh Jacobs faces fresh abuse allegations from three women in police recordsThree women contacted police after Jacobs’ May arrestOne alleged the Packers star threatened to kill herLawyers call allegations ‘uncorroborated’ and ‘old’AgenciesSat 31 Oct 2026 13.35 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 13.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs police investigated the battery case involvingGreen Bay Packersrunning back Josh Jacobs following a May altercation with his then-girlfriend, multiple other women contacted them to detail their own allegations against him.Those accounts were included in evidence regarding Jacobs’ battery case that the Hobart/Lawrence Police Department released on Friday night in response to a public records request. Green Bay TV station NBC 26 first reported the records’ release.Jacobs pleaded no contest on 10 September to misdemeanor counts of battery and criminal damage to property. He was arrested on 26 May, three days after an incident in which a woman said he threw her to the ground.He was one of the NFL’s most feared runners. Now Larry Johnson fears what football did to his brainRead moreIt is unclear how the latest allegations will play into the NFL’s investigation into Jacobs. The league placed him on the commissioner’s exempt list in August after charges were filed against him, causing Jacobs to miss the Packers’ first six games of the season.The NFL is still investigating Jacobs over the incident that led to his May arrest, so the league could impose further discipline on the running back.Jacobs’ lawyers – David Z Chesnoff, Richard A Schonfeld and Clarence F Duchac III – issued a statement on Saturday on their client’s behalf:“The Brown County District Attorney’s office had these uncorroborated, old, and previously unreported allegations for months. They conducted their own exhaustive investigation, along with the police department, and the D.A. determined that only two misdemeanor charges were warranted. They then entered into a plea agreement with Josh Jacobs. Josh has repeatedly expressed his remorse and is honoring the terms of the agreement.”The Packers had no immediate comment.According to the records released on Friday, one woman contacted police after Jacobs’ arrest to say she had experienced a similar incident with him around 2023. She later said the incident had actually occurred on 5 January 2022.The woman said she had communicated with Jacobs for about six months before spending around 11 hours at his home. She said that after she told Jacobs she had not come there for sex, he became angry, slapped her across the face and told her not to disrespect him.She said he took her phone and threw it into a swimming pool when she attempted to leave, and that he grabbed her by the hair, threw her on to a bed, pinned her down, threw her to the floor and said: “I should kill you right now.” She said Jacobs also spat on her.The woman said she had not previously reported the incident to law enforcement because she remained friends with Jacobs afterward and was concerned her allegations would not be believed. She said she contacted police this time because she believed it showed a pattern of behaviour similar to the allegations in the May case.View image in fullscreenJosh Jacobs scored two touchdowns in the Green Bay Packers’ Thursday night win over the Carolina Panthers.Photograph: Michael Owens/Getty ImagesAnother woman told police she had sex with Jacobs in April 2021. She said his condom broke, so she told Jacobs to get tested for sexually transmitted infections because they had both been involved with other people.The woman said Jacobs later removed her from the residence, grabbed her by the arms and biceps, pushed her against a wall and threw her belongings out. She told police she sustained bruises to her arms and swelling around her ribs.Hobart/Lawrence police said they obtained records from that incident indicating that officers observed “no visible signs of injury, bruising or damage consistent with a physical altercation”.Another woman said she met Jacobs through social media and that he flew her to a residence in May 2022. She described an altercation in which Jacobs grabbed her by the hair, placed his hands on her head and neck, dragged her, scratched her chest and took her phone after it fell to the floor.The woman said she suffered bruises to her arm and scratches to her chest and neck. She said she did not report the incident to police because she was not a US citizen at the time and Jacobs told her she could be deported.Jacobs is a three-time Pro Bowl selection who led the NFL in rushing in 2022 for the Las Vegas Raiders, where he played when the three previous incidents were alleged to have occurred. He joined the Packers in 2024.He returned two weeks ago and scored twice in the team’sThursday night win over the Carolina Panthers, celebrating one of the touchdowns by briefly placing his hands behind his back. The move drew immediate backlash from viewers in light of his off-season arrest, but Jacobs said he was modelling his celebration after a gospel song called Break Every Chain.The records released on Friday also offered more details of the 23 May incident that led to Jacobs’ arrest. According to the criminal complaint released in August, the woman told police Jacobs grabbed her and threw her to the ground as she was trying to exit through a garage door, causing her to hit her head. Police said Jacobs also took her phone while she was on the ground.The records released on Friday noted that the woman said that while they were still in the home, Jacobs lunged at her, pinned her on the bed with his body weight on her chest and put his hand over her mouth and nose, leaving her feeling unable to breathe.She also indicated that she believed she briefly lost consciousness when the confrontation moved to the garage.Explore more on these topicsGreen Bay PackersNFLUS sportsShareReuse this content

title: He was one of the NFL’s most feared runners. Now Larry Johnson fears what football did to his brain | NFL | The Guardian
description: Once among the NFL’s most punishing running backs, Larry Johnson opens up about memory loss, intrusive thoughts and his fears over football’s lasting toll
Author: Andrew Lawrence
Headline: Once among the NFL’s most punishing running backs, Larry Johnson opens up about memory loss, intrusive thoughts and his fears over football’s lasting toll
Content: Kansas City Chiefs running back Larry Johnson looks at the scoreboard during a game against the San Diego Chargers at Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City, Missouri, on 25 October 2009.Photograph: Jamie Squire/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenKansas City Chiefs running back Larry Johnson looks at the scoreboard during a game against the San Diego Chargers at Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City, Missouri, on 25 October 2009.Photograph: Jamie Squire/Getty ImagesNFLHe was one of the NFL’s most feared runners. Now Larry Johnson fears what football did to his brainOnce among the NFL’s most punishing running backs, Larry Johnson opens up about memory loss, intrusive thoughts and his fears over football’s lasting tollAndrew LawrenceSat 31 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn his heyday, Larry Johnson was the NFL tailback you’d least want to line up against, the steamroller in pads who had defensive players and coaches questioning their life choices on every down. But since Johnson walked away from pro football in 2011, after seven seasons in the league and an All-Pro run with theKansas City Chiefs, he’s the one doing the soul-searching, grappling with the toll all that gridiron glory has taken on his brain.Johnson, who still cuts a fit and formidable figure at age 46, can scarcely recall his glittering career, much less its highlights. “I go up to maybe 2006, 2007,” he tells me. “Anything before or three years after, I really don’t remember.”When Johnson was thriving as a pro in the mid 2000s, chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a degenerative brain disease associated with repeated head impacts, was not yet widely recognized as a risk of playing football. The NFL, however, had evidence that head injuries could cause lasting neurological damage, yet spent much of the decade publiclydisputing the linkas former players sought disability benefits for neurological problems – and were largely denied.It wasn’t until Will Smith starred in the movie Concussion as Bennett Omalu – the forensic pathologist who sounded the alarm on CTE in American football players after examining the brain of Mike Webster, the Hall of Fame center who died in 2002 afteryears of cognitive declineand a range of behavioral problems – that Johnson began joining the dots between football and his own personality swings. Johnson has long suspected he suffers from CTE, even though the disease can only be diagnosed after death. A studypublished on Wednesdayof former NFL players who died between 2008 and 2023 found that 74.5% had CTE. Of the nearly 400 players whose brains were donated for postmortem examination, 93.5% showed evidence of the disease.Johnson’s NFL career was defined by physical punishment, and he was a violent runner who welcomed the blows. Ahead of the 2003 draft, Johnson seemed like everything a team could want in a franchise running back. He had size (6ft 1in, 230 lbs) and speed (4.45s 40-yard dash). He capped a four-year career at Penn State by sweeping the Doak Walker Award for the nation’s best running back and the Maxwell and Walter Camp awards for the nation’s best player after rushing for more than 2,000 yards on fewer carries than anyone in history. He had backing from Joe Paterno, whenthat still meant something, and more hands-on guidance from his father, Larry Johnson Sr – the former Nittany Lions defensive assistant who’s now Ohio State’s associate head coach.But when the Chiefs selected Johnson 27th overall as insurance for franchise running back Priest Holmes, they did so over the objections of head coach Dick Vermeil, who had watched a parade of Penn State runners disappoint in the pros and figured Johnson would be no different. Vermeil singled out Johnson’s preparation habits and maturity, joking that he needed to “take the diapers off”. But Vermeil had to eat his words after Holmes went down with a season-ending neck injury midway through the 2005 season and Johnson stepped in to rack up 1,750 yards and 20 touchdowns in nine weeks. (“Well, he’s a talent,” the coachconcededlater.)View image in fullscreenJay-Z, left, and former NFL running back Larry Johnson attend a pre-fight party at Lavo in Las Vegas on 1 May 2009.Photograph: Denise Truscello/WireImageThe following season Vermeil retired and Herm Edwards took over, and the bombastic defensive guru made Johnson the centerpiece of the Chiefs offense. He ran for 1,789 yards on a whopping 416 carries – anNFLrecord that isn’t likely to be threatened in the current era of pass-happy offense and running by committee. Whenever Johnson publicly shares his CTE fears, fans often find themselves looking back at the season for answers. Was that the beginning? Too many blows? “People forget: I didn’t get hurt during those 416 carries,” he says. “I didn’t really start until 2006. I was in the league for three years – maybe the only first-round pick battling just todress. If Herm had told me straight up, ‘I’m gonna run you 416 times.’ I would’ve been like, Why can’t we do 500?”Johnson reveled in his star status, famously signing on as an ambassador for Jay-Z’s Roc-A-Fella record label as it was growing into a lifestyle brand. The Chiefs workhorse was frequently spotted partying with LeBron James and other members of Jay-Z’s inner circle at the rapper mogul’s bygone 40/40 Club in New York, helping get Jay-Z in the door with the NFL and paving the way for his later relationship with the league office and commissioner Roger Goodell. Johnson celebrated touchdowns bytenting his hands into a diamond, a gesture popularized by Jay-Z and his associates known as “throwing up the Roc”.But the southern Maryland native never quite cottoned to the scrutiny that came with the spotlight. He was slammed in the press for demanding a trade and threatening to sit out as leverage for a new contract. He clashed with Chiefs coach Todd Haley – questioning his credentials to succeed Edwards – and disparaged fans and media with homophobic slurs, prompting suspensions before he was eventually released by the team.Johnson drew more troubling headlines for his alleged assaults on women: a Kansas City nightclub patron accused him ofspitting a drink in her face, and an ex-girlfriend accused him of beating andstrangling herat the Bellagio in Las Vegas. Between 2003 and 2012, he was arrested five times in cases involving allegations of violence against women – resulting in convictions for disturbing the peace, domestic battery and assault, with penalties that stopped short of jail time. Johnson shies from blaming football for those incidents, but it’s hard not to wonder what the game left behind in a man so handsomely rewarded for violence – or how much the game messed with his head. Johnson began playing tackle football at age nine, taking helmet-to-helmet hits long before he reached the NFL.double quotation markAs twisted as it may sound, the thing I wanted to do was to die on the football fieldLarry JohnsonLife after football was deeply unsettling for Johnson. “I couldn’t find anything that really will test your manhood and also test your character like football,” he says. “I enjoyed lining up eight in a box and then trying to get five or 10 yards – and then I’m getting 50. As twisted as it may sound, the thing I wanted to do was to die on the football field. I always felt like I had to go to war, like I had to fight even when I don’t have to fight.”He had hoped to transition into nonprofit work, but found the 9-to-5 office environment stifling. A hair-trigger sensitivity to light, noise and group settings made it impossible for him to hold down a job. He fought with the mother of his young daughter, Jaylen, over school pickup schedules; during a two-year court fight, with Johnson’s own mother acting as a go-between, he finally realizedhewas the one misremembering the times. He enrolled in a master’s program with a cohort of NFL retirees, but says he quit after flipping out on a professor during a group project.All the while, Johnson wrestled with intrusive thoughts and inner voices telling him to harm himself and others. The voices come in waves, he says, “almost like a suggestion. Certain things scare me. I can’t be close to balconies anymore. If I’m walking, I’ll think,What if something falls out of the sky? Just a constant state of paranoia.” To cope, he isolated himself for long stretches and self-medicated with drugs and alcohol – making matters far worse.Johnson’s father had little idea of his son’s quiet suffering until the ex-Chiefs star went public in a2017 Washington Post profile. Johnson feared that his father might not understand or relate to what he was going through; he went from checking in with his dad for any reason, even if it was just to say he was heading home after a game, to pulling away from his great mentor. The Post article, though, “gave my father new eyes,” Johnson says. “People would tell him, ‘That’s a really good thing your son did.’ I think that made him a little bit more accepting. [Now] we’re back to our relationship – as if I’m still in the house, you know?”Johnson had another major breakthrough around the same time, when the NFL granted him lifetime disability benefits, giving him the financial security to focus on his health without worrying about making ends meet. In a league infamous for publicly denying former players’ claims and usingrace-normingto limit disability payouts (disputes that were ostensibly addressed ina revised league settlement), that victory shouldn’t be taken lightly. Johnson knows how fortunate he was to last seven years in a league where the average running back’s career is around 2½ years, leaving little time to build a safety net. He believes the modern trend of devaluing running backs only serves a league that’s “trying to lessen payments.”View image in fullscreenNow 46, Larry Johnson says he struggles with memory loss and other neurological symptoms that he fears may be linked to the repeated blows he absorbed during his NFL career.Photograph: Jamie Squire/Getty ImagesJohnson’s daily life is still punctuated by bouts of confusion. Light and noise still bother him, and he gets irritated anytime he hears himself slurring words or otherwise struggling to put sentences together. But Johnson has better ways of coping. Jaylen is old enough to drive herself – and her dad – around now, sparing him the embarrassment of getting lost on routine trips orconfusing the TV remote for a car key fob. Johnson spends a lot of time talking through his feelings with his wife, who knows when to prod and when to leave him be. All of it helps keep the voices at bay, but he still hears them. He likens the intrusive thoughts to a movie. “Yours might last for a scene,” he says. “Mine is like a sequel. Then there’s part three and hidden features. It’s like Marvel at the end of the movie. It engulfs me.”Social media tends to be where Johnson gets in trouble these days, courting controversy with conspiracy theories about Jews, Kobe Bryant’s death and Jay-Z, with whom he has since fallen out. Away from the online fray, though, Johnson keeps a cool head in group chats with former teammates, even as it frustrates him that his peers never want to talk about what they’rereallygoing through. “All they’re talking about is each other’s birthdays and going out and drinking,” he says. “We are in an era where if you admit you were hurt, you’re soft – you know what I mean?”His new dream is to create an app that connects former pros struggling with their mental health with people who understand what they’re going through – former NFL clinicians like Susan Wilson, his team therapist at the Chiefs. “I would love to be able to have asymposiumfor retired guys,” Johnson says, “so they can hear not only the horror stories, but share their similar histories of how to deal with mental health. It’s been too hush-hush and taboo for such a long time because guys are embarrassed.”CTE researchers are always keen to build relationships with former players, too. Last month, Emory University announced a partnership with the Concussion & CTE Foundation and Boston University on amedical studyof former football players experiencing depressive and cognitive symptoms. The study is testing whether an FDA-approved drug that reduces inflammation can also improve those symptoms, recruiting men aged 30–55 in the Atlanta area who have played at least 11 years of tackle football.Whether researchers are any closer to diagnosing and treating CTE in living patients remains an open question. “CTE is both a complex physiological and psychological issue,” says Concussion & CTE Foundation co-founder Chris Nowinski,a longtime advocate. “Learning you have CTE can have a positive mental impact for some, and a negative one for others. That’s why it’s critical to have a multi-pronged approach advancing diagnosis, treatment and mental health support.”Johnson tries not to let his emotions get the better of him when watching football now. He appreciates the safety measures the league has introduced to protect players, but laments what they’ve taken away from the physical brand of football he once defined. It broke the ex-Chief’s heart to see his former AFC rival Chris Johnson opening upabout his ALS battle. “To watch these players who could basically run 4.5, 4.4 40s be in wheelchairs, like, that haunts me,” he says. “If this could happen to Chris Johnson orSteve Gleason, it can happen to any of us, right?”In an effort to keep tabs on his own neurological condition, Johnson has taken to posting videos of himself on social media and scrutinizing them for signs of decline – the ultimate mental health self-scout. Early replies describing his delivery as “mean” or “condescending” helped him modulate his behavior and even led to some online friendships. With a firmer handle on his general well-being, Johnson thinks differently about being tested for CTE now, while he’s alive.“When I first said that, it was like, yeah, I would want to know,” he says. “But at the end of the day, I know I would obsess over it. I would be paying attention to every little micro movement and emotion. I would drive myself crazy thinking I don’t have much time, so let me act out. If there was a way we could figure out before then, at least I would know the damage. Whether I know it or whether I can feel it, I know something is there.”Explore more on these topicsNFLCollege footballCollege sportsUS sportsKansas City ChiefsConcussion in sportConcussion (2015)featuresShareReuse this content

title: Hyrox athlete who soiled herself puts ‘confronting’ matter behind her to win return race | Australia sport | The Guardian
description: Joanna Wietrzyk claims victory in first event of season in Hamburg after saying in a pre-race social media video that she is ‘truly so sorry’ for events in Beijing
Author: Martin Pegan
Headline: Joanna Wietrzyk claims victory in first event of season in Hamburg after saying in a pre-race social media video that she is ‘truly so sorry’ for events in Beijing
Content: Joanna Wietrzyk has returned to Hyrox competition with a win in the women’s event in Hamburg after suffering a bout of diarrhoea during a race in Beijing.Photograph: Poly Fei/SOPA Images/LightRocket/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJoanna Wietrzyk has returned to Hyrox competition with a win in the women’s event in Hamburg after suffering a bout of diarrhoea during a race in Beijing.Photograph: Poly Fei/SOPA Images/LightRocket/Getty ImagesAustralia sportHyrox athlete who soiled herself puts ‘confronting’ matter behind her to win return raceJoanna Wietrzyk claims victory in first event of season in HamburgAustralian says pre-race that she is ‘truly so sorry’ for events in BeijingMartin PeganSat 31 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Australian athlete who sparked outrage when winning a Hyrox event in Beijing despite soiling herself during the race has returned in style with victory in the first event of the new season in Hamburg.Joanna Wietrzyk won the endurance sports event in China last month but forfeited the points and soon faced a stinging public backlash as footage of her continuing through demanding exercises and using communal equipment withfaecal matter running down her legswent viral on social media.There’s a long history of athletes pooing themselves mid-race – why, and how can you avoid it?Read moreThe 24-year-old posted a statement on social media with an apology in theaftermath of the incidentbefore stepping away from the public eye. The Melbourne-born athlete returned to speak on a pre-race video this week where she said she was “truly, truly so sorry to everyone that I affected”.Wietrzyk, the world record-holder in the Hyrox women’s solo event, added the attention that had stained her reputation had been “very hard” and “very confronting” to deal with before she put the storm behind her to win the Hyrox event on her comeback to competition on Friday.“I’ve had some time to reflect over the past six to eight weeks of everything that happened in Beijing and firstly I want to say that I’m truly, truly so sorry to everyone that I affected whether they were spectators or participants out on that race floor, for my decision to choose to continue to race,”Wietrzyk saidin a post on Instagram. “Having that time to reflect, I’ve really learnt a lot from the situation and I am very, very sorry for it all.”She added: “It has been a very hard situation to navigate for me and very confronting as well, so all the support, whether it was personally or through my team has been honestly so incredible and it goes a far longer way than I can truly express right now.“I’m super excited to go back to doing what I love.”Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueHyrox is an increasingly popular fitness competition that sees participants alternate between running a kilometre and doing fitness exercises at shared high-intensity stations – including a rowing machine, sled pushes, burpee jumps, medicine ball throws and lunges while carrying a sandbag.The competition launched in Germany in 2017 and is now held in locations across the world with the 2026-27 season to include races in London, Bangkok, Las Vegas and Lyon after the opener in Hamburg.Wietrzyk took an early lead in the Elite 15 competition when winning the fitness event in Hamburg in 56:10.21 ahead of American pair Lauren Weeks (56:24.37) and Vivian Tafuto (57:55.34).skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHyrox apologised and pledged immediate rule changesafter Wietrzyk was allowed to finish and win the Beijing race in September even as she suffered from a bout of diarrhoea.
