The proposal’s foes have out-fundraised supporters by nearly10-1.But whatever the election’s outcome is on 3 November, campaigning to tax the wealth of the country’s nearly 1,000 billionaires has enormous potential nationwide.In early August, the California Democratic Party executive board, hardly a bastion of class struggle,votedto give the party’s endorsement to Prop 40. But, undeterred, Newsom has gone all-out to fight the billionaire tax proposal as well as to boost another ballot measure that would nullify any such tax.double quotation markRefusal to back Proposition 40 runs directly counter to standard rhetoric from Democratic politicians about standing up to the ultra-wealthy on behalf of the disadvantagedWhen I contacted a former chair of the state party’s Progressive Caucus, he was matter-of-fact about the alliance of big tech moguls with the current and next governor. “When it comes to Newsom and Becerra opposing the billionaire tax,” said Amar Shergill, a Sacramento-based attorney, “you need know only two things. First, Newsom needs billionaire money for his presidential campaign. Second, Becerra needs to pay back the billionaires that made him governor. The rest of the corporate Democrats in office are some version of these stories.”Newsom became governor in 2019, following Jerry Brown’s second eight-year stretch in the job. His unique style aside, Brown has long been a kind of prototype for the state’s Democratic leadership now typified by Newsom.“The way you have to approach the political process is something like piloting a canoe,” Brownsaidin 1979 during his first stint as governor. He explained: “If you paddle a little bit on the left side, then you paddle a little bit on the right side, you keep going right down the middle.”This year, Brown has stayed out of the battle over Proposition 40. In late October, when I emailed the former governor to ask whether he supports it, he replied: “I have not discussed the proposition. There is already a plethora of opinions on the measure.”Weeks ago, duringa BBC interview, Brown lamented: “The gains for those who succeed at the top are getting bigger and richer, and the sustenance at the bottom and the middle is getting less and less.” He added: “We obviously need a wealth tax. If Tesla wants to give Elon Musk a trillion dollars over 10 years, then the people have to take back 99% of it. Now, can you get that? No, not at this point. Can you get it in one state? No, that would not work. Can you get it in one country? Probably not. So it would take an international agreement to tax the very wealthy, so that you can’t accumulate at the level that they are today.”Brown and Newsom share a fondness for voicing lofty principles while kicking them very far down the road, tacitly equating deference to corporate power with realism. Newsomsays– with scant details – that he would support a federal tax on billionaires. Meanwhile, he claims that approval of Proposition 40 would cause many of California’s more than 200 billionaires to move out of the state, with disastrous results.“Proposed tax hikes on the rich invariably produce grim warnings of millionaire flight which then don’t eventuate,” the journalist Harold Meyerson recentlypointed out. “Even if they did in this case, as apaperfor the National Bureau of Economic Research has documented, the revenue gain of roughly $100 billion that the [billionaire] wealth tax would yield wouldn’t be offset by reductions in the income tax revenue produced by the flight of every one of those 200 billionaires until 25 years had passed. If just 50 of those 200 billionaires fled, it would take a full century.”The survival of American democracy depends on taxing billionairesRead moreA large majority of the 45 Democrats in the California delegation to Congress richly deserve the “corporate” label. The official website of the Proposition 40 campaignlistsonly two congressional endorsers in the state. One of them, Representative Ro Khanna, has emerged as California’s most visible and vocal politicianadvocatingfor Prop 40.“It’s the most important ballot initiative in America and in the world,” Khannadeclaredduring a recent interview on MS Now. Looking ahead, he asked: “Are we going to continue to cater to a donor class that has hollowed out jobs, hollowed out the working class, and lost us two elections to Donald Trump?”That kind of rhetorical question could progressively reframe the race for the Democratic presidential nomination in 2028.“This is a fight for the soul of the Democratic party,” Khanna told me last weekend. “Will we be beholden to billionaire donors and offer platitudes without policy likeGavin Newsom, or will we reclaim our FDR courage and offer a bold vision for our nation’s future?”Exactly 90 years ago,speakingat Madison Square Garden on the last day of October 1936, the then president Franklin Delano Roosevelt scorned the rightwing plutocrats of the day: “They are unanimous in their hate for me – and I welcome their hatred.” Leaders of today’s Democratic party have failed to earn such hatred.Norman Solomon is the director of RootsAction and executive director of the Institute for Public Accuracy. His latest book isThe Blue Road to Trump Hell: How Corporate Democrats Paved the Way for AutocracyExplore more on these topicsCaliforniaOpinionGavin NewsomUS midterm elections 2026US economyWest CoastDemocratsUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Racists used to say ‘Go back where you come from’. Now they exclaim ‘Deport!’ | Ghassan Hage | The Guardian
description: ‘Deport!’ oozes an entirely different sense of power – one where the racist imagines they can call upon the state to act on their behalf
Author: Ghassan Hage
Headline: ‘Deport!’ oozes an entirely different sense of power – one where the racist imagines they can call upon the state to act on their behalf
Content: The rise in state deportations around the world has helped to legitimise the use of racist language, writes Ghassan Hage.Photograph: Alan Schein Photography/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe rise in state deportations around the world has helped to legitimise the use of racist language, writes Ghassan Hage.Photograph: Alan Schein Photography/Getty ImagesOpinionRaceRacists used to say ‘Go back where you come from’. Now they exclaim ‘Deport!’Ghassan Hage‘Deport!’ oozes an entirely different sense of power – one where the racist imagines they can call upon the state to act on their behalfSat 31 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 19.59 EDTShareThere is a rise in racist rhetoric surrounding deportation. This is clearly influenced by the increased use of deportation against immigrants and asylum seekers worldwide, particularly in the US.But my concern here is not so much the governmental practice itself as the racist language that it has helped disseminate and legitimise: I write something on X, and some random racist who dislikes what I wrote decides that because my name is Ghassan Hage I must be a potentially deportable subject and simply writes “deport” as a comment. Nasser Mashni, the president of the Australia Palestine Advocacy Network, notes in Crikey that “deport” is “the comment most often left on anything I post”.On the face of it, there is not much difference between the exclamation “Deport!” and the racist injunction “Go back where you come from”. Both seek to delegitimise someone’s national belonging and fantasise their removal from national space. But despite the similarities there are important differences.Australia has never driven migration into reverse by design. Would slamming on the brakes be calamitous?Read moreIn White Nation: Fantasies of White Supremacy in a Multicultural Society, I argued that “Go back where you come from” was at the heart of the fantasy of white supremacy of subjects who felt entitled to decide who should stay in the nation and who should leave it. Nonetheless, it should be noted that at the time I wrote this, in the 1990s the exclamation operated more like a lament: “I am entitled to tell you to go back where you come from, but I have no means of forcing you to do so, even though I wish I could.”Apart from not caring where the other “goes back” to – a significant point I leave aside here – “Deport!” oozes an entirely different sense of power. One can immediately note that, formally, the exclamation is directed not at the racialised person but at the state. “Deport!” imagines a relation of complicity between the racists and the state whereby the racists can call upon the state to act on their behalf. In practice, however, the racialised person remains the principal addressee. The message is: “Look, I am asking my state to deport you.” Whereas with “Go back where you come from” the racist fantasises a claim of ownership of the nation but not necessarily of the state, with “deport” there is a claim of ownership of both.As I did in White Nation, I am using “fantasy” in a psychoanalytic sense to understand the way subjects frame their pursuit of both what is desirable and possible. The latter is important: racists are not delusional when their fantasy registers a shift in the political culture of the state. It is the significance of this transformation in racists’ relation to an increasingly racist state that I wanted to highlight here. Those who look at Pauline Hanson’s current discourse and see a continuity with her 1990s pronouncements, without noticing the sense of power that permeates her pronouncements and that derives from this shift, miss something important.This transformation also affects the relation of anti-racists to the state. In Australia, there has historically been a difference between First Nations anti-racism and immigrant anti-racism. The latter has tended to have more faith in the state. Today, particularly in the shadow of the state’s pitiful response to the pulverisation of Gaza and its inhabitants, immigrants from colonised background have increasingly come to experience the institutionalised racism of the state in the way First Nations people do: more as a harmful ecology, a form of generalised toxicity that is being diffused throughout the societal environment than just an event or a structure.‘I can’t sleep at night’: international students forced to navigate the impact of Labor’s sudden visa changesRead moreWhile thinking through the way racism in the shadow of Gaza has become more of a toxic ecology, I read an ethnography of sewage workers in Paris, Basses Oeuvres, by the anthropologist Agnès Jeanjean. I found it particularly stimulating and suggestive. In one passage, a sewage worker draws a distinction between garbage workers and sewage workers. Garbage workers, he argues, can maintain a certain distance between themselves and the garbage they handle. Sewage workers can’t. “On est dans les égouts et on a les égouts en nous” (“We are in the sewers and we have the sewers in us”), he said.To the extent this distinction holds, we might say we anti-racists today are more like sewage workers than garbos. We must continuously work on de-polluting ourselves and de-polluting our anti-racist instruments and strategies, even as we are trying to de-pollute – and decolonise – the environment in which we live.Ghassan Hage is honorary professor of anthropology at the University of Sydney. He is the author of Is Racism an Environmental Threat? and The Racial Politics of Australian MulticulturalismExplore more on these topicsRaceOpinionMigrationAustralian immigration and asylumAustralian politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: The real problem with Britain’s Political Traitors show is that no one is very faithful to anything for long | Robert Hutton | The Guardian
description: For Westminster’s special budget edition of the series, politicians have played to their strengths. Bombast, duplicity, distrust: it’s all second nature, says journalist and author Robert Hutton
Author: Robert Hutton
Headline: For Westminster’s special budget edition of the series, politicians have played to their strengths. Bombast, duplicity, distrust: it’s all second nature, says journalist and author Robert Hutton
Content: The Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch (left) and the  Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.Composite: Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenThe Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch (left) and the  Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.Composite: Guardian DesignOpinionThe TraitorsThe real problem with Britain’s Political Traitors show is that no one is very faithful to anything for longRobert HuttonFor Westminster’s special budget edition of the series, politicians have played to their strengths. Bombast, duplicity, distrust: it’s all second natureSat 31 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 11.49 EDTShareYou join us on a steam train in Scotland as we head to the next episode of the BBC’s hit show Political Traitors. It’s like the celebrity edition, except that everyone is less comely – politics being the practice ofshow business for ugly people. For this week’s task, the players have to construct a “budget” of tiny crowd-pleasing measures, carefully balanced by invisible tax rises.What makes the show so compelling is that the players don’t know the whole story. Only those of us on the outside can see what’s really going on. WhileJohn and Andyrun around shouting about how they have faithfully met their “fiscal rules” in the third year of the forecasts, on our sofas at home we know that this incantation is entirely meaningless.But people who’ve been on the show say that when you’re in the midst of it, it feels completely real. So much so that there are ongoing questions for the producers about safeguarding. Liz, who was a sensation of chaotic energy when she briefly appeared in 2022, is the most obvious example of someone who shouldn’t have been allowed to take part. She waslast heard explaining her plan to colonise Mars.If the series has any value beyond entertainment, it’s for the insights it offers into human psychology, especially the way people convince themselves of narratives that are objectively nonsense. Take Kemi, from the current run. After the banishment of Keir earlier this year, she could be heard explaining to anyone who would listen that this was the result ofher brilliant inquisitions at the roundtable.We could all see that the other players, after debating why on earth Keir hadn’t already been stabbed in the back, had concluded that although he was 100% faithful, he was also 1000% loser.Nevertheless, there’s something rather charming about Kemi’s total conviction that she’s a masterly player on course for triumph. It’s easy for us to laugh, but you have to remember that she doesn’t have access to the information we do, such as opinion polls and byelection results.That information gap is the joy of the show. Several times Nigel hasseemingly revealed himself to be a traitor, and his close ally Nathanwas actually unmasked as one, but still no one seems able to put two and two together.View image in fullscreenThe prime minister, Andy Burnham, and the chancellor, John Healey, visiting the Rolls Royce factory in Derby, October 29.Photograph: WPA/Getty ImagesSome players adopt a strategy of trying to fly below the radar to avoid being noticed. One current player, Ed D, has been so successful that many viewers have forgotten he exists and refuse to believe he ispart of the game at all, even after his triumph in the water slide task.Each morning, the players meet over breakfast TV for a heated discussion in which they all insist that whatever has just happened proves their theory is right. Then there’s the dramatic moment of discovering who has been banished, or simply walked off the set. In one compelling episode in 2022, almost all the players quit in the hope of forcing Boris to admit he’d been lying. Even then, to viewers’ delight, he still had the support of the loyal Nadine.In last month’s “conference” task, the players were handed the severed head of a deceased teammate and had to mimic their distinctive cry. Kemi, predictably, chose Maggie, although her impersonation looked more like pastiche. Andy, on the other hand, reckons he can do a mean Harold. He’s rejected any suggestion that he should try copying Tony, one of the game’s most successful players, but he’s failed to brush aside the lingering suspicion that he’s simply doing an impression of Keir.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe format has been sold around the world, with changes for local markets. The French edition involves a runoff vote. TheIsraeli versionis so complicated that no one understands anything about it except that somehow Bibi keeps winning. And the American one is louder, brasher and far more expensive. It also seems to be played entirely by idiots who have failed, despite an impossible number of very clear clues, to identify their obvious traitor.Although the players change at an alarming rate, the one constant in the British show is the host, Lindsay. With his ridiculous outfits and his catchphrases – “Order! ORDER!” and “Mr Holden, I think you need to leave” – he is fast becoming a national treasure. And now, as he says at the end of every roundtable, the time for talk is over.I’m joking, of course. In this version of the show, the time for talk never ends.Robert Hutton is a journalist and authorExplore more on these topicsThe TraitorsOpinionKemi BadenochNigel FarageAndy BurnhamJohn HealeyLabourConservativescommentShareReuse this content

title: Relying on AI is rotting your brain. But here’s what you can do about it | Carly Dober | The Guardian
description: Each new tech product is designed to make our lives easier and keep us mindlessly entertained. Switch off: embrace discomfort – and boredom, says psychologist Carly Dober
Author: Carly Dober
Headline: Each new tech product is designed to make our lives easier and keep us mindlessly entertained. Switch off: embrace discomfort – and boredom, says psychologist Carly Dober
Content: A humanoid robot walk past a protest outside an OpenAI developers’ conference in San Francisco, California, 29 September 2026.Photograph: Heather Diehl/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA humanoid robot walk past a protest outside an OpenAI developers’ conference in San Francisco, California, 29 September 2026.Photograph: Heather Diehl/Getty ImagesOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)Relying on AI is rotting your brain. But here’s what you can do about itCarly DoberEach new tech product is designed to make our lives easier and keep us mindlessly entertained. Switch off: embrace discomfort – and boredomSat 31 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 12.20 EDTShareEver longed for your own personal assistant? In the ever quickening tech race, Meta has recently launched Muse, anew AI personal agent. Unlike traditional chatbots, this little AI tool will be able to fill out forms for you, organise calendars, pay bills and make reservations. Meta describes Muse as a personal agent “built for everyone”. The launch comes at a time when AI agents have been making headlines for hacking intogovernment websites,public agenciesand businesses. However, my immediate concern is a little closer to home.I work as a psychologist, and I’m often talking to clients about lifestyle habits that lead to short-term gain but incur long-term pain. Our brains have a beautiful way of preferring the path of least resistance, of doing what is easiest to preserve our resources. And with the demands of modern life feeling so overwhelming for so many people, the urge to scroll after a long week or defer to a chatbot because you are exhausted is incredibly seducing.Tech bros pushing their products on to us is nothing new (we all rememberthe metaverse, right?), but the message is now seemingly at fever pitch for mass AI adoption and how integral it is for human development. It is helpful to remind ourselves what we are being asked to give up, to whom and why, and to consider the potential risks before we hand over our precious data.Some technology, such as large language models (LLMs) and social media that has an infinite scroll algorithm, seem to have a dose effect: too much reliance on this technology can lead to particular cognitive biases being activated, brain chemistry beingdepleted, moods andmental health being affected, and evenneurological skillsbeing atrophied, to name but a few of the documented risks.Overusing artificial intelligence affects the brain and learning by bypassing the mental effort required to build deep neural connections, a process known as cognitive offloading. Frequent AI use fosters a passive acceptance of information, reducing the internal friction and inquiry that drive genuine curiosity and problem-solving. The brain depends on mental struggle and overcoming failure to rewire and strengthen our neural pathways. Bypassing that friction reduces our overall cognitive reserve over time.Our tendency to favour or give greater credence to information supplied by technology (such as ChatGPT or Claude), and to ignore a manual source of information that provides contradictory information (a textbook, for example) even if it is correct, illustrates the phenomenon of automation bias. Automation complacency is closely linked – an overlapping concept that refers to the monitoring of technology with less frequency or vigilance because of a lower suspicion of error and a stronger belief in its accuracy, even when we know that LLMs often generate inaccurate answers.Social media is designed to be so addictive because its business model relies on maximising user attention, while people give up their privacy because the immediate psychological rewards outweigh the abstract risk of data exposure. Most people say they value their privacy, but their behaviour says otherwise. This contradiction is known in behavioural economics as theprivacy paradox.Digital tools make life incredibly convenient – you can order a car with the touch of a button, a hot meal can be delivered to your door, and you can order and return outfits without ever exchanging a word with another person. People gladly trade their location data, contacts and browsing history in exchange for free maps, personalised shopping recommendations and seamless communication. Many individuals falsely believe that because they aren’t committing crimes, their data isn’t valuable. They don’t realise that aggregate data is used to manipulate purchasing habits, influence political votes and predict private life events.Privacy policies are also intentionally long and confusing, and written in dense legal language that is inaccessible to the vast majority of users. Users face “consent fatigue” and simply click “Accept all” whenever the pesky window pops up while they are browsing because they feel they have no real choice.There is a way out of the muck, though. Become more discerning about what information you share online; consider turning your location off unless you’re using navigation apps; reject cookies tracking you; hell, even start to poison your data if you really want to engage in some online anarchy. Does the online store you bought a T-shirt from once really need to know your full legal name and date of birth?To avoid AI overreliance, you need to startintroducing “friction”into your days – deliberate obstacles that break the automatic loop of seeking instant gratification. From a psychological perspective, AI is highly addictive because it eliminates this friction, offering immediate rewards with zero cognitive effort – and our brains need cognitive effort to remain sharp. Every time you try to work out a problem or read a book instead of the comments section, that is your brain doing a push-up.If you’re struggling to rein in your social media or AI usage, a good way to start is by logging out of online sessions. Forcing yourself to manually type your credentials every time creates a massive psychological barrier. Also, try restricting your AI usage strictly to a desktop or laptop computer: removing ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini from your phone eliminates the urge to use it while walking, lying in bed or waiting in line. Scrolling on our phones or talking to a chatbot impedes much of the necessary mind-wandering time that our brains need to function at their best.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMeta releases Muse Spark Open, a new ‘open-weight’ AI modelRead moreWhen you feel the urge to ask an AI a question or have it write something for you, force yourself to wait about 30 minutes. Use this time to brainstorm, look at a book or simply sit with the problem. Often the urge passes or you solve the problem yourself. Commit to writing the first draft of any email, letter or presentation entirely by yourself. Embrace the discomfort of maybe getting things wrong. Instead of asking an AI for a recommendation or an explanation, ask a friend or colleague, or check a reputable website. The delay in waiting for a human response builds patience, and we need to practise this skill in order to retain it.Dedicate specific hours of your day to completely screen-free activities. Read books, write with pen and paper or go for a walk without your phone and see how differently things feel for you after six weeks of consistent effort. Intentionally building friction into the frictionless online experience is hard – but I promise that your brain will thank you for it.Carly Dober is a psychologist living and working in MelbourneExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionSocial mediaMetacommentShareReuse this content

title: When you’re traduced, abused and gaslighted – believe me, Black History Month matters  | Hugh Muir | The Guardian
description: There is always debate about the concept’s necessity and efficacy. But with nativists in their pomp, it’s good to focus on who we are and why, says Hugh Muir, Opinion executive editor
Author: Hugh Muir
Headline: There is always debate about the concept’s necessity and efficacy. But with nativists in their pomp, it’s good to focus on who we are and why, says Hugh Muir, Opinion executive editor
Content: Illustration: Guardian Design; ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock; Manuel Harlan; Jeff Moore/PA;  Laura McCluskeyView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian Design; ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock; Manuel Harlan; Jeff Moore/PA;  Laura McCluskeyOpinionBlack History MonthWhen you’re traduced, abused and gaslighted – believe me, Black History Month mattersHugh MuirThere is always debate about the concept’s necessity and efficacy. But with nativists in their pomp, it’s good to focus on who we are and whyWhat forces shaped four generations of Black Britons? | The panelSat 31 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 04.05 EDTSharePityBlack History Month UK, assailed on all sides. Those on the right seek to end the celebration on the basis that it amounts to special treatment for a group that doesn’t deserve it. History should be colour-blind: society should not differentiate, they say. We are not racist, we just want fairness. But often, they are – and they really don’t.On the other side of the argument are the progressives, notably minority progressives, who say the idea of a month to consider Black history is demeaning because it should already have a year-roundplace in our teaching and consciousness. There is a further view that any beneficial effect the month once had has been diluted by unimaginative repetition and commercially motivated virtue signalling. Playerstaking the kneein the Premier League? Been there, done that: yawn!I have long taken the glass-half-full approach. The ideal would be for Black history to be incorporated into the social and educational culture – and perhaps one day it will be. But in the meantime, I’ll take a mandated, month-long focus on the Black contribution to the way our society has evolved. And it seems very necessary this year, when the very notion of belonging in Britain and other major western countries has been so under attack.A year in which we have clearly seen that a political party, with pretensions to lead the country, attracts activists with ugly racist and nativist views – at national and local level – with the same efficiency that magnets attract iron filings. Our expectations are different now. When transcripts of the thingsReform folk say in privatereach the public domain, the old-fashioned Tory dog-whistle seems comparatively quaint.View image in fullscreenA book by Michelle Obama was among those removed from school shelves.Photograph: Paras Griffin/Getty ImagesThis is a year in which we have again seen the confidence and daring of those who cuddle close to pseudo-scientific theories assertingwhite superiority and black inferiority. The racial eugenicists are back from the fringes, championed down their venal path by Donald Trump, whose leadership of the free world gladhands nativists, targets Black officials androutinely belittlesBlack enemies as “low IQ”.It’s been a year in which toxic politics and the mainstreaming of intolerance – against minorities of many categories – has led to racist unpleasantness on our streets and in the workplace. There is a snapshot from the Royal College of Nursing: racist abuse of NHS nurses – including use of the N-word – up 86% in therecent past. All part of what one NHS official called “a rising tide of racism”.Another snapshot of the increasingly hostile environment is from parliament. What happened, via social media, when Labour MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy posted a video in support of Black History Month?Vile abuse, of course: “Some of a kind that I had not necessarily seen in that volume before. I had people calling me the N-word, people telling me to eff-off and go back to where I came from, and people sending monkey photographs.”Another snapshot from Chichester, Sussex, where a diverse group of actors recently went to perform A Midsummer Night’s Dreamand were shamefully menaced.“I don’t know if I have witnessed and/or experienced as much racism, xenophobia and homophobia as I saw in those six weeks,” said the actor and comedian Munya Chawawa. Britain is a good place. The vast majority of our fellow citizens are decent and kind. But it’s now easy, far too easy, to unwittingly enter hostile territory.So in years like this, when there are obvious, concerted, targeted, and well-funded attempts to undermine Black people and the Black experience – not least thetargeting of booksby Black authors by “anti woke” crusaders – it becomes more difficult to be sanguine about concepts such as Black History Month. It then becomes a good thing, perhaps an essential one, to remember and to highlight – if only over a calendar month – who we are, who has shaped us and how we have indisputably helped to shape Britain as a vibrant, diverse, first world power.Today, at the end of thisBlack History Month, Guardian Opinion has asked Black Britons representing four generations to tell us how their own Black British identities have evolved, for we have been here long enough now to compare notes on the different stages of our lives on this island. A twentysomething sees the joy and pain of being here very differently to their elderly siblings, to their parents, to their grandparents.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCall it reflection with a purpose. In a time like this, it seems more vital than ever to know who we were, who we are – and the foundations on which we all stand.Hugh Muir is executive editor, OpinionDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsBlack History MonthOpinionRaceReform UKcommentShareReuse this content

title: Massive Attack, Bob Marley, bell hooks and grime: what forces shaped four generations of Black Britons? | Arlo Parks, Eunice Olumide, Ade Adepitan and Vanley Burke | The Guardian
description: For Black History Month, figures from the arts, culture and sport reveal the people and ideas that made them who they are today
Author: Arlo Parks
Headline: For Black History Month, figures from the arts, culture and sport reveal the people and ideas that made them who they are today
Content: (L to R:) Lauryn Hill, Margaret Ekpo, Bob Marley, Skepta and Nelson Mandela.Composite: Redferns/Fourth Estate/Luath Press/Mariner/Corbis/VCG/Getty/Rex/Shutterstock/Alamy/Guardian DesignView image in fullscreen(L to R:) Lauryn Hill, Margaret Ekpo, Bob Marley, Skepta and Nelson Mandela.Composite: Redferns/Fourth Estate/Luath Press/Mariner/Corbis/VCG/Getty/Rex/Shutterstock/Alamy/Guardian DesignOpinionBlack History MonthMassive Attack, Bob Marley, bell hooks and grime: what forces shaped four generations of Black Britons?Arlo Parks,Eunice Olumide,Ade AdepitanandVanley BurkeFor Black History Month, figures from the arts, culture and sport reveal the people and ideas that made them who they are todayWhen you’re traduced, abused and gaslighted – believe me, Black History Month matters | Hugh MuirSat 31 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 10.16 EDTShare‘British music has shaped me completely’Arlo ParksSinger and songwriter, 26What book has most inspired you?All about love by bell hooks taught me so much about the nuances of connection and desire; it helped me make sense of the world and embrace my sensitivity. She had such a compassionate and inspired approach to truth-telling that I try to carry with me wherever I go.What albums or artists have most shaped your sense of self?British music has shaped me completely. In Rainbows by Radiohead taught me to yearn, bend genres and embrace minimalism. Blue Lines and Mezzanine by Massive Attack moulded my taste in drums and song structure. Dummy by Portishead encouraged me to be as vocally naked and unafraid as possible. [The song] Archangel by Burial taught me to embrace the grime and the magic and the grey of London.What cultural moments have felt most significant to you?Radiohead headlining the Pyramid stage at Glastonbury. Tate Modern opening its programming into the late night. The founding of Notting Hill carnival, and Meltdown festival at the Southbank Centre.If you werePM for the day, what would be your first priority?Protecting and advocating for young people’s health and education.Which Black historical figure has most influenced you?It would have to be a cluster of figures for their fearlessness, vulnerability and dedication to their crafts: Zadie Smith, Steve McQueen and the painter Donald Rodney.View image in fullscreenThe writer Zadie Smith at her home in London, September 2020.Photograph: IBL/ShutterstockWhat political development in the UK has most disappointed or uplifted you?I’ve been most disappointed by the rise in anti-trans rhetoric and discrimination. I’ve been most uplifted by theArts Everywhere fundand the general commitment to increasing public access to art.What is most misunderstood between generations?That it’s impossible for generations to truly connect. I think that with some care and attention we could find common ground, grow and truly understand each other.What is a “good life”?A life full of love, generosity and adventure.What would you change about your life?Nothing. I feel really lucky and am looking forward to seeing where life takes me.‘I’m interested in people who refuse to be reduced to a single identity’Eunice OlumideModel, actor, author and activist, 39What book has most inspired you?I really did enjoy the Loud Black Girls anthology. It’s a wonderful constellation of extraordinary voices, contradictions, ambitions and histories. As someone who has spent much of her life moving between different worlds, I’m interested in the people who refuse to be reduced to a single identity.What albums or artists have most shaped your sense of self?Growing up in Edinburgh, my relationship with identity has always been layered. Music was one of the places where those layers could coexist without requiring an explanation. I have toured the world with artists from Lauryn Hill, the Roots and Skepta to Wu-Tang Clan and Roots Manuva. They have all in different ways challenged the idea that we must make ourselves smaller to fit into the world.View image in fullscreenRZA and Ghostface Killah of Wu-Tang Clan performing at the O2 Arena in London, March 2026.Photograph: Simone Joyner/Getty ImagesWhat cultural moments have felt most significant to you?The emergence of grime as a defining British sound. It brought the ingenuity, language and lived realities of young people from communities too often treated as peripheral into the centre of British culture. It was a reminder that culture does not need permission to become influential.If you were PM for the day, what would be your first priority?I would bring education, culture and economic opportunity much closer together. I’d usher in properly funded creative education, meaningful careers guidance, paid routes into industries that have historically relied on unpaid internships, and a serious commitment to ensuring that young people from every background can participate in Britain’s cultural and economic life.Which Black historical figure has most influenced you?Margaret Ekpo was an inspiring Nigerian women’s rights activist and politician who fought for equality and the empowerment of women. At a time when women were often denied a voice in politics, she bravely stood up for their rights and encouraged them to participate in decision making.What political development in the UK has most disappointed or uplifted you?The repeated pressure on public services, education and the arts concerns me deeply. These are not peripheral concerns; they shape our ability to participate in society, develop our talents and understand one another. What has uplifted me is the progress made in recognising the breadth of Britain’s history and the people who have shaped it.What is most misunderstood between generations?I think each generation underestimates the difficulty of the world the other has inherited. Older generations can sometimes mistake the language of younger people for a lack of resilience, when it may actually be a more sophisticated vocabulary for identifying problems that were previously endured in silence. Younger generations, meanwhile, can underestimate the ingenuity and sacrifices of those who navigated a world with fewer of the freedoms and resources we now take for granted.What is a“good life”?To have been a source of utter joy and kindness to the world. To use my inspiration to help and heal. Loving my family, doing good and letting the rest be. In the end it’s not what you own or worry about, it’s who you loved and the good you left behind.What would you change about your life?Absolutely nothing.‘My first act as PM? Bring in conscription for teaching’Ade AdepitanPresenter, disability advocate, former wheelchair basketball player and gold medal-winning Paralympian, 53What book has most inspired you?King Leopold’s Ghost by Adam Hochschild opened my eyes to history. I have always had this craving for more knowledge about Africa, the world and why it is the way it is. It talks about the origins of racism and race theory, and where we are socially and politically in the world – you can see the roots of it from this book.What albums or artists have most shaped your sense of self?I gotShut Up and Dance’salbum Dance Before the Police Come when it came out in the 1990s. It is a seminal album from a time when British music was still trying to find itself. It is like a cross between hip-hop, breakbeat and dance – they were like the Prodigy before the Prodigy. I felt like the album had the right amount of anger and cultural references. Soul II Soul were pretty influential when I grew up, and Massive Attack were big for me as well.What cultural moments have felt most significant to you?The London 2012 Olympics and Paralympics. The opening ceremony was a real celebration of Britishness, of who we are and who we had become. It talked about everything from Black culture to white British culture, and we all celebrated it.View image in fullscreenThe London 2012 Olympic opening ceremony in Stratford, London, 27 July 2012.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesIf you were PM for the day, what would be your first priority?There are so many things like accessible housing and transport, but I just couldn’t get away from education. I get asked to go to a lot of schools to do talks and assemblies and I can’t understand how we can’t see that the difference between private and state education is so stark in terms of resources, facilities, everything. It is insane that we have a two-tier system with such a wide discrepancy. I would ringfence a certain percentage of GDP to go into state school education. Or introduce something like a kind of conscription for people who have been highly educated or have a degree to teach. I think everyone at some point should have to do a stint in teaching and put back into society.What Black historical figure has most influenced you?James Baldwin, because he was so articulate and an incredible communicator. He grew up in probably the most divisive and dysfunctional country in the world: the US. In a country where you could literally get shot for stating those types of views, he was brave enough to make it look at itself.What political development in the UK has most disappointed or uplifted you?What has most disappointed me is that a lot of our policies and political leaders have allowed their politics to be shaped by anger. Angry rhetoric about immigrants, about benefits; anger about taxes, or the country being overregulated. Arguably, if we hadn’t listened to some of these very vocal groups and allowed ourselves to be shaped by them, we may not have had Brexit. More appropriate regulation, rather than a focus on less regulation, might have avoided a tragedy such as Grenfell.What has most uplifted me is people starting to take more notice of politics. I think when I was growing up there was a lot of apathy when it came to political ideas. We were not as aware of what was going on. But people now have been forced to [take notice], because we have been in a period of high political flux and [experiences] like Covid have made us examine who we are.What is most misunderstood between generations?My generation thinks the millennials’ lives are really easy: “They are not as resilient as we were.” But then millennials will say: “You guys didn’t have to deal with the kind of world we had to.” We had 9/11 and that turned the world upside down. Then the next generation says: “Look at us; we are dealing with social media and cannot afford to buy a house.” We allow ourselves to be put into these groups and these groups are then put against each other.What is a“good life”?It’s about feeling happy and fulfilled. If you manage to find your thing, no matter whatever else happens to you in life you will always be able to go back to that. For me, it’s sports and family – they anchor me.What would you change about your life?What I regret is that a lot of my success came after my parents passed away or their health deteriorated, so we couldn’t enjoy as much.I would have loved my dad to have been a grandfather to [Ade’s children] Bolla and Zayla, and for my mum to have had more time while she was well with Bolla, and to have met Zayla. I would have liked things to have aligned when I was at my best and they were at their best. That would have been nice.‘No political development has uplifted me – we always return to the status quo’Vanley BurkePhotographer and artist, 75What book has most inspired you?The books by the Black photographers Gordon Parks and James Van Der Zee. They most influenced my visual style.What albums or artists have most shaped your sense of self?Catch a Fireby Bob Marley and the Wailers undoubtedly had and continues to have an impact on me. His lyrics are so visual. Notable mentions: Burning Spear’s Marcus Garvey, Culture’s Two Sevens Clash, Stevie Wonder’s Songs in the Key of Life. The work of Nina Simone. So many great albums, it’s difficult to choose one.What cultural moments have felt most significant to you?The release of Nelson Mandela, perhaps because I was in Africa for the first time when it happened. This significant moment offered hope not just for South Africa but also beyond the shores of the continent.If you were PM for the day, what would be your first priority?Acknowledging the evils of the enslavement of African people over centuries, the teachings of colonial history and its impact on British society, and having serious plans about how we can pay reparations for the labour of enslaved Africans.Which Black historical figure has most influenced you?The visionary Marcus Garvey offered hope for the Black people; he was not just a thinker but he also got things done. He was one of the most accomplished orators of all time. His thoughts and philosophy continue to reverberate throughout Africa and the diaspora.View image in fullscreenMarcus Garvey in 1924.Photograph: Photo 12/Universal Images Group/Getty ImagesWhat political development in the UK has most disappointed or uplifted you?No political development has uplifted me because we always return to the status quo, which is disappointing. Thatcher’s legacy and its continued legacy on the working classes, the selling of council houses, the dismantling of the manufacturing industry, privatisation and closing the coal mines. Her policies benefited a few but resulted in many of the issues that blight our communities today.What is most misunderstood between generations?Most people – especially the younger generation – are plugged in and switched on to their own universe, leaving very little time to communicate with each other. Meanwhile, the bridging generation is having to deal with an ever-changing work-life balance, making it difficult for them to provide the necessary support bringing both sides together.What is a“good life”?Not having to be conscious of race on a daily basis or even at all. But that isn’t going to be possible in my lifetime. And being able to pay your bills.What would you change about your life?I’ve been quite happy with my life. I’m not sure I would change anything, perhaps tweak a few things. Changing one thing can have detrimental consequences on the rest of your life.Explore more on these topicsBlack History MonthOpinionRaceArlo ParksAde AdepitanVanley BurkecommentShareReuse this content

title: Jump scares, leather gloves and squeaking moth noises: theatre horror masters on how they make their shows so scary | Stage | The Guardian
description: Whether in the immersive haunted horror show Blackout or the campily satisfying 2:22: A Ghost Story, ‘tis the season to be scared witless. Meet the theatre-makers who are putting the horror into Halloween
Author: Kate Wyver
Headline: Whether in the immersive haunted horror show Blackout or the campily satisfying 2:22: A Ghost Story, ‘tis the season to be scared witless. Meet the theatre-makers who are putting the horror into Halloween
Content: Devil in the details … Ami Okumura Jones and Ty Fanning in Paranormal Activity.Photograph: Matt CrockettView image in fullscreenDevil in the details … Ami Okumura Jones and Ty Fanning in Paranormal Activity.Photograph: Matt CrockettStageJump scares, leather gloves and squeaking moth noises: theatre horror masters on how they make their shows so scaryWhether it’s immersive chiller Blackout or the campily scary 2:22: A Ghost Story, ‘tis the season to be scared witless at the theatre. But what’s the secret to making an audience gasp in terror?Kate WyverSat 31 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 08.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was 1am. Total darkness. Locking up a wedding venue, Sam Beech’s car sensor went off: there was something behind him. “It went on for half an hour,” the writer and director recalls, “on the front bumper, then round the back. But every time I looked, there was nothing.” It kept going, snuffling around the car. So he stopped looking. “I thought: ‘If I don’t look behind me, it won’t get me.’” Since then, Beech, the creator of one of a plethora of horror shows currently haunting the stage, admits, “I don’t like driving in the dark”.Beech’s experience was eerily similar to a scene in Andy Nyman’s hit 2010 playGhost Stories, which Beech had seen four times, so the gnarly end the character had met on stage filled his mind when the sensor went off in the dark. Now, the uncanny experience has fed into his own new horror showBlackout(touring the UK to 27 February), which uses everything that made him so scared that night: the quiet, the absence, the idea of something lurking in the shadows. “It’s the Jaws effect,” says Chris Fisher, the illusions designer behind the stage show ofParanormal Activity(at London Ambassador’s theatre to 27 February, and touring the UK), which had me sheepishly checking under my bed for several nights and stopped just short of nightmares. “It’s scarier to see the fin and hear the music,” Fisher says, “than it is to see the mechanical head of the shark.”On stages across the country, theatre-makers are hoping to make their audiences grab the arms of strangers next to them. But it’s easy to go wrong with horror, Fisher says: “It often goes too far, too hammy. Too – and I say this affectionately – Blithe Spirit.” But when you get it right, he says, discounting Noël Coward’s farce about an eccentric clairvoyant, “people leave with a newfound understanding of what theatre can do”.View image in fullscreenFear factor … Blackout.Photograph: Craig FullerFor years, 1987’s The Woman in Black was the reigning champion of achieving a proper nail-biting scare on stage. On a sparse set, the show invited the audience to imagine a pony and trap as the story set off, priming them, like Beech’s stalking shadow and Fisher’s Jaws theory, to fill in the gaps for themselves. It was unrivalled for years, but recently, perhaps kicked off by the success of Ghost Stories, there’s been an increasing flood of shows trying to eke out new ideas of horror plays. The campily satisfying haunted house thriller2:22: A Ghost Storyis ever-touring and the hallucinatoryStranger Things: The First Shadow(which also features Fisher’s illusions) is going strong in London’s West End. Farther west in the city, at the Bush theatre, Mei Leng Yew’s recent debutThe Hungry Ghostplayed with Chinese traditions and queer obsession to create a nightmarish story of possession. Going down the route of psychological horror, the immersive touring experienceSinsuses audience participation to determine what happens on stage. This Halloween season, the ghosts and ghouls have busy schedules.double quotation markIt only takes one mistimed moment for your brain to go: I didn’t believe that“Maybe 2.22 was so successful that it just initiated a cascade,” says comedian Kirsty Mann, who tests her audience’s belief in ghosts with a true tale of her haunted house in the comedy-horrorCorpse, which is coming to London’sSoho theatrein February after an Edinburgh fringe run. “These things come in cycles,” she says. “But people go to the theatre for escapism and horror is the ultimate escapism. There’s so much awfulness in the world right now, people are turning more to the fantastic, and with horror, you’re not just following the story. You’re totally separated from reality.” Now, finding the scariest night out possible has become “almost a drug”, Fisher says, for audiences chasing the high of the collective fright. “It’s like being on a rollercoaster,” says Mann, who saw Paranormal Activity three times in one month.The line between successful scare and unimpressed shrug is a fine one. “It’s a bit like comedy,” says Carolyn Downing, sound designer onThe Silence of the Lambs, the stage adaptation of the psycho-killer movie that is touring the UK to 26 June. “It has to be super-precise. It only takes a mistimed or misaligned moment, and your brain’s quick enough to go: ‘I didn’t believe that.’” The success of that minuscule moment relies on the atmosphere created by dozens of people backstage. “It’s all about the buildup,” Downing says. Achieving the perfect jump scare requires the increase in tension, the wrongfooting, and the offbeat fright just as you’ve relaxed. “It won’t scare you if you’re half expecting it,” she says.View image in fullscreenPhantom of the theatre … Sophie Lenglinger and Robin Morrissey in The Haunting of Hill House.Photograph: Pamela RaithHorror works best, set designer Ti Green believes, “when your understanding of the rules are pulled apart”. For the stage adaptation of Shirley Jackon’s 1959 gothic novelThe Haunting of Hill House, Green wanted to build a world that looked solid and dependable. “That’s the first step,” she says. “The second is to dismantle everyone’s sense of safety.” Jackson’s story is a quintessential haunted house, with a group of ghost seekers wandering around a decrepit mansion. Paying homage to Jackson’s description of “Hill House, not sane”, much of Green’s set is made of translucent gauze, so depth and vision can play with the idea that everything is constantly in flux, making it feel, she says, “as if the house is doing it, not as if the theatre is doing it”.In Blackout, Beech aims for the opposite effect: he wants the theatre itself to feel haunted. Having created the award-winning Statfold Scream Park, he is moving his experience in horror events on stage with this touring show that plays in each venue for just one night. “Five hundred people walk into a theatre and choose to accept something they know isn’t real,” he says, setting up the show, which is framed as a rehearsal. With the audience as ghosts to the action, Blackout aims to dissect and strengthen the classic tropes of horror: “darkness, silence, negative space”. As in The Woman in Black, the agreement to suspend disbelief allows the paranormal to take a step closer.double quotation markThe juiciness of horror is that you can zoom in on sound, make it feel visceral and intenseThese conventions of horror on stage are not cheat codes. “Anyone can go and buy a magic trick and try to perform it,” Fisher says, “but they’re not actually doing real magic. It’s all about how you present it, what story you put with it. It’s the same with horror.” Many of the principles of good illusion – and good horror – have remained largely unchanged over time. “For Paranormal Activity, I went back to the ways that Victorian magicians or spiritualists would have done it,” Fisher says. “The majority of the illusions could have been used for hundreds of years.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIllusions such as Fisher’s have become a significant selling point for modern horror on stage, perhaps, as Mann suggests, because they give a “wow factor” that is hard to recreate on screen with the ubiquitous powers of AI and CGI. “In live theatre, if you pull off an amazing trick,” she says, “you can have that moment of, ‘Holy shit, how did they do that?’”View image in fullscreenCell mates … Mollie Gallagher and John Partridge in The Silence of the Lambs.Photograph: Marc BrennerMaximising the bodily experience of sharing the space, theatre has the opportunity to be even scarier than film, allowing the fear to slip off the stage and follow you home. “The really scary stuff is when it taps into a deep fear you have,” says Mann. In Corpse, which uses minimal set and choice illusions by John Bulleid, she pushes on the bruise of the feeling: this could happen to me.Other shows have the challenge of a direct comparison with their originals; that Paranormal Activity, The Silence of the Lambs and The Haunting of Hill House, which is touring the UK to 21 November, are all adaptations says something of the endurance of spooky stories. For The Silence of the Lambs, Downing felt a responsibility to achieve the iconic sound of moths, which marks a significant turning point in the story. Using foley techniques, she’s previously made the sound of birds with flapping leather gloves, but the moths needed to be smaller and finer. Her list of moth-making ingredients includes rustling leaves, swooshing paper, rubbed hands and the real recorded squeaking of death’s-head hawkmoths. “The juiciness of horror is that you can zoom in on sound,” she says, “make it feel visceral and intense.”This is key; a horror play has to be felt. So much of that feeling being handed over to the audience, Fisher says, is down to the actors. “Like with illusion, when you see something again and again, you become a bit jaded with it. It’s the same thing with horror scares. It’s so important to keep those reactions as if they are experiencing it for the first time, because that’s what we’re doing.”Halloween in the UK is growing. “We’re about 10 or 15 years behind America,” says Beech. “I think that’s probably the same with horror shows and audience appetite.” As demand grows, so do these theatre-makers’ ambitions. “I want to keep pushing it,” says Fisher. When the Paranormal Activity team recently locked the show in New York, he says, “we all sat down for dinner, together for the first time in months, and were like, ‘What shall we do next?’” He nods to me: “Make sure you have those nightmares.”Explore more on these topicsStageHalloweenTheatrefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘The sexy stuff has got to be coming to an end, right?’: Rivals star Aidan Turner on beards, ballroom dancing and putting Poldark to bed | Aidan Turner | The Guardian
description: His dashing lead role in Jilly Cooper’s bonkbuster didn’t hurt the actor’s pin-up status, but now, he protests, he’s 43 – and a dad
Author: Rebecca Nicholson
Headline: His dashing lead role in Jilly Cooper’s bonkbuster didn’t hurt the actor’s pin-up status, but now, he protests, he’s 43 – and a dad
Content: All portraits: Stephanie Siân Smith/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAll portraits: Stephanie Siân Smith/The GuardianAidan TurnerInterview‘The sexy stuff has got to be coming to an end, right?’: Rivals star Aidan Turner on beards, ballroom dancing and putting Poldark to bedRebecca NicholsonHis dashing lead role in Jilly Cooper’s bonkbuster didn’t hurt the actor’s pin-up status, but now, he protests, he’s 43 – and a dadSat 31 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAidan Turner has a tactical beard. For the last two decades or so, the actor has found himself in roles that have made him a smouldering pin-up. Audiences really love to look at him. You can buy mugs that say, “Today I don’t feel like doing anything … exceptAidan Turner.” There are entire Reddit forums dedicated to sharing photographs of him looking hot. He knows this about himself, just like he knows that people want to ask him about it. “I do get asked these questions,” he says, a little wearily. “I do get the, you know, word ‘smoulder’ or ‘sexy’, and all that kind of shit.” So right now, he has a full beard, in the hope that he will not be accused of, for example, smouldering. “I thought it wouldn’t happen so much with the beard,” he sighs. “I thought I could get away with it. I was going for ‘dad’.”The job of actors is to sell a story as well as they possibly can, and over the years plenty of the stories that Turner has sold have involved romance and sex. He appeared in Les Liaisons Dangereuses at the National Theatre in London this summer, and even the New Yorker noted how much he smoulders. In some ways, Turner is one of those male performers who is, well, a little bit objectified. The fact that he is a good actor, and also known for being sexy, places him in a peculiar bind. If he doesn’t gamely play along, if he points out that he’s getting a bit tired of it actually, then he risks being seen as a killjoy. Sure, there are worse burdens to bear, but at times the star ofPoldarkandRivalsfinds himself in a curious position.Turner is 43 now. (He is literally a dad – he and his wife, the American actor Caitlin FitzGerald, have got a small son.) His early roles showed off his ability to handsomely, pensively brood. He was a vampire in the sci-fi seriesBeing Human, and played Dante Gabriel Rossetti in Desperate Romantics, writing moody poetry in soft light. Then, in 2015, he starred in the BBC’s hugely popular adaptation of Poldark, which turned him into a household name. As Ross Poldark, an 18th-century soldier, he loved, fought and, very famously, swung a scythe. The attention that came with it made his career, but it also put him off sexy roles for a while. Then a few years later, Rivals came along.View image in fullscreenTurner with his wife, Caitlin FitzGerald, in 2024.Photograph: Kate Green/Bafta/Getty Images for BaftaRivals is outrageously fun and smutty. It adapts Jilly Cooper’s Rutshire Chronicles novels, the kind of books that would once have been known as bonkbusters, into big, brash television. In her fictionalised version of the Cotswolds in the 1980s, Cooper brought together aristocrats, MPs and cut‑throat television executives. Everyone is having sex with everyone; everyone is ready to stab their neighbour in their back, and probably have sex with them at the same time. Everyone, that is, except Turner’s character, Declan O’Hara, a serious‑minded broadcast journalist who is unusually faithful to his wife, Maud – and also dashingly handsome. So here Turner is again, fielding questions about intimacy coordinators, sex scenes and his very full moustache.double quotation markJilly Cooper’s parties were exactly what you would imagine. The champagne never stopped flowing, and her dogs were everywhereThe moustache was his idea. “Isayit was my idea,” he begins, then corrects himself. “It fuckingwasmy idea.” Turner swears like it is going out of fashion. He has just finished today’s photoshoot, so we have gone to find a quiet spot to chat, and have ended up in a basement, surrounded by bikes and cleaning products and tools. He is out of the fancy clothes and back in his east London dad uniform of white T-shirt, navy chore jacket and jeans. He explains that he had turned up for the Rivals job with a full beard, and if they were going to shave it off, he told them, he had no intention of using a stick-on prosthetic. “You end up eating hairs all day and if you smile it falls off,” he says. “I think everyone on set has now learned the lesson of no stickies.” So they shaved him down to a moustache first, and decided they liked it, and that’s what stuck. It also gave Declan a bit more gravitas. “I don’t want to make this about getting into character or anything. All that stuff gives me the creeps, actors talking about that,” he says, squirming. “But [the moustache] is really helpful, because Declan feels older to me. Like, he’s a bit more of a grownup than I am.” Turner grew up in Dublin and has the accent to prove it, but Declan has a Westmeath accent, a bit deeper than his own, which he borrowed from his father, Pearse. “So with that, and the geography teacher outfits, everything feels more mature.”View image in fullscreenRivals has been a juggernaut for all involved. The TV series is nostalgic and knowing, horny and hilarious, but the new episodes find the show in a more gloomy mood. It opens with a funeral – don’t panic; I counted, and it only takes 15 minutes to get to a sex scene – and trouble is brewing for Declan and Maud’s marriage. “It’s a big one,” Turner nods, though spoiler etiquette dictates he cannot say too much.The fact that Rivals can swing so comfortably between profound grief, camp backstabbing and joyful infidelity gives it a very particular tone. Why does Turner think that audiences have lapped it up? “I mean, I was born in ’83, and there is this yearning for that nostalgia, I suppose. And Jilly Cooper has a certain tone. She was looked over for many years. It was seen as this low-rent, smutty kind of literature, and I don’t know if a lot of people gave it a chance. That doesn’t seem to be the case any more.” He has noticed that it appeals to lots of age groups, and for the first time in a while people in their 20s are coming up to him in the street. “Rivals is funny, and it knows exactly what it is,” he offers. “It’s unapologetic. It’s on the front foot and it’s out there, going, this is what we’re doing, this is who we are.”View image in fullscreenTurner as Declan O’Hara in Rivals.Photograph: Robert Viglasky/ Disney+Cooper was heavily involved in the first season, and they were in the middle of shooting the second whenthe author diedsuddenly, at the age of 88. Turner has fond memories of her. “She was famous for throwing these parties at her house in the Cotswolds that were just exactly what you would imagine,” Turner says. “They were so much fun. The champagne never stopped flowing, and her dogs were everywhere. She was so spirited.” He was filming the immediate aftermath of those funeral scenes when he sensed that something was going on. “It was eerie already, and I mentioned to Victoria [Smurfit, who plays Maud] that this feels weird. It feels very dark, and,like, not Rivals. And then we took a break, and I knew something was up.” The line producer broke the news to the cast that Cooper had died.Five weeks earlier, Turner says, he had been at one of those famous parties. “And she was making speeches and drinking champagne and introducing me to people. She was her brilliant, funny, filthy self.” Cooper would often swing by the set. “I’m just glad that she got a chance to see the show, to see where it was going and how it was looking, and she was really proud of it.”Given the amount of sex involved in Rivals, it is no surprise that they use intimacy coordinators to assist with the choreography. Turner remembers the time before intimacy coordinators were commonplace, and he finds it much better, and much easier, now that they are readily available on sets. In the past, he remembers working with directors who were hands-off or awkward when it came to sex scenes. “They just kind of leave it to you. And I don’t know whether that’s a really good thing, you know, because it’s, like, what the fuck do we do? And is this OK? And does this work?” Having a professional who is there to figure that out is really useful. “I think it’s important, especially in a show like this, to sell the scene and to do what we’re doing, because there are so many different types of sex in this show. It helps us a lot.”Turner was in his early 30s when he got the lead in Poldark, the BBC’s second adaptation of the Winston Graham novels, about a soldier returning home from the American revolutionary war. It turned you into a pin-up, I suggest. He takes a breath so deep that it could fill a Cornish tin mine. “I suppose they were positioning Ross to be that,” he concedes, carefully. “There was a sex in Ross, wasn’t there, I suppose,” he says, with a chuckle, “that previously wasn’t there.” He mentionsthe photographof him taken behind the scenes, in a field, topless, with a scythe. For the last 10 years, it has appeared again and again, which, he says, is “all quite embarrassing. It kind of went everywhere.” In it, Turner is being touched up by the show’s makeup artist Jacqui Fowler, who is often airbrushed out of the shot, much to his disdain. “She’s there with the makeup brush, brilliant Jacqui, and I don’t know what she’s doing … ”Was she painting his muscles? (I meant enhancing them, rather than adding them.) “No! That was something I fucking worked hard for,” he laughs. “I was 12 years younger. It was probably a lot easier to get in shape. But I was, like, no, this guy is a farmer. He’s on the horse all the time. We never really see him eating. When he is, it’s fucking gruel. He’s probably quite lean.” So Turner decided that he needed to get in shape, too. As with the Rivals moustache, it was his idea to go topless in the scything scene, and he had no idea that it would still be talked about a decade later. “I made some friends on the show that I’m still friends with now, and I’m proud of it. It had a really strong audience, and we tried to do something different with it, and I think we did. But all of that stuff wasembarrassing, because it just kind of follows you around a little bit. But it might not have been successful if we didn’t have any of that at all.”View image in fullscreenTurner as Ross Poldark with Eleanor Tomlinson as Poldark’s wife, Demelza.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyFor a few years afterwards – until Rivals, in fact – Turner resisted taking roles that he knew would require him to be sexy. DidPoldarkput him off? “It did, yeah,” he says. In photoshoots now, for example, he might politely decline to pose in a way that seems suggestive. “It just feels different, at 43, and being a dad,” he shrugs. Then again, he admits, he is here to talk about Rivals. Also, he has just finished Les Liaisons Dangereuses, that famously sex-focused play, in which his character Valmont manipulates women into bed, for sport and for the sheer sociopathic thrill of it. “And you’re, like, well, I mean, you’re asking for it, dude!” he laughs. He is nothing if not self-aware. “But then, I feel like this sexy stuff has got to be coming to an end. Right? Tell me it’s done.” I think that’s up to him. “For sure, and it is. But the roles are getting more interesting, and less about … that.”Turner has never done social media and says he has never felt any pressure to sign up to it. “No. You would definitely get more free shit if you had a few million followers on Instagram. I do meet people and I’m, like, where did you get that? And they’re, like, oh, it got sent to me.” But he knows it’s not worth it. “I don’t need those trainers. Most people I know are on it, but I don’t really want to share those things. And I don’t think I’d be very good at doing it. I would probably get it wrong. I’d probably either overshare, or not do it enough.”Turner does not strike me as an oversharer. He mentions early mornings taking his son to school after a late night at the theatre, or trips with him to the West End to see The Lion King and Paddington, but otherwise he is tight-lipped on life outside work. “I draw the line at the personal stuff. And plus, I’ve always just felt, like, who wants to hear from me? I always felt that, in the early days of Twitter or X or whatever. It takes so much confidence, doesn’t it, to go, ‘People want to hear exactly what I have to say in this sentence.’ Wow. Theballson that. Jesus. I’d love some of that courage.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhen not being forced to examine the embarrassment of being objectified as a man in your 40s by horrible, intrusive journalists, Turner is great company. He is funny; he is as charming, as you might expect; and he is more than happy to discuss big, state‑of-the-world stuff. Take this morning. He was listening to a podcast aboutMeta’s new AI assistant, he says. “They will do shit for you. They’ll order food and deliver it to a friend of yours, and they’ll make sure that if you want to get paid, you’ll get paid, and they’ll make sure your mortgage gets done every month, and they’ll do everything. But you’ve just got to give them all of you.” He realised, for the first time, that he was scared of what might happen next. “There could be a moment where it’s, like, no, sorry, Aidan, there is no money for you. We need that money for a datacentre.” The podcast talked about how helpful AI could be, as well as how destructive. “But this has already been downloaded by millions of people, and I’m, like, we’re walking straight into this fire, aren’t we? This might be coming for us faster than I thought.”double quotation markI was actually quite a shy kid, and there’s still a lot of that in thereView image in fullscreenDoes he worry about AI coming for his job? The late Gene Wilder’s voice has been reactivated for a Netflix reality show;Tilly Norwood, the world’s first AI actor, has been unleashed on Hollywood, to middling results. “It will get better and better, and it’s about how comfortable we are when it does get amazing and we can’t tell the difference,” he says. “I don’t know whether I want to read a novel from an AI author. I want the human. I want the connection.” Maybe he is showing his age, he says, “but I don’t want to write us off yet. I don’t want a painting that’s been generated by AI. I want to see oil and canvas and acrylic. Call me old school, but I want the humans to win that battle.”Turner lives in London now, with FitzGerald and their son. He moved to the city in his 20s, after a few years of doing theatre in Dublin. “My first TV job brought me over, and I never really went back,” he says. “I love London. For me, it’s still one of the most exciting cities in the world.” The couple have lived in the US for short periods of time, too, though neither was keen on settling there. For political reasons? “I’m not going to lie.  Guns scare me, and we have a young child, and I don’t want to worry about that every day. I know we have our own problems in this country, but the guns thing scares me. I think the healthcare system is completely fucked [in America]. God forbid you’re not very wealthy, because if you get sick and you don’t have much money, or even if you’re doing all right, it will take everything. That just seems crazy to me.”Turner grew up in Clondalkin, in the west of County Dublin, with his brother and his parents. “We were a working-class family. My dad retired a few years ago, but he was an electrician, and my mum is an accountant.” He had a grandmother who did amateur dramatics, but otherwise there was no history of performing in the family. When Turner realised he wanted to go to drama school, at 18, “there was a certain mould being broken, there”. But, he says, he did have some experience of being on stage. “It would be remiss of me not to say that there was an unusual part of my childhood where I danced,” he begins.View image in fullscreenHe was not just a casual dancer. He danced ballroom and Latin American from the age of six to 17, and at one point he came third in the All-Ireland dance championships. “That’s weird as fuck,” he laughs. “I mean, not odd, but just not the norm for a kid from west Dublin, which is quite poor. My mum and dad spent a lot of money to fund that.” He describes the world of competitive dancing in vivid detail. “There were trophies everywhere, and we went to a competition and it was tails and suits and numbers on the back, and fake tan and Elnett hairspray and pushy mums.“I went to schools that were quite rough, and I danced right up until I was 17,” he continues. “And I told everyone!” Was he given a hard time for it? “I don’t think they believed me, that’s my theory.” He has seen old friends who have since read about his dancing years, and they told him that they didn’t think he was being serious. “These are working-class boys, who are 14, 15, and we’re all drinking cider on a Friday night and smoking cigarettes and doing whatever else. And you tell them that you’re away to Blackpool this weekend, that you dance, and theymightbelieve you. But they don’t want to take part in this conversation. They move away. They still want to be your mate, but they don’t have the faculties to deal with this conversation.” He gave up dancing when his dance partner got injured, and while on a break, he applied on a whim for drama school. “I was actually quite a shy kid, and there’s still a lot of that in there,” he says. Acting made him less self-conscious, and he knew straight away that it was the life for him.View image in fullscreenStyling: Lewis Munro, assisted by Louis Wesnes. Grooming: Jessica Doyle. Brioni blazer; Burberry shirt; Mithri trousers; Giorgio Armani pocket square; Jimmy Choo shoes; Gieves and Hawkes tie. Blue Celine shirt; Loewe checked jacket. Black shirt: Mithridate; black scarf: Soho Scarves; cream trousers: BrioniRivals season two review – if I could give this exquisite bonkbuster 10,000 stars, I wouldRead moreTurner has roles coming up that take him beyond the heart-throb. He is waiting for work to start on Grendel, the live-action adaptation of the 1971 novel, which tells the story of Beowulf from the monster’s perspective. Is he playing a monster? “No, no, he’s a warrior. He’s a shit warrior,” he jokes. “I don’t even know how much I can talk about that. I hope it’s still happening.” He also plays the Apostle Andrew in Terrence Malick’s forthcoming biblical epic, about the life of Jesus Christ, currently known as The Way of the Wind, though Malick is, famously, not a fast worker, and it was filmed in 2019. “Surely it’s coming out soon? I don’t know,” he says.But he has also, briefly, returned toThe Diplomat, Netflix’s popular political thriller, reprising his role as the British spy Callum Ellis. And there is no denying it: Callum is a sexy guy. “Oh, come off it. I amnotsexy in The Diplomat,” he says, firmly. “That is all you.” He really does think, or hope, that this era is almost behind him. “It must be coming to an end,” he says. But what if he’s got another 20 years of it left? “Ohno,” he says, laughing. Then groans, as if he cannot think of anything worse.Rivals season two returns to Disney on 11 November.Explore more on these topicsAidan TurnerTelevisionPoldarkBeing HumanPeriod drama (TV)DramainterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Yaga: chicken bones? Saltburn parties? This folk horror is so debauched, it’s hilarious | Television | The Guardian
description: Heated Rivalry’s Hudson Williams and Carrie-Anne Moss star in this audacious mystery about a Slavic witch. There’s supernatural weirdness, detective work … and a hero who looks a lot like Tim Key dressed in leather
Author: Rhik Samadder
Headline: Heated Rivalry’s Hudson Williams and Carrie-Anne Moss star in this audacious mystery about a Slavic witch. There’s supernatural weirdness, detective work … and a hero who looks a lot like Tim Key dressed in leather
Content: Chilled to the bone … Carrie-Anne Moss as osteo-academic Katherine in Yaga.Photograph: Bell Media/SkyView image in fullscreenChilled to the bone … Carrie-Anne Moss as osteo-academic Katherine in Yaga.Photograph: Bell Media/SkyThe watcherTelevisionYaga: chicken bones? Saltburn parties? This folk horror is so debauched, it’s hilariousHeated Rivalry’s Hudson Williams and Carrie-Anne Moss star in this audacious mystery about a Slavic witch. There’s supernatural weirdness, detective work … and a hero who looks a lot like Tim Key dressed in leatherRhik SamadderSat 31 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHalloween was once a simpler time, when neighbourhood kids would dress up as mythical serial killers, the undead or bedsheet-wearing ghosts. At some point, following America’s lead, it became sexy and cat-forward. It has now become a sort of conceptual art show.
