I’ve heard people this year planning to go to parties dressed as Erling Haaland, Prom Carrie (Prime Video edition) and Bad Bunny’s half-time Super Bowl show. It’s horrifying.The perception of witches has evolved, too. Once understood to be a malignant version of the crone archetype, sympathy for witches has grown. They have been embraced as a feminist image of the older woman, free of patriarchal command and possessed of a powerful rage. In recent years, Maleficent, Elphaba from Wicked and Marvel’s Scarlet Witch have given witches a pop edge. Some of my most intense friends proudly wear slogan T-shirts proclaiming themselves descended from the witches whom society failed to burn.Now, in swoops Yaga (Sat, 9pm, Sky Atlantic), a quasi-horror mystery series from Canadian streamer Crave. They are known for making Heated Rivalry (matching oversized jerseys? Huge Halloween outfit this year). Yaga is another genre-bender. It opens with a cocky detective, Charlie Rapp, arriving in the quiet fishing town of Whittock, present day. He’s investigating the disappearance of Henry Park, son of a wealthy local family. As the case grows violent, it brings evidence of cult activity to light, and increasingly hints at the existence of a dark, supernatural figure behind events.To those unfamiliar with Slavic folklore, Baba Yaga is a forest-dwelling hag who lives in a hut on chicken’s feet, flies around in a pestle and mortar, and eats children. It is her voice that bookends every episode in a taunting monologue, though her exact involvement with Henry’s disappearance is a grisly little puzzle. I’m a few episodes in, and it’s still unclear if she is a literal character in the play or the embodiment of its theme: women being sick of men’s shit.The men are certainly a rum bunch. Charlie Rapp is our hero – yet his credentials are questionable, and he flirts with every woman in town, including his police partner Carson. Henry Park – played by Heated Rivalry’s Hudson Williams – is vain, adulterous and given to druggy parties. Williams also plays Henry’s slippery roommate Logan. The show has fun with the unlikely physical resemblance between them, as when Logan answers the door to the surprised detectives. “I have brown eyes and glasses,” he explains with a straight face. He’s also naked under his overalls, FYI.The women are formidable, including Clark Backo’s drily unimpressed take on police detective Carson. She’s introduced as a fan of romantasy (or what her superior officer describes as “fairy smut”). Carson is unenthusiastic about pursuing the case of the missing rich kid. “Billionaires aren’t real people,” she shrugs. Even more no-nonsense is Carrie-Anne Moss as an older, morally ambiguous osteo-academic. When Charlie sits beside her at a bar and asks what excites her, she replies: “Sex. And bones.”Given the bones, and the overalls, you may be thinking: “Stuff the spooky business, are there hella sexy shenanigans?” Yes and no … The theme of Henry’s parties, which take place Gatsby-like in his absence, is Dark Solstice. Expect masked ball eroticism, fetish wear and debauchery and, elsewhere, an erotic encounter that had me laughing at the audacity. But it’s never wholesome fun. There are chicken bones in unexpected places, and Rapp in particular is haunted by horror imagery. While sex is on the menu, the male gaze is under the microscope.Playwright-creator Kat Sandler has, so far, found room on the broom to make Yaga pointed but playful, and fun while tackling the darkest of subject matter. There are Ukrainian covers of pop songs, a hero who looks like a leather-trouser version of Tim Key, and Saltburn-esque parties. But what I really want, whisper it, is for an actual witch to appear, rather than the political idea of one. I’m basic, and like pointy hats. Will this be another Blair Witch situation? How far will the witch-tease go? I’m crossing my fingers and burying the hair of a bat.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionThe watcherfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Never big enough’: inside the booming penis enlargement industry | Documentary films | The Guardian
description: In a revealing documentary, a looksmaxxing-influenced world where ‘your social capital is tied to your appearance’ has led to more men wanting more
Author: Andrew Lawrence
Headline: In a revealing documentary, a looksmaxxing-influenced world where ‘your social capital is tied to your appearance’ has led to more men wanting more
Content: ‘With very few exceptions, almost none of the partners in the movie wanted them to do this.’Photograph: World of WonderView image in fullscreen‘With very few exceptions, almost none of the partners in the movie wanted them to do this.’Photograph: World of WonderDocumentary films‘Never big enough’: inside the booming penis enlargement industryIn a revealing documentary, a looksmaxxing-influenced world where ‘your social capital is tied to your appearance’ has led to more men wanting moreAndrew LawrenceSat 31 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 11.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMan’s obsession with his member is a tale as old as time, writ large in sky-scraping edifices, in allusions that flatter (big dick energy) or offend (prick), in the countless artifacts across the ages that venerate male potency – a porn star’s description of Donald Trump’s “toadstool” penis. But it’s the booming intimate wellness industry – AKA the rash (ahem) of fillers, therapies and cosmetic procedures that have come into vogue since the little blue pill rocked the market – that most intrigued Daniel Lombroso, the esteemed documentarian who made his name at the Atlantic and the New Yorker dissecting male fragility.‘A cultural moment’: smash hit doc You Can See Everything continues to dazzle AmericaRead more“A lot of the stories I worked on at those places were kind of fringy subculture and oftentimes adjacent to white nationalism,” says Lombroso, who became aware of the rising demand for penile enhancement procedures while reporting on plastic surgery trends at the New Yorker. “I started calling all these practitioners. But to make an embedded film the way I do, you need someone who’s very open.”A 2024 study of US Google searchesnotedan increase in interest in penile-enhancement injections from 2013 through 2022. Lombroso’s 90-minute film, Manhood, puts male self-esteem issues at the heart of the trend on a cold, chafing examination table. Our guide throughout is Bill Moore, a capitalist in scrubs who gives fresh meaning to the phrase bedside manner. We meet him at home, tongue-kissing a pet lap dog while snuggled up under the covers with his male partner. We behold the full splendor of his naked body, nipped and tucked in retreat from the ravages of time and his own unforgiving eye. “Nobody would suspect I’ve ever had anything done!” he says with bracing cluelessness.We see Moore hawk outpatient penile enhancement procedures from his Dallas strip mall office for $15,000 and $20,000 a pop and tout the lowly glow-ups as career-changing, sex-life turbocharging, depression-curing – whatever patients need to hear to fork over the dough, really. “Everybody wants a boat that’s one foot longer,” one guy says as Moore sticks a long numbing needle into his nether regions. “The boat is never big enough.”We see many of these patients (though customers is the better word, since, again, Moore isnota doctor), their faces more obscured than their ink-marked private parts. The inclination toward anonymity owes as much to the physical embarrassment Moore’s clientele bring into the room as to the irony of receiving this kind of care from an out-and-proud gay man – the megachurch pastor, the border patrol agent. It’s wild to see Moore act as a machismo whisperer to men who might perceive him as less than masculine, especially as he reflects on the guilt and fear of rejection he experienced before coming out to conservative Christian family members in the deep south (not that his mother having dementia doesn’t help).Throughout the film, Lombroso manages to point out these and other paradoxes without casting judgment. “I’m not deep in the looksmaxxing world, but part of what Clavicular and those guys understand is that your social capital is tied to your appearance,” Lombroso says. “Does your penis size matter? Probably not. But there are all these stats about the huge percentage of American men who obsess over it, which was foreign to me. And it connects all these other things we talk about – like how many older American men don’t know how to make a best friend.”None of Moore’s customers embodies male loneliness quite like Ruben, a father of five who is so desperate to enlarge his penis that he moves his family in with an ex to raise money for an enhancement procedure. “I have to sell my house this weekend, and I’m going to Bill after.” Lombroso recalls Ruben telling him in a phone call. “I was like, ‘OK, I’ll be there tomorrow.’ The only way to make a film like this, because I’m in New York and this was in Texas, was to fly out on a whim every time and just capture things as they happened.”Ruben fills his days listening to Joe Rogan prattle on about the marginalization of manly men and spends nights performing at comedy open mics in bars to crickets – and zero friends in the crowd. His jokes about child abuse are as wince-inducing as the circular logic of upgrading his manhood. He believes it will help protect and provide for his family, even as it fundamentally destabilizes them. “He’s actually a very loving father,” Lombroso says. “A good guy. But he escapes into these worlds like many of us do, and I think eventually it caught up to him.”Meanwhile, Lana, Ruben’s poor wife, overwhelmed by the succession of shocks his big dick sidequest has imposed on their lives, is pushed ever closer to divorce. “With very few exceptions, almost none of the partners in the movie wanted them to do this,” Lombroso says. “You see Lana kind of against it, but not taking too strong of a stance.”But the film takes its strangest turn with David, a handsome young man who seeks out Moore’s help repairing the damage from an enhancement procedure botched by another dubious quasi-physician – Victor Loria, a gruff George Costanza-type who brags about growing up in a “connected” family (“We lived the Goodfellas life,” he says, wondering “when are we going to jail, basically”) and keeps a large malpractice insurance disclaimer nailed to his front office wall like Martin Luther’s 95 Theses. Loria is the film’s villain, in case that wasn’t clear.View image in fullscreenA still from Manhood.Photograph: World of WonderDavid seems plucked from a casting call for the reality TV series Botched, a naive keen to hit control-Z after going under the knife too young and, perhaps, steer others away from rushing down that same path. But as his arc unfolds and his OnlyFans porn-acting past is revealed, it turns out he and Moore have more in common than just deeply religious parents who viewed homosexuality as an abomination. They share a bed, too – with Moore’s partner and the dog. That David risks permanent damage from this corrective procedure only heightens the stakes around the throuple bombshell.Lombroso calls the effort to compel David’s participation in the film “one of the hardest acts of persuasion I’ve ever done. It took the entire film to convince him. We were going to use AI face replacement. But right around the rough-cut stage, when we realized he was the heartbeat of the story, we flew him into New York and showed him – and he loved it. Told his family everything. Now he’s touring with the film. It’s the best.”Weaving between David’s feelgood story, Loria’s villainy and Ruben’s allegory is Moore – the honest broker who still lulls customers into thinking he’s a doctor, who travels to conferences to show actual doctors how to get in on the male-enhancement gold rush, and who sells his wares as an antidote to all the cosmetic procedures women can get to feel better about themselves. His massive house and impressive car collection speak more plainly to his motives in this space than his riffs to customers about self-esteem or the blarney about posting their post-op results on his company website.Moore’s company PhalloFill, which specializes in “girth enhancement”, has expanded to 32 locations across the country. He hopes to make the procedure as common as Botox. “Bill tried to get me to have my penis enlarged,” says Lombroso. The thought never occurred. “I said my mom would never forgive me.”But the great shame in Manhood isn’t that Moore and other practitioners in this charcoal gray area of medicine lavish their customers with patience and empathy. It’s that few see the tender treatment for what it is: gender-affirming care. “That’s why this movie has a very light touch,” Lombroso says. “So many of these things are funny and self-evident, especially to smart viewers. It’s fun to have these tough conversations and not tell people exactly how to feel in every moment.”Manhood is now playing in select US cinemas with UK and Australia dates to be announcedExplore more on these topicsDocumentary filmsPlastic surgeryMen (Society)Men's healthMen (Life and style)Body imagefeaturesShareReuse this content

Bharti, Paresh, Harminder and Maz never stopped missing the country they were born in, but they made a new home in Britain, and they made Britain better: it would be hard, for example, to calculate the size of the debt we owe Bharti for her 40 years as a social worker safeguarding children in care. Every minute of Escaping Idi Amin contains an urgent lesson to learn.”Jack SealeRead the full reviewPick of the restThis City Is OursBBC iPlayer; available nowSummed up in a sentenceJames Nelson-Joyce returns in this terrifically acted, high-stakes crime drama in Liverpool – and it’s as lovable as it is bloody.What our reviewer said“We can expect more of the following: convoluted drug deals conducted over congealing ragu; shouting; tiny-skulled henchmen with chests of astonishing bulbosity, as if someone had squeezed their legs like tubes of toothpaste and all the meat had been forced up to their armpits; beards.”Sarah DempsterRead the full reviewThe One About Matthew PerryNetflix; available nowSummed up in a sentenceThe star’s friends and family celebrate his life – and give respectful insight into his troubles as well as his career triumphs.What our reviewer said“It remains at heart a simple, sad story. But this unexpectedly candid, thoughtful, genuinely intimate film gives it nuance and depth, and a voice to wider sorrows – including what a shame it was that Perry could not enjoy his talent or appreciate the joy it gave as fully as his audiences always did.”Lucy ManganRead the full reviewFurther readingThe hidden life of Matthew Perry: ‘He would say: I need to stop and get help’You may have missed …LupinNetflix; available nowView image in fullscreenFormidable foe … Omar Sy in Lupin.Photograph: Emmanuel Guimier/NetflixSummed up in a sentenceThe French super-thief returns for a fourth series; the budget is bigger, the stakes are higher and there are lots of Houdini-style twists and thrills to be had.What our reviewer said“Omar Sy, whose performance is magnetic as always, has graduated to co-showrunner and wants to lean harder into the show’s “superhero”-like qualities. absolute most of being in the right place at the right time.”Andrew PulverRead the full reviewThe DevilsIn cinemas nowSummed up in a sentenceKen Russell’s 1971 possessed-nuns tale stars Oliver Reed out nowSummed up in a sentenceCollecting traditional songs of female struggle and strength, the Irish singer invests them with staggering power.What our reviewer said“John ‘Spud’ Murphy’s production brilliantly brings out earthy, granular details, from the sucking-in of air through Peat’s concertina bellows on Cailín Deas to the disruptive thwack of Eleanor Myler’s drums.”Jude RogersRead the full reviewPick of the restView image in fullscreenKali Malone: Burning SongIdeologic Organ; out nowSummed up in a sentenceThe US artist takes a newly compact approach to her craft, and trades technical composition methods for pure emotion on another sombre masterpiece.What our reviewer said“The heavy opening notes of Map the Path are solemn yet startlingly direct for Malone, feeling for the first time as if she’s lifting her fingers from the keys and shaking the listener by the shoulders.”Laura SnapesRead the full reviewIgor Levit: ResistanceNo Silence/Sony; out nowSummed up in a sentenceThe German pianist performs these works by Beethoven and Schoenberg – linked by Napoleon – with his characteristic exquisite touch, in interpretations full of poetry.What our reviewer said“Levit rightly sees Liszt’s piano realisation as a masterwork in and of itself and his dramatic interpretation is full of poetry, often surprisingly gentle, and with breathtaking pianissimos … In a time of bullies and despots, this is essential listening.”Clive PagetRead the full reviewView image in fullscreenThe Big Moon: ForeverFiction; out nowSummed up in a sentenceAfter frontperson Juliette Jackson lost half her hearing, she wrote sad songs and felt frustrated. So she pivoted, writing herself a happy ending. The results are joyfully convincing.What our reviewer said“The album’s sense of finding joy in sometimes difficult circumstances crystallises on the wonderfully titled You Remind Me That I’m Dying (And That It’s Good to Be Alive), those words providing what may well be this year’s most bittersweet euphoric chorus.”Dave SimpsonRead the full reviewOn tour …Macklemore’s Free Palestine tourReviewed at 3Arena, Dublin, 26 OctoberView image in fullscreenShow of hands … Macklemore in Dublin.Photograph: Zoe RainSummed up in a sentenceSeveral unannounced guests feature on the first European date of the rapper’s sold-out benefit tour, including video messages from Mark Ruffalo and Cynthia Nixon.What our reviewer said“There’s something very striking about the fact that the local artists who’ve heeded Macklemore’s call to help out are evidently committed to the cause behind it: you never get a sense of anyone rocking up in order to grab brownie points or reflected glory.”Alexis PetridisRead the full reviewFurther readingIf you really hate it when music and film stars do politics, here’s the answer: give us politics that worksExplore more on these topicsCultureThe week in reviewsTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: From Wicker to Zelda: Ocarina of Time: your complete entertainment guide to the week ahead | Culture | The Guardian
description: Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgård star in a new fantasy romance, and Nintendo’s revered 1998 classic gets a fresh coat of paint
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgård star in a new fantasy romance, and Nintendo’s revered 1998 classic gets a fresh coat of paint
Content: Wooden performance … Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgård in Wicker.View image in fullscreenWooden performance … Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgård in Wicker.Going out, staying inCultureFrom Wicker to Zelda: Ocarina of Time: your complete entertainment guide to the week aheadOlivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgård star in a new fantasy romance, and Nintendo’s revered 1998 classic gets a fresh coat of paintSat 31 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleContents1Going out: Cinema2Going out: Gigs3Going out: Art4Going out: Stage5Staying in: Streaming6Staying in: Games7Staying in: Albums8Staying in: Brain foodView image in fullscreenGoing out:CinemaWickerOut nowAnyone who has ever fantasised about having a husband made out of wicker (surely a universal dream) will want to get themselves along to this Olivia Colman romantasy about a loner fisher who does exactly that. With Alexander Skarsgård, Richard E Grant, Peter Dinklage and Elizabeth Debicki.NightbornOut nowSeidi Haarla gives a wonderfully unhinged performance as a woman convinced there is something wrong with her newborn baby: the hellish crying, her bleeding nipples … surely this child is a monster? All will be revealed in this tense but humorous supernatural drama, with Rupert Grint having fun as the sceptical new father.PrimetimeOut nowRobert Pattinson continues a recent hot streak with a characterful turn as Chris Hansen, the TV personality famous for fronting To Catch a Predator, the US hit that lured and publicly exposed men who were interested in having sex with teenagers. Directed by Lance Oppenheim (also on a hot streak with You Can See Everything).I Love BoostersOut nowShoplifting, teleportation, the consequences of sweatshop labour, designer fashion, workers’ rights and demons who suck out your soul while performing oral sex: here’s a comedy from Boots Riley that has it all. Keke Palmer, Naomi Ackie and Taylour Paige star as Bay Area shoplifters the Velvet Gang, with Demi Moore as a powerful designer.Catherine BrayGoing out:GigsView image in fullscreenSeeing red … The Avalanches.Photograph: Dean PodmorePitchfork music festival LondonVarious venues,2to 9 NovemberThe always divisive music website returns with another city festival lineup featuring the best in alternative soundscapes. Highlights include the Avalanches, Olof Dreijer, Jacob Alon and Keiyaa, plus Nigel Godrich’s new project Dragonflies, while the best band name goes to Psychedelic Porn Crumpets.Michael CraggPapa Roach1to 9 November; tour starts GlasgowTwenty-six years after their breakthrough with second album Infest, the perpetually angry nu-metallers are still going strong. Expect a heavy focus on that album – Last Resort is pretty undeniable in a live scenario – and follow-up Lovehatetragedy on this huge arena tour.MCGuildhall School’s Opera Double BillSilk Street theatre, London,2to 9 NovemberStudents on one of the country’s leading conservatoire opera courses perform two mid-century works: the UK premiere of Gian Carlo Menotti’s comic one-acter Amelia Al Ballo and Bernstein’s jazz-soaked modern classic Trouble in Tahiti. Expect high-energy professionalism and a chance to pick out the opera stars of the future.Flora WillsonFergus McCreadieThe Glasshouse, Sage Two, Gateshead,5 NovemberSince 2021, young pianist/composer Fergus McCreadie has grown in stature within the restless evolution of contemporary global jazz as a Mercury prize nominee, the traditional folk music of his Scottish homeland, and at the cutting edge of chamber music. The Glasshouse’s Innovators programme and Chamber Music Scotland showcase this adventurous wildlife-inspired co‑commission.John FordhamGoing out:ArtView image in fullscreenOn the fence … Neisser Yoel Gálvez Tabares.Photograph: James Clifford KentWinston Taylor Photo PortraitprizeNational Portrait Gallery, London,5 Novemberto 17 JanuaryThe biggest photographic portraiture prize in the country has rebranded – you might know it better as the Taylor Wessing – but is otherwise unchanged: expect the finest photography by established pros and amateurs alike, featuring work from James Clifford Kent’s long-term project Yuma, including his portrait of aspiring pentathlete Neisser Yoel Gálvez Tabares.Mad BloomsburyCharleston Firle, Lewes,4 Novemberto 11 AprilCoinciding with the centenary of Virginia Woolf’s essay On Being Ill, this show looks at how the Bloomsbury Group – the likes of Roger Fry, Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant – dealt with ideas of madness, disability and neurodiversity.Steve McQueen: ResistanceLeedsArtGallery,6 Novemberto 25 AprilDeeply moving documentation of how acts of resistance and rebellion have transformed the UK, all conceived by the brilliant Turner prize-winning artist and Oscar-winning director Steve McQueen.The Nue Black AestheticDesign Museum, London,6 Novemberto 8 AugustThis display of more than 100 objects celebrates the black creatives who are shaping the future of design in Britain, including Taiba Akhuetie, Ini Archibong and Tejumola Adenuga.Eddy FrankelGoing out:StageView image in fullscreenIt’s a scream … Jordan Brookes.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianJordan BrookesTouring to27 November; starts BristolIn 2019, the Surrey-raised standup expressed his long-held ambition to become “the existential Michael McIntyre”. In his excellent new show, The Part of You That’s Always Screaming, Brookes reaches those heights, with an unlikely combination of laugh-out-loud observational comedy and genuinely terrifying evocations of the abyss.Rachel AroestiPeanut Butter and BlueberriesLeeds Playhouse, to 7 NovemberAfter opening to strong reviews at Kiln theatre, Suhaiymah Manzoor-Khan’s thoughtful romcom transfers to Leeds. It’s about two university students and practising Muslims who move to London from the north, fall in love – but come up against harsh realities and rumbling racism.Miriam GillinsonHamlet Hail to the ThiefBarbicantheatre, London, to 23 JanuarySteven Hoggett and Christine Jones’s music- and movement-infused Hamlet lands in London. The backbone of the show is Radiohead’s 2003 album Hail to the Thief, which frontman Thom Yorke has stripped back, rewired and threaded through the show with electrifying intent.MGLuail: NōsThe Mac, Belfast,to 7 NovemberOnly formed two years ago, Luail is Ireland’s all-island national dance company, spanning Northern Ireland and the Republic. Their triple bill includes works by Belfast’s own Oona Doherty, Liz Roche and a classic from Akram Khan.Lyndsey Winshipskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenStaying in:StreamingView image in fullscreenSeeing double … Hudson Williams in Yaga.Photograph: Bell Media/SkyYagaSky Atlantic,31 October, 9pmHudson Williams swaps romance for folklore fantasy as he follows his star-making turn in Heated Rivalry by playing two characters – the missing scion of a wealthy family and his odd housemate – in Kat Sandler’s adaptation of her own play. Could a witchy professor be the key to it all?The Rise of the Rockstar ChefBBC Two/iPlayer,5 November, 9pmThe collective yearning for 2000s monoculture continues to be stoked with this documentary series about three of the decade’s rule-breaking, gamechanging chefs: Marco Pierre White, Heston Blumenthal and Gordon Ramsay (whose own production company is behind the show). Catnip for 00s nostalgists.The GreatestPrime Video,4 NovemberBoxing dramas are a Hollywood mainstay, but this year the genre is migrating to the small screen with the likes of Fightland, A Thousand Blows and this new Muhammad Ali biopic, whose first season chronicles the vertiginous early 1960s rise of the then Cassius Clay (Jaalen Best).Allies in ExileBBC Four/iPlayer,3 November, 10pmBBC Four’s Storyville strand has long brought the world’s best feature-length documentaries to television. Now briefer films will be showcased too, starting with this one following the arduous journey of two Syrian film-makers through the UK’s asylum system. An Unknown Substance, about the poisoning of a Russian politician, airs afterwards.RAStaying in:GamesView image in fullscreenMissing Link … The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.Photograph: NintendoThe Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of TimeSwitch 2; out5 NovemberThe only major game challenging GTA 6 this month is this lively, stylish remake of Nintendo’s 1998 adventure classic, in which series hero Link becomes a time traveller to save the land of Hyrule from evil warlock Ganondorf. A nostalgic treat for the ages.Wherethe Seeds FallPS5, Switch 2, PC; out5 NovemberAn intriguing action adventure which follows the human inhabitants of a vast tree as they set out to descend its branches and rediscover the land they were once forced to flee. Part mystical role-playing game, part climbing challenge.Keith StuartStaying in:AlbumsView image in fullscreenIt’ll come out in the wash … Ex:Re AKA Elena Tonra.Photograph: El HardwickEx:Re – Save AsOut nowWith her band Daughter currently between albums, Elena Tonra returns to her Ex:Re solo moniker via this second album of textural alt-rock. Songs such as Sleep creep along with a hint of menace, while opener Radio Station spins off into a trippy road trip anthem.DIIV – Zirp!Out nowAmerican alt-rock curios DIIV return with this AG Cook-produced fifth album. While steeped in their typically opaque, shoegazey textures, songs such as the pop-adjacent Kid and chunky lead single The Fountain dial up the melodies and frontman Zachary Cole Smith’s hushed vocals.Chloe Qisha – FantasizeOut nowAfter quitting a psychology degree for pop stardom, Malaysia-born, UK-based singer-songwriter Qisha found instant success with 2024’s sultry I Lied, I’m Sorry. She increases the sex chat on this debut album, specifically on gloriously overblown banger YDH, AKA young, dumb and horny.The Big Moon – ForeverOut nowLondon quartet the Big Moon return with a sunnier take on their brand of indie rock. Created as an imaginary utopia after a period of upheaval in frontwoman Juliette Jackson’s life, songs such as the buoyant Three Things and Fun offer sweet solace.MCStaying in:Brain foodView image in fullscreenProvocationsPodcastFor the numerically challenged, this new series hosted by Nihal Arthanayake is essential listening. Experts break down the big stories in finance, such as changes in lending policies and how technology can affect banking.Interior MotivesYouTubeOn the surface this video series looks like a flippant guessing game pairing pictures of domestic interiors with their owners, but it in fact uncovers fascinating truths about the ways our homes reveal our hidden selves.Concorde: The Untold StoryPBS America,2 November, 8.40pmEncompassing everything from engineering breakthroughs to espionage and political hand-wringing, this film on the race to build the first supersonic airliner between Europe, the Soviet Union and the US makes for surprisingly engaging viewing.Ammar KaliaExplore more on these topicsCultureGoing out, staying inDanceTheatreTelevisionArtGamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Guide #267: Robert Pattinson embraced his inner lowlife and became one of the best actors of his era | Culture | The Guardian
description: In this week’s newsletter: Sandra Hüller and Anne Hathaway might have been in more films this year – but Pattinson’s remarkable run confirms him as one of the best performers of his generation
Author: Gwilym Mumford
Headline: In this week’s newsletter: Sandra Hüller and Anne Hathaway might have been in more films this year – but Pattinson’s remarkable run confirms him as one of the best performers of his generation
Content: Rogues gallery .. Robert Pattinson in (clockwise from top left) The Odyssey, Dune: Part Three, Primetime and The Drama.Composite: Universal/Warner Brothers/AP/A24View image in fullscreenRogues gallery .. Robert Pattinson in (clockwise from top left) The Odyssey, Dune: Part Three, Primetime and The Drama.Composite: Universal/Warner Brothers/AP/A24The Guide newsletterCultureThe Guide #267: Robert Pattinson embraced his inner lowlife and became one of the best actors of his eraIn this week’s newsletter: Sandra Hüller and Anne Hathaway might have been in more films this year – but Pattinson’s remarkable run confirms him as one of the best performers of his generationGwilym MumfordSat 31 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 04.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor prolific actors, 2026 has been a banner year. The roles have kept piling up for a small cohort of stars, the roles have kept piling up, to the point where you wonder how they found the time to do vital things like sleep, shower or scarf down nuclear-fallout-covered chicken wings on YouTube interview shows.Just look at Sandra Hüller, who by the time December ends will have racked up six projects in 2026, ranging from austere cold war road-trip movies to migraine-inducing Marvel blockbusters. Anne Hathaway, meanwhile, has since January appeared as – deep breath – a psychologically tormentedfading pop star, a catatonicpopular novelist, a suburbanitefending off hungry dinosaurs, anIthacan queenfending off hungry suitors and reluctant fashion journo Andy in the belatedDevil Wears Prada sequel. (Hathawaydidalso have time to go on thenuclear chicken wings show, but was unable to partake, due to being heavily pregnant.)Robert Pattinson’s 2026 output looks almost leisurely compared to Hüller and Hathaway’s, though by normal standards the four films that he will have starred in by the end of year is an impressive haul. More impressive still is the quality of work, a remarkable run of roles that cements his status as one of the best performers of his era. And most certainly the best player of lowlifes: his 2026 has been a true rogues’ gallery, with every shade of scumbag accounted for.This malcontent tendency is magnificently on display inPrimetime, in UK and Irish cinemas now. Directed by Lance Oppenheim – film-maker wunderkind also behind the much-talked-about You Can See Everything – this clammy, queasy drama recalls the heyday (and ultimate demise) of To Catch a Predator, the US network reality show notorious for its stings on putative paedophiles. Pattinson plays the show’s preening host Chris Hansen, famous for his habit of sidling into the middle of an operation and casually confronting his target. Hansen’s slick, nightly news exterior disguises a grubby desire to bend the show’s ethics to breaking point, his motivations complicated by a trauma-inducing incident early in his career, and Pattinson does a great job at showing glimpses of the frayed, angry, fearful figure behind the squeaky-clean veneer. (Hansen, it should be noted, has declared the film “a completely made-up work of fiction” and “an insult to the thousands of men and women who work hard every day to protect children from predators”.)Before Primetime came The Odyssey, and another oleaginous figure for Pattinson to ooze into. His alpha-suitor Antinous was, by design, a more two-dimensional character than Hansen; a crawling, craven antagonist primarily present for audiences to bristle at and Odysseus to dispatch with extreme prejudice. Still, Pattinson nails the assignment, with a performance that some critics saw as “stealing the show” – some achievement in a gargantuan three-hour epic featuring giants, men transforming into pigs and the like.Compared to the lowlifes of Primetime and the Odyssey, Pattinson’s character in gleefully black comedyThe Dramais positively well adjusted. Indeed, initially gentle art historian Charlie is the recipient of no little sympathy in the early stages of the movie, having been broadsided by a horrifying detail – which, six months after the film’s release, I’m still wary of revealing – from the past of his bride to be (played by Zendaya, another prolific 2026 star, and one who now shares three films with Pattinson). But as Charlie unravels, his cracked decision-making and general brittleness becomes deeply unlikeable. By the day of the wedding itself, you’re half-rooting him to fail miserably – a remarkable turnaround, and testament to Pattinson’s gift for unlikability.There is of course one more performance to come this year and it’s a big onein Dune: Part Three. Pattinson plays Scytale, a shape-shifting manipulator set on usurping Timothée Chalamet’s space-messiah Paul Atreides. Another antagonist then – though Atreides’ slide into antihero-dom at the end of the previous Dune might complicate things. Still, with his dead eyes and general air of quiet menace in the film’s trailers, it’s hard to imagine Pattinson’s character will be handing out cupcakes and kittens.But what is it that makes Pattinson so adept at playing sleazeballs? Certainly his playing against type, a former Twilight heart-throb gone to seed, seems effective. It helps too that he picks roles better than just about anyone, often working with auteurs who seem to understand his magnetic/repellent duality. It’s a shame that this sort of role tends to get sidelined for worthier, more outwardly heroic parts when it comes to awards season: no one seems to be including Pattinson in their Oscar best actor prognostications.Perhaps that suits him fine – his choice of role hardly seems to be an impediment at the box office.The Odysseyis one of the highest-grossing films of the year, Dune: Part Three will probably join that bracket when it arrives in December, and both The Drama and Primetime have massively punched above their indie-film weight. And if you have had enough of him on the dark side, next year he reprises his role as the Dark Knight in the second of the latest Batman films. In the meantime, though, if you want a wrong’un played right, just call for R-Patz.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTo read the complete version of this newsletterplease subscribeto receive The Guide in your inbox every FridayExplore more on these topicsCultureThe Guide newsletterRobert PattinsonThe OdysseynewslettersShareReuse this content

title: ‘We freed Patrick Stewart!’ Star Trek’s Marina Sirtis on breaking in her beloved but very serious co-star | Patrick Stewart | The Guardian
description: She was scared of him but soon loosened the Shakespearean up – then watched him give Star Trek depth, even insisting scenes be rewritten for her. Captain Picard’s right-hand woman salutes her fabulous friend
Author: Tim Jonze
Headline: She was scared of him but soon loosened the Shakespearean up – then watched him give Star Trek depth, even insisting scenes be rewritten for her. Captain Picard’s right-hand woman salutes her fabulous friend
Content: ‘Star Trek was a punchline before he came along’ ... from left, LeVar Burton, Stewart and Sirtis.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Star Trek was a punchline before he came along’ ... from left, LeVar Burton, Stewart and Sirtis.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyPatrick Stewart‘We freed Patrick Stewart!’ Star Trek’s Marina Sirtis on breaking in her beloved but very serious co-starShe was scared of him but soon loosened the Shakespearean up – then watched him give Star Trek depth, even insisting scenes be rewritten for her. Captain Picard’s right-hand woman salutes her fabulous friendMarina Sirtis as told toTim JonzeSat 31 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’d been warned about Patrick by friends who’d worked with him at the Royal Shakespeare Company. They said: “Marina, you can’t beyouaroundPatrick Stewart. He’s all about the work. He takes itveryseriously and he won’t abide you mucking about and trying to make people corpse.”We had been cast together onStar Trek: The Next Generationand, because of what I’d heard, I was a bit scared, a bit intimidated. And let’s be honest – Patrickwasvery serious about the work. But there was a concerted effort by the rest of us to beat it out of him. We were from a younger generation and we wanted to shake up this Englishman who was so typical of his generation – stiff upper lip and a Yorkshireman to boot. You know, the kind of person who was not exactly renowned for showing their emotions. Early on Patrick told us all that we weren’t there to have fun, and you should have seen the looks he got. I’m a cockney: I’ve got a Spurs tattoo and we all looked at him in the same way I look at an Arsenal fan. But we did loosen him up. And – he’s said this himself – I think we actually freed him. We gave him a freedom that he said he’d never really felt before.double quotation markHe told the writers he really had to look into my eyes – not Data’s – to reach the emotions he neededOf course it went both ways. We learned so much from him, how could you not? We learned from his professionalism and his absolutely insane talent. He brought gravitas to the role.Star Trekwas a bit of a punchline before Patrick came along – it’s not any more. Patrick gave it depth – here was this consummate Shakespearean actor playing the captain of a starship. It just shifted everything.View image in fullscreen‘It was the absolute privilege of my life to work with him’ … Sirtis and Stewart at the Sag awards in 2011.Photograph: Abaca Press/AlamyHe had reservations about taking the role, and his friends – who loved him and were looking out for him – told him not to do it. They thought it would be the end of his career, whereas it was probably the best decision in showbusiness at that time. He handled fame with grace. He didn’t flaunt it. Never got too big for his boots. Early on, a review in a paper described him as an “unknown Shakespearean actor” and we blew it up and stuck it on his trailer door. Someone less self-deprecating might not have liked that but he left it up there for years. He knew it was all good fun.Before meeting Patrick I was just a jobbing actor who did a bit of telly. I’d grown up dirt poor and had a difficult childhood, so we came from very similar backgrounds. I kept my cockney accent because I wanted people to know where I came from. Patrick was the same – not through his voice, but through his demeanour and actions. He was down to earth, a regular bloke. The fact that he supportedHuddersfieldTown shows you who he is – he didn’t go for Leeds or one of the glamour clubs.We’d both experienced childhood trauma and came out with our stories after we had finished working together. We never sat down and went into it all. But when people have gone through something like that, there’s something in their demeanour, something that you can see in them, that you feel in them.A month before Covid hit, my husband died. I was on my own in my house in Los Angeles for a year with just my dogs for company. Patrick was one of the very few people who invited me over for lunch, socially distanced in his garden. It had occurred to him that I was grieving and on my own – and he did something about that. It’s a mark of who he is.View image in fullscreen‘Our relationship on screen was a two-way street’ … in Star Trek: The Next Generation.Photograph: APC/THA/ShutterstockHe was always on my side. In one of the Star Trek movies we did there was a scene written for Picard and Data, where Picard tells the story of how his family were burned in a fire. Patrick went to the writers and producers and asked if they could rewrite the scene to have me be in it instead of Brent Spiner. He said that Brent’s character Data was an android, and that he really needed to look into my eyes in order to reach the emotions he needed. So our relationship on screen was a two-way street, which sounds ridiculous saying that out loud! I don’t know how I’ve got the cheek to say that when I’m talking about Patrick Stewart! But we did help each other.It’s also because of Patrick that I am now in the annals of my football team. When Tottenham played Huddersfield in 2018, we both did interviews about the game and it was officially named in the match day programme as the Star Trek derby. That’s now a part of Tottenham history and, as anyone who knows me will tell you, that means more to me than winning an acting award!It was the absolute privilege of my life and my career to work with him. We were very, very close and stayed in touch right to the end, even though it became difficult to speak to him on the phone because of his health. He went quickly in the end and it makes me very sad that I didn’t get a chance to say goodbye. To say: “Thank you Patrick. Thanks for everything, mate.”Explore more on these topicsPatrick StewartStar TrekTelevisionHuddersfieldTottenham HotspurfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Selma Blair says she is ‘so sorry’ to those she alarmed following alleged air incident  | Selma Blair | The Guardian
description: Actor pleaded not guilty to allegedly kicking a nurse and a police officer after an incident on flight from Los Angeles to New York
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Actor pleaded not guilty to allegedly kicking a nurse and a police officer after an incident on flight from Los Angeles to New York
Content: Selma Blair said in her statement that she has never intended to hurt or frighten anyone.Photograph: Ryan Murphy/APView image in fullscreenSelma Blair said in her statement that she has never intended to hurt or frighten anyone.Photograph: Ryan Murphy/APSelma BlairSelma Blair says she is ‘so sorry’ to those she alarmed following alleged air incidentActor pleaded not guilty to allegedly kicking a nurse and a police officer after an incident on flight from Los Angeles to New YorkPress AssociationSat 31 Oct 2026 01.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSelma Blair has spoken for the first time since being charged with assault after a mid-air assault incident, saying she is “so sorry” to anyone “that I hurt, I frightened, that I alarmed”.Blair pleaded not guilty to state assault charges over allegations she kicked a nurse and a police officer after an incident involving crew members on a flight from Los Angeles to New York earlier this month.At the time, her representatives said her alleged behaviour had been brought on by a severe medical emergency.Selma Blair charged with assault of police officer and nurse after allegedly attacking flight attendantsRead moreIn a videopostedto Instagram, Blair said: “I know I’ve been quiet for a couple weeks since October 11. And you deserve to hear from me directly, and I’m sorry that it’s taken this long.“There is a legal matter going on, and my lawyers have asked me to not say anything about that day, and I’m listening to them.”The actor said she took the matter “very seriously” and that the “very simple and the truest thing I know about myself is that not one day ever have I intended to hurt or frighten anyone”.“And so to the people that I disappointed, that I hurt, I frightened, that I alarmed, I am so sorry,” she said, adding that she appreciated everyone who had reached out to her in support since the incidents.Blair then assured fans that her service dog Scout, who accompanied her on the flight, was doing well. She was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in 2018 and got the Labrador as a service dog five years ago.The actor concluded: “So, right now I’m going to be taking care of my health. And my son. And thinking of you all with my gratitude and love.”Blair, 54, was detained by police when the Delta flight landed in New York and was taken to hospital for evaluation.A police officer taking her to Jamaica hospital medical centre alleged in charging documents that while securing Blair to a stretcher, the actor pulled one of her legs from the straps and kicked her repeatedly around the face, neck and chest, causing serious pain and substantial swelling.Later, a nurse moving Blair said the actor kicked her in the chest.She was arraigned on two counts of second-degree assault late the following day at a court in Queens, where a judge set her bail at $20,000 (£15,141) cash or $60,000 dollars bond and set the next hearing for January.Her lawyer Shawn Barnes told the judge that her actions were not intentional.He said the actor missed several doses of “a powerful medication that controls severe neurological symptoms,” according to the New York Daily News and New York Post.Mr Barnes said she boarded the flight in Los Angeles amid a heavy workload and hit her head during the flight.He said these factors, along with the altitude, led to “a state of severe confusion and disorientation”.Explore more on these topicsSelma BlairShareReuse this content

title: ‘They cheer like it’s football’: Celebrity Traitors fans hit bars to watch climax | The Traitors | The Guardian
description: One south London bar provided Claudia Winkleman-themed cocktails and its very own banishment ceremony
Author: George Francis Lee
Headline: One south London bar provided Claudia Winkleman-themed cocktails and its very own banishment ceremony
Content: Shock in Arch Clapham as comedian James Acaster revealed he was a reluctant traitor.Photograph: Andy Hall/The GuardianView image in fullscreenShock in Arch Clapham as comedian James Acaster revealed he was a reluctant traitor.Photograph: Andy Hall/The GuardianThe Traitors‘They cheer like it’s football’: Celebrity Traitors fans hit bars to watch climaxOne south London bar provided Claudia Winkleman-themed cocktails and its very own banishment ceremonyGeorge Francis LeeSat 31 Oct 2026 07.53 EDTFirst published on Sat 31 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCries, cheers and boos emanating from pubs across the country on Friday night were less likely to be linked to any sports fixture than the nation coming together for the dramatic climax of the BBC’s The Celebrity Traitors.The cloak and dagger reality show, in which contestants attempt to deceive or deduce who among them are “Faithfuls” and “Traitors” for a charity cash prize, drew inmore than half of the UK’s TV audiencein its debut episode earlier this month.The popularity of the Claudia Winkleman-hosted programme was so great that fans left their living rooms and flocked to public venues to watch the second series of the show.The series’s psychological mind games are what appealed to Calum, a regular viewer and account manager from Edinburgh who was waiting to watch Thursday’s semi-final at a bar in Clapham. “For me, it’s how good people are at lying and then how that translates into normal life. You can almost second-guess anyone you’re around,” he said.The intensity from fans had not only caused venues to screen each episode of the hit show, but offer an entire night of entertainment inspired by the programme. In south London bar Arch Clapham, attenders sipped Claudia Winkleman-themed cocktails, ate “100% Traitor” chocolate coins and twice took part in their very own banishment ceremony. Banishment, in which contestants vote out a peer they suspect to be a Traitor near the end of each episode, provokes some of the most visceral reactions from fans.View image in fullscreenPunters at Arch Clapham participating in a Celebrity Traitors game during the semi-final screening on Thursday.Photograph: Andy Hall/The GuardianCalum and his friend Ali had previously “stumbled” into Arch Clapham’s watch party for the first series’s finale of The Celebrity Traitors last year, and they were captivated by the crowd’s excitement. “There were people cheering like it was football,” Ali said. “I’m not personally too into sports, but I like having the atmosphere.”This year’s run of treacherous celebrity TV had 3 million more viewers than the previous year’s iteration. Ali explained that the programme had encouraged friends, co-workers and even strangers to discuss each episode, with many seeking to avoid spoilers at all costs.He said: “I think back in the day, everybody was watching X Factor. There’s not really been anything since then that everyone’s been watching, so it’s quite nice. You can probably pick out a random person and they’ve probably been watching.”Brandon Bolland, a supervisor at Arch Clapham, said the bar had screened every episode of the latest series after the previous two finales of The Traitors’s standard and celebrity versions drew in a lot of punters. “We were packed. It was really, really popular,” he said.During Thursday’s semi-final, those attending the Traitors-themed night were equally jubilant and appalled when comedian James Acaster shocked audiences by revealing he was a reluctant traitor.It was these bombshell TV moments – such as when actor Richard E Grant made the unexpected decision to reveal he was a Traitor in the game’s first episode – that made the act of watching the show together more enjoyable, Bolland said.He added: “It’s like watching the World Cup when this is on. People are jeering and shouting like they’re watching a football game.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBlue Planet III features cloudier footage to prove authenticity amid AI boomRead moreAnother notable moment for fans that caused loud scenes was when fan favourite Miranda Hart was murdered earlier in the series, he added.This year’s highly anticipated finale saw stars such as comedian Romesh Ranganathan and actor Michael Sheen attempt to uncover the two remaining traitors: TV personality Maya Jama and content creator Kenny Oghenovo Ojuederie (known as King Kenny).For Siobhan, an IT account manager, the social manipulation and subterfuge in these sections are the show’s biggest draw. “That whole psychology aspect and how they can play that is super interesting to me,” she said.Siobhan’s love for the Traitors led her to introduce her parents to the show, and has led to a number of vocal outbursts. She added: “I’m talking to the TV when I’m watching it!”Despite players being required to manipulate one another, some find the show’s format to be a comforting watch. Ziad, who attended the watch party with his husband, said the programme stood out “in a day and age where reality TV is solely about fights and political divide”.“It’s the closest you get to a feelgood show,” he added.While viewers were united by their Traitors fervour, they also shared a love of the game’s cut-throat rules. This was made clear when the Clapham bar hosted its own roundtable discussion once the semi-final had finished, and the only Guardian journalist present was deemed a Traitor and banished.This article was amended on 31 October 2026. Miranda Hart was murdered in the game, not banished as an earlier version said.Explore more on these topicsThe TraitorsBBC OneBBCfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: Halloween weirdness with Heated Rivalry’s Hudson Williams | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Carrie-Anne Moss also stars in fun, creepy drama Yaga. Plus, Sir Tom Jones takes his bow as The Voice UK concludes. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: Carrie-Anne Moss also stars in fun, creepy drama Yaga. Plus, Sir Tom Jones takes his bow as The Voice UK concludes. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Turn down the heat … Hudson Williams in Yaga on Sky Atlantic.Photograph: Sphere Abacus/SkyView image in fullscreenTurn down the heat … Hudson Williams in Yaga on Sky Atlantic.Photograph: Sphere Abacus/SkyTV tonightTelevision & radioTV tonight: Halloween weirdness with Heated Rivalry’s Hudson WilliamsCarrie-Anne Moss also stars in fun, creepy drama Yaga. Plus, Sir Tom Jones takes his bow as The Voice UK concludes. Here’s what to watch this eveningPhil Harrison,Graeme Virtue,Priya Elan,Jack SealeandSimon WardellSat 31 Oct 2026 02.15 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 02.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYaga9pm, Sky AtlanticWitchy weirdness for Halloween in this drama starring Carrie-Anne Moss and Hudson “Heated Rivalry” Williams. It hits plenty of familiar beats (mismatched cops, missing rich kid, mysterious coastal community) but lands them in a fresh way. Noah Reid is PI Charlie Rapp who has been hired to find the heir to a local fishery. He’s paired with sceptical cop Carson (Clark Backo) and once they start digging, things get stranger and stranger.Phil HarrisonGriff Across the Alps8pm, Channel 4Conquering Europe’s most dramatic mountain range is no joke but Griff Rhys Jones has a twinkle in his eye during his travelogue. The journey begins in France, where each outdoor exertion (abseiling, ibex spotting) is offset with something more relaxing (spa soaking, a slap-up feast).Graeme VirtueThe Voice UK: The Final8.30pm, ITV1Overshadowed by the axing of Sir Tom, this competition finale will see Jones and other judges Kelly Rowland, will.i.am and two of McFly duetting with their last remaining artists. Next season, could guest mentor Cheryl join and pull the show out of irrelevancy? And can we please upgrade those ugly red chairs?Priya ElanThe F Ward9pm, Channel 4Hospital dramas can generally be divided into snarky and wholesome, and this Aussie import is firmly in the latter camp. It focuses on a bunch of interns who, after various screw-ups, are in the last chance saloon. When a storm floods the hospital, they have no choice but to grow up. Anna Friel stars.PHGhostwatch: The Night That Terrified Britain9.15pm, Channel 5View image in fullscreenSarah Greene prepares for Mr Pipes in Ghostwatch.Composite: BBCThe BBC’s 1992 pseudo-investigative chiller Ghostwatch is still regarded, by those lucky enough to have caught it live, as the last word in TV horror. Where else could you see Sarah Greene abducted by a poltergeist called Mr Pipes while a horrified Michael Parkinson looked on? This documentary looks at how they did it.PHMarble Hall Murders9.25pm, BBC OneLesley Manville’s sleuthing literary editor cracks two twinned cases, one real and one fictional, in the season finale – so there’s a scene where suspects gather beneath a gazebo to find out whodunnit, then another in a drawing room. The unmasking of another wrong’un is a satisfying bonus.Jack SealeFilm choiceAli G: Who Iz I (Sacha Baron Cohen, 2026), Prime VideoHot-footing it from cinemas, Sacha Baron Cohen’s satirical documentary dusts off his deluded 90s Staines wideboy rapper for a series of pranks taking aim, mostly, at American Maga and anti-woke folk and their zeal to protect the border from immigrants. Morgana Robinson co-stars as the very pregnant “me Julie”, with Ali G heading to the US on the promise of a new show to fund impending fatherhood. Your enjoyment of all this will depend on your taste for gross-out gags and political provocation, and a character whose time has arguably passed.Simon WardellBoorman and the Devil (David Kittredge, 2025), 8pm, Sky DocumentariesIf you’ve ever read one of his books, you’ll know the great British film-maker John Boorman (Point Blank, Deliverance) is a wonderful raconteur. And in David Kittredge’s deep-dive documentary, he’s great value as he recalls his time directing Exorcist II: The Heretic, a disastrous, glorious mess of a horror sequel that almost killed his career – and him. Stars Linda Blair and Louise Fletcher add further context to a cautionary tale that includes a drunken Richard Burton, locust wrangling and Boorman falling prey to a sand-based fever.SWThe Fog (John Carpenter, 1980), 9pm, Sky ArtsMuch of the plot of John Carpenter’s classic 1980 horror yarn will be familiar to viewers of recent Apple TV homage Widow’s Bay. A California coastal community is assailed by ghostly forces from the sea hidden in a mysterious fog – the result of a 19th-century curse – and nobody is safe; not Adrienne Barbeau’s local radio DJ Stevie, nor hitchhiker Elizabeth (Jamie Lee Curtis) nor fisher Nick (Tom Atkins). Carpenter’s mastery of low-budget film-making is evident here: he does so much with a bit of dry ice, a few backlit figures and his own ominous electronic score.SWFanny and Alexander (Ingmar Bergman, 1982), 9.20pm, BBC FourView image in fullscreenFanny and Alexander.Photograph: ScreenProd/Photononstop/AlamyIngmar Bergman delved fruitfully into his own childhood for this resonant three-hour period drama (cut down from the even better five-hour TV original). The titular children are part of a large, well-off Swedish family who own a theatre in their town. Their emotional, magical life is brilliantly evoked in sumptuous Christmas celebrations, but the kids’ joy is short-lived when their mother is widowed, then marries a cold, cruel bishop who prioritises “purity and austerity”. An intoxicating masterpiece.SWTalk to Me (Danny and Michael Philippou, 2022), 10pm, Film4Prior to their teeth-clenchingly brilliant Bring Her Back last year, Australian twins Danny and Michael Philippou had already explored the grisly scope of grief in this nail-biting 2022 horror. A group of teenagers are introduced to a party game that involves holding a severed hand – which may have been a medium’s – and summoning a dead person, which you invite to (briefly) possess you. But when Mia (Sophie Wilde), who lost her mother a year ago, agrees to let her best friend’s kid brother Riley (Joe Bird) try it out, things go bloodily wrong. Great, ghostly goings-on from an up-and-coming duo.SWLive sportPremier League Football: Chelsea v Man United, 11am, TNT Sports 1United’s head coach Michael Carrick remains nominally in charge for the trip to London. Tottenham v Crystal Palace is at 5pm on Sky Sports Main Event, with Aston Villa v Fulham at 7.45pm.Prem Rugby Union: Bath v Sale, 3pm, TNT Sports 1Followed by Northampton v Gloucester at 5.15pm.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Being hated is very bracing’: Helen Garner on surviving three marriages and being called a ‘rotten feminist’  | Helen Garner | The Guardian
description: Her unsparing fiction and true crime writing have made her one of Australia’s most controversial and celebrated authors. The author discusses relationships, resilience – and finding global recognition five decades into her career
Author: Emma Brockes
Headline: Her unsparing fiction and true crime writing have made her one of Australia’s most controversial and celebrated authors. The author discusses relationships, resilience – and finding global recognition five decades into her career
Content: Helen Garner.Photograph: Jillian FreyerView image in fullscreenHelen Garner.Photograph: Jillian FreyerHelen GarnerInterview‘Being hated is very bracing’: Helen Garner on surviving three marriages and being called a ‘rotten feminist’Emma BrockesHer unsparing fiction and true crime writing have made her one of Australia’s most controversial and celebrated authors. The author discusses relationships, resilience – and finding global recognition five decades into her careerSat 31 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 18.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfew years ago, whenHelen Garnerhad an idea to write a book about Australian rules football, her heart soared then immediately sank. The impetus was Ambrose, her teenage grandson, who played for a local team. Garner enjoyed watching them and wanted to put this into writing. Then the dreary thought: “I’ll have to swot, read the rulebook.” People to whom she mentioned the idea assumed she’d be writing a polemic, “like what it means in society and how terrible it is and what violence means. And I’m going: ‘What a bore.’”As anyone familiar with Garner’s almost 50-year writing career will know, there is nothing more igniting to the 83-year-old than the invitation to outrun boredom by going off in an unauthorised direction. Garner, who is speaking to me via video call from her home in Melbourne, occupies that tiny category of writers famous enough to be recognised in public. Stopped by strangers in the street, she’s often treated to their strong views about her work. As a result, perhaps, she has perfected a very Garnerian obstinacy, enabling her to resist other people’s bossy opinions which, in the case ofThe Season, meant no tedious explainers about the rules, history or sociology of Aussie rules football. Instead, says Garner, she envisaged following a single season of Ambrose’s U16s team, the Flemington Colts, as “a nanna’s book”. During publicity, she’d turn up to an event at a library to find “the first five rows packed with nannas; all these white-haired women with hankies in their hands. And I feel nobody writes about nannas. I mean, sentimentally, yes; but I want to say what they’rereallylike.”To say what something is really like is the ethos behind all of Garner’s books and it has, on occasion, landed her in spectacular trouble. It has also won levels of devotion from readers who have turned her into an almost guru-like figure in her 80s, turbocharged by the publication last year of her wisdom-heavydiaries– which won the Baillie Gifford prize – and helped, one suspects, by her ability to combine insight and erudition of the highest literary order with a style that is at times comically down to earth. (A classic example: referring to the controversy around The First Stone, the 1995 book she wrote about feminism, Garner says: “I gave a lot of people the shits.” It’s not a line one can imagine, say, Marilynne Robinson delivering.)The current mania around Garner is a long-overdue correction for a writer who, outside Australia, was ignored and condescended to for decades. In 1987, in a typically sniffy reference to Garner in the TLS, her work was referred to as “Mills& Boon for bohemians”, yet she is now credibly hailed as a contender for the Nobel prize, can fill 900-seat venues in New York, and has seen practically her entire back catalogue reissued in the US. (Carrie Bradshaw was shown carrying a copy of Garner’s 2014 book, This House of Grief, in a scene from And Just Like That … and Dua Lipa interviewed her on her podcast.) All of which Garner shrugs off, referring to herself as an “old kind of warhorse” who was never interested in prizes in the first place, not least, she says, because “you have to put on that look that you’re pleased for the other person”, even when – a typically bracing admission – “their book was not as good as mine”.View image in fullscreenNoni Hazlehurst and Colin Friels in the 1982 film of Monkey Grip.Photograph: RGR Collection/AlamyThe fact is that Garner has always cut through the flab and waffle of so much literary culture in pursuit of something more honest. In her first novel,Monkey Grip, published in 1977 and based on her rackety life at the time, Garner told the story of Nora, a woman with a young child living in a bohemian shared house in Melbourne and on-off dating a heroin addict called Javo. Garner had arrived at this point in her own life partly as a result of fleeing a rigid, repressed childhood in the town of Geelong near Melbourne. As the oldest of six kids, she had frequently clashed with her father, a wool merchant and “a rather domineering person”, she says, who bullied her meek stay-at-home mother and kept no books in the house. After attending an Anglican girls’ school, Garner won a place at the University of Melbourne, where she spent the best part of three years in the pub. “It was a strange time. Once you get estranged from your parents, you go galumphing across the landscape seizing this and throwing out that. I look back and I see a lot of damage. We trampled through each other’s lives.”This sense of damage would become more profound in Garner’s late 20s after a short-lived marriage to Bill Garner, whom she’d met at college and with whom she had a daughter, Alice. The pair split up when Alice was two and Garner moved into a series of hippy shared houses. It was an unstable life that had what Garner now calls a “kind of berserk quality to it – there was a lot of smashing and breaking that went on”, and only became more precarious when Garner, who had been working as a teacher, “opened my big mouth” and was fired from a school in Victoria for giving an impromptu and explicit sex education lesson. At the same time, she fell in love with a heroin addict and, a few years later, looking back over her diaries from that period, realised she wanted to write about it, embarking on Monkey Grip with the modest ambitions that enabled its fresh, uncontrived voice. “It was a private thing, writing down in a notebook what I thought about what was happening in my life,” she says. “So, I didn’t compare what I had written with anything great or mighty. I thought I’d just tell the story of what  happened.”Looking back now, she finds the novel “rather naive and undefended”.But it thrills her, 50 years on, that Monkey Grip is not only still in print, but highly popular. She was in a shop, recently, “and there was a young bloke who said: ‘Aren’t you Helen Garner? I’m reading Monkey Grip, and we’re living the life!’” She laughs and assumes a look of mock horror. “And I thought: ‘Ooh, don’t do that.’” I’d always assumed Javo had died way back, but fans of the book may be interested to know the real-life Javo is alive and well and living in Hobart, Tasmania, where he has a wife and grandchildren. After offering his spare room to Garner’s own 25-year-old grandchild who was visiting that part of the world recently, he wrote to Garner, “to say how marvellous it was to see our two grandchildren together”.double quotation markI did feel sad. I thought: God, everyone hates me, this is terrible. But I didn’t regret it for a minuteMonkey Grip, which was written with the electric, offhand energy of a young writer yet to grow self-conscious, caused a sensation in Australia and was followed by a series of short, brilliant novels, includingThe Children’s BachandCosmo Cosmolino, before Garner pivoted to nonfiction in the mid-1990s. (She’d return to fiction in 2008 withThe Spare Room, based on Garner’s experience of nursing her close friend through cancer. The book has recently enjoyed an operatic adaptation in Melbourne.) And in the background, always, Garner maintained her diaries, recording her second marriage to Jean-Jacques Portail, a journalist whom she met in Paris, where she moved for a couple of years in the late 1970s while living on a writer’s grant and trying to write her second novel. Portail moved back to Melbourne with Garner, and they split up in 1985. A few years later, Garner moved to Sydney to be nearer to the writer Murray Bail, the man who would become her third and (to date) final husband, and who dominates the last volume of her diaries.Alongside entries about fashion, art, friendship, nature and the end of her marriage to Bail, the diaries offer readers a chance to witness the epic battle between Garner’s extremely robust writer’s ego and its near-constant collapse. A typical entry, from 1997, reads: “I have to admit to myself that I feel irrelevant, small, hollow, untalented, worthless – and frightened. The energy required to maintain self-command is so great that I am always tired. How repellent one is. If only I were writing something.”I’m curious about how Garner reconciles these two things – confidence and self-doubt – particularly in the wake of The First Stone, her first nonfiction book, in which she interrogated the case of two female students at the University of Melbourne who accused the master of their college of groping them. A mid-90s cause celebre in Australia, Garner foreshadowed culture wars to come by presenting the story as a possible overreaction on the part of the women, putting the boot in, she says, “to what I thought was a rather punitive form of feminism. I got into a hell of a lot of trouble. Really, it was quite astonishing, the amount of hostility I copped. I was thought to be a rotten feminist; a heretic. I heard that someone on a judging panel said: ‘If this book by Helen Garner even gets on the long list, I will’ … thunderous threats …’” Garner says: “I just laughed. Because I think it’s a sort of compliment.”The First Stone was much more subtle and ambivalent than its detractors allowed, being a real intellectual reckoning with a complicated subject. Given the response, I’ve always wondered how Garner came back from it. “I had the shit kicked out of me! People savaged me. And it took me a while, but when I got over it, I thought: ‘Well, I survived that, and now I’m free. I can write what I really want. And I won’t have to see if it comes out pure.’ Being hated is very bracing. It’s not destructive. Well, it could be; if I’d published that book now … but the internet didn’t exist then. I did feel miserable and sad and I thought: ‘God, everyone hates me, this is terrible.’ But I didn’t regret it for a minute.”Because it was the book you wanted to write? “Yeah. And I made mistakes in it; but I got a lot of amazing letters. I reckon I got about 800 and I answered every one. It was quite an exercise; someone would cover me with loathsome abuse and I’d write back: ‘Thank you for your kind letter …’ And the good letters I got were long and thoughtful, saying: ‘I read your book and I’d like to tell you something that happened to me.’ And that made me think I opened up the subject for people to talk about calmly.” It can’t have hurt that thebook was a huge bestseller.“Yeah, and thatreallygave them the shits. And they’d go around saying: ‘Oh, yes, of course Helen’s motivation was purely commercial.’”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markIt’s the hardest thing people ever do, being married. Harder than having kidsIt helped that Garner had a career in freelance journalism to fall back on, particularly when she got stuck on a book,This House of Grief, which told the story of the trial and conviction of Robert Farquharson, who murdered his three children to get back at their mother, and which took eight years to finish while the various appeals played out. After the success of Monkey Grip, Garner dashed off a second novel, “and it was crap, and my publisher correctly bounced it back. That was a nasty moment, but they were right. Justbecause you’ve written one book doesn’t mean you know how to write the next one.” But while better novels followed, including The Children’s Bach, published in 1984 and widely considered her masterpiece, she moved permanently to nonfiction after The First Stone, coming to specialise in a kind of literary true crime with a series of devastating books built around high-profile murder trials.That shift was brought about in part by her marriage to fellow novelist Murray Bail. Garner’s account of the collapse of that marriage appears in How to End a Story, her third volume of diaries, and it’s quite something; at one point, in a fury at the insidious, unfaithful Bail, she throws cups, an espresso machine and a saucepan full of beetroot soup across the kitchen. Garner writes that Bail belittled and gaslit her, and dismissed her work as inferior to his. “I thought my marriage was the worst marriage in the world and I was the world’s biggest wimp for going along with it,” she says. Since the diaries came out, however, a lot of people have said to her “‘that book is my marriage.’ And that sort of shocks me – they’re talking about a marriage they’re still in. But it can be terribly difficult. I reckon it’s the hardest thing people ever do, being married. Harder than having kids.”She regards having her only child, Alice – at the age of 26 and without any great planning – as the greatest good fortune of her life. And the happiest she has ever been, she says, has been during these past decades of living next door to Alice and her husband and three children. Bail, meanwhile, comes out of the diaries looking very bad indeed. Any feedback from him since publication? “The answer to that is no. And either he hasn’t read it or he’s saying he hasn’t read it. I haven’t had any contact with him now since long before I published the diaries. We parted badly and painfully and it’s never been mended.” She sighs. “He also published a memoir in which he summed up my part in his life in about three sentences. I was roundly dismissed. And I went on like it was the collapse of civilisation. But. You know. Bless him.”Given the relative literary reputations of Helen Garner and Murray Bail these days, she can afford to be generous. And, of course, one of the delights of the diaries is the schadenfreude of watching a man flex his superiority over a woman who will, in time, be regarded as one of the great writers of our age. Splitting up gave her just the impetus she needed, she says. “I felt very liberated by no longer living in close companionship with someone who had ideas about literature which were too severe and didn’t suit my work. He had this hierarchy of forms, and I subscribed to them for a long time because I’d been educated to think that as well.But after I split up with him, I relaxed into being a nonfiction writer. And I stopped doing it defensively. I thought: ‘Actually, this is my natural form.’ And I still feel that very strongly: I’m out here, and I’m good at this, and it’s really fun to do, and it gets you out of the house, rather than stewing in your own self-hatred.”View image in fullscreenJudy Davis and Elizabeth Alexander in the stage adaptation of The Spare Room.Photograph: Brett Boardman/The GuardianSo it was with The Season, in which for the space of winter training Garner showed up every week at the football ground to watch her grandson and his cohorts play. Garner went through her customary period of thinking it was all a mistake, that the book was a terrible idea and she’d never be able to drag it over the line. The toughest experience she ever had with this kind of self-doubt was during the writing of Joe Cinque’s Consolation, her deeply affecting 2004 book about the killing of Joe Cinque, a young engineer from New South Wales whose girlfriend injected him with ‘Get in there and do it!’ heroin and was later convicted of manslaughter. “I actually told Maria Cinque, his mother, that I wasn’t going to write the book. I wrote her a letter and said I’m really sorry, I’m going to have to give up, I can’t do this. And she rang me up and said: ‘What do you mean you can’t do it? We gave you our story, you said you were going to do it, you’ll do it! Do it!’ God, I nearly died of shame. I look back on that and think you need someone who’s going to kick you right up the arse. Don’t you think? You don’t want someone who’s going to say: ‘Oh, darling, it must be so hard, I really feel for you.’ You want someone to say: ”This is Garner’s circuit, from idea to execution via collapse, shame and eventual, dogged persistence. A few days before our conversation,Anne Carsonwas announced as the winner of the Nobel Prize in literature, a decision thoroughly approved of by her Australian peer. Taped up on the wall of her office, Garner has a poem of Carson’s, which she looks at in times of dire need. “If I ever had a tattoo, I’d have that last line tattooed on me,” she says. “I just think it’s so marvellous.” The poem describes a stormy night at sea, fraught with peril, existential and otherwise. “And the last line is: ‘Nothing for it just row.’”The Season by Helen Garner is published in the UK on 5 November by W&N.
