title: What we’re reading: Ian Rankin, Louise Kennedy and Guardian readers on the books they enjoyed in October | Books | The Guardian
description: Writers and Guardian readers discuss the titles they have read over the last month. Join the conversation in the comments
Author: Ian Rankin
Headline: Writers and Guardian readers discuss the titles they have read over the last month. Join the conversation in the comments
Content: View image in fullscreenWhat we're readingBooksWhat we’re reading: Ian Rankin, Louise Kennedy and Guardian readers on the books they enjoyed in OctoberWriters and Guardian readers discuss the titles they have read over the last month. Join the conversation in the commentsIan Rankin, Louise Kennedy andGuardian readersSat 31 Oct 2026 05.04 EDTLast modified on Sat 31 Oct 2026 05.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIan Rankin, authorI’m a huge fan of Muriel Spark, but wasn’t sure I needed another biography of her, yet James Bailey’sLike a Cat Loves a Birdwas a winning blend of detail and readability.A Bad, Bad Placeby Frances Crawford is a prize-winning debut crime novel set in 1970s Glasgow. It’s clever, authentic and humane with unforgettable protagonists and pitch-black humour.The Heights by Ian Rankin is published by Orion (£25). To support the Guardian order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.David, Guardian readerI’ve loved (most of) China Miéville’s books (I think that he and Alan Moore are the real doyens of “weird” fiction) – butThe Rouseis surely his opus: sometimes prose-poetry, sometimes stream-of-consciousness, with shades (literally) of Lovecraft and MR James running through a bleak, unsettling yet compelling tale. I strongly suggest you take a very deep breath and launch into an adventure (lasting more than 1,200 pages) that will leave you dazed and amazed!Louise Kennedy, authorI normally read one book at a time but, perhaps because I am on the road at the moment, I have three on the go. Emma Cline’s short story Arcadia almost killed me, and I’ve been a devotee ever since.Switzy,her new novel, accompanies on his final journey a man whose wealth and privilege offer no protection from the dementia that has begun to addle his poor brain. Edith Wharton’sThe House of Mirth: so far, charming, pretty Lily Bart is in charge of her story, but an encounter with a man who appears not to wish her well suggests there may be trouble ahead. John McGahern’sMemoiralready has my heart rent in twain, to paraphrase an old Irish ballad, and he hasn’t even finished primary school.Stations by Louise Kennedy is published by Bloomsbury (£20). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Sophie, Guardian readerAlmost Lifeby Kiran Millwood Hargrave is a beautiful and heartbreaking love story that transported me back in time to Paris in the late 1970s and 80s. The main characters, Laure and Erica, as well as the other characters, soon feel like friends – friends who are human and imperfect, and who sometimes make frustrating decisions, but who are all the more lovable for it. It’s elegantly and smartly written, and paints such vivid pictures – I rarely read past my bedtime these days, but I stayed up late for this one, torn between wanting to finish and never wanting the book to end. It captures the feeling of love and being in love so well.Mark, Guardian readerThis year, I’ve set myself the challenge of only reading books by writers who aren’t part of the Anglosphere, with each writer being from a different country. It’s certainly forced me to read stuff outside my comfort zone – which is how, this month, I’ve ended up readingIndependent Peopleby Halldór Laxness, a 500+ page novel about an Icelandic farming family. Over the course of about 20 years in the early 20th century, we follow the hardships and privations of a stubborn farmer who insists he fend for himself to maintain independence on his own land.I expected this book to be unrelentingly grim reading – and in parts it is, especially in the almost indifference to death. But it’s also very humorous in its characters’ cynicism towards one another. It’s beautifully atmospheric in its prose, particularly the changing of the seasons and their effect on the dramatic landscape of the farm. Reading so much literature in translation has given me an appreciation of when it’s done well (without ever knowing the original text), and the translation by JA Thompson, in collaboration with Laxness, is sublime.Explore more on these topicsBooksWhat we're readingIan RankinEdith WhartonEmma ClineChina MiévilleShareReuse this content

title: ‘Dark green dust’: the best (and worst) supermarket green teabags, tested and rated | Tea | The Guardian
description: Green tea can be a mixed bag – we sipped our way through the supermarket shelves to find the ones worth boiling the kettle for
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: Green tea can be a mixed bag – we sipped our way through the supermarket shelves to find the ones worth boiling the kettle for
Content: The quality of green tea varies considerably.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Robert BillingtonView image in fullscreenThe quality of green tea varies considerably.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Robert BillingtonThe FilterTeaReview‘Dark green dust’: the best (and worst) supermarket green teabags, tested and ratedGreen tea can be a mixed bag – we sipped our way through the supermarket shelves to find the ones worth boiling the kettle forThe best (and worst) supermarket teabagsTom HuntSat 31 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy mother-in-law has a mug that reads: “By replacing your morning coffee with green tea, you can lose up to 87% of what little joy you still have left in your life.” Some people will never like green tea, while others will probably have tried only poor-quality, over-brewed bags filled with the dust and fannings left over from the production of whole leaf tea. Only one of today’s teas contains whole leaves, and the difference is hugely noticeable, though that’s not to say the more economical bags are undrinkable. Some are single-origin or organic, and are certainly satisfactory, so long as you brew them properly.Due to the large surface area of these tiny broken leaves, you need to be careful not to over-brew them. To stand the best chance of making a half-decent cup, use water at 80C – you can achieve that temperature by quarter-filling a cup with cold water, topping it up with just-boiled water and leaving it to brew for about 90 seconds. You’ll end up with a much sweeter cup, with nuanced kelp, edamame and toasted-straw flavours (all of which are, admittedly, acquired tastes).The best supermarket green teabagsBest overall:Clearspring organic Japanese senchaView image in fullscreen£3.99 for 20 sachets at Victoria Health (20p/sachet)£4.10 for 20 sachets at Ocado (21p/sachet)★★★★☆Small, individually wrapped bags of green fannings and brown stems with a classic umami, earthy aroma. Chamomile-yellow in colour with a distinct, savoury scent alongside a sweet, brothy tone. Quite astringent, so I’d recommend a shorter brew time. Bags free from plastic.Best bargain:Duchy Organic green teaView image in fullscreen£2.50 for 50 bags at Waitrose (5p/bag)★★★☆☆Dark green dust fannings and brown stems with a seaweedy aroma, from a single estate (Korakundah in the Nilgiri mountains, southern India). A clear, buttercup-yellow brew that holds a bright and complex flavour with a sweet start, an astringent finish and a full mouthfeel. Organic and Fairtrade.And the rest …Pukka organic supreme matcha green teaView image in fullscreen£4.74 for 20 sachets at Asda (24p/sachet)£5 for 20 sachets at Tesco (25p/sachet)★★★★☆A small, individually wrapped bag of organic dark green fannings and brown stems made from a blend of sencha, Vietnamese and Indian green teas, plus 2% South Korean matcha. A sweet, oceanic aroma, a golden-yellow colour and a honeyed, floral and grassy flavour with hints of citrus. Bright and sharp, with a mild astringency.Teapigs Mao Feng green teaView image in fullscreen£3.50 for 15 bags at Waitrose (23p/bag)£5 for 15 bags at Amazon (33p/bag)★★★★☆The only whole tea leaf in the test comes in a plant starch pyramid teabag full of large, broken dark green leaves with a kelpy scent. A light and clear green-lemon colour and complex, brothy, seaweed aroma. Bright and crisp with an earthy-umami depth, bright, fruity quality and mild astringency. One star Great Taste award in 2025, industrially compostable bags, and this week’s best splurge.Tesco green teaView image in fullscreen85p for 20 bags at Tesco (4p/bag)★★★☆☆Dark green fannings with brown flecks produce a chamomile-yellow cup with clarity, toasted straw aroma, vegetal notes and a strong, astringent finish. title: Jackson Boxer’s recipe for roast apples with toffee sauce and soured cream | Food | The Guardian
description: Autumn on a plate: come in from the fireworks and warm up with this sweet, rich caramelised apple treat
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Autumn on a plate: come in from the fireworks and warm up with this sweet, rich caramelised apple treat
Content: Jackson Boxer’s roast apples with walnuts and soured cream.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Eden Owen-Jones.View image in fullscreenJackson Boxer’s roast apples with walnuts and soured cream.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Eden Owen-Jones.FoodJackson Boxer’s recipe for roast apples with toffee sauce and soured creamAutumn on a plate: come in from the fireworks and warm up with this sweet, rich caramelised apple treatJackson BoxerSat 31 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIlove a tarte tatin: it’s one of those perfect recipes that contains only a few key ingredients at its core – in this case, butter, sugar, apples and pastry – yet it brings out the absolute best qualities from each: the sugar dark, bittersweet, caramelised, and tempered by the acidity of the apples, the texture softened but held by the combination of butter and fruit pectin. The only problem is that the whole thing happens behind a screen of puff pastry, meaning that tarte tatin takes a great deal of practice and repetition to reach the right level of caramelisation blind. So, here, I’ve dispensed with the pastry altogether, making it a much easier preparation. For the intrepid, this is delicious cooked over a bonfire, where the smoke adds an incredible extra dimension; it also functions as a warming treat after a chilly evening out watching the fireworks.Roast apples with walnuts and soured creamThis basically follows my method for making tarte tatin, but without the need for pastry – nor to turn out a pan of seething caramel at significant danger to the skin on your wrists. The butter and sugar in the presence of the apples produce a beautiful and slightly acidic toffee sauce, while the fruit retains enough bite to stand up for itself and avoid disintegrating into mush. By drying out the quartered fruit in the fridge first, you ensure a nice, even caramelisation of the sugar and helps the apples maintain their shape and integrity. That said, you can also dry them in an oven set to 80C (60C fan)/gas very low for 30 minutes.Prep5 minDry2 hrCook45 minServes46 apples– braeburn or discovery, for preference100g unsalted butter, softened100g caster sugar500gsoured cream, to serveA few pinches ground cinnamon, to serve100g toasted walnuts, to servePeel the apples, cut them in half and then into quarters, then cut out and discard the cores. Put the apple pieces on a tray and leave uncovered in the fridge for two hours to dry out.Heat the oven to 210C (190C fan)/410F/gas 6½. Press the butter all over the base of an ovenproof nonstick pan, so it covers the entire flat surface, then scatter the sugar evenly over the top. Arrange the apples cut-side up on top (I like to shape them into a fan), then put the pan on a medium heat to melt the butter and caramelise the sugar for five to 10 minutes, gently shaking the pan every few minutes, until the sugar has melted to a dark caramel. Transfer to the oven and bake for 30 minutes, until everything is deliciously brown and bubbling.Remove, leave to cool for 10 minutes, then divide between warmed bowls and serve with a generous spoon of soured cream, a dusting of cinnamon and some toasted walnuts.Jackson Boxer is chef/owner ofBrunswick House,VesperandDove, all in London, and culinary director ofCowley Manornear Cheltenham andthe Henriettain LondonExplore more on these topicsFoodBonfire NightFruitDessertBakingBritish food and drinkNuts and seedsrecipesShareReuse this content
